"In Donetsk, 3,000 to 5,000 strikers demonstrated from early morning until dusk. They listened to speeches and hoisted banners in the central square in front of the regional Communist Party office."

"Thousands of ordinary citizens marched and rallied outside the Kremlin walls today to demand that the Communist Party concede failure and turn its remaining wealth and power back to the nation. With the party having finished a two-week congress of anxious debate and intramural intrigue, the protesters took to the rainy streets to express outrage and mockery and to resolve that a full-scale political opposition will be created to drive the party from power."  "The decree was announced on the Soviet evening news following an anti-Communist demonstration by an estimated 100,000 people in central Moscow. It comes two days after Gorbachev, in apparent reaction to the defections of several high-profile leaders from the party, pledged to work with non-Communists in governing the Soviet Union."

"Demonstrators demanding multi-party elections blocked a rail line in Samtredia in the Georgian Soviet Republic yesterday. Goods bound for Georgia, including medicine, wheat and gasoline, have been diverted to other areas of the Soviet Union since the protest began on Thursday."  "Such a concession by the Georgian government would demonstrate the devastating effect of the protest blockade on the republic. From last Thursday 800 people, some from political groups in Tbilisi, have camped across the rails at the crucial junction of Samtredia, 130 miles northwest of the capital."  "TRAINS began to run through the Soviet republic of Georgia again yesterday as protesters called off their six-day blockade after a government pledge to hold multi-party elections in the republic on October 28. Zviad Gamsakhurdia, a prominent leader of the protest, said the blockade had forced Givi Gumbaridze, Georgia's president and Communist party first secretary, to make significant concessions."

"On Monday, 200 people blocked traffic in Leningrad, 300 staged a similar protest in Gorky, and 3,000 people rallied at a plant in Yaroslavl, an independent Soviet news service, Interfax, reported."  The main reason of the protest was cigarette shortages.

"Scores of angry smokers blocked a street next to Red Square for several hours today as public outrage over a summerlong cigarette shortage boiled over. The protest, in a driving rain in Revolution Square adjacent to the Lenin Museum, ended when a truck delivered a dozen cases of cigarettes to a nearby tobacco kiosk. A line of more than 230 people formed immediately."

Location of Protest: Lazdijai (near the Soviet border with Poland)
Notes: "About 20,000 people rallied today near the Soviet border with Poland to protest K.G.B. control of travel to and from Lithuania. ''For 40 years these people have been telling us where to go and what to do; they've been our jailers,'' said one middle-aged woman pointing at K.G.B. guards at the border. ''Now we want to decide for ourselves.''"  "THE KGB deployed troops along the Polish-Soviet frontier yesterday as about 30,000 Lithuanians, carrying national flags and singing patriotic songs, massed at the border. The protesters, calling for control to be assumed by Lithuania's separatist government, crowded in pouring rain against a border fence set in a birch and pine wood. The protest also marked the anniversary of the 1939 Molotov-Ribbentrop pact."

"Rioters in the Soviet city of Chelyabinsk smashed cars and shop windows and tried to storm a Government office in a third successive night of protests over food, tobacco and other shortages, the official press agency Tass said today. Some 1,500 people marched on the regional Communist Party headquarters in the Ural Mountains city late Friday night and held a rally demanding better supplies of food and consumer goods. Earlier, Tass said a crowd of drunken youths gathered near the Interior Ministry office in Chelyabinsk, which had been a target of protests since Wednesday. The press agency said security forces had rounded up several teen-agers armed with firebombs."

"Townspeople said the women marched onto a main street, attracting German television news cameras. But no action was taken against them, and at week's end soldiers and wives said there had been no official retaliation. Pent-Up Frustration Though the women said the protest was specifically against the prospect of moving into temporary housing in winter, some also said the eruption represented ''pent-up frustration at the hasty withdrawal.''"

"Tens of thousands of protesters marched to the Kremlin today to demand the resignation of Prime Minister Nikolai Ryzhkov and immediate adoption of a plan to shift the Soviet Union to a free-market economic system. The demonstration in central Moscow added to political pressure on Ryzhkov to step down in favor of a government of national unity that would include some non-Communists. It came on the eve of a crucial session of the Supreme Soviet, the nation's standing legislature, that is to choose between rival programs put forth to rescue the Soviet Union from its growing economic crisis."

"Nationalist protesters attacked K.G.B. headquarters in the capital of the republic of Georgia, smashing windows and hurling documents into the street, Soviet press agencies and newspapers reported today. The attack early Monday in the city of Tbilisi followed a demonstration by members of the Round Table, who declared the formation of a Free Georgia bloc of political parties for elections next month, the press agency Tass reported. The demonstrators demanded the release of a nationalist, David Gelashvili, who was arrested on charges of illegally storing firearms and attacking a police station, according to Tass and the independent Postfactum agency."

"Tens of thousands of people in Ust Kamenogorsk in Soviet Kazakhstan held angry demonstrations today to protest an explosion two weeks ago at a nearby nuclear fuel plant that officials said could endanger the health of more than 100,000 people. Kazakhstan's president, Nursultan Nazarbayev, sent a telegram to Prime Minister Nikolai Ryzhkov saying the Sept. 12 accident at the Ulbinsky metallurgical works near the Chinese border spewed dangerous gases over parts of the city and asked that the eastern region of the vast Central Asian republic be declared a disaster area."

"Tens of thousands of Ukrainian nationalists marched today through Kiev, the republic's capital, calling for greater independence from the central government in Moscow. ''Mother Moscow: We want to be orphans,'' declared a banner held aloft by cheering protesters as they streamed along the city's main street, the Kreshchatik. The Ukraine is one of 13 Soviet republics that have taken steps toward greater autonomy from Moscow. The only one that has declared immediate independence is Lithuania."

"Tens of thousands of Ukrainian nationalists marched in the capital, Kiev, to protest against the Communist Party and the republic's leaders. Protesters carried the traditional flags and chanted slogans for independence, and a delegation was allowed to enter the Supreme Soviet to present its list of demands. Police observed the demonstration but did not try to interfere."

"WEARING a white headband with the inscription ''I'm on hunger strike,'' one activist swigged water under the warm autumn sun. ''It's my tenth day without food but I do take water,'' Taras said. Some 200 others, recognisable by their headbands, are doing likewise. A few have been on absolute deprivation but of these, two were taken away by ambulance and put in intensive care yesterday."  "STUDENTS on hunger strike in Kiev scored the first important victory of their two-week campaign against the Ukraine's Communist-led government yesterday when President Leonid Kravchuk announced that his prime minister, Vitali Masol, had decided to resign. The decision has yet to be ratified by the republican parliament.  The announcement, relayed live over loudspeakers from the parliament, provoked a storm of noisy celebration in the untidy tented camp that the students have set up in a central city square under the shadow of a massive red granite statue of Lenin. At the same time at least three separate groups of marchers were moving through the streets of Kiev, the Soviet Union's third largest city. Waving flags and chanting anti-government slogans, they included large numbers of people too old to be students as more and more workers added support to the hunger strikers. The protest began on October 2 inspired by students from Kiev's two universities and from the militant western Ukrainian city, Lvov. Since then numbers have risen as other workers have joined the protest. Letters of support and cash donations have come in from all over Ukraine."  "REJOICING at what appeared to be their absolute political victory over the Ukrainian government, students in Kiev decided in a mass vote yesterday to call a temporary halt to their two-week-old hunger strike."

"About 100,000 Ukrainian students marched through the center of Kiev today demanding the resignation of the republic's Communist government. The students, carrying Ukrainian nationalist flags, gathered at a park near Parliament. The police watched closely but did not intervene. Protesters demanded that the Ukraine, a powerful Soviet republic, quickly adopt a new constitution to establish its independence from Moscow."

"ON the evening of Sunday, Dec. 2, in a burst of violence as sudden as it was deadly, five soldiers and at least three townsfolk died in a clash in the quiet Uzbek city of Namangan. Tens more were injured and thousands of demonstrating Uzbek youth and police battled in two days of riots that followed."

"Hundreds of people rallied yesterday in Moscow to denounce dictatorship in the Kremlin and to support Eduard A. Shevardnadze, who resigned as Foreign Minister on Thursday to protest the growing influence of hard-liners. The rally, attended by an estimated 1,500 people, came at the start of a critical week, in which Mikhail S. Gorbachev seeks parliamentary approval for an increase in his powers as President."

"Tens of thousands of people rioted in a Siberian city today in protest against having to celebrate New Year's without alcohol, the official press agency Tass reported. The shortage of spirits for the New Year's holiday, the most festive day on the Soviet calendar, "overfilled the cup of tolerance of city residents," the report said. The rioters -- in the city of Chita, 2,976 miles east of Moscow -- blocked traffic and lit bonfires to protest the lack of wine, vodka and other goods, Tass said."

"RADICALS in the Russian Federation, who make up a virtual majority in the huge republic's parliament, want it to withdraw economic co-operation from the Soviet authorities and even leave the Soviet Union unless Moscow backs down in Lithuania. The threat by the Democratic Russia bloc, grouping politicians from Vladivostok to Leningrad, was the most serious challenge to President Gorbachev among scores of denunciations of army behaviour by nationalists and liberals round the Soviet Union."  "Other radical politicians led 3,000 people in a march from Red Square to the Communist party central committee. Protesters chanted ''Hands off Lithuania'' and ''Freedom for Lithuania'' as they marched past KGB headquarters waving huge Russian and Lithuanian flags."

"That sadness may be deepest in the Soviet Union, where thousands of protesters turned out in Moscow's Red Square to voice their disgust with the killing of civilians in Lithuania. They're keeping the spirit of glasnost and democracy alive despite the Kremlin's reversion to the tactics of intimidation and the ''big lie.''"

"WORKERS in Moscow and many other parts of the Russian Federation staged a two-hour strike yesterday to protest against Soviet army action in Lithuania and honour the memory of those who died. The strikes were a prelude to a demonstration planned for Moscow on Sunday to demand the resignation of President Gorbachev."  "A lunchtime rally in the city centre attended by a few thousand people heard speakers from Democratic Russia and other reformist groups deliver warnings that Lithuania was only the first republic to suffer army action. Placards called for Mr Gorbachev, Marshal Dmitri Yazov, the defence minister, and Boris Pugo, the interior minister, to be ousted, along with Leonid Kravchenko, the newly appointed head of the state broadcasting organisation."

Location of Protest: Moscow, Leningrad, Kiev, Sverdlovsk, Donetsk, Kishinev and Kaliningrad
Notes: "More than 100,000 people marched to the Kremlin under cold gray skies today to denounce the bloodshed in Lithuania and President Mikhail S. Gorbachev's increasingly hard line. Chanting "Dictatorship won't do!" and "Communists out!" the vast throng filled the broad Manezh Square outside the Kremlin with placards and the national flags of Russia and the Baltic republics in the largest demonstration to date of liberal displeasure with Mr. Gorbachev's new course." "Demonstrations against the crackdown in Lithuania were also reported in the cities of Leningrad, Kiev, Sverdlovsk, Donetsk, Kishinev and Kaliningrad."

"Reflecting growing concern that Boris N. Yeltsin, the leader of the Russian republic, is being singled out by the Kremlin for a political fall, tens of thousands of people took to the streets today to voice support for him and demand the resignation of his rival, President Mikhail S. Gorbachev. They rallied on a cold, windy day outside the Kremlin, carrying signs that read, "Boris, you're right" -- an endorsement of Mr. Yeltsin's withering criticism of President Gorbachev that has been met by a torrent of official denunciation and warning."

"More than 100,000 people marched through this capital today demanding Mikhail S. Gorbachev's resignation and urging a "no" vote in the referendum on Soviet unity a week from now. The rally and similar ones in several other Soviet cities contributed to making next Sunday's referendum a showdown between President Gorbachev with his coalition of Communists, centrists and conservatives, and the liberals, nationalists and reformers who have rallied behind Boris N. Yeltsin, the leader of the Russian Republic." "HUNDREDS of thousands of people all over Russia joyfully demonstrated their support yesterday for Boris Yeltsin's ''declaration of war'' on the Soviet leadership, pledging noisily to vote against President Gorbachev's proposed new union treaty in Sunday's plebiscite."
"More than 100,000 Muscovites defied a strong show of military force and Mikhail S. Gorbachev's ban on public meetings to rally today behind his rival, Boris N. Yeltsin."

"MORE than 25,000 workers gathered in the central square of the Byelorussian capital of Minsk yesterday to protest the massive price rises introduced earlier this week."  "The demonstration in the normally quiet and conservative city of Minsk marks a significant escalation of labor unrest. The march appears to be the work of the newly formed independent Byelorussian Confederation of Labor, which held its first congress on March 31."

"Tens of thousands of workers rallied in Minsk today, as Georgian leaders called for widespread strikes and Siberian miners intensified their demands, all on the day after President Mikhail S. Gorbachev proposed a yearlong moratorium on strikes and protests."  "The Byelorussian protest peaked, temporarily at least, after two days of unusual street demonstrations in Minsk by tens of thousands of workers displeased by the Gorbachev Government's new retail price increases and its general lack of success in reversing the economic disintegration."  "STRIKING workers in Belorussia returned to the factories yesterday after the republic's beleaguered Communist party leadership agreed to talks on their demands."

"Soviet Muslims angry at the high cost and limited number of pilgrimages to Mecca rioted today and tried to occupy the government headquarters in the capital of the autonomous republic of Dagestan, the ass news agency reported."

"Thousands of Lithuanian demonstrators in Vilnius picketed the local headquarters of Soviet "black beret" special forces troops for the third day yesterday, calling for their withdrawal from the secessionist republic. The units are believed to have carried out several attacks on republic border posts, which are considered illegal by Moscow."

"Within hours of learning that Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev had been stripped of power in a military-backed coup, tens of thousands of Muscovites gathered all around the capital to argue and plead with the army troops and tank crews who had seized control of the city just after dawn today."

"At least 50,000 Russians defied the Soviet Union's new communist hard-line rulers Aug. 20 and demonstrated at the Russian parliament against the overthrow of Mikhail Gorbachev. Tens of thousands of people also rallied in Leningrad, journalists said. Soviet miners Aug. 20 followed a general strike call by Russian President Boris Yeltsin, but in the key Tyumen oil fields a labor official said workers backed Yeltsin but stopped short of a strike, fearing they could pitch the country into civil war (see story, Page 1)... "

"Four demonstrators were wounded today by special police in Georgia using guns and truncheons to break up a rally demanding the resignation of the republic's nationalist president, journalists said. The local journalists said 5,000 supporters of the opposition National Democratic Party gathered outside government buildings in the Georgian capital, Tbilisi, to demand the resignation of the President, Zviad Gamsakhurdia, a nationalist."

"The holiday was marked in Moscow only by two small rival demonstrations. A couple of thousand hard-core communists waving red flags and banners denouncing Mr. Yeltsin and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev gathered at the giant statue of Lenin in October Square. "Hands off Lenin!" and "Down with the Dictatorship of the Bourgeoisie!" read their posters."

"In the consumers' struggle in the marketplace, the general form of protest thus far has been a flat refusal to buy the more drastically overpriced products. Shoppers were refusing to purchase milk in various regions, and the police were called out in Vladimir in the face of "milk disturbances" in which protest but no violence was reported."  "The first expressions of angry protest were reported today among the battered consumers of Russia as they tried to cope with drastically rising food prices."

"About 10,000 Communist supporters demonstrated in Moscow yesterday to protest rising prices and demand the resignation of Russia's Government. Some carried Soviet flags and pictures of Stalin."  "The demonstration was called by several successor organizations to the Communist Party, including Working Russia, the Russian Communist Workers Party, the Russia Party and the Liberal Democratic Party."

"THE disgruntled people of St Petersburg turned out yesterday to air their complaints when President Yeltsin arrived in their city on the last leg of a five-region tour of Russia. Taxi drivers and ambulancemen were reported to have staged token strikes to protest against high food prices and poor supplies."

Protester Group Identity: members of the hard-line Russian Communist Workers Party and the United Front of Working People
Notes: "In St. Petersburg, an estimated 3,000 people, many of them members of the hard-line Russian Communist Workers Party and the United Front of Working People, rallied against the lifting of price controls by the Russian President, Boris N. Yeltsin."

"Over at Manezh Square, opposite the Kremlin, a crowd of about 7,000 gathered under red banners to voice anger over the plight of the "working class." Many harshly criticized the government, saying it had implemented policies without properly taking into account how they would affect the population."

"Several thousand opponents of the Russian Government marked Armed Forces Day yesterday by demanding the restoration of the Soviet Union. Police officers removed protesters from a vehicle."  "The protest was the latest of several by groups opposed to the new order, primarily staunch Communists but also clutches of nationalists, monarchists and soldiers. Many demonstrators were elderly, pensioners who shouted that they had worked their entire life for the Soviet state and had been left penniless."

"The high point of the communist demonstration, which attracted the usual crowd of 25,000 or so, was a joyfully received prediction that America would be punished for its imperialist sins by an earthquake geological rather than social."

"THOUSANDS of striking Russian doctors and health service workers chanted slogans outside the Kremlin yesterday to press home their demands for a big pay rise."  "Up to 100,000 of Moscow's 350,000 health service employees, and colleagues from more than half the other regions of Russia, are taking part in an escalating series of industrial protests, whose current phase involves refusing to work in outpatients' clinics. However, the doctors, many of whom are paid less than 1,000 roubles (Pounds 6 at the market rate) a month, have held off calling a total strike pending a decision that President Yeltsin is expected to make today."

"RIOT police and supporters of Russia's conservative political opposition clashed on the streets of Moscow last night, paralysing the northern suburbs during the rush hour. Police and interior ministry troops moved in to halt an anti-government march called to demand airtime for the opposition on television."  "The clashes were the first between police and demonstrators in Moscow since the opposition rally on February 23. The organisers, a group called ''Working Russia'' which allies former Communist hardliners and extreme nationalists, had called a protest outside the television centre as part of their campaign for broadcasting time. The city authorities banned the demonstration."

"Immediately after the killing, several hundred black students from the university, went on the rampage, smashing shop windows, overturning cars and demolishing the free-market kiosks which sell mainly alcohol and cigarettes. The Omon riot police were called in to restore order and patrolled the campus through the night, alongside the regular police."  "Yesterday afternoon a protest march organised by the students down the main thoroughfare past the scene of the killing was broken up violently by the Omon, who beat the marchers with truncheons and fists and chased them back on to the campus. A Western eyewitness said that the Omon commander was ''beaming from ear to ear'' as he ordered his men out of the bushes on either side of the road in what was effectively an ambush."

"More than 1,000 pro-Communist demonstrators rallied yesterday around a statue of Lenin in Moscow to call for a revival of the Soviet Union and the removal of President Boris N. Yeltsin's Government. "

"Thousands of pro-Communist veterans and pensioners marched through Moscow today, denouncing President Boris N. Yeltsin as an "agent of America" and urging the military to rise against him. In the biggest pro-Communist demonstration in months, crowds of mostly older Muscovites turned out for Defenders of the Fatherland Day. The holiday was known as Soviet Armed Forces Day until last year."

"On the other side of Red Square, about 10,000 ultranationalists and communists paraded under red hammer-and-sickle flags of the former Soviet Union and signs that denounced Yeltsin. The demonstrations were the largest display of political activism on the streets of Moscow since the abortive coup attempt."

"Barred from marking May Day in Red Square, hundreds of Communists and their supporters battled the riot police with staves, spears and stones today, leaving dozens of people injured and promising more demonstrations to come. The clash on Gagarin Square, under a tall monument to the first man in space, was the first outbreak of political violence in Moscow since the coup attempt in August 1991. At least 80 policemen and as many rioters were injured, including one policeman who was reported in critical condition after he was crushed between two moving trucks. Several news photographers and television cameramen were roughed up."

"Mixing proud memories and bitter anger, some 15,000 war veterans, Communists and nationalists flowed to the center of Moscow today to mark the 48th anniversary of victory over Nazi Germany. But with Red Square finally opened to the demonstrators, there was no repetition of the violence that erupted at May Day marches last weekend."

Location of Protest: in front of the Council of Ministers in Moscow
Notes: ""If we can't find a mutually satisfactory compromise with the government on this issue we will start making political demands - even [for] the resignation of Yeltsin himself," adds Mr. Katalnikov, speaking at a protest yesterday of 100 miners in front of the Council of Ministers in Moscow."

"At the demonstration's peak, the authorities said, there were about 2,000 people ranged under red flags and a banner reading, "We're Russian, God is With Us." The protesters wrecked several sidewalk kiosks, ripped up metal fences and smashed a sign advertising a new McDonald's hamburger restaurant nearby. Witnesses reported seeing rows of gasoline bombs, but none were thrown."

"About 10,000 demonstrators had gathered at Moscow's October Square, marching down a main boulevard, breaking line after line of riot police in the process. As the demonstrators reached the White House, they overwhelmed the riot forces, pouring over barriers of police water-cannon trucks and barbed wire. Police fired automatic weapons into the air in an attempt to stop the demonstrators. But many police fled in panic."

"An estimated 20,000 workers, ex-servicemen and communist diehards paraded through the capital in a lively but ultimately doomed attempt to recapture the spirit of Soviet May Day parades. Viktor Anpilov, a rabble-rousing communist hardliner who heads the splinter Russian Communist Workers' Party, said: ''We will fight to overturn this hateful regime ... there can be no peace with a government which has started market reforms ... down with the bankrupt government.''"

Protester Group Identity: Workers (the Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia)
Notes: "In protest against this intolerable situation, the Federation of Independent Trade Unions of Russia organized mass demonstrations in the country's major cities on Oct. 27, demanding that workers be paid the back wages due them. The federation represents 50 million workers out of a total labor force of 70 million."

"RUSSIAN diehard Communists yesterday commemorated the 77th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 in what turned into the biggest demonstration so far this year against President Yeltsin's government. About 15,000 people marched through Moscow with banners denouncing Mr Yeltsin and calling for the restoration of the Soviet Union. About 8,000 marched in St Petersburg. Speakers at the Moscow rally denounced Mr Yeltsin and his administration as ''thieves'', ''drunkards'' and ''a pack of wolves''."

"THE main Russian army column advancing into Chechenia was stopped in its tracks yesterday by the appeals of a crowd of unarmed civilians and a Russian democratic politician. Russian troops advancing in tanks and troop carriers towards Grozny, capital of the rebel republic, had their way blocked by hundreds of Chechens waving placards. Their officers appeared to be confused and frightened by contradictory signals from Moscow and the prospect of large-scale civilian casualties. At noon yesterday the demonstrators at Davydenko, 40 miles from Grozny, blocked the main road leading into Chechenia from Ingushetia to the west. They carried placards reading: ''Russian soldiers, do not shed the blood of the people.''"

Location of Protest: the line on the western edge of the capital (Grozny) and stretched along the only open highway to the border of Dagestan
Notes: "As Russian planes and mortar shells battered the Chechen capital today, more than 100,000 people formed a remarkable, 40-mile human chain to protest the assault on Grozny. The demonstrators, called to their task by a radio broadcast, began the line on the western edge of the capital and stretched along the only open highway to the border of Dagestan, where regiments of Russian troops have been waiting for a week."

"In Moscow, about 2,000 workers grimly waved red flags as they encircled the Russian government headquarters for four hours. Many protesters called for the resignation of President Boris Yeltsin and his government. "What else can we do when our families are starving?" Sushko asked. In St. Petersburg, about 60,000 protesters marched down Nevsky Prospekt, the main thoroughfare."

"TENS of thousands of communist hardliners staged May Day demonstrations across Russia yesterday calling for President Yeltsin's downfall and vowing to return to power four years after they were ousted."  "In Moscow, where up to 30,000 flag-waving communists marched past the capital's newly opened luxury shops, car showrooms and restaurants, a similar message was heard. ''We want jobs, not unemployment benefits,'' read one banner in the crowd. Another said: ''The Government is bankrupt get out.''"

This protest is against government's policy towards kidnapping crisis...  "In Budennovsk today, public officials and citizens gathered to welcome back the "human shields" who accompanied the Chechen gunmen back to their homeland as part of Monday's deal to end the hostage crisis. Many local residents also staged a demonstration demanding both the government's resignation for allowing the incident to occur and the expulsion of ethnic Chechens from Budennovsk." "A three-day cease-fire in Chechnya, also declared as part of the deal to win freedom for the hostages, seemed to be holding today as talks continued in Grozny, the Chechen capital. But Russian commanders threatened to break off talks and resume fighting if the Chechens do not hand Basayev over to Russian law enforcement authorities, a demand the Chechens are unlikely to meet."

"Pulling up in chauffeur-driven limousines and surrounded by bodyguards, a group of Russia's richest men gathered today outside the former K.G.B. headquarters to protest the murders of dozens of businessmen. The demonstration was provoked by the fatal poisoning of a prominent banker, Ivan Kivelidi, earlier this month."

"TENS of thousands marked the 78th anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution in central Moscow yesterday with one of the biggest Communist demonstrations since the collapse of the Soviet Union. Marchers with red flags filled every corner of Teatralnaya Square outside the Bolshoi Theatre in a demonstration that was partly an outpouring of nostalgia, partly a huge election rally for the Communist Party."

This is a protest as a part of national strike by miners. There is certain information that miners gathered in order to protest.   "Some of the strongest protests came in Vorkuta, in the icy Arctic, where thousands of miners held a demonstration and voted a resolution demanding the resignation of Yeltsin and his government "for carrying out a policy of popular impoverishment and breakup of the national economy.""  About response - "Securing a respite from election-year labor unrest, the Russian Government tapped its severely strained budget today to persuade striking miners to go back to work. After rushing money to the miners and assuring them that a hefty $2.2 billion would be allocated to the coal industry this year, Russian officials persuaded the Russian Coal Workers Union to end a two-day strike by about half a million miners."

"The roads this weekend were filled with angry Chechens in flatbed trucks and old cars. Russian military leaders here decided to permit a large anti-Moscow demonstration in the shattered capital, Grozny. They also let the mothers and wives of policemen taken hostage in Pervomayskoye come here to plead for their loved ones with General Maskhadov. After listening to them impassively he said there was nothing he could do about their problems."

"The protesters, whose numbers have swelled to about 2,000, asserted that the Russian authorities were responsible for the blast, which heightened the tensions in the city. Situated in front of the grounds of the ruined presidential palace in Grozny, the six-day-old demonstration has been generally peaceful."

"Russian soldiers fired tear gas and machine guns in the central market and near the presidential palace to prevent others from joining the demonstration, witnesses said. They said one woman was killed and several people were wounded. But the Russian news agency Tass said no one was hurt."

"Hundreds of thousands of Russian coal miners went on strike today over back pay, idling at least 180 mines from the Far East to central Russia. Teachers and power plant workers joined the strike in many regions."  "In another protest, dozens of retired workers who have not received their pension checks blocked the Moscow-St. Petersburg railway near the town of Tver. Russian television showed demonstrations in depressed coal towns across the country and raised the prospect of coal shortages as winter approaches. Coal accounts for more than 80 percent of Russia's heating fuel and over half of the fuel used in electric plants."

"More than a dozen employees at St. Petersburg's nuclear power plant took over the control room on Thursday and threatened to shut down the plant that provides most of the city's power unless they received months' worth of back pay. This morning 400 of their colleagues joined the protest, and announced a hunger strike. Federal officials rushed to the scene to assess the hazard. By noon today, the Government had flown more than a billion rubles -- $200 for each worker -- to the plant and promised to deliver the rest within a week."

"Millons of private frustrations spilled over into public anger yesterday as demonstrators turned out in cities across Russia to protest against chronic delays in their wages and pensions.   The "day of action" called by Russia's main trade union federation was the biggest antigovernment protest in the country since the collapse of the Soviet Union. The number of marchers and strikers fell well short of organizers' predictions, however, and the day passed peacefully."

"Protesters in Moscow add their voices to tens of thousands who massed across Russia yesterday to demonstrate against the non-payment of wages. But their numbers were far fewer than the millions predicted by opposition leaders."  "Thousands of Russians demonstrated today to protest unemployment, delays in wage payments and the government's general economic policy. Since there is no government, it was hard for the demonstrators to know whom to blame for what."

"SERGEI KIRIYENKO faced his first major crisis as Russian Prime Minister yesterday as tens of thousands of workers downed tools and joined demonstrations across the country over the non-payment of wages. Mr Kiriyenko, whose appointment was confirmed three weeks ago after a month-long tussle between President Yeltsin and the Communist-dominated Duma, met the leaders of Siberian miners who have been on strike for the past two weeks to demand wages overdue by up to six months. The miners have blocked both rail routes across Siberia, prompting Aman Tuleyev, Governor of Kemero vo region, to declare a state of emergency. Mr Kiriyenko said after his talks that Mr Yeltsin had signed a decree ordering wages to the miners to be paid in full ten days ago. There seemed no likelihood, however, that the miners would give up their protest until they received the money. They have been joined by protesters in other sectors. About 200 scientists in the Far East region of Vladivostok blocked major roads out of the city on Tuesday and in Moscow yesterday, thousands of teachers and students marched on the Education Ministry to protest against a lack of funding."

"Angry coal miners blocking tracks have brought rail traffic across Russia to a near standstill in protest of unpaid wages, paralyzing scheduled trains and posing a new challenge to the Kremlin."  "Prime Minister Sergei Kiriyenko, who began the week facing down turbulence on Russian financial markets, today launched a counteroffensive to the miners' strike. He expressed sympathy with strikers' demands and sent his deputies scurrying to the railroad protest sites, canceling some planned foreign trips."

"Hundreds of Russian scientists joined coal miners camped outside government headquarters in Moscow to protest unpaid wages and demand more funds for their sector. "Hungry scientists -- Russia's shame!" and "Without science Russia will become a colony!" read banners carried by the protesters, many of whom had walked in from towns outside Moscow. Under Communist rule, Soviet authorities had generously funded science, which they saw as an important propaganda tool in their ideological battle with the West."

"Millions of workers have not been paid for months. Protesters have shut down mines and blocked the Trans-Siberian railroad. Several provincial towns are paralyzed, with electricity and gas shut off because of unpaid bills. Teachers and defense workers have joined the miners in protest. At least three regional governments have demanded that Yeltsin resign."

"Red banners flapping in the breeze, Communists and trade unionists led a nationwide strike today to protest President Boris N. Yeltsin's rule. In Moscow, thousands of protesters marched toward the Kremlin during a brilliantly sunny day to demand that Mr. Yeltsin resign. In Vladivostok, the improverished port city on Russia's Pacific Coast, strikers briefly blocked a road."

"The woman was among some 10,000 marchers who turned out for the main event of the Nov. 7 commemoration, a march organized by the Russian Communist Party from the statue of Lenin on October Square through the center of Moscow to the old K.G.B. headquarters. By most accounts, the turnout was better than in recent years, evidently reflecting the impact of the latest economic crisis, which hit in August."
This was a protest against a new lash to make the Prigorod region part of North Ossetia.

"Thousands of protesters paraded through Moscow to mark the 82nd anniversary of the Russian Revolution and vent their anger at President Boris Yeltsin and the social and economic upheaval in Russia. About 10,000 people--many elderly and poor--marched from the former October Square to Lubyanka Square, site of the former headquarters of the KGB secret police. Their common refrain was that Yeltsin was to blame for the loss of Soviet-era stability and the country's economic collapse."

"In his first interview journalist Andrei Babitsky reveals the torment of his captivity at the hands of Russian forces in Chechnya....The country's best-known journalists put together a special one-off newspaper in protest, and 2,000 anti-war activists gathered outside the Kremlin."

"On a day when the United States again called for a political settlement to the Chechen war, about 200 people gathered outside the Bolshoi Theater in downtown Moscow for a rare protest against the conflict. The protesters, which included members of the well-known Soldiers' Mothers Committee, circulated a petition calling on Acting President Vladimir V. Putin to settle the conflict peacefully. The demonstrators also approved a statement opposing what they called the growing militarization of Russian society and restraints on press freedom."

"Chechen rebels staged a series of attacks on Russian facilities in the capital, Grozny, and other parts of the breakaway republic, killing six soldiers and wounding 18, officials said...More than 1,000 residents of Alkhan-Kala rallied Saturday to protest the beating of civilians and looting of homes by Russian troops."

"As many as 20,000 people crowded Pushkin Square in central Moscow today to defend free speech and Russia's major private television network in one of the largest public displays of support for democratic liberties here in the post-Communist era. Reformist politicians, soap-opera stars and even a world champion gymnast joined the rock-concert protest to pressure President Vladimir Putin's government to call off its 10-month financial and legal campaign against NTV, the only real source of television news in Russia not under the Kremlin's control."
Police estimated turnout at 6500, but protest organizers estimated turnout at 25000.

"Russian forces sweeping through villages near Grozny, Chechnya's capital, have killed several rebels, officials said today. On Chechnya's western border, in Ingushetia, a hunger strike by people demanding an end to the war drew more and more participants, with 82 refugees in the region refusing food. About 1,000 others supported them in a demonstration in the border town of Sleptsovskaya."

"The police briefly detained four people in Moscow after a rally today in defense of Grigory Pasko, a journalist whose work on the Russian Navy's handling of nuclear waste led to a treason conviction, NTV television reported. According to the report, the four were among about 50 protesters gathered outside the headquarters of the F.S.B. domestic intelligence service, which once housed the K.G.B., to demand Mr. Pasko's release."

"The Moscow city government unveiled plans for a monument to Mikhail Bulgakov...A small but growing group of residents has held protests, written letters and begged the stolid Moscow city government to scrap its plan...On Saturday, in the snow, against a backdrop of yellow backhoes, a crowd of about 300 residents rallied against changes to the park...They say the monument will ruin the quiet park, which has remained relatively unchanged since it was set aside as a public space in the early 1800's."
Protests were against a plan by Putin to cut pensioner's benefits.

"A Russian army colonel serving a ten-year sentence for the murder of a Chechen girl dropped his appeal for a pardon yesterday after more than 1,000 Chechens staged a rare protest to urge President Putin to block his release. The demonstration in the Chechen capital, Grozny, was the largest in the region in five years and highlighted a dilemma for Mr Putin, who needs to appease Russian hardliners in the wake of the Beslan school siege without undermining the Kremlin-backed Chechen administration."
Protesters called for the resignation of Kalmykia's president, Kirsan Ilyumzhinov.
Protests were held in additional cities throughout Russia, though they are not identified specifically, and over 300,000 protesters took part throughout the country.
Protesters demanded the regional President's resignation over seven murders linked to his son-in-law.

Protests were against cuts in state subsidized transportation, prescriptions, and housing for the elderly. Additional protests were reported in Barnual in Siberia and Togliatti on the Volga River over the next two days, but there is no indication of whether these protests had at least 50 participants.

"In St. Petersburg, at least 15,000 demonstrators blocked streets in the largest protest so far in a weeklong wave of protests across Russia against a new law abolishing a wide range of social benefits for the country's 32 million pensioners, veterans and invalids. Demonstrations were held in at least three other cities in the Moscow region, as well as in the capital of Tatarstan."

"Hundreds of residents of Beslan blocked a southern highway for a second day, protesting their local government's handling of the investigation of the school hostage siege in September that ended with more than 300 deaths, more than half of them children. The residents, who have built tents across the Rostov-Baku highway near the town, are demanding the resignation of Aleksandr S. Dzasokhov, the president of North Ossetia, where Beslan is. They have also voiced no confidence in a commission of the Russian Parliament that is investigating the terrorist attack and the government's handling of the siege, according to Russian news reports."

"The protests were sparked by a new law replacing benefits such as free public transport for pensioners, military personnel and police with cash payments that critics say are far too low...In the southern city of Stavropol, several hundred pensioners picketed the regional administration building and some threatened to commit suicide by setting themselves on fire if their demands were not met."

"The protests were sparked by a new law replacing benefits such as free public transport for pensioners, military personnel and police with cash payments that critics say are far too low...On Tuesday, more than 5,000 people attended a rally in the centre of the western city of Nizhny Novgorod, halting traffic temporarily as the biggest protests of Mr Putin's five years in office continued."
"In Moscow on Thursday, 150 civilian workers gathered outside the Defense Ministry to demand the same level of raises given to those in uniform."

"An estimated quarter-million Russians took to the streets Saturday in a wave of demonstrations and counter-demonstrations over a controversial retirement benefits plan, which has prompted the first murmurings of serious opposition to the government of President Vladimir Putin.  Dissatisfaction with a new law that replaces benefits such as free transportation and subsidized drugs for millions of pensioners with tiny cash payments has drawn thousands of people onto the streets in the past month. And Saturday, at over 200 rallies in 70 cities, from St. Petersburg to the Far East, the country witnessed the most widespread demonstrations of Putin's presidency."

Protester Group Identity: opponents of the president of the Bashkortostan region, Murtaza G. Rakhimov
Notes: "Here on the southwestern edge of the Urals, a popular uprising against a regional government is posing one of the most significant challenges yet to President Vladimir V. Putin's political control, raising the possibility that civic protest may be spreading into Russia from its periphery. Heartened by the political upheavals in two of Russia's neighbors, Ukraine and Kyrgyzstan, thousands here have staged a series of demonstrations since February calling for the ouster of the president of the Bashkortostan region, Murtaza G. Rakhimov."

Protester Group Identity: communists, trade unionists, and opposition supporters
Notes: "TENS of thousands of communists, trade unionists and opposition supporters marked May Day yesterday with protests over the Kremlin's moves to overhaul the Russian welfare system and tighten its grip on power...In Moscow 20,000 trade unionists marched to demand that the minimum wage be brought up to the cost of living. Around 5,000 communists with pictures of Lenin and Stalin and hammer-and-sickle banners also marched down the main avenue to the Kremlin. Gennadi Zyuganov, the Communist Party leader, praised Stalin for securing the Soviet victory over Nazi Germany -the 60th anniversary of which Russia will celebrate on May 9."

"A RUSSIAN judge began yesterday to deliver what is widely expected to be a guilty verdict on Mikhail Khodor-kovsky, the oil tycoon who was once Russia's richest man, prompting scuffles between riot police and his supporters outside the courtroom. Judge Irina Kolesnikova read out six of the eleven counts against Mr Khodorkovsky before adjourning the hearing after three hours, as about 300 people protested outside against what they call a show trial."

"THE Russian oil tycoon Mikhail Khodorkovsky was sentenced to nine years in a prison camp yesterday in the climax of what was widely seen as the show trial of the post-Soviet era.... Near by, about 50 supporters of Khodorkovsky shouted "Shame!" and blew whistles in protest, but they were kept behind barricades and were outnumbered by police armed with machineguns."

"Public sector workers in Russia have united in a demonstration calling for "significantly" higher salaries. More than a million teachers, doctors and other state-paid workers took to the streets, some bearing banners saying: "A bureaucrat's dog could not live a single day on the wage that a teacher gets." Russian nurses earn as little as 1,600 roubles (ÃÂ£32) a month."

"THOUSANDS of Russian motorists staged a national protest yesterday in support of a Siberian railway worker jailed for causing a car crash that killed a senior government official... Mr Shcherbinsky was sentenced to four years in prison on February 3 for failing to get out of the way of the speeding Mercedes, which police said had been travelling at more than 90mph...On Saturday more than 1,000 people joined a demonstration in support of Mr Shcherbinsky in his hometown of Barnaul, in Altay."

Police interfered in a coordinated slow-driving protest by pulling over cars for alleged traffic violations and preventing reporters from taking photographs. However, they did not take any actions that fit into the coding scheme as responses to the protest.

This was a protest demanding government intervention following a number of corrupt housing schemes that sold apartments to multiple buyers, then disappeared with the money. "On May 19, several hundred people pitched tents on the lawn in front of the White House government headquarters." We have come to demand help," protester Boris Kazyonov said. "All we get from [the authorities] is brushoffs and empty promises." It was a short-lived protest -- riot police broke up the encampment after dark. But it was a rare example of civil disobedience and made the issue a political embarrassment for the Kremlin."
Protests were against Vladimir Putin. Though the number of protesters is not given, the presence of riot police suggests at least 50 participants.

"An unusually large and unruly protest against the government of President Vladimir V. Putin ended here Saturday in clashes with the police and the arrest of opposition leaders. Rally organizers and the police said more than 100 people were arrested after a midafternoon scuffle between marchers and riot police on the main street, Nevsky Prospekt, in the heart of the city's tourist district."

"Riot police officers swarmed on a group of several dozen journalists and demonstrators on Saturday in Nizhny Novgorod, Russia's third-largest city, cutting off a protest against the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. The police, vastly outnumbering the protesters and wielding night sticks and metal shields, detained about 30 people, the Interfax agency quoted a spokesman as saying. A protest organizer said the number of people detained at the raid was more than 100, plus another 100 who had been arrested in an earlier roundup. Among those detained were several foreign and Russian journalists, including a photographer for The New York Times who was later released."

"Garry Kasparov, the former chess champion turned opposition politician in Russia, was arrested with nearly 200 other protesters during a rally in Moscow on Saturday that ended in clashes with riot troops. The rally, the third so-called Dissenters' March held by a loose antigovernment coalition known as Other Russia, was noteworthy because authorities aggressively pursued the organizers, including President Vladimir V. Putin's former prime minister, Mikhail M. Kasyanov, whom the police jostled but did not arrest. Mr. Kasparov was later fined and released."

"Riot police officers dispersed an opposition rally in St. Petersburg on Sunday, rounding up and arresting protesters and their leaders in a chaotic street scene. The crackdown, on several hundred people who had gathered for an authorized rally but who then began an unauthorized march, followed a similar police action on Saturday in Moscow after a protest that attracted several thousand people. Interior Ministry troops lined the streets in both cities, dispersing the protesters with truncheons."

"Among those detained at a Moscow airport was Garry Kasparov, the former chess champion, who was on his way to the latest in a series of protests organized by Other Russia, a loose opposition coalition he leads. Protests so far in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Nizhny Novgorod have ended in arrests and clashes with the police, sometimes violent ones. A rally and march in Samara went ahead with several hundred in attendance, according to news media accounts, and no immediate reports of unrest."

"Opposition leader Garry Kasparov was among dozens of activists detained Saturday, as riot police eventually quashed a thousands-strong rally against President Vladimir Putin that spilled into the central streets...Up to 3,000 Other Russia supporters turned up midday Saturday for a sanctioned demonstration on Prospekt Akademika Sakharova, near the Krasniye Vorota metro station. While pushing a general anti-Putin message, demonstrators also to protest violations of election law allegedly committed against opposition parties ahead of the Dec. 2 State Duma vote."

"On a second day of rallies against President Vladimir V. Putin, riot police officers broke up a protest in St. Petersburg on Sunday, detaining numerous marchers, including two prominent politicians. The unrest came a day after a similar event in Moscow ended with the arrest of Garry Kasparov, the former chess champion and opposition leader, whose coalition, Other Russia, has declared that Mr. Putin is turning Russia into a dictatorship. A judge sentenced Mr. Kasparov to five days in jail. Similar demonstrations across Russia this weekend, a week before parliamentary elections, were either banned or squelched by the police."

"Anti-government protesters in the largely Muslim republic of Ingushetia clashed with riot police Saturday, throwing rocks and firebombs a day after the government started a major security operation in the troubled southern Russian region. Police responded by firing live rounds over the heads of some of the 300 protesters who tried to gather in Ingushetia's main city, Nazran. Heavily armed riot police blocked side streets and beat protesters with rubber truncheons. At least one person was injured."
"Police officers in central Moscow blocked an area where demonstrators from the opposition coalition Other Russia gathered Monday to protest the results of Sunday's presidential elections."

"Dozens of protesters were taken in by the Russian police for trying to hold an unsanctioned rally in Moscow. "When it comes to modern authoritarian leaders, President Vladimir Putin ranks high for ruthlessness and repression. The anti-government demonstrations were the largest in more than five years, drawing tens of thousands of people into the streets in scores of cities despite a sweeping ban on unsanctioned rallies. The protests called for the resignation of Prime Minister Dmitri Medvedev; their proximate cause was a 50-minute video produced by Aleksei Navalny and other opposition allies and viewed more than 13 million times on social media. The video alleged that Mr. Medvedev had receive bribes from prominent oligarchs that enabled him to maintain fancy estates, vineyards and yachts in Russia and overseas. The protests also reflected broader public discontents, including unhappiness with the economy and the government's suppression of peaceful demonstrations. "Farmers' protests against the low milk purchase prices are peaceful for now, but they are ready to raise their opinion more aggressively. On Friday farmers distributed free milk in Riga's Dome Square. Interest of residents, especially elderly people, was huge. More than 1,000 people arrived for the start of the campaign."

"About 200 police officers and firefighters gathered for a picket outside the Latvian Interior Ministry on Friday to demonstrate their attitude to the government, the interior minister's performance and next year's budget. The protest ended peacefully. The Latvian police trade union (LAPA) has drawn up demands to Interior Minister Mareks Seglins. Policemen's demands include a wage increase that would fully compensate for inflation, a tax drawback system and ration compensations to basic wages. Policemen also demand that the government pay their life and medical insurance, provide them with modern uniforms, secure places in nursery schools for their children, ensure a pay increase for next year, work out a new remuneration system and improve working conditions. Officers also demand that a social dialogue be launched on the most pressing issues."

Protester Group Identity: Latvian United Trade Union of Policemen (LAPA)
Notes: "About 300 policemen on Saturday participated in the rally organized by the Latvian United Trade Union of Policemen (LAPA)....Policemen from Kuldiga, Rezekne, Jekabpils, Ventspils and other Latvian cities came to the protest campaign, but the majority of the participants are from Riga. Many policemen arrived to the rally with their families and children. Participants of the rally were carrying posters, saying "We require human worthy wage", "A cop is a human being, too", "Ice age for wages while prices are growing" and others."

"About 500 people have gathered for a picket outside the Latvian government building to protest against inadequately low wages. The majority of participants are teachers from Latvian cities of Tukums, Dobele, Liepaja, Jelgava, Jurmala and other places. There are also representatives of the State Fire and Rescue Service (VUGD) and medics, State Environment Service among the participants."

"Violent protests over political grievances and mounting economic woes shook the Latvian capital, Riga, late Tuesday, leaving around 25 people injured and leading to 106 arrests. In the wake of the demonstrations, President Valdis Zatlers threatened Wednesday to call for a referendum that would allow voters to dissolve Parliament, saying trust in the government, including in its ability to deal with growing economic problems, had ''collapsed catastrophically.''...The rioting broke out Tuesday after around 10,000 people protested in historic Dome Square over the economic troubles and grievances involving corruption and competence of the government."

"WORKERS have clashed with police across Europe in a day of demonstrations against job and public spending cuts...some 1,000 Latvian trade unionists protested outside Prime Minister Valdis Dombrovskis' office in Riga."

"About 700 people had gathered this Monday in Riga for a protest against the Latvian government's plans to reduce the number of government-funded students also at the higher education institutions subordinated to the Culture Ministry, observed BNS. The protesters, mostly young people, were holding posters appealing to Culture Minister Sarmite Elerte and protesting against the planned reform. The protesters staged a march, which ended at the government building in downtown Riga."

"Latvian President Valdis Zatlers on Thursday received at his office in Riga Castle several participants of a protest against a hike in electricity tariffs of Latvia's Latvenergo power utility, presidential spokeswoman Ilze Rassa told BNS. The president heard eight protesters who voiced their grievances over the increased electricity tariffs and taxes. The protesters handed Zatlers a petition against the increased Latvenergo tariffs with people's signatures. The petition will be passed on to the prime minister, the economics minister and the regulator, as well as the State Audit Office and the ombudsman. About a thousand people on Thursday staged a rally outside Riga Caste to protest against the hike of Latvenergo tariffs, effective from April 1."
The protest was against energy tariffs.

"Outgoing Latvian President Valdis Zatlers was greeted with ovations by the crowd that had gathered at the parliament building on Thursday morning when the lawmakers are expected to elect a new Latvian president. Zatlers is one of the two presidential candidates, and the people, who had gathered at the parliament building for a demonstration in support of the rule-of-law in Latvia, greeted him, loudly voicing their support to him. Today we show support to an honest Latvia," the outgoing president told the crowd before entering the parliament building. Over a thousand people have gathered at the Latvian parliament for a demonstration organized by the pro-transparency NGO Delna to show public support to the rule-of-law and the fight against corruption and oligarchs in Latvia."

"THOUSANDS OF Latvians have protested against the malign influence of tycoons in politics, after the Baltic state s president was ousted following a dispute with MPs over the issue. More than 6,000 Latvians rallied in the capital, Riga, just days after parliament voted to replace head of state Valdis Zatlers, who sought to dissolve the chamber for its refusal to strip legal immunity from an MP suspected of involvement in a corruption scandal."

Protester Group Identity: students of the Latvian Culture College
Notes: "Some 70 students of the Latvian Culture College on Tuesday had gather in front of the Cabinet of Ministers house in Riga to protest the government's decision to merge their college with the Latvian Culture Academy. Students where singing, whistling and chanting slogans of protest, as well as holding posters with slogans like "Castration of Culture", "Practice in Ireland", "Don't Drive Culture into Exile", "No Directors -- No Song Festivals" and others. The Latvian Culture Ministry argued that the reorganization was necessary to prevent program overlap and to ensure a more efficient use of resources."

THIS IS A PROTEST AGAINST THE EUROPEAN UNION: "On Wednesday afternoon more than 300 farmers gathered in Riga by the European Union (EU) House to protest against unfair payments from the EU, BNS noticed. Even though there are many participants, the protest campaign is peaceful."

"The picket staged by supporters of the leftist pro-Russia Harmony Center outside the parliament building in Riga on Monday morning has drawn some 2,000 participants. So far, the protest has been passing without any incidents. Police spokeswoman Sigita Pildava told BNS that about 2,000 people had gathered for the picket by 9.30 a.m. Guntars Markitans, chief of the public order police, told BNS that no incidents have been reported so far."

"The Latvian Education and Science Ministry has not prepared any budget saving proposals so far and has argued against further funding cuts for higher education. Latvian Education and Science Minister Roberts Kilis announced this on Friday as some 700 students from various higher education institutions gathered in downtown Riga for a protest demonstration, to respond to unofficial information that budget measures planned by the government for 2012 will also include funding cuts for higher education."

"Several hundreds of people have gathered by the parliament on Thursday morning to protest against next year's budget to health care sector, BNS noticed. There were people with black balloons, posters saying "Our silence would harm your health", "The government -- love medics because you will not be healthy forever!", and others. Health Minister Ingrida Circene came to greet the protesters."
The protest was against the government's decision to join the Anti-Counterfeiting Trade Agreement (ACTA) and restrictions on freedom of expression in general.

Protester Group Identity: employees of the Latvian State Probation Service
Notes: The protesters, employees of the Latvian State Probation Service, demanded a five-day work week.
THIS WAS A PROTEST AGAINST THE EUROPEAN UNION. The protest was specifically against unfair EU direct subsidy payments.

Protester Group Identity: students and lecturers from several Latvian universities
Notes: The protest is only noted as "against Latvian Education and Science Minister Roberts Kilis."

"Leader of the Lithuanian Liberty Union (LLS) Vytautas Sustauskas could be imposed an administrative penalty for coordinating an unsanctioned gathering near Vilnius City Hall last Saturday. Early this week Sustauskas should be handed an official report on the last week's event, and the data will be passed over to court later. About 200 remonstrators gathered near the City Hall where a Vienna Dance was held for the elite of society on Saturday night. The protestors saluted the guests, including the Lithuanian president, the parliamentary chairman, the PM and foreign diplomats residing in the country, and yelled "cheats" and "shame on you.""
The protesters came to support a smaller number of protesters from the Vilnius Marketplace on strike over police actions.
This was a protest against an increase in telephone rates which called on the government to intervene.

Protester Group Identity: Lithuanian Workers' Union (LDS) and workers of the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant (INPP)
Notes: "A group of about fifty members of the Lithuanian Workers' Union (LDS) and workers of the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant (INPP) gathered outside the Government's House on Friday protesting against the forthcoming closure of the plant and demanding clarity in their social guarantees. Some 20 LDS members started the protest action at about 11 a.m. local time and were later joined by another 30 INPP employees, who arrived from the city of Ignalina, some 110 kilometers northeast of Vilnius."

Protester Group Identity: staff members of the Mazeikiu Nafta (Mazeikiai Oil refinery)
Notes: "A few hundred staff members of the Mazeikiu Nafta (Mazeikiai Oil refinery) gathered outside the company's building on Friday to protest against sale of the Lithuanian oil concern to foreigners and to demand for social guarantees. The Friday's protest action came as a continuation of the one held by the Lithuanian Liberty Union (LLS) on Thursday, when a couple dozen of the Mazeikiai Oil's employees picketed outside the refinery overnight. At about 9 a.m. on Friday, another 200 hundred of the oil refinery's staff joined the ten people who had stayed there since the Thursday protest action... The workers passed a resolution, asking the government to call a trilateral meeting with Williams representatives and sign an agreement, which would provide employment and social guarantees for the staff in the future. If the government does not call the meeting, Mazeikiai Oil's staff members intend to stage protest actions in the Lithuanian capital in the short run."

"Farmers in the Lithuanian northern district of Joniskis have blocked the main road as a last-ditch attempt to exert pressure on the government to get their money due to them since last year for sugar beet they had supplied. About 120 agricultural machinery stands lined up on the hard shoulder of the Siauliai-Riga highway close to Joniskis. The traffic has not been entirely blocked because the police has made its presence there. Coordinators of the picket action say that about 300 people are participating in the protest. Joniskis farmers demand for full settlement for the sugar beet, criticizing the unclear pricing of this year's harvest. Until the start of the picket, the farmers had not received about 30 percent of the money for the sugar beet supplied last year. According to a governmental resolution, the accounts were supposed to be settled by June 1."
The protest was originally restricted to the road between Marijampole and Kalvarija, but on July 13 became national.

"Former Lithuanian president Algirdas Brazauskas was among the participants of a rally staged in the Independence Square outside the parliament on Friday to protest against the deal between the Lithuanian government and Williams International of the U.S. One of the largest protest rallies of the past several years was initiated by the Vilnius University and attended by about 3,000 people -- mostly college students and a large number of lawmakers and other politicians. Participants of the protest action spoke of insufficient funding of the education and science, voicing dissatisfaction with the government's plans to sign an agreement with Williams on investment in the country's oil sector."

Protester Group Identity: Lithuanian Trade Unions' Centre (LPSC) and the association of the Lithuanian Trade Unions (LPSS)
Notes: "The Lithuanian Trade Unions held a noisy protest march in Vilnius on Tuesday against increasingly deteriorating people's living standards in this country. The march was organized by the Lithuanian Trade Unions' Centre (LPSC) and the association of the Lithuanian Trade Unions (LPSS). About 1.5 thousand people, mostly pensioners, gathered outside the House of the Government to voice their demands."

"The Lithuanian capital city's police force held a warning protest march on the main street in Vilnius in an attempt to draw the government's attention to inadequate financing of the force. This was the first ever public protest action held by police officers since the restoration of independence almost ten years ago. About 400 uniformed policemen and firemen took part in the protest action under rather unfavourable winter conditions of wet snow."

"Vilnius beat cops refused to leave their division offices for a few hours Thursday night, demanding they be told when their salaries will be paid. Around 50 police officers, ending their shift at midnight, turned in their weapons but refused to leave the building until someone told them when their late paychecks would be issued. The police officers' wages are about one week late, although they were told a portion would be paid this year. Officers complained they didn't have money to buy their children gifts before Christmas and can't pay their utility bills."

"Russia has not appealed to Lithuania with a request to provide treatment to Russian servicemen wounded in Chechnya, the Lithuanian Foreign Minister, Algirdas Saudargas, has said. An unauthorized picket was staged outside the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Vilnius on Friday protesting against the proposal put forward by the Lithuanian Citizens' Alliance to provide treatment for Russian wounded soldiers in Lithuania. The picket, of about 50 people, urged the Foreign Ministry to forward a clear-cut official stance on the Alliance's initiative and to make sure that entry visas to Russian servicemen who fought in Chechnya were not issued."

"The most acute problem in Lithuania is this that all Lithuanian politicians have already established themselves in Europe leaving the people behind in poverty-ridden Lithuania, the president of the Lithuanian Workers Union (LWU), Aldona Balsiene, has said. LWU organized on Wednesday a two-hour rally outside the Government's Office protesting against the government's "policy of impoverishing people", with over 500 people, mostly pensioners from various regions of the country, taking part. Protests were voiced against the government's policy of "giving in to the demands of the World Bank to keep reducing social guaranties" and against the Kubilius-led government's refusal to listen to workers' demands."

Protester Group Identity: Lithuanian Liberty League, the Lithuanian National Party 'Jaunoji Lietuva' (Young Lithuania)
Notes: "Protesting against the government's failure to pay subsidies on time, farmers of Central Lithuania blocked on Wednesday one of the main highways not far from Panevezys. About 300 farmers and representatives from agricultural cooperatives blocked the highway using agricultural hardware in the vicinity of Vilnius-Siauliai and Kaunas-Ryga crossroads."

Protester Group Identity: farmers and representatives from agricultural cooperatives
Notes: "A barrage of accusations were levelled at the Lithuanian President, Valdas Adamkus, by the right-wing patriotic forces at a rally held on Wednesday outside the parliament. The rally was organized by the Lithuanian Liberty League, the Lithuanian National Party 'Jaunoji Lietuva' (Young Lithuania) and some other minor right-wing patriotic parties. According to the police estimate, 150 to 200 people took part in the rally. Placards carried by some protestors testified to profound resentment over the conferred state awards last week to the first prime minister after the restoration of independence, Kazimiera Prunskiene, and the interior minister Marijonas Misiukonis."

Protester Group Identity: Drivers of private taxies, buses and mini-buses
Notes: "Drivers of private taxies, buses and mini-buses on Monday staged a rally outside the parliament protesting against the government's plans of making cash registers compulsory in vehicles carrying passengers. About thousand drivers arrived in Vilnius from various parts of the country to take part in the rally. The chairman of vendors and small business association, Eduardas Sablinskas, told journalists that private passenger carriers were not supporters of drastic measures. However, he said, if the government "having started its second hundred days in office, is set to ignore this action, private passenger carriers will be forced to take long-term protest actions.""

"On Saturday, the Amalgamation of Lithuanian Trade Unions (LPSS) staged a protest action suggesting that people under any rule want to eat. The rally was organized by the LPSS chairman, a member of the Social Democratic Party Algirgas Sysas, whose ideas were supported by the Center of Lithuanian Trade Unions and the Lithuanian Workers' Union. Dagys told the Lietuvos Aidas that protests can be held when there are troubles to complain about, adding that not a single protest rally organized by trade unions has been a success. About one thousand of participants of the protest action marched along the central street of the Lithuanian capital and staged a protest rally outside the parliament on Saturday."
The protest actually extended to March 30, but there is no indication that there were at least 50 people present after March 17 so the final coded day is March 17.
The protest was against government plans to restructure the management of the train system, potentially resulting in lost jobs.
The protesters demanded that more funds be allocated to the police, and that police officers be permitted to take on second jobs.

The protest demanded "that the local administration should not follow governmental resolutions changing the procedure of paying social allowances, which would deprive two thirds of the city's 4,000 people with low income of relief (1)."

"Lithuania's unregistered national social party made some anti-Semitic remarks and statements insulting the country's administration in a protest rally staged outside the municipality of the second city Kaunas on Wednesday. Speaking to a 150-strong crowd, the party's leader Mindaugas Murza said that they "had come to rescue the nation and would soon attract thousands of supporters." Some participants wore straps with symbols resembling Nazi swastikas. In an address to the Lithuanian president, participants of the protest rally censured the work of the parliament and the Baltic state's law-enforcement institutions."

Protester Group Identity: Lithuanian Freedom Union, Lithuanian People's Union For a Just Lithuania, Young Lithuania and the Union of New Nationalists and Political Prisoners
Notes: "A protest organized by representatives of radical parties in parliament against the policies of the current administration burned an effigy of current Lithuanian prime minister Rolandas Paksas on Thursday. Participants in the protest held on Independence Square in Vilnius expressed their dissatisfaction with increases in consumer telephone tariffs, decreases in pension payments to working pensioners, the liberalization of labor relations and plans to legalize gambling. Around 300 elderly people took part in the meeting organized by the Lithuanian Freedom Union, Lithuanian People's Union For a Just Lithuania, Young Lithuania and the Union of New Nationalists and Political Prisoners. They held signs demanding the government not impoverish pensioners. As the meeting ended, around 150 angry participants moved from the Mazvydas National Library towards the parliament."

The number of protesters is not noted, but the article stated that the protest was a threat to the president retaining power, which suggests a large group of people and certainly at least 50 participants.
The protesters supported President Paksas, who was impeached.

"Riots broke out once again in the Baltic states on Friday, this time in the Lithuanian capital, Vilnius, where a group of 7,000 gathered to protest planned economic austerity measures. A smaller group began throwing eggs and stones through the windows of government buildings until the police moved in, using tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse the crowd."

"WORKERS have clashed with police across Europe in a day of demonstrations against job and public spending cuts... Some 400 protesters rallied in an illegal demonstration in the Lithuanian capital of Vilnius to demand authorities drop harsh austerity measures such as salary cuts."

"Several hundred gay and lesbian rights activists have gathered for a parade in Lithuania"s capital, attracting a large protest and a bigger police presence. The activists have planned to march along Vilnius" central commercial avenue, which has been barricaded and surrounded by hundreds of police, many in full riot gear, to prevent disturbances. Approximately 200 protesters have assembled on a large central square adjacent to the avenue. The Saturday parade, dubbed "the March for Equality," is only the second such event for Lithuania, a predominantly Catholic nation of 3 million people that activists say has not done enough to ensure gay, lesbian, and transgender rights."
