"Thousands of workers in the Ukrainian capital protested sharp price increases that took effect today as a result of deep cuts in state subsidies. More than 5,000 workers from a defense plant demonstrated for several hours along with leaders of the Socialist Party, made up mostly of former Communist Party members."

"Kiev: Thousands of mineworkers in eastern Ukraine took to the streets in protest against threatened price rises which would dramatically reduce their standard of living. Almost half the 204 pits in the region were closed."

"About 45,000 miners and other workers in the heavily Russianised coal-producing Donbass region joined a mass protest on Monday in Donetsk, the regional capital, against low wages and rampant inflation, and called for Mr Kravchuk's resignation. The pit protests have widened into a political strike joined by transport workers, health staff and students."  "PRESIDENT Kravchuk of Ukraine yesterday gave in to striking miners' demands for a referendum on his leadership and early parliamentary elections, as the mood in the former Soviet republic worsened and fears grew that the country faces political and economic chaos."

"Orthodox protesters prevented the head of the Uniate Catholic Church from holding a service in a Kiev church today, rekindling religious animosity in the former Soviet republic.  Dozens of Orthodox believers blocked the entrance to St. Cyril's Church, where the Catholic Cardinal, Myroslav Ivan Lubachivsky, was to lead a service, with Government officials and members of both faiths in attendance. Cardinal Lubachivsky eventually left to hold the service at the future site of a Uniate cathedral."

"The funeral for the leader of the breakaway Ukrainian Orthodox Church turned violent yesterday, with police using nightsticks and tear gas on angry mourners who wanted him buried in a state cathedral. About 200 riot police beat followers of Patriarch Volodymyr when they tried to push past a police cordon blocking their path to St. Sofia's Cathedral, the city's holiest Orthodox shrine, after a funeral service in a nearby church. The government rejected the church's request to bury the patriarch at St. Sofia's, now a state museum."  "But mourners fought their way through the cordon. Some hurled the cover of the opened coffin at policemen blocking their path and others hit them with nationalist flags. Riot police sprayed tear gas on the 1,000 followers as they approached."

"A protester in Kiev, Ukraine, is thrown into a police van. He held a sign yesterday demanding the defense minister retire. A group sought dismissal of the Defense staff for the destruction of a missile silo."

"Ukrainian miners protest THOUSANDS of striking Ukrainian coal miners demonstrated in the industrial city of Donetsk yesterday as tensions mounted in their eight-day protest. Waving banners with Soviet-era slogans, miners from across the nation cried out for back wages and increased subsidies to their state-owned industry. They shouted down the regional governor when he tried to speak."

"Coal miners blocked a rail line in eastern Ukraine to protest unpaid wages. The standard of living has dropped in Ukraine, once the Soviet Union's breadbasket, in part because of corruption and a slow pace of privatization. Millions of workers from police officers to teachers have gone unpaid for months."

"Ukrainian university lecturers and students have called for the dismissal of education minister Mykhaylo Zhurovsky and the adoption of an 'emergency budget' to save the country's higher education system and pay their salaries and grants. They want a law making officials who delay salaries and grants liable to prosecution. The demands were voiced at a rally in Donetsk, organised by the regional council of trade unions of teachers and scientists, but reflect opinion nationwide. Salary hold-ups have become common for state-paid staff in the post-Soviet countries. The Ukrainians' protest was fuelled by Ukraine's switch from its temporary quasi-currency, the karbovanets, to what is hailed as the 'real and fully convertible' hrivna."

"Ukraine police clashed with some of the 1,000 protesters who rallied yesterday in Sevastopol to demand that Ukraine return the home port of the Black Sea Fleet to Russia. The protesters want a referendum to determine the future status of the city, which lies on Ukrainian soil on the Crimea Peninsula but is populated mostly by ethnic Russians."

"Policemen push demonstrators back as they try to advance towards the Kiev city administration building yesterday during an "empty saucepans procession." Women from Ukraine decided to demonstrate before the March 8 International Women's day to draw attention to the disastrous economic situation that affects the majority of Ukraine's population."

This protest is a good example of the nostalgia with the old regime, which is one of the biggest dangers for the consolidation of the new regime.   "Angered over unpaid wages and pensions, tens of thousands of people across Ukraine marched today to demand a return to Communist rule. Interior Minister Yuri Kravchenko was quoted by the Interfax-Ukraine news agency as saying that as many as 85,000 people had taken part in the demonstrations, which were called by left-wing groups."

"A group of hungry miners' wives and children recently marched to the Komsomol mine and blocked the entrance, shutting down the operation. In the smoggy, perilous and dirt-poor Donbass coal belt of eastern Ukraine it was an act of desperation."

"Up to 6,000 protesters yelling "Pay us, pay us" spilled on to the streets of Kiev on Thursday demanding the Ukrainian government deal with back wages and pension of some $ 2.65 billion. Miners, teachers and pensioners joined in the protest. One miner complained, "The last time we were paid was 12 months ago." Miners banged their helmets on the ground in unison in front of the central bank yelling "Wages, wages" and "Work, work." Others carried signs saying "A hungry miner is Ukraine's shame.""

"Young protesters dressed in black carry candles and a banner saying ''For a nuclear-free Europe'' at a rally in central Kiev. The chief of Ukraine's Chernobyl nuclear power station, site of the world's worst nuclear accident, says he plans to restart the plant's reactor No. 3 next month after repairs. Shut down last year after cracks were found in the cooling system's pipes, the reactor is the only one of four which has functioned since the No. 4 reactor exploded on April 26, 1986."
Protests were over student loans and demanded the resignations of Prime Minister Viktor Yushchenko and his deputy Yuriy Yekhanurov.

"Ukrainian police launched an early morning attack on opponents of President Leonid Kuchma yesterday, pulling down a makeshift tent camp that had become a focus of protests against him. To cries of "Shame, shame" and "Kuchma out!" 400 policemen took about an hour to surround and evict 100 occupants from 50 tents on Kiev's elegant Kreshchatyk street. The camp was set up in December by protesters demanding that Kuchma resign over claims he had ordered the abduction of a reporter whose headless corpse was found in November -- the country's biggest scandal in a decade. Kuchma has denied all involvement."

"About 100 demonstrators braved the subzero cold to chant "Ukraine without Kuchma" in front of the Interior Ministry building, at the base of the hill crowned by Mr. Kuchma's presidential edifice, the old headquarters of the Communist Party. The demonstrators demanded the arrest of Interior Minister Yuri Kravchenko."

"Thousands of protesters waving Ukrainian flags and chanting, "Ukraine without Kuchma," streamed into Kiev today in a mostly peaceful protest march demanding the resignation of President Leonid D. Kuchma, who is struggling to overcome a deepening political crisis. The crowd, estimated at 3,500 to 5,000, tried to break through a police cordon around the presidential administration building but was turned away, witnesses said. Ukrainian television reported a number of scuffles among the protesters, the police and counterdemonstrators. The crisis is being fueled by the continuing release of recordings of Mr. Kuchma's private conversations with senior aides and political figures in which his voice is heard ordering the abduction of a prominent journalist, threatening a judge and discussing how to protect the head of one of Ukraine's largest energy companies after he had reportedly "put a hundred million, at least" into his "pocket.""

"Thousands of demonstrators marched through the capital of Ukraine today, the second such outpouring in a week, demanding the resignation of President Leonid D. Kuchma and calling for new presidential elections. Up to 5,000 people watched as a wreath of black and white ribbons was laid at the entrance of Ukraine's state intelligence service to celebrate the news that Mr. Kuchma had on Saturday fired its top two officers, Leonid Derkach and Veleriy Strogov. The two had been criticized for orchestrating a crackdown on freedom of the press and suppressing Mr. Kuchma's political opponents."

"Hundreds of protesters chanting "Yulia!" marched through Kiev demanding the release of Yulia V. Timoshenko, the former deputy prime minister arrested on corruption charges that she claims are politically motivated. Ms. Timoshenko, left, waged a battle last year to bring transparency to the corrupt energy sector. The Interfax news agency said up to 1,000 marchers from Ms. Timoshenko's Fatherland Party picketed the prosecutor general's office in central Kiev, the scene of large protests against President Leonid D. Kuchma this winter."

"A tribute yesterday to a famed poet turned into the bloodiest protest in a three-month campaign against President Leonid Kuchma, with several people injured as demonstrators hurled bottles and a molotov cocktail and riot police used tear gas. Snaking across the capital, the protests grew throughout the day, swelling to as many as 18,000 people, police said -- a huge gathering for this usually quiet city. Dozens of protesters were arrested and thousands of police were deployed throughout the city. The injured included six police, several protesters and a photographer. The violence took protest leaders by surprise, after a series of peaceful rallies demanding Kuchma's ouster. The campaign was sparked in December by accusations that Kuchma was involved in the killing of a journalist, but has been fueled by anger at his failure to solve Ukraine's economic ills. The protests began with Kuchma's traditional wreath-laying at a monument in a small park to Ukrainian poet Taras Shevchenko."

"About 4,000 students marched through the western Ukrainian city of Lviv today calling for the arrest of President Leonid Kuchma and providing clear evidence that mass protests in the former Soviet state have yet to die down. Kuchma is accused by his opponents of involvement in the kidnapping of a journalist whose headless corpse was found outside Kiev, the capital, in November. The president denies the charge and has rejected growing calls for him to resign. The peaceful protest in Lviv, which has one of Ukraine's oldest universities and is the focal point of Ukrainian nationalism, was prompted by the arrest of 200 people Friday after a demonstration in Kiev turned violent."

"Yesterday's demonstration was more a show of unity than of force. Closely watched by riot police peering from behind grey blankets covering their bus windows, about 1,000 activists from Ukraine's main socialist and nationalist groupings gathered before parliament and marched to the prosecutorgeneral's office to demand the release of Yulia Timoshenko. The centrist politician was jailed by Mr Kuchma after she angered his supporters in the lumbering privatised industries by demanding that they pay energy bills in cash."

"THE roar of 10,000 protesters packed into the streets around Ukraine's parliament building counted for little yesterday when deputies inside completed a swift grab for power that will almost certainly reverse the country's timid attempt to shake off Russia's influence and align itself with Europe. "Police wielding truncheons fought with demonstrators in central Baku calling for the resignation of President Heidar Aliyev at an unauthorised rally Saturday and made around 20 arrests, police officials said. Around 80 members of the youth wing of the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan took part in the demonstration on the city's Fountain Square, spokesman Yashar Aliyev told reporters. They were outnumbered by the 100 policemen posted on the square, he said. Some of the protestors, who were chanting slogans calling on Aliyev to resign, received slight injuries in the fighting, he added without elaborating."

"Thousands of demonstrators gathered Saturday to protest against President Geidar Aliev's government, accusing the president of lacking the moral authority to rule this former Soviet republic. "We want all the national forces of the country to unite for a struggle against the present authority which does not have the moral right to manage the country," Ali Kerimli, chairman of the opposition People's Front party said at the protest rally. "Despite evidence of the hopelessness of the present government, it seeks to continue its existence." ... The demonstrators also rallied against what they claim are Aliev's repressive policies against political dissenters, and they urged the government to create a commission to investigate the problems facing the national army, such as corruption and poor morale. About 2,000 people attended the protest meeting, which was sanctioned by the government."

"Azerbaijani police wielding truncheons arrested 35 demonstrators after violent clashes with around 1,000 supporters of an opposition coalition who staged an illegal anti-government rally in central Baku on Saturday, officials said. Fifteen policemen were injured as the demonstrators, chanting "resign", attempted to break through a police cordon set up around the city's central square, the officials said in a statement. The rally was called by a coalition of 26 opposition groupings who are demanding the resignation of President Heidar Aliyev and his government and the holding of early elections. An earlier eyewitness estimate of the number of protestors attending the unauthorised rally was 2,000."

"Hundreds of women opposition activists rallied in Azerbaijan's capital on Saturday to demand President Geidar Aliev's resignation, accusing him of trying to impose a dictatorship. The demonstration in front of a movie theater in the capital Baku was organized by a coalition of 30 opposition groups and parties in this ex-Soviet republic. The women carried banners in Azerbaijani, Russian and English with slogans such as "Down with Dictatorship!" They accused Aliev, Azerbaijan's Soviet-era leader, of cracking down on opposition groups and independent media and of corruption."

"Three opposition leaders in Azerbaijan were arrested in the capital Baku on Saturday, amid violence as police sought to break up a demonstration calling for the resignation of President Heidar Aliyev. Arif Gadzhiyev, the secretary of the country's main opposition Musavat Party, was among those arrested during the rally by 400 anti-government protestors near Baku's Freedom Square. An AFP reporter saw others covered in blood after around 800 police, who had earlier set up roadblocks around Freedom Square, moved in to disperse the crowd."

"Swinging batons and rushing at demonstrators, Azerbaijani police on Sunday broke up a protest called by the opposition to demand the resignation of President Geidar Aliev and his government. Up to 50 people were detained as they tried to reach the site of the planned protest on Freedom Square in the center of Azerbaijan's capital Baku, said Saida Gojamanli, the director of the non-governmental Office for the Protection of Human Rights and Legality. Several of the protesters were injured, and police said five officers were hurt. Deputy city police chief Yashar Aliev said 23 people were detained as they tried to reach the officially unsanctioned protest. About 300-400 people tried to take part in the demonstration."

"At least one protester was killed and dozens of policemen were hurt after a night of rioting in a village near Azerbaijan's capital Baku, local news reports said Tuesday. Protesters in the village of Nardaran, 30 kilometers (18 miles) east of Baku, fired on police and threw stones and petrol bombs according to the private ANS TV station. Police said that 35 of their officers were injured. They said the situation was now calm. A crowd of 300 to 400 local residents came out on to the streets of Nardaran late on Monday to protest the arrest of seven villagers on charges of disturbing the peace."

"About 1,500 people rallied Saturday in the Azerbaijani capital to demand the resignation of President Geidar Aliev. The protest came a day after Aliev vowed to proceed with a constitutional referendum set for next month despite a U.S. call to postpone it to allow more debate. The referendum will put before voters proposals that would significantly change how the president and parliament are elected. Carrying signs reading "Resignation" and "Freedom," the protesters marched to a square in central Baku, where Nureddin Mamedli, a leader of the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan, read a resolution calling for early presidential elections and the release of all "political prisoners, including the illegally arrested residents of Nardaran.""

"More than a thousand people protested against the authorities Wednesday in Nardaran, a town in eastern Azerbaijan described by the authorities as a hotbed for Islamic radicals. The town, 30 kilometres (18 miles) from the Azeri capital, Baku, has been a focus for unrest since rioting broke out there between police and local people on June 3 leaving one man dead and dozens hurt. Men who gathered in the town square Wednesday chanted "Allahu Akhbar," or "God is great" while women stood under trees at the edge of the square covered from head-to-toe in burkha robes. There were no police at the rally as Nardaran has become a no-go area for the authorities since June's rioting. Burnt-out police vehicles still litter the streets and the walls are daubed with religious slogans."

"Some 3,000 people demonstrated here Tuesday against a forthcoming referendum on constitutional changes in the Caucasian state of Azerbaijan, saying the poll is a ploy by rulers to tighten their grip on power. Marchers, made up of opposition party supporters, chanted slogans including "We say no to fake referendum," and "Leave our constitution alone." Police said the protest passed off peacefully. All opposition parties in the former Soviet republic have called for a referendum boycott. They say 79-year-old President Heidar Aliyev intends to use the changes to the constitution to smooth the way for his son, Ilham, to succeed him. The opposition claims the referendum will be rigged in favour of the governing group."

"Nearly 10,000 anti-government demonstrators marched through Azerbaijan's capital Saturday in a rally opposition leaders said was a dress rehearsal for next year's presidential elections. The demonstration in Baku, the second mass rally in three weeks, is seen as a sign of growing discontent with the rule of 79-year-old President Heidar Aliyev, who is seeking a third term in office. "This is proof that the people do not want to live any longer under these rulers," Sardar Dzhalaloglu, leader of the opposition Democratic Party, said at the rally as protesters shouted slogans calling on Aliyev to resign."

Nearly all 3,000 officer cadets at Azerbaijan's top military academy staged a mass desertion overnight to protest staff corruption and tough living conditions. "The staff have started taking bribes, our sons are walking around hungry all the time and they go for weeks at a time without being able to take a bath," one father complained.

"An estimated 10,000 people took to the streets of Azerbaijan's capital, Baku, Saturday in the biggest demonstration against the government of this volatile former Soviet republic for at least two years. The massive street protest was prompted by anger at a referendum on constitutional change in the country last month which the opposition and international observers said was marred by large-scale ballot rigging. The protesters marched peacefully through Baku, chanting "The government must resign," and "Give us Work.""

"A crowd of about 1,000 people protested in a village outside the Azerbaijani capital Baku on Monday, calling for the release of more than a dozen people detained following a June clash with police and demanding that the police who opened fire during that clash be brought to justice. The village of Nardaran, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) outside Baku, has become a flashpoint for anti-government protests since the June violence, in which one village resident was killed and 65 others injured, 15 of them with gunshot wounds. Police said some 80 officers were also injured. Residents said they were simply demanding better services, including gas for heating and cheaper drinking water. However, the government says the village is a center for Islamic extremism. Police have set up checkpoints around the village and arrested several residents and Islamic party activists in connection with the June violence."

There were furious protests in the eastern Azerbaijan town of Nardaran Friday after a leader of a four-month revolt against the government was abducted by gunmen believed to be police. Nardaran, 30 kilometres (18 miles) from the Azeri capital, Baku, has been a no-go area for the authorities since local people rioted with police in June resulting in the death of one resident.

"More than 6,000 opposition protesters took to the streets of the Azerbaijani capital Baku on Sunday to demand that President Geidar Aliev resign. The protesters said Aliev should step down because of his "inability to free occupied Azerbaijani land seized by Armenians." They were referring to Nagorno-Karabakh, an ethnically Armenian enclave inside Azerbaijan that has been under the control of pro-Armenian forces for most of the past decade. They also demanded that the government create conditions for free and fair elections, cease pressure on independent media, and release residents of Nardaran, a village outside Baku that has become a flashpoint for anti-government rallies."

Organisers of the rally said 40,000 people turned out while police put the figure at 5,000. Observers estimated the true figure was about 20,000, making it one of the biggest protests in Azerbaijan for several years."

The demonstration is the latest in a series of rallies linked to this October's presidential elections, when 79-year-old President Heidar Aliyev will be running for a third term in office. Demonstrators chanted "resign" and adopted a resolution demanding that the elections should be free from the ballot-rigging and intimidation that has marred previous votes in the south Caucasus republic."

"Police on Sunday blocked opposition demonstrators from holding an unauthorized protest rally in the Azerbaijan capital and arrested at least 20. The demonstrators tried repeatedly to penetrate police lines surrounding Fizuli Square, a frequent site for political rallies, but were turned back. According to the city police department, about 150 people took part in the attempted protest and 20 were arrested on charges of violating public order. But Jalal Sardaroglu, head of the Democratic Party of Azerbaijan, which organized the protest attempt, several thousand people took part and about 100 were arrested. The party wanted to held the demonstration to press its demands for resignation of the current government and for the return of exiled party head Rasul Guliyev to take part in this year's presidential elections."

"Armed police clashed Tuesday with up to 100 opposition demonstrators in central Baku, suppressing an unsanctioned protest against Azerbaijan's new electoral code. As many as 20 demonstrators were arrested and many were beaten by uniformed police and other individuals in civilian clothes. Earlier in the day the police stopped an elderly woman who in a sign of protest had tried to set herself alight by dousing her body in petroleum. The demonstration was organized by the Center of Coordinated Opposition, a coalition of nine opposition parties calling for the retraction of a new electoral code, the resignation of President Geidar Aliev and an end to unethical behavior in Azerbaijan's parliament. Only one member party, Adalyat, was not represented. The protesters had planned to march on the Azerbaijani parliament, but were dispersed by a cordon of police armed with truncheons and shields. The violent clashes began when a group of about 100 demonstrators managed to regroup, but were held off from reaching the parliament buildings by blows from the police."

In Malmo on Thursday night, young people threw stones at police and set fire to cars and rubbish bins. The shipyards, which build both vessels and offshore oil platforms, have been hit by slowdowns in both the oil and shipping industries. As many as 4,000 people have been laid off, and the industry fears 15,000 to 25,000 jobs could disappear in all. About 12,000 shipyard workers and 10,000 oil industry employees staged a one- hour protest yesterday in hopes of pressing the government to take steps to stimulate the industry. Muslims and atheists have been granted the right to proclaim their faith - or lack of it - from loudspeakers over Oslo. The catch is they have to do it quietly in Norway's capital. A neighbourhood council late yesterday granted a permit for a mosque in the old town Gamle Oslo, to broadcast ''Allahu akbar" (''God is great") on outdoor loudspeakers once every Friday. The Norwegian Heathen Society won permission to broadcast ''There is no God" in its calls to meetings, to protest the noise of church bells and now Muslim imams. The council said the loudspeaker calls must not exceed three minutes or a noise level of 60 decibels - the level of normal conversation - which might not be heard over city traffic. Abid Raja, of World Islamic Mission, called the ruling a ''victory of great symbolic importance" but said he might object to the 60-decibel limit. ''If that is true, either they misunderstood or we've been tricked. What is the point of a call to prayer that is a whisper? We'll have to try it on Friday and see if anyone can hear it." The application drew protests, mainly from conservative Christians in a country where more than 90 per cent of the 4.5 million population belong to the state Lutheran Church. About 150 people marched here Saturday, chanting ''Jesus is great." Their signs read: ''Is Oslo going to be an Islamic city? No!" There were at least as many counter demonstrators because many Norwegians support the application.

Norway was set to become the latest European country to suffer blockade chaos today amid the continent's growing fuel crisis. Motorists rushed to fill their tanks ahead of blockades of Norway's main fuel depots planned for later today. The blockades by hauliers and commercial fuel users came as further protests against high diesel and petrol prices were being organised in Sweden and Spain.  Organisers said about 900 trucks would be mobilised to begin sealing off the five depots with trucking unions considering blocking a further four. Norwegians, Danes, Germans, Hungarians, Italians, Iranians, Finns, Belgians and Ameri cans were among those rounded up by Swedish police, along with two British women aged 24 and 26, who were deported, and a 41-year-old British man, Paul Robinson, who is to appear in court on a charge of incitement to riot. THE Danish authorities are trying to cope with the latest pressure group taking direct action in support of their cause. But this group does not fall into the usual category of youths demanding the legalisation of cannabis or squatting rights in empty property. Most of the members of the so-called C-Team Riot group are well into their 70s and constitute a sort of Hell's Geriatrics outfit.  For the past week, they have been taking over public buildings, such as a Copenhagen old people's home which is threatened with closure despite a general shortage of beds and a waiting list of 655 elderly people needing residential care. They have openly copied many of the techniques of civil disobedience developed in the 1960s. But despite their breaking the law, the police and authorities are at rather a loss to know how they should react. About 50 people are involved in the sit-in, but C-Team activists claim to have the support of 10,000 pensioners in the Copenhagen area alone. Hans Frimodt-Moller, one of the organisation's founding fathers, is keen that politicians should not take all the blame. In a Europe that has a distinctly ageing population, he wants to raise awareness of how individuals treat older members of their families. How can it be, he asks, that "there is enough money to pay 300,000 unemployed people to do nothing, but there is no money for home helps?"

DANISH police late last night fired on rioting squatters protesting against the referendum vote. At least one demonstrator was shot in the stomach, three others were taken to hospital and 20 riot policemen were injured.   The riot police, who also used tear gas, opened fire after several of them were hit by bricks or stones hurled by the rioters in the working-class Noerrebro district of the city, where banners had been strung up declaring the area an ''EC-free zone''. The squatters set up barricades of containers against the police and lit bonfires. A police spokesman said that about 300 squatters were throwing cobblestones at officers. ''It is very violent,'' he said. ''Last year after Denmark's 'No' vote we did not have any trouble.'' The disturbances intensified when about 300 demonstrators used trash containers and boards from a construction site to barricade a main avenue. The police fired tear gas and repeatedly charged with riot shields and dogs.

Five policemen were injured and one rioter was jailed after protests flared for a second night on Wednesday after Denmark's acceptance of the European Community's Maastricht treaty in a second referendum. In the violence on Tuesday, Danish police shot and injured 11 youths and squatters in the most serious street unrest in Denmark's modern history, leaving 26 police injured in the five-hour battle. In Wednesday night's briefer clash, police refrained from using small arms, employing only tear gas to quell mobs of about 200 stone-throwing youths. Police said that 19 people had been detained for two weeks on charges of violent behaviour and disturbing public order.

Danish police arrested at least 100 people in Copenhagen yesterday in violent street clashes after authorities evicted left-wing squatters from a youth centre, a police spokesman said. Authorities took control of the building in the Norrebro area in a raid that saw officers land on the roof in helicopters.

Denmark's riot-torn capital was hoping to avert further mayhem after the eviction of squatters from a city building prompted a third straight night of trouble during the country's worst street violence for 14 years. More than 600 arrests have been made and police reinforcement have been brought in from Sweden to deal with the violent backlash after an anti-terror squad carried out a long-standing threat to clear the Ungdom-shuset youth centre in Copenhagen's NÌürrebro district. The graffiti-covered red-brick building has been a base for anarchists and homeless young people since 1982 and its struggle has become a symbolic one for left-wing groups. Since the police moved in, sympathisers from neighbouring countries have joined the protests, which have shattered the city's tranquillity. In a clash on Saturday, more than 30 people were arrested in the NÌürrebro and Christiania districts after protesters built and then lit barricades and hurled Molotov cocktails and cobblestones at riot police who responded with tear gas. The violent protests have reawakened memories of the organised anti-globalisation protests which gathered force in the early part of the decade. Of the 643 people arrested in Copenhagen, 218 have been remanded in custody on preliminary charges of rioting, while 15 people have been released and others are awaiting court appearances.

Groups of youths torched schools and cars in a sixth consecutive night of violence across Denmark, mostly in immigrant neighborhoods, police said Saturday. Forty-three people were arrested. Police said they weren't sure what triggered the spate of vandalism in cities including Copenhagen, Aarhus, Ringsted and Slagelse. Some observers said immigrant youths were protesting perceived police harassment but suggested that reproduction of a cartoon of the prophet Muhammad in Danish newspapers Wednesday may have intensified the unrest.

When Danish police officers raided a church this week in Copenhagen to dislodge Iraqi refugees living there, they hoped to end a three-month-long stalemate. Instead, the raid, and videos that are said to show the police beating the refugees' supporters, have generated intensive news coverage, sparked a demonstration by thousands who demanded the Iraqis be allowed to stay in Denmark and led to a hunger strike by some of the refugees.  The trouble began Wednesday when the police arrived at the church to detain about 20 men who had been living there with permission from the church's leader. Officials said they wanted to round up the men, who had been denied asylum, because they were not keeping in touch with the authorities who were working on their deportations. When the men refused to leave the church, the police said they began to remove them against their will. But local activists who supported the refugees and had learned of the raid blocked the police vans in an attempt to stop the detentions.  Videos that are said to show the confrontation that followed show some activists being dragged away and one being clubbed by the police. Police in Niger fired on student protesters Friday, killing at least five, according to a news account. Witnesses in Niamey, the Nigerian capital, said students clashed with about 100 police who blocked their route to the city center, the news agency Agence France-Presse reported. Hundreds of school and college students, most from the University of Niamey, since Thursday have protested a government freeze on hiring civil servants, including university graduates, AFP reported. Students in the northcentral African country also have protested alleged corruption in the military government of President Ali Saibou, who returned to Niamey late Friday from a drought conference in neighboring Bissau. Police first fired tear gas at demonstrators and then charged the crowd several times. Some of them fired into the crowd, the agency quoted witnesses as saying. The police reportedly acted to disperse hundreds of student strikers when they tried to march from the university across the Niger River to the main business district. President Ali Saibou's military Cabinet, continuing an emergency meeting begun over the weekend, praised "the valor of the forces of law and order" who opened fire Friday to disperse a rally of about 3,000 high school and university students.

Striking teachers said they also were protesting the arrests of two colleagues detained on suspicion of encouraging student unrest. This protest is believed to have at least 100 participants due to the fact that several unions were involved.

A total of 335 detainees escaped from Niamey prison here late on Tuesday during a riot over alleged police corruption, the official ANP news agency reported Wednesday. The police had been given authority by former president Seyni Kountche to sell 14 kilos of heroin, seized in 1987, to pharmaceutical laboratories, and use the money to buy materiel. Soldiers demanding overdue wages staged a brief mutiny in central Niger Saturday, taking control of Zinder town and its airport before returning to their barracks, a local correspondent for Niger's national radio said. The source, contacted by telephone, however told AFP that the soldiers warned they would resume their action if their demands were not satisfied "within 48 hours". They were demanding to be paid three months overdue wages and pressing for the cancellation of budget cuts made by the Niger government last month, according to the source. Mutinous soldiers in Niger on Tuesday ignored an appeal for calm by President Mahamane Ousmane and took 11 hostages, including the deputy head of the army's general staff, Moussa Moumouni Djermakoye. Colonel Djermakoye and others were taken hostage in Zinder, Niger's second city 750 kilometres (470 miles) east of Niamey, informed local sources told AFP. Soldiers from three of Niger's main army garrisons began a revolt Saturday and said they will not release their hostages until financial and political demands are met. Soldiers at the garrison in Maradi 550 kilometres (340 miles) east of Niamey also joined the mutiny Tuesday, according to local witnesses contacted by telephone. Mutinous soldiers at five garrisons on late Tuesday freed all of the military and civilian hostages they had been holding in a dispute over financial and political demands, Interior Minister Ousmane Oumarou said. Mutinous troops, who began their action on Saturday, had insisted they would not free their captives until their demands had been satisfied, namely the payment of back wages, cancellation of budgetary austerity measures and the resumption of patrols -- suspended June 10 -- against Taureg rebels in the north.

Hundreds of high school students rampaged through Niamey on Tuesday, ransacking buildings and erecting burning barricades, on the second day of a strike called over a grants dispute and the closure of the city's university. They ransacked public buildings in the centre of the city and set fire to a police post, also attacking the capital's French high school, the Lycee la Fontaine, which had refused to join the strike.  Riot police had regained control by around 1:00 p.m. (1200 GMT) as the protestors fled their barricades. Police arrested numerous demonstrators but no injuries were reported. Pupils of all public and private schools in Niamey began an indefinite strike Monday, calling in particular for the payment of five months' worth of overdue grants. The protest is backed by the main educational trade union, USN, which called Tuesday in a statement for a "greater mobilisation (to) maintain union action until the demands are met." The riot was the latest in what have become daily disturbances by students upset with the cash-strapped government's failure to pay education grants for the past nine months. The government closed Niamey University last week because of the unrest.

On Thursday, women's organisations mounted a demonstration to protest against the closure of Niamey University following clashes there between police and students demanding the payment of arrears in grants. The march was declared illegal by Niamey authorities, who sent in police to disperse the demonstration. Given the response by the government, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

About 8,000 people demonstrated in front of Niger's parliament building Tuesday in protest against the banning of a women's march that had been planned for last week, witnesses said. The demonstration was headed by several politicians, including Tanja Mamadou, president of the National Movement for a Developing Society (MNSD), the former sole ruling party and now the main opposition grouping. Tuesday's protest ended without incident at about 11:30 a.m. (1030 GMT).

Almost 1,000 university students and secondary school pupils demonstrated in Niger's capital on Wednesday to call for the release of their union leader, Boubacar Siddo, arrested a week earlier. The demonstrators held a rally outside parliament, where deputies have been in a special session since Monday, and then went to government headquarters before dispersing calmly shortly before midday. Siddo, the secretary-general of the USN students' union who was arrested on January 19, has stated that the authorities have charged him with "incitement to rebellion" because of statements he made to the press.

A student died Friday of injuries sustained in campus clashes with Niger police that left four other students wounded, students told the official ANP news agency. The general secretary of the UEU students' union, Ousmane Abdourahamane, confirmed the report to AFP, adding that the fatal casualty, Tahirou Harouna, 25, was hit "right in the face" by a teargas canister. Four of his colleages were injured, "two seriously," Abdourahamane added. The police had intervened when several hundred students demonstrated for several hours late Thursday in protest against the government's failure to pay grants that had become several months overdue. The police threw tear gas canisters and sought to dismantle barricades of blazing tyres put up by the students, who responded by hurling stones, Abdourahamane said. The government of Niger agreed late Wednesday to study the grievances of students who earlier gave the government 48 hours to punish those responsible for killing a student here last Friday. Students are also demanding backpayment of grants in arrears since 1992, and an increase in the basis grant to compensate for January's devaluation of the CFA franc. The government had already paid in full the grants owing from last year and the year before, which had cost 2.8 billion CFA francs (four million dollars), and would pay grants outstanding for the first trimester by this week, he said.

Niger's three leading opposition politicians were arrested Sunday, the day after a violent anti-government protest that killed an opposition supporter. At least 20 people were injured and hospitalized on Saturday when police clashed with opposition militants who blocked streets with barricades of burning tires. Niamey hospital authorities said one man died of his wounds. Opposition parties had called for a civil disobedience campaign, saying they were being marginalized by the government. The trouble began the day after President Mahamane Ousmane, this desert nation's first democratically elected leader, celebrated his first anniversary in power. The three opposition parties that called the protest won 33 of the 83 seats in the national assembly. Given that this protest was brought forth by the opposition parties and that at least 20 people were injured with clashes (implying violence), this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.  Three opposition leaders were arrested yesterday, a day after a demonstrator died of wounds suffered during a clash with police at an anti-government protest. Whereabouts of the three legislators was not known.

One student was injured here Friday after protests over non-payment of grants led to violent clashes between police and demonstrators in the Niger capital, an AFP correspondent reported. The demonstration by around 100 students demanding the payment of four months' grant arrears began at 10:00 a.m. local time (0900 GMT). It turned violent after police tried to dismantle barricades erected by students across the Kennedy Bridge over the River Niger.

Three people were killed and 38 injured when two Niger army soldiers threw grenades into the crowd at a pro-Tuareg rally at Agades, 750 kilometres (470 miles) north east of Niger's capital Niamey, a Tuareg leader said Sunday. Rebel leader Mano Dayak told AFP that the grenades, of which he said there were three, were thrown during a rally organized Saturday by the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDPS), which is essentially a pro-Tuareg organization. The town is situated deep inside Tuareg rebel-held territory in the northern central belt of the country which has been the scene of clashes between autonomy-seeking rebels and government forces since 1991. A grenade attack killed six people during a rally of Tuaregs, the ethnic group seeking greater autonomy in Niger, the Interior Ministry said Monday. Three more people died of their wounds Sunday and Monday at a hospital, authorities said. This protest is believed to have at least 100 people, since 36 people were injured; the response is coded as ignore because the killings from the grenade are not clearly from the government.

Thousands of Muslims gathered in the capital's main mosque and demanded the government halt an AIDS education and prevention campaign. In the meeting Saturday, Islamic groups said the radio, television, and poster campaign would encourage adultery, and they threatened to tear down posters that have been put up in villages nationwide. ''The radio and the television belong to the people of Niger, and we will not tolerate the Western destruction of the moral and religious codes of our society,'' said a statement after the meeting. The groups are particularly angered by the campaign's encouragement of the use of condoms to prevent acquired AIDS. More than 5,000 Muslims gathered at the grand mosque in Niger's capital yesterday to denounce condoms and the government's anti-AIDS and birth-control campaigns. The Muslims, who oppose secularization of their 98 per cent Muslim country, said promoting the use of condoms to fight AIDS encourages debauchery among the young. They gave the government what they called a final warning to stop publicizing condom use and also to ban the screening of pornographic films. Niger has experienced a surge of Muslim fundamentalist protests ranging from the smashing of billboards that promote family planning to attacks on girls in miniskirts.

Niger's main human rights movement on Wednesday staged a march to back a hunger-striker from neighbouring Nigeria, who was detained a year ago and accused of masterminding an air hijack. Niger police say they suspect him of being behind the hijacking of a Nigerian Airways aircraft to Niamey in October 1993, though he was not aboard the jet when it was diverted from an internal flight. Launching his hunger-strike, Yussuf wrote to top police authorities alleging that he had been physically and mentally tortured in a bid to drive him insane. He stated that he had been beaten by police, deprived of visits and reading materials, and fed like a dog. About 100 demonstrators responded Wednesday to the appeal from the ANDDH, which issued a copy of Yussuf's letter, and marched on government buildings in Niamey to call for an immediate end to his "arbitrary detention".

Campaigning for Niger's second democratic election began Wednesday with street demonstrations and competing demands from unpaid government workers, university students, and hard-line Muslims. Trade union leader Ibrahim Mayaki said workers are angry that the government is spending money on elections when clinics have no medication and workers have not been paid for months. Students are threatening protests if the new government does not pay arrears in grants going back four months. The congress of trade unions is demanding the government pay five months of unpaid salaries to workers and warning that ''otherwise the coming elections are going to suffer.'' Fundamentalist Muslims opposed to the government's family planning and AIDS programs say they will disrupt the election campaign if ''the defense of Islam'' is not included in parties' manifestoes. The wide range of demographics this protest covers implies there was at least 100 people participating.
NIAMEY, Niger - About 3,000 people march peacefully in Niamey in protest against possible cancellation of the 1994-1995 academic year in the landlocked West African State of Niger.

Clashes erupted during a protest June 2, and four students were arrested. Students from Niamey's high schools have held periodic demonstrations since January to protest late payment by the government of their annual grants for educational materials such as books, pens, and papers. Given the response by police, this protest is believed to have at least 50 participants.  JUNE 6: NIAMEY, Niger - Police release eight of the 12 students remanded in custody after violent demonstrations in the nation's capital, Niamey, the previous week.

Police hurling tear-gas grenades and swinging batons broke up a demonstration Tuesday by high school students demanding freedom for fellow students arrested in an earlier protest. There were no reports of injuries or arrests. Students from Niamey's high schools have held periodic demonstrations since January to protest late payment by the government of their annual grants for educational materials such as books, pens, and papers. Clashes erupted during a protest June 2, and four students were arrested. The protesters Tuesday demanded they be freed unconditionally. Students barricaded streets with tree trunks and burning tires and threw rocks at police. After police gained control, the students returned to their schools.

On Thursday last week, Niamey university students, angered by the non-payment of up to eight months bursary arrears, torched two private vehicles and clashed with security forces for 24 hours. The government decided to close down the students halls but allowed lectures to continue. NIAMEY, Niger - Eleven students are arrested following clashes with police in which three of their colleagues sustained injuries. Clashes with police implies crowd dispersal as a response.  This protest is coded as having at least 50 participants due to how many people were arrested and how popular other student demonstrations have been.

Riot police brutalised and then arrested seven students who converged at Parliament building in Niamey, the capital, on Thursday. The students were among hundreds of other colleagues from various institutions in the capital, preparing a rally in support of University students who had their campus closed Friday.

NIAMEY: More than 2,000 students and school pupils held a violent demonstration in the Niger capital Niamey to claim a year's arrears in grants. In one incident, a dozen vehicles were wrecked and a few passers-by were hit by stones thrown by the demonstrators. Riot police prevented the demonstrators from reaching the city centre after they left the university campus. They were also protesting against a cut in the budget for grants and the dissolution of a commission responsible for helping newly qualified students. (Niger-students)

The military junta in Niger imposed an indefinite ban on demonstrations and public meetings from Tuesday night after presidential elections marked by tension and the abrupt sacking of senior election officials.  Shortly after the ban was issued, police used tear gas grenades to disperse supporters of political parties who were preparing to hold a demonstration, according to an AFP reporter in Niamey. As results were being made public, Interior Minister Idi Ango Omar slapped a ban on all demonstrations and public meetings throughout the country, in response to protests at the dissolution Monday of the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI) which had clashed several times with Mainassara over the organisation of the poll. Police also used tear gas late Tuesday to disperse political activists after the interior ministry announced a ban on public meetings and demonstrations. Given the response by the police, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

Riot police used tear gas Wednesday to disperse a crowd of hundreds of opposition supporters after Niger's junta leader General Ibrahim Bare Mainassara won presidential elections here. The supporters, who had started to gather outside the headquarters of the party led by former president Mohamane Ousmane, one of the losing candidates, were reportedly due to attend a meeting organised by the four parties who put up candidates in the poll. Soldiers lobbed tear gas into crowds of stone-throwing demonstrators protesting election results But Boubacar Sidikou, an opposition party member, said, "we're going to march and hold meetings in spite of the ban." The military ruler who seized power in a coup last January was declared president Wednesday, and opposition parties immediately cried fraud. One of Gen. Ibrahim Mainassara's first official acts was to ban public meetings and opposition parties. Soldiers lobbed tear gas at hundreds of demonstrators who threw stones at them during an opposition march to protest the election results.

Sixteen people, including a police officer, were slightly injured Thursday during a demonstration in the eastern Niger town of Zinder, birthplace of the former head of state defeated in a presidential poll, police sources said. Some 94 people were arrested in the incident, which involved a "significant number" of violent demonstrators, local police superintendant Dodo Kadri told AFP by telephone. The demonstrators, identified as supporters of Mahamane Ousmane -- the president ousted in a January coup then defeated in a presidential poll by General Ibrahim Bare Mainasara -- armed with machetes and other non-firearm weapons, also set fire to a police station, according to Kadri. Authorities in Niger on Friday imposed a curfew in the eastern town of Zinder a day after police clashed with hundreds of people protesting a presidential poll won by the country's junta leader. Sixteen people, including a policeman, were slightly injured during Thursday's clashes in Zinder, the country's second largest city. It is also the birthplace of Mahamane Ousmane, the president that General Ibrahim Bare Mainassara ousted in a January coup and defeated in this week's presidential election.

Earlier on Sunday, police occupied the headquarters of Issoufou's party after supporters held a demonstration against a supreme court decision to reject a bid by Issoufou and another candidiate to annul the poll results. About 10 people were arrested at Saturday's protest, witnesses said. There was no official confirmation that anyone had been detained. Given that 10 people were arrested, at least 50 people is assumed to have participants in this protest.

Police in Niger's capital used tear gas Thursday to disperse students marching towards parliament in protest against the non-payment of grants, witnesses told AFP. Some students were detained, said the witnesses, who reported no injuries in the incident, which involved around 500 students. Police used tear gas grenades to break up the protest as the students approached the parliament building. As well as the payment of several months of grant arrears, the students are also demanding the grants be increased and the conditions for eligibility be revised.

NIAMEY, Jan 11 (AFP) - Police used truncheons and teargas Saturday to break up a demonstration mounted by eight opposition parties in Niamey, the capital of Niger. Hours later, three top opposition leaders were put under house arrest in Niamey, a source close to the opposition, reached by telephone, told AFP's Abidjan bureau. Police were seen rounding up and arresting dozens of demonstrators after authorities in Niamey banned the protest, saying it was subversive. After the demonstration was broken up Saturday, protestors scattered through the capital and set fire to car tyres on several crossroads, blocking traffic in the town. Issoufou, president of the Nigerian Party for Socialism and Democracy, told a private radio station: "This struggle is going to continue until democracy is restored." Thousands of anti-government protesters clashed with riot police Saturday who fired tear gas after the demonstrators forced their way past barricades and tried to stage a march. Protesters armed with rocks and sticks set up burning barricades of tires and tree branches in the roads, creating massive traffic jams in the capital.

More than 2,000 people took part Saturday in a rally in Niger's capital to demand the unconditional release of three opposition leaders who were arrested on Tuesday. The rally, organized by women members of the opposition coalition Front for the Restoration and Defense of Democracy, had been authorized by the police. Niger's president, General Ibrahim Bare Mainassara, announced Thursday on national television the release of the main opposition leaders and their supporters.

Thousands of students and schoolchildren took to the streets of Niger's capital Thursday to press demands for unpaid allowances as well as for more teachers and classroom space. space. Riot police were deployed in the town centre and near the university, blocking the path of other students hoping to join the demonstration. The schoolchildren say they need more classrooms because many of the straw huts used have been destroyed by rain and roaming animals.  Riot police were deployed in the town centre and near the university, blocking the path of other students hoping to join the demonstration. They later stormed the campus, firing tear-gas grenades and beating up several students before withdrawing, but leaving 10 students injured, Ibrahim Saley, a student leader, told newsmen.

Some 1,000 students demonstrated for payment of scholarship arrears in Niger's capital Monday, while schoolteachers went on strike to demand unpaid backpay. Early in the morning, students blocked a key bridge over the Niger river, forcing some commuters to make the crossing by canoe and prompting gendarmes to deploy to prevent students reaching the city centre, where President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara was due to inaugurate an exhibition at the national museum.

Students and school pupils on Monday gathered in their hundreds in Niger's capital to commemorate the gunning down and wounding of several of their number during a pro-democracy rally eight years ago. The students and children boycotted classes to meet near Niamey's Kennedy bridge and shout slogans against successive governments for failing to deal with security force members who shot three students dead and seriously wounded several others on February 9, 1990.

Mutinous soldiers in eastern Niger have taken several officers and civilian officials hostage, travellers from the region said here Monday. Among those held by soldiers who mutinied in the Diffa region Saturday to protest their living and working conditions were the deputy commander of the region and senior local administrative officials, the same sources said. The mutinous soldiers arrived Saturday in Diffa region, 1,150 kilometers (720 miles) east of Niamey, the sources said. The hostages were being held in a military camp in Bosso, near the Chadian border, the sources said. A high-level military delegation was due to travel to Diffa to negotiate with the mutineers, but bad weather prevented their aircraft taking off, informed sources in the capital said. Residents of Diffa, where the soldiers imposed a curfew Tuesday night, said calm had returned although three gunshots were heard in the town's barracks an hour after the curfew began. The mutineers in Diffa, located 1,150 kilometers (720 miles) east of Niamey, on Wednesday released three of at least four civilian officials and army officers they had held since Saturday, Tounkara said. Speaking from Diffa, home to some 20,000 people, a civil servant said: "Residents were very frightened Tuesday evening and laid low after sunset." Given that soldiers were able to take over a region of 20000, this protest is assumed to have at least 50 soldiers participating. Aside from their salary demands, the mutineers in Diffa want two of their superior officers to be relocated. Mutineers in Diffa, 1,150 kilometers (720 miles) east of Niamey, who rose up a week ago, on Saturday freed two civilian hostages; the sub-prefect of Diffa and secretary-general of the prefecture, whom they had been holding since the start of the rebellion, informed sources in Diffa said. However the mutineers were still holding three superior officers, namely the Diffa battalion commander, a captain and the commander of the Nr.3 defence zone based in Zinder, who was seized after going to Diffa with money to pay wage arrears. This protest is recorded as ending on March 1st because it seems to go past February 28th, but does not have a clear end date; the fact that they released many hostages on the 28th implies that the protest ended soon after.

Soldiers in northern Niger mutinied Wednesday in apparent solidarity with army colleagues who at the weekend took control of an area in the far east to demand settlement of back pay. Gunshots were heard in Agadez, where mutineers seized the region's prefect, Lieutenant-Colonel Mai Manga Oumara, and two other officers, Defence Minister Yahaya Tounkara said in the capital. The mutineers in Agadez, located 750 kilometers (470 miles) northeast of the capital, joined colleagues in Diffa, N'Gourti, Bosso and N'Guima, near the borders with Chad and Nigeria, who since Saturday had been demanding back-pay settlements and other allowances. The mutiny has strong support across the country, implying that there were likely at least 50 soldiers participating.  Troops in two of at least four mutinous garrisons in Niger ended their protest and released five hostages Friday after military authorities paid some of the salary arrears that fuelled the uprising, one of the freed hostages told AFP. "The mutineers' demands, which were purely material, have been met," said Oumar, who added that a curfew imposed by the soldiers in Agadez had been lifted. The national press agency reported officers from the capital had delivered half of four months of salary arrears as well as other allowances to the troops.

An army mutiny in the impoverished former French African colony of Niger spread Thursday to the country's second city Zinder where soldiers demanding back pay stormed a radio station. Also Thursday, disgruntled soldiers took three new hostages in the northern mining centre of Arlit. Soldiers in Zinder, a regional army command centre 750 kilometers (470 miles) east of the capital, Niamey, stormed a radio station to press demands for settlement of four months' unpaid wages and imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew on the city, where residents reported gunshots in the morning. Mutinous troops in a southeastern Niger military command centre ended their uprising Saturday and released four hostages as they began receiving half of the salary arrears which fuelled their protest, an official there told AFP. A military official said the mutineers in Zinder, 750 kilometers (470 miles) east of the capital, had returned to their barracks and that calm had returned to the previously panic-striken town. It was not clear, however, whether the backpay demands of gendarmes who joined the protest were being met. Given that soldiers were able to take over the second-largest city in the country, this protest is assumed to have at least 50 participants.

Several people were seriously injured Monday in northern Niger during a violent clash between opposition militants and security forces at a political rally, the opposition charged. "There were several serious injuries and many arrests" in the incident in Tahoua, 400 kilometers (250 miles) northeast of here, a local opposition official told the private radio station R and M broadcast from Niamey. Demonstrators took several security officers hostage demanding the release of their arrested colleagues, the spokesman said. The official said the eight parties belonging to the opposition coalition, the Front for the Restoration and Defense of Democracy (FRDD), organized the rally calling for the resignation of President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara. Several policemen and civilians were reportedly injured and several arrests were made during the clashes in Tahoua, about 550 kilometers (330 miles) northeast of the capital, the radio station known as ''RM-FM'' said Monday. The protesters were demanding the ouster of Nigerien President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara, the radio station said citing anonymous government officials. Due to the several people being injured as well as the number of opposition parties in the coalition, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people participating.

Several people were injured Saturday in the southern Niger town of Maradi as security forces used teargas to break up an opposition demonstration, corroborating sources said. The demonstrators in the town, 550 kilometers (340 miles) east of the capital, were carrying clubs and slingshots, placed burning tyres on several crossroads and ransacked several kiosks, the sources said. Since last weekend, Niger's opposition has held demonstrations across the country, calling for Mainassara's resignation. Given widespread opposition support, the several people injured, and the police response, this protest is believed to have at least 50 participants.

Opposition militants in Niger barricaded roads with flaming tires, tree trunks and electricity pylons Sunday in the towns of Zinder and Maradi, state radio reported. In Zinder in the center, the country's second city, the demonstrators set fire to the headquarters of President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara's Rally for Democracy and Progress party (RDP). In Maradi in the south, demonstrators jostled RDP officials there for an afternoon meeting, including party secretary-general Colonel Abdulrahaman Saidou, whose bodyguard was injured and hospitalized, the radio said. Several people were injured in Maradi on Saturday when police used teargas to break up an opposition demonstration. Sources said the demonstrators, carrying clubs and slingshots, placed burning tyres on several crossroads and ransacked kiosks. Opposition activists took to the streets of Niger's second-largest city, Zinder, setting fire to a police station and to the regional headquarters of the ruling party, officials said. In the town of Maradi, supporters of an eight-party alliance demanding the resignation of President Col. Ibrahim Bare Mainassara ransacked buildings, built barricades and burned tires during a turbulent weekend. But officials and witnesses said the ruling Rally for Democracy and Progress proceeded with a meeting there in support of Mainassara, protected by a heavy police turnout. This protest is believed to have at least 50 participants due to the levels of violence and the widespread opposition support.

Security forces on Sunday broke up an opposition demonstration in several working-class parts of Niger's capital Niamey, witnesses told AFP. Private radio said clashes between protesters and security forces left "several injured," adding that "many arrests" were made. Street protests have been held over the past two weeks demanding the resignation of President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara. Opposition militants set up barricades of burning tyres at major streets in Niamey today in a flare-up of political violence in the Niger capital, witnesses said. Paramilitary police fired teargas at several locations to break up groups of demonstrators protesting at the rule of President Ibrahim Bare Mainassara, they said. Police chased and arrested several protesters. An unknown number of people were wounded, the witnesses added.

Opponents of President Ibrahim Bare Mainassare in Niger, one of the world's poorest countries, staged the latest in a series of protest rallies in the second city of Zinder on Saturday. Demonstrators built barricades of burning tyres and tree trunks to block roads in the city but refrained from attacking property, and police did not intervene, a local official said. The rally was the latest to be organised by the Front for the Restoration and Defence of Democracy, an opposition umbrella group. The group has organised a wave of protests since mid-April, some of which have turned violent.

Police in Sierra Leone have despatched armed reinforcements to the small town of Mile 91, after rioting secondary school students burnt a police station and six cars on Thursday, a police chief said Friday. Students wielding sticks set light to a police station in Sierra Leone and damaged two cars in protest at the treatment of an unlicensed motor cyclist, police said Tuesday. "He then mobilised support from the students, who grouped and marched to the police station, chased out the personnel and set the building alight," Gbekie explained at a news conference. The pupils also damaged two cars parked in the complex and destroyed a new police office complext under construction, in the town of Lumpa, 20 miles (30 kilometres) east of the capital. Very few people inside Sierra Leone had expected that President Ernest Bai Koroma would take his anti-corruption crusade into the highest echelon of political power in his otherwise impoverished country. Since his All People's Congress (A.P.C) came to power in 2007 following nationwide elections, President Koroma has been speaking regularly about adopting a zero-tolerance policy towards corruption. Several times in the past, he's warned members of his government of the consequences of fraudulently enriching themselves. He had warned his officials that "no longer shall we have sacred cows" in the campaign against graft and that he would not prepared to stand in the way of the anti-graft body if it indicted anyone for mismanagement or outright embezzlement of the national coffers, no matter how highly placed the accused is. If anyone was surprised to see Mrs. Kabbah in the dock a number of weeks ago, it would have been because she is a very senior member of the current A.P.C. - controlled government in Freetown. Mrs. Kabbah's high-profile case pits her against the powerful Anti-Corruption Commission. Crucially, too, she is a high-ranking member of the governing party, and her friends came from all over the country to put on a visible reminder. Outside the premises of the court, there were scenes that easily resembled a political rally, as dozens of women clad in red were chanting slogans and calling on the A.P.C. to intervene on behalf of one of their own. Inside the courtroom proper, several riot policemen stood guard, in part, to put paid to any planned breach of the peace.
