"In the capital Bujumbura, soldiers marched through the streets today to disperse demonstrators bent on ousting President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya. About 200 Tutsi youths gathered in the main square late in the morning, and offices and shops quickly closed their doors. Within minutes, about 200 soldiers arrived, walking eight- and 10-abreast through the streets with their automatic weapons raised. One soldier kicked a man who didn't get off the street fast enough."

Notes: "Hundreds of demonstrators marched through Bujumbura on Saturday to protest against foreign military intervention to quell ethnic violence in Burundi. The protestors, rallied by former president Jean-Baptiste Bagaza, converged on Bujumbura football stadium where thousands of other supporters of the former leader were already assembled. Bagaza, a Tutsi, who exerts powerful influence in the Tutsi-dominated army and among young Tutsis, has denounced the Burundian government for calling for military assistance during a regional summit in Arusha, northern Tanzania, last Tuesday."

"Several hundred Tutsi students from the university of Bujumbura protested here Thursday against the possibility of a foreign military peacekeeping force being deployed in their strife-torn country." "The students called for the immediate departure of "genocidal president" Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, a Hutu, and expressed strong support for the Tutsi-dominated armed forces."

"Tutsi opponents of Burundi's Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya took to the streets of Bujumbura on Friday to protest against "all foreign intervention" in their violence-wracked nation. Some 2,000 to 3,000 were seen taking part in the demonstration, although organizers -- mainly Tutsi political parties -- claimed that the turnout was in excess of 10,000."

"Activities ground to a halt in Bujumbura Friday, as workers in strifeThe work-stoppage was organized workers' union to protest the death of about 100 workers killed last week in the central town of Teza, in an attack on a tea packaging factory." "The Unions have urged government officials to abandon their ambivalent attitude to the crisis in the country and put an end to the continuing massacres."
"Some 2,500 Burundian students, pupils and jobless people demonstrated in Bujumbura Monday in opposition to proposals for a regional military force that is to try and restore order in the country."

"Vowing to resist foreign military intervention, some 10,000 protesters marched Friday through the streets and called for the overthrow of the coalition government. It was the largest demonstration since Hutu President Silvestre Ntibantunganya and Tutsi Prime Minister Antoine Nduwayo appealed June 25 for outside assistance - which they later acknowledged would be military aid - to end ethnic violence in the tiny central African nation. The United Nations also has called for international help."

Anti-riot police and soldiers on Saturday dispersed a thousand, mainly Tutsi, demonstrators who crowded into a downtown quarter of the capital in defiance of the government to air their opposition to peace talks with Hutu rebels. Before the gun and baton-wielding security forces broke up the rally near Bujumbura's central market, the protesters waved placards condemning negotiations with Hutu political and rebel leaders, whom they called the ''perpetrators of genocide'' against minority Tutsis. As policemen pummeled protesters after cornering them in the street, about a dozen of protesters were whisked away in police cars. Shop owners closed their doors and onlookers fled to their houses.

Hundreds of people marched through the streets of the Burundian capital Friday after trade unions in the war-torn country launched an open-ended strike to protest at the "failure" of the current government. "The government is violating union rights... the economy has broken down, citizens can no longer meet their basic needs," said a statement from the country's main trade union grouping, the Confederation of Burundi Trade Unions, COSYBU. Police were out around the protesters.

Several hundred people marched through the city centre here Saturday to protest against the government and the peace talks aimed at ending Burundi's seven-year civil war. Over a two-hour period, police dispersed demonstrators who tried to reach two main squares. There were few clashes as the protestors melted away into the crowd at a market when police intervened. Police used tear gas once against a group of people trying to reach the market square while shouting anti-Arusha slogans.

Up to 40 members of a radical Tutsi party were arrested here Saturday for trying to demonstrate against the dissolution of the country's army, which they say is the only shield against the genocide of their people. A heavy riot police detail was deployed on Independence Square, where members of PARENA (Party For National Recovery) had tried to mount their protest. Party Secretary-General Remy Nkengurutse said about a dozen party activists had been arrested, some in pre-dawn raids on their homes.

Ten radical Tutsi militants and a correspondent for the Associated Press news agency were arrested by gendarmes in Burundi at a demonstration against the Arusha peace accord, witnesses said Thursday. AP correspondent Aloys Niyoyita, who was released six hours later, told AFP he had been "beaten and abused by the gendarmes." Some 100 protesters took part in the demonstration, organised by Power of Self-Defence-Amasekanya, which groups young Tutsis opposed to the Arusha peace accord signed in August 2000.

Burundian police on Sunday opened fire on a group of some 5,000 high school students who were staging a protest to demand payment for cleaning up the capital, Bujumbura, one of the protesters told AFP. But Interior Minister Salvator Ntihabose said a 13-year-old youth who was injured when the demonstration was violently dispersed was not fired on by the police.

Police in Burundi fired in the air Wednesday to disperse 1,000 secondary school pupils demonstrating for a solution to end a strike by their teachers, government officials told AFP. It was the second day of clashes between the pupils and security forces. Wednesday's unrest took place in the central town of Gigega, where the children were trying to gather in the town's centre, according to a local administrator.

Police in Burundi's capital used baton charges Wednesday to disperse hundreds of moped-taxi drivers who were protesting against a ban on their trade, an AFP journalist reported. Several policemen were hurt by stones. The drivers were demonstrating for a second day in front of the interior ministry when about 30 police officers charged and struck out with their batons. The protesters, who numbered about 500 according to police, responded by throwing stones.

Police in Burundi's capital fired into the air Thursday to disperse hundreds of bicycle-taxi operators protesting against a ban imposed to prevent rebel incursions. In several parts of the city, police clashed with the taxi operators, some of whom had vented their anger on other cyclists delivering goods rather than passengers and who were not subject to the ban. They slashed tyres, spilled milk churns and in some cases beat up the riders.

About 100 peasants from southwest Burundi Thursday entered the fourth day of a sit-in in front of the agriculture ministry in Bujumbura to demand the government restore land they say was seized from them. "We are owners of land in Gatakwa since 1982, we have developed these marshes and today eager officials have dispossessed us and divided up this land," said one of the demonstrators, Egide Ntabandi, 45. The peasants, including women with babies on their backs, arrived from Gatakwa, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) south of the capital, to begin the sit-in on Monday morning. They spend the night under the stars, wash their laundry and spread it out atop the hedges, and say they are "determined that justice will be done," said Ntabandi. The government on Wednesday established a mediation committee "to solve the Gatakwa problem once and for all," said the committee's chairman, Anicet Niyongabo, governor of Bururi, which includes Gatakwa.

About five thousand prisoners held in Burundi's largest jails and accused of offences related to the central African country's civil war have demanded their freedom, a rights group said. The detainees, most of whom have not yet been brought to trial, consider themselves to be "political prisoners" and object to getting different treatment from politicians granted immunity under a peace pact signed in 2000.

On Prince Louis Rwagasore road at the INSS building, everything was fine except after the clash between police and several hundred demobilized former fighters. The building which is occupied by US NGO PADCO [expansions untraced] and is located on the road mentioned was besieged by several hundred angry demobilized former fighters starting this morning. In the building's corridors, the inner court and the parking was full of former fighters who refused workers entry. Police who intervened a little late were almost unable to eject them from the building and opted to negotiate with them to secure the people who had been taken hostage.

Burundian police used clubs and belts to break up a protest Wednesday in support of the former head of the president's political party, who was arrested last month. Dozens of police officers charged the crowd of hundreds in the capital, resulting in several injuries, including a woman who fainted for several minutes, an AFP journalist saw. "It's unacceptable. The police do not have the right to charge people who are demonstrating peacefully," said Pierre-Claver Mbonimpa, head of the Association for the Defense of Detained Persons and Human Rights.

Eighteen students were injured on Thursday in a clash with police when they marched on Burundi's education ministry to protest at poor food in their technical college, students and officials said. The high school students came from Bubanza, 35 kilometres (about 20 miles) north of Bujumbura, "where they wanted to march on the ministry of education," Bubanza Provincial Governor Pascal Nyabenda told AFP. "I couldn't allow that, so I asked the police to stop them," he said, while protesting students said the police did so by opening fire and clubbing some of them with batons at Mpanda, 12 kilometres outside the capital.

About 2,500 Burundian prisoners rioted in the country's largest jail, leading police to intervene with tear gas, a prison official said Tuesday. Many of the inmates of Mpimba jail in the capital Bujumbura barricaded themselves off late Monday against warders trying to restore order and tried to break doors. Police had to be called in during the night, said Anaclet Gasanirwa, director of correctional facilities.

Demonstrations held in Burundi today degenerated resulting in three people, including a police officer, being injured. The demonstrations were held by students in the capital, Bujumbura, to demand an increase in their university allowances. Policemen intervened and dispersed them using truncheons and tear gas.

A Burundi opposition leader was on Tuesday charged with contempt for the president, his lawyer said, following his November 3 arrest alongside 37 party members for holding an illegal meeting. Dozens of policemen were deployed near the court where around 150 supporters gathered to protest against Alexis Sinduhije's arrest.

Hundreds of Burundians gathered in a show of support for opposition party leader and former journalist Alexis Sinduhije, whose trial on charges of contempt for the president opened here Friday. More than 100 Burundian police forces, some of them in anti-riot gear, had gathered since the early morning to bar demonstrators from approaching the high court in the capital Bujumbura. "What the police is doing here is a violation of the law... All this further proves that it is a political trial," Francois Nyamoya, a close friend of Sinduhije's, told AFP.

Thousands of Burundians demonstrated Friday in the capital to demand the outlawing of homosexuality after senators rejected a draft law last month that would criminalize the act. Up to 20,000 people turned out for the government-planned protest against homosexuality, which organizers described as a foreign practice that is tarnishing morals.

Hundreds of former child soldiers for Burundi rebels staged a mutiny at a demobilisation camp to demand better conditions, an official said Tuesday. Some 340 child soldiers from the National Liberation Forces (FNL), Burundi's last active rebel group, have been in Gitega, 100 kilometers (60 miles) east of Bujumbura, since early April awaiting demobilisation. "The 340 child soldiers gathered at Gitega demobilisation centre mutinied yesterday evening," head of the centre Romain Ndagabwa, told AFP in a telephone interview.

Former Burundi rebels clashed with riot police when a protest in the capital Bujumbura turned violent and eight people were arrested, police said Tuesday. Police spokesman Pierre Chanel Ntarabaganyi said that about 300 members of the former National Liberation Forces (FNL) were involved in the violence during Monday's protest and that "police intervened to restore calm and arrested eight ring-leaders." Demonstrators threw stones at police and passing cars, said Ntarabaganyi, adding that in any case, the protest was "illegal". "The police charged while we were calmly asking for our money, they beat us, threw tear gas and pursued us to the market place," said David, a 25-year-old former fighter who declined to give his full name. Hundreds of the former fighters had demonstrated outside the offices of the service responsible for demobilising fighters from the small central African country's 13 years of civil war.

Clashes erupted in Burundi's capital Saturday in the first violence linked to last week's disputed local polls, with several people wounded and arrested, an opposition party and officials said. The election commission has announced the ruling party won more than 60 percent of Monday's vote but eight opposition groups allege there was massive fraud and have demanded a re-run. The opposition National Liberation Forces (FNL) said people began demonstrating in Bujumbura's Kinama quarter when they found "several ballot boxes filled with balloting papers, some of them not counted."

Burundi's police on Friday blocked a demonstration organised to demand justice for an assassinated anti-corruption activist and briefly detained two activists. The demonstration had been organised to commemorate the second anniversary of the murder of Ernest Manirumva, a former deputy of the central African country's Olucome corruption watchdog who was stabbed to death in 2009. "We don't understand why the regime is preventing us from marching to demand justice for the third time in a year. It is a right enshrined in the constitution," Pacifique Nininahazwe, who heads a civil society platform of some 150 associations and non-governmental organisations, told AFP. "We want justice to be done, because two years after his death, the trial hasn't produced anything," he said in Bujumbura, where a small group of demonstrators were barred from holding their march.

About 100 journalists marched here Tuesday to press for the release of a jailed colleague, the decriminalisation of press offences and to mark World Press Freedom Day. "We're demonstrating, on the international day for press freedom, to demand first and foremost the release of our colleague, Jean-Claude Kavumbagu, who has been jailed for months and risks a life sentence," Alexandre Niyungeko, the president of the Burundian Union of Journalists, told AFP. The state prosecutor in mid-April called for life imprisonment for Kavumbagu, who has been in detention since July 2010, accused of treason for having doubted the ability of Burundi's security forces to prevent an attack by Somali insurgents on Burundian soil.

At least 900 inmates detained at Ruyigi prison with a capacity of 300 on Tuesday morning rioted to protest against deteriorating living conditions, local media reported.  Media quoted prisoners as saying that they have spent a whole week without receiving beans rations, the staple food in the prison of Ruyigi.  The inmates rioted in an attempt to get out of the prison and the deteriorating living conditions.

Lawyers in Burundi announced a week-long strike on Monday in protest at the arrest of one of their colleagues for "complicity in espionnage". Around 100 lawyers gathered outside the courthouse in the capital Bujumbura in support of Suzanne Bukuru, who was arrested and imprisoned on July 15 for helping French journalists get an interview with victims she is representing in a rape trial involving a French man, according to legal sources.

A prosecutor Friday asked an appeal cout to uphold the life sentence handed to Burundian journalist Hassan Ruvakuki over terrorism charges. "Hassan Ruvakuki is a terrorist," said prosecutor Emmanuel Nyandwi on the last day of an appeal hearing in Gitega, central Burundi. "He does not have the right to hide behind his journalism profession to kill. That is why I ask the court to uphold the life sentence which was given to him the first time," added Nyandwi amid protests by crowds gathered in and out of the courtroom.

Both have a case to make, but some see the government's National Commission for Land and Property (CNTB) as favouring one side over the other, said Pacifique Ninahazwe, a prominent civil society figure. "The CNTB is increasingly deciding in favour of returnees and ethnic Hutu more generally, rather than recognising that both returnees and residents face problems," Ninahazwe told AFP. "If this continues it will lead to other potentially devastating conflicts." In one recent case in Burundi's capital Bujumbura, riots broke out as police tried to evict a Tutsi family from their house in order to give it back to a Hutu family, former residents 40 years ago. "We are here to oppose injustice, to oppose the CNTB, which is undermining reconciliation in Burundi society," shouted a member of the thousand or so youths who gathered at the protest. In that case, the standoff lasted six hours, left more than a dozen people hurt and resulted in the arrest of 20 youths.

Rioting broke out in two overcrowded prisons in Burundi, leaving one civilian and one inmate dead and at least 16 others wounded, a police spokesman said Friday. At Mpimba prison, the country's largest, in the capital Bujumbura, police stepped in to put down the rioting on Thursday, and two people were killed by the rioters, the spokesman, Pierre Nkurikiye told AFP. It happened as some 100 Muslims were visiting the prison to pray with inmates at the end of the Islamic holy month of Ramadan. "Two people were killed -- one of the Muslims who was visiting and one detainee, killed by rioters," Nkurikiye said.

"demobilized soldiers in mozambique's second largest city beira staged a peaceful demonstration on friday, demanding the authorities provide them with jobs and help resolve their economic problems, radio mozambique reported today."

"Mozambican police opened fire on a crowd of demobilised soldiers in the central city of Chimoio on Monday, killing one and wounding at least six. Radio Mozambique reported that the police started shooting when the angry crowd tried to force its way into the building housing the offices of the Manica provincial government."

"about 200 mozambican government troops in dondo training center in the country's central province of sofala raised a riot on monday, shooting dead some local residents. according to the local daily "noticias" today, the soldiers with weapons in hands detained the head of the training center and the officer in charge of financial affairs as hostages, demanding the higher authorities pay their wages in arrears."

"riots happened in some districts here today with some residents robbing shops and attacking vehicles on the streets. the mozambique police rushed to the spots to disperse the rioting people. the riots were caused by a fare hike announced yesterday by some private passenger transporters."

"riots erupted today in xipamanine district in maputo, capital of mozambique, when some residents attacked private minibuses and injured some people. today's riot was again caused by a demonstration in protest against the 100 percent increase of bus fare, which was announced by private bus owners on november 23 following a 28 percent fuel price rise."

Protester Group Identity: former guerrilla soldiers of the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO)
Notes: "Some 200 former guerrilla soldiers of the Mozambican National Resistance (RENAMO) opposition Monday held over 50 vehicles including a United Nations police car after mounting a road block in central Manica Province, UN sources said."

Location of Protest: the main road from Mozambique's capital Maputo to South Africa and Swaziland
Notes: "Hundreds of demonstrators blocked the main road from Mozambique's capital Maputo to South Africa and Swaziland with barricades Monday in protest at bus fare rises, eye witnesses said."

"Rioting soldiers killed two policemen and a civilian in a protest Monday in northern Nampula province, the state news agency reported. The soldiers, based at a United Nations-supervised assembly camp, barricaded a main road to the nearby port of Nacala. Clashes with police sent to restore order left one soldier and the two policemen dead, and another policeman was seriously wounded, the Mozambique Information Agency (AIM) said."

"about 400 soldiers of the mozambique national resistance (renamo) to be disbanded raised riot on monday in renamo headquarters in maringue. the mutineers blockaded the roads linking the headquarters and the outside and held a renamo major general as hostage, according to the local press."

"citizens in the suburbs of maputo, capital of mozambique, today held a grand demonstration again to protest against the government for increasing charges of mini-buses. the citizens poured into the streets this morning and held demonstrations. they also blockaded the roads leading to the city center. a mini-bus was burnt by the angry citizens and another two seriously damaged. the police clashed with the demonstrators and the situation got worse."

"Around 80 army mutineers caused panic as they wreaked havoc with a tank in the suburbs of Maputo Wednesday morning, Radio Mozambique reported. The mutineers, who began their protest Tuesday night, threatened and robbed civilians in Machava suburb of the capital, forcing many residents to flee to neighbouring Liberdade suburb."  "Dozens of mutinous government soldiers terrified residents by driving two tanks through a Maputo suburb Thursday, robbing civilians and firing a missile at a house, Radio Mozambique reported."

"some mozambican soldiers went rioting for government subsidy on thursday evening in gaza province, the local press reported on friday. the rioting soldiers blocked roads and held hostage provincial governor eugenio numaio and passengers on vehicles intercepted on the roads, the report said."
"At least eight people, among them demobilised Mozambican troops, were injured Wednesday during clashes with riot police in demonstrations over their welfare."

"Angry mobs stoned cars and blocked streets in riots that erupted in at least three different sections of the capital Friday over the rising cost of food and transport. ... The riots were sparked by a 500-percent increase in the price of a 50-kilogram (110 pounds) sack of rice, a staple food, and a 33-percent price hike in bus fares. Witnesses reported that hundreds of people, mostly men, attacked the open-air Janeta market in central Maputo. Some attacked passing cars and blocked traffic with burning tires."

"About 300 demobilised soldiers early Tuesday invaded the premises of a bridge and road construction company in northern Nampula province demanding jobs. The troops took several people hostage at Tamega company in Monapo town, but later released them."

"calm has returned to mozambique's central port city of beira today following an unauthorized "peace demonstration" which led to clashes between protesters and police on monday. four protesters were injured while 14 others were arrested by the police during the demonstration, organized by the largest opposition party, national resistance of mozambique (renamo) protesting against rise of living expenses and government mismanagement."

"Mozambican police arrested 36 people after riots broke out in several cities following protests organised by the main opposition Mozambique National Resistance (MNR-Renamo) party, reports said here Tuesday. Authorities used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse demonstrators, notably in Nampula and Angoche in the north of the country and Beira in the centre, the Portuguese news agency LUSA reported. reported."

These protests are part of Labor Day celebrations.  "Thousands of workers in Mozambique took part in traditional 1st May celebrations, marching with banners with demands for better pay. This was an immediate reaction to the government announcement of minimum salary increases of 13,5.%. The minimum wage now stands at 353.886,00mts, where it was formerly 311.000,00, about $30 US dollars."

Twenty-two people, including six police officers, were killed and 113 more injured yesterday in Mozambique during demonstrations against the outcome of last December's general election, President Joaquim Chissano said
Maputo's port and the railways in southern Mozambique hit a near standstill Monday as hundreds of workers went on strike to demand salary increases.
An estimated 30,000 Mozambican workers marched through the streets of the capital Maputo Thursday under tight security to demand better wages and conditions.

Protests by former migrant workers, better known as Magermanes, are frequent in Maputo, where they turn out in their hundreds accusing the government of reneging on payment of benefits due to them after they spent years in the 1980s labouring in the then East Germany.

Thousands of workers on Saturday marched through some main streets of Maputo, the capital of Mozambique, for the traditional May Day demonstration, under the slogan "For employment, development and social justice."

Workers have staged regular protests in Mozambique, demanding payment. About 300 majermanes briefly occupied part of the Mozambican parliament building on June 30, demanding to speak with parliamentary chairman Eduardo Mulembue. Mulembue agreed to meet with them, and took their concerns to President Joaquim Chissano.

Magermans protest in different locations of Mozambique in the first day. Later, the protest concentrates in Maputo which ends with the occupation of the German Embassy. The number of protestors reduce to 40 in the 15 of July. But, three days later the protestors abandoned the embassy.

Students at Eduardo Mondlane University (UEM), the largest institution of higher education in the Mozambique, went on strike on Tuesday in protest against the government's new scholarship regulations.

Police opened fire on a crowd protesting against transport price hikes in Mozambique's capital yesterday, killing one person, a police official said. Thousands of people joined the protests in Maputo, burning tyres and throwing stones at police vehicles. Police fired rubber bullets as they attempted to clear the streets. The government said it would meet transport operators to try to negotiate an end to the stand-off, but explained it had little control over rising transport fares. - (Reuters)

Thousands of Mozambicans have clashed with the police in another wave of protests over the rising cost of living in the booming but impoverished southern African nation, state-owned radio reported. The Mozambican capital, Maputo, was rocked by street demonstrations last week that saw angry crowds loot shops, destroy vehicles and burn electricity poles. Three people were shot and killed by the police and more than 150 were injured.
Hundreds of protesters took to the street in Mozambique's capital Monday to protest health ministry policies that they say are jeopardizing HIV care in one of the world's worst affected countries.

Protester Group Identity: former workers of Matola Coal Terminal
Notes: 157 workers who were sacked last month from the Matola Coal Terminal (TCM) in Maputo port demonstrated on Wednesday outside the Maputo Provincial Labour Directorate, demanding that TCM double the redundancy pay it has offered.

one person died and three others were injured in a clash on Friday between the Mozambican police and a crowd of about 300 people who attacked a health post at Macaroja, in Moma district, in the northern province of Nampula.

Seven people have died in disturbances caused by disinformation about the spread of cholera in the central Mozambican district of Gurue, in Zambezia province, reports the Beira daily paper "Diario de Mocambique".

The cities of Maputo and Matola on Wednesday morning saw unrest with streets being obstructed with rubbish and large obstacles such as electricity poles and burning tyres. Passing vehicles were stoned.

Mob violence led to the destruction of six homes of neighbourhood secretaries in the town of Namialo, in the northern Mozambican province of Nampula, on Wednesday night, according to a report in Friday's issue of the Maputo daily "Noticias".

About 1,000 women demonstrated on Friday in front of the City Council heaquarters in the central port of Beira , demanding just compensation for land and crops they are losing because of the construction of the new Beira port coal terminal.

Traffic was interrupted along Mozambique's main north-south road at Palmeira, some 100 kilometres north of Maputo, for four hours on Monday, when a crowd blocked the road, demanding that the local police hand over two individuals accused of murder.

Several hundred people claiming to be demobilized soldiers and their families demonstrated in a park close to the Mozambican Prime Minister's office in central Maputo on Tuesday, demanding additional payments from the government.

The disturbances in Moatize were clearly on a much larger scale than initially suggested by a laconic report in the Maputo daily "Noticias". About 500 people blocked both the railway and the nearby main road and threatened to destroy train carrying coal. Traffic along the Sena line was halted for about 24 hours.
Under the slogan "Decent Jobs, Fair Wages, Peace and Justice at Work", thousands of workers marched through the streets of central Maputo on Tuesday in the traditional May Day parade.

According to a report in Tuesday's issue of the Maputo daily "Noticias", the students were protesting against the decision to annul the second quarter assessments in eight subjects, where academic fraud was alleged.
More than 200 inmates of the main prison in the central Mozambican city of Beira rioted on Wednesday in protest against poor food and health conditions.
The Mozambican police claimed on Thursday evening that the situation has returned to normal in Maputo and the neighbouring city of Matola after disturbances in protest at an increase in bus fares.

A group of around 350 demobilised soldiers gathered at the AntonioiRipinga athletics track, in front of the office of Prime Minister Alberto Vaquina on Tuesday, to demand pensions from the government of no less than 20,000 meticais (about 664 US dollars, at current exchange rates) a month from the government.

At least two people were injured, and two others are reported dead in clashes in Mecufi district, in the northern province of Cabo Delgado, between police and mobs claiming that health workers are causing rather than curing cholera and other diarrhoeal diseases

Protester Group Identity: former agents of the Mozambican intelligence and security service (SISE)
Notes: Hundreds of former agents of the Mozambican intelligence and security service (SISE) demonstrated outside SISE headquarters in Maputo on Wednesday, demanding higher pensions.
The Mozambican riot police (FIR) on Tuesday morning used tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannon to disperse a demonstration by a group of demobilised soldiers in central Maputo.

Members of the Mozambican Forum of Demobilised Soldiers on Tuesday again attempted to stage a demonstration in front of Prime Minister Alberto Vaquina s Maputo office to press their demand for a pension for all demobilised troops of 20,000 meticais (about 664 US dollars) a month.

The Mozambican police on Tuesday once again used water cannon to disperse a group of demobilised soldiers who were attempting to march on the office of Prime Minister Alberto Vaquina, in pursuit of their demand for a pension for all demobilised troops of 20,000 meticais (about 664 US dollars) a month.

Over 100 residents of the T3 neighbourhood, in the southern Mozambican city of Matola, demonstrated outside the local police station on Wednesday, in protest against the police murder of a minibus driver the previous night.

Thousands of people marched through the streets of Maputo on Thursday, demonstrating against government inertia towards the wave of kidnappings in Mozambican cities, and calling for an end to violence and a return to peace.

"Residents in the city of Lichinga, capital of the northern Mozambican province of Niassa, on Monday protested to President Armando Guebuza about the poor state of communication in the province, particularly the road and railway linking Lichinga to Cuamba, the other major urban centre in Niassa."

"Maputo: Mozambican women's organisations planned to protest outside the country's parliament, the Assembly of the Republic, today against articles in a new draft of the penal code. Today's protest will also be directed at other provisions in the penal code which the women's organisations say discriminate against women and children."

"About 1,000 supporters of women's rights marched in Maputo last week to express their anger over the code. Riot police prevented them from reaching the National Assembly but a small group was allowed through to deliver their concerns to the Speaker,Veronica Macamo. Before the march Macamo had contacted the directors of the two leading women's NGOs to try to persuade them to call it off."

"About 800 people, claiming to be former workers of the long defunct state company Minas Gerais de Mocambique (MAGMA), have occupied the tantalite mine at Muiane, in the central province of Zambezia, reports the independent television station STV."

"Municipal cleaning staff went on strike on Wednesday in the central city of Quelimane, claiming that the municipality owes them their New Year's Bonus for the last three years. The New Year Bonus, commonly known as the thirteenth month?, since it is equal to an extra month's wages, has become a tradition in Mozambique, and workers now regard it as a right. The strike began on Wednesday morning and dozens of cleaning workers gathered in protest outside the municipal council offices. The mayor, Manuel de Araujo, went to speak with them, admitted the debt, and promised that the council would pay it."

"Rioting supporters of Mozambique's former rebel movement Renamo threw up barricades of burning tyres and other detritus on Wednesday evening in the Munhava neighbourhood of the central city of Beira. This blocked the main road from Beira to Zimbabwe, thus making it temporarily impossible for vehicles to enter or leave the city. The pretext for the riot was the rumour that a car had been spotted with fake ballot boxes containing pre-marked ballot papers. So far there is no reliable information as to whether there was any truth in the rumour."

"Policemen opened fire today on hundreds of stone-throwing university students who were protesting a doubling of the price of corn meal, Zambia's staple. No details were immediately available on casualties. But residents of a Lusaka suburb, Kalingalinga, said they saw at least two people fall when police officers fired their rifles at demonstrators."  "ZAMBIAN anger at an ailing economy erupted yesterday and thousands of people rampaged through the capital, Lusaka, in an orgy of looting and violence. Riot police and paramilitary forces used first tear gas and finally live ammunition as they attempted to drive the crowds, led by students, away from Cairo Road, which forms the city's business district, after they smashed shop windows, looted and overturned vehicles."

"about 3,000 students from the university of zambia in lusaka staged a protest on thursday to demand payment of their allowances. according to local press reports today, students complaining of starvation due to lack of money, left the great east road campus and marched to the bursaries committee office in longacres, six kilometres away from the campus, in protest against the committee's delay in paying them allowances. however, they were stopped by armed policemen on the way. armed policemen and paramilitary troops sealed the saddam hussein boulevared road near the bursaries committee office and had a hard time blocking the movement of the students. the confrontation between the police and students lasted about three hours until officials from the ministry of higher education and the bursaries committee obtained some money from the bank of zambia and paid the students part of their allowances."

"about 300 angry young zambian vendors protesting against government removal of street vendors clashed with the police yesterday in ndola city of copperbelt province, local sources said here today. the vendors took to the streets looting property and smashing windows of shops in protest against government seizure of their goods and continued police harassemnt following the recent ban on street vending. police fired teargas canisters to disperse the mob. no casulties were reported."

"more than 300 workers from the zambia national housing authority were arrested today for "unlawful" procession and assembly in lusaka, the zambia news agency zana reported. the workers had reportedly downed tools this morning and marched in downtown lusaka demanding higher pays against the background of sharp devaluation of the kwacha currency and widespread price hikes for major commodities. they were later rounded up by riot police and taken to the lusaka central police station on the charge of illegal parade, zanasaid."

Protester Group Identity: wives of ndola copper refinery workers
Notes: "about 300 wives of ndola copper refinery workers were detained on tuesday for staging an illegal demonstration in protest aginst the heavy taxation on their husbands' salaries. according to reports reaching here today, the women, dressing in their husbands' working overalls and helmets, marched to the refinery on tuesday, but were intercepted and detained by the police in front of the refinery and were sent to masala police station by bus. learning the incident, their husbands stormed the police station, saying that they would not leave until they saw their wives. a trade union official finally persuaded them to leave, said the reports."

"zambian police today arrested about 170 student from university of zambia for unlawful assembly, police officer bartholomew jere has confirmed. but secretary-general of the students union of the university, alfred zulu, who escaped from the arrest, claimed in his address to the on-going congress of the opposition united national independence party (unip) that 1,000 students were arrested by the police. it was reported that the arrested students were tring to proceed to kafue round-about, downtown lusaka, to hold their planned rally in defiance of a police order cancelling their earlier permit. jere said that the arrested students are now being held at lusaka's edwin imboela stadium. he assured the nation that law and order will be retained as the police throughout the country are on guard against any possible riots."

"Riot policemen opened fire today on student demonstrators, killing one and critically wounding another, a police spokesman said. It was the first violent confrontation between the police and students since democratic elections in November ended three decades of authoritarian one-party rule in Zambia. The police spokesman, Bartholomew Jere, said eight officers were being held for questioning. About 2,000 demonstrators had gathered outside a magistrate's court."  "About 2,000 demonstrators had gathered outside a magistrate's court on the second day of a class boycott to protest the court appearance of 144 classmates charged with taking part in an illegal march Sunday, the spokesman said."

"Thousands of unemployed youths fought pitched battles with police and looted several shops in the capital Lusaka today, protesting government economic policy. Riot police fired teargas and shot into the air to disperse the rioters. A police spokesman said at least 75 people were arrested. Business in the capital ground to a halt as tens of thousands of panicked people fled the city center. Trouble started when police officers from the Lusaka local authority tried to close down hundreds of illegal vendors in the sprawling Soweto market near the city center."

"more than 500 zambian students of lusaka-based evelyn hone college, who gathered at the ministry of science, technology and vocational training to protest bad conditions in their campus, were arrested by the police today. the students marched from their college to the ministry to seek audience with the minister over problems at the college."

"Sixteen blind people were arrested after they ran amok breaking windows and doors and beating up workers at the Zambia Council for the Handicapped (ZCH) here, it was reported Wednesday. According to the Times of Zambia, about 100 blind people demanding payment for a rehabilitation project for disabled people attacked the workers with walking sticks and iron bars as their guides helped them to wave the weapons."

"hundreds of street vendors ran riot in northern zambian city of ndola on tuesday when the police tried to evict them from the city center, "times of zambia" reported today. the riot erupted when the police seized fresh fish from vendors in a bus stop in the downtown area as a measure to evict them from the street. rioting vendors stoned cars on the street, looted shops and set makeshift stalls on fire. all shops were closed and the streets were sealed in the affected area."

"over 400 students from the chipata teacher training college in zambia's eastern province this morning marched to the provincial education office in chipata to protest poor diet and filthy conditions at the college. the students, who formerly wanted to see the provincial permanent secretary, were intercepted by the police on the way and deviated to the provincial education office, according to a report from chipata, the provincial capital."

"hundreds of zambian civil servants from various government departments today held a rally before the ministry of finance here to demonstrate their resolve to go on a strike scheduled for march 3. operations of the ministry came to a partial standstill during the day as the rally lasted from the morning to the afternoon."

"Calm returned to Chingola on Wednesday, after thousands of residents rioted on Tuesday to protest the high crime rate in the Zambian copper mining town in the Copperbelt Province. Copperbelt Police Chief, Martin Nasilele said on Wednesday that Chingola which had been rocked by sporadic gunfire throughout Tuesday as policemen fought the rioters was quiet on Wednesday morning. The riot in which thousands of residents fought pitched street battles with police was sparked off by the shooting to death of a 22-year-old man in the early hours of Tuesday by suspected armed bandits."

"Recent student protests and a walk-out by opposition parliamentarians last Friday, seem to have convinced the Zambian government not to push ahead with the controversial bills to re-name the University of Zambia and the Lusaka International Airport."  "Two weeks ago, students at the University of Zambia rioted after police denied them authorisation to march to parlimentary buildings to petition against government's intention to rename the campus after a fallen national hero."

"University of Zambia students yesterday barricaded the entrance to the campus demanding immediate payment of the promised K90,000 meal allowances. The students, who were chanting anti-MMD slogans, blocked the main entrance with huge boulders and tree trunks and for nearly five hours turned the campus into a no-go-fortress. They stoned any cars that tried to drive into the campus."

Protester Group Identity: supporters of the opposition United National Independence Party
Notes: "Zambian police Thursday shot in the air and fired teargas to disperse supporters of the opposition United National Independence Party (UNIP) outside a court trying senior UNIP members on charges of treason."  "The crowd responded angrily after magistrate Francis Nsokolo ruled that he could not summon the director of public prosecutions to appear before him to explain why the case is being delayed, as it was improper."

"Zambia's largest university was ordered closed after two days of riots. Police using tear gas and billy clubs broke up a planned march on the presidential palace in Lusaka by students who seek reform of the country's voter-registration policies. They also intended to ask President Frederick Chiluba to reopen dialogue with seven opposition parties. Those parties are boycotting next week's elections because the constitution bars some of their candidates from competing. At least 17 people were injured in the rioting."  "on monday hundreds of riot police surrounded the university and fired teargas canisters to block the rampaging students from marching to the state house where they wanted president f. chiluba to, among other things, ''assure'' them of peace after this year's general elections."

"A Zambian opposition alliance Saturday staged a peaceful demonstration here in its bid to force the newly re-elected government of President Fredrick Chiluba out of office. Some 4,000 supporters of former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), the Liberal Progressive Front (LPF) and six other small parties that form the alliance took part in the protest march along the city's busy Independence Avenue."

"HE UNITED National Independence Party (UNIP) today held an unusual demonstration which attracted about 500 supporters and which was in favour of the party's boycott of the November 18 parliamentary and presidential elections. The protest march started at about 11 hours Zambian time after organisers, who arrived at the starting point at about at about 10 hours could not muster enough supporters at first."  "An estimated number of 1,000 demonstrators of Zambia's allied opposition parties, demanding for fresh elections, stunned the onlookers when some of the women demonstrators confronted the police with their nudity. The women, who are members of former President Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), said their action was to press President Frederick Chiluba, who won a second-term of office in November, to call for fresh elections."

" Students at the Lusaka campus of the University of Zambia boycotted classes Monday, in protest against the non-payment of their book allowances by the government. Dozens of riot police kept vigil outside the campus early Monday after students hurled stones at vehicles along the Great East Road in the capital, Lusaka. Police have blocked the main entrance to the campus and arrested eight students."

"On Saturday, April 12, hundreds of journalists in Lusaka went on a demonstration against government's plans to legislate for a Media Council, reports the Zambia Independent Media Association (ZIMA/MISA-Zambia). The demonstration aimed at raising public awareness about the impact of the proposed Media Council of Zambia (MCZ) on the public's right to freedom of expression."

Protester Group Identity: former workers of the liquidated Lima Bank
Notes: "Scores of former workers of the liquidated Lima Bank, a lending institution for farmers, recently staged a protest at the Ministry of Agriculture to demand payment of their terminal benefits. The workers, who were joined by their wives and children., demanded that they be paid their dues promptly because they and their families have been starving since the firm was closed about a month ago."

"ore than 1,000 Lusaka City Council (LCC) unionised workers downed tools yesterday, each demanding K30,000 arrears from the K1.5bn released by the Ministry of Local Government and Housing. The workers were retrenched from the Chitakale Tea Estate, about 90 kilometres (50 miles) south of the commercial capital Blantyre in June and claim the state-run business owed them some 90,000 dollars.

Parliament reconvened Tuesday under heavy security a day after a violent protest against moves to impeach President Bingu wa Mutharika. Hundreds of the president's supporters besieged Parliament on Monday, stoning vehicles belonging to opposition lawmakers. Extra armed police were deployed Tuesday along approaches to New State House, where lawmakers meet in the capital, Lilongwe, police spokesman Willie Mwaluka said.

Vendor Mabvuto Khaiya told AFP the protestors, estimated to number 10,000, had marched to open ground outside Kamuzu Stadium to "pray to God so that the government should rescind its decision to evict us from the streets."

Police smashed stalls and fired tear gas Wednesday to disperse rioting street vendors who were resisting government attempts to evict them. It was the second day of clashes this week in Malawi's commercial capital, Blantyre, as police enforced a Tuesday deadline to move the vendors to designated flea markets.

Up to 10,000 villagers were mobilised by Malawian President Bingu wa Mutharika's party here Tuesday to pressure an opposition-dominated parliament to stop blocking a budget vote. The villagers -- hundreds of whom walked barefoot and wore party colours -- were trucked in from remote parts of the densely-populated south. They held up placards lambasting the opposition and chanted anti-opposition slogans.

Protester Group Identity: National Voices on The Budget civil group
Notes: Malawian rights activists on Tuesday staged a peaceful march in a bid to pressurise the opposition to drop demands to expel 41 lawmakers and instead debate the budget of the impoverished country. It follows weeks of political wrangling as Malawi's powerful opposition continues to demand that parliamentarians who switched allegiance to President Bingu wa Mutharika be expelled before the budget is debated.

Meanwhile, scores of riot police foiled a solidarity march organised by about 400 of Muluzi's supporters. The police came in full force to nip in the bud the demonstrations, which had just started from the headquarters of his United Democratic Front. The marchers carried placards, some which read "Free Muluzi now, Bingu is a dictator."

More than 100 villagers in Malawi demanded Thursday more compensation from the government for land on which US pop star Madonna  is building a girls academy. Madonna,  who has adopted two children from Malawi, led a groundbreaking ceremony last week for the school being built on the outskirts of the administrative capital Lilongwe.

More than 100 members of a Christian sect barricaded themselves in an abandoned building in southern Malawi over their refusal to give their children the measles vaccine. Members of Seventh Day Apostolic Church say their doctrine forbids them from taking medication when they fall sick.

Nationwide protests began today under tight security, with hundreds of demonstrators in Malawi's two main cities gathering to rally against high fuel and food prices and increasing crackdowns by the government of Malawian President Bingu wa Mutharika. In the capital city of Lilongwe, and in the commercial city of Blantyre, hundreds of young men and women gathered at rally points, dressed in red, and began to march in small groups through the cities chanting "Bingu leave, Bingu leave." The protests began in the early morning hours, after a day of intimidation by young pro-government thugs prowling the city with machetes on Tuesday, and after a pro-government citizens group successfully lobbied for an injunction against civil society and opposition groups participating in the demonstrations.

Around one thousand people marched in cities across Malawi Thursday against tough government reforms, challenging the nine-month-old government of President Joyce Banda. Authorities deployed 3,000 police on the streets of major cities ahead of the march, fearing a repeat of nationwide rioting and looting in 2011 that left 19 people dead.

Police in Malawi on Thursday used tear gas to disperse school pupils marching against a public workers strike, police said. "Police fired tear gas to bring peace," Nicholas Gondwa told AFP. The police said the they were forced to fire tear gas at the school pupils' protest because it had been hijacked by hooligans.

The arrest of the "coup plotters" sent shock waves through Malawi, fuelling anger at Banda's government, which has been much feted by the international community. Malawi police fired teargas at around 500 people protesting the arrests outside police headquarters in Blantyre, but the protesters failed to disperse and retaliated by throwing stones. Another group of protesters, estimated to be in the thousands, gathered nearby, blocking the main highway to the capital Lilongwe with boulders and branches. Banada called an emergency cabinet meeting to discuss the crisis.

Malawians marched on the streets of Blantyre in anger at their government on Thursday after a damning audit revealed that corrupt officials had stolen over $30 million from state coffers. The protest organised by non-governmental organisations attracted hundreds of street vendors, activists, lawyers and housewives. "It hurts to see all those monies stolen from the government when hospitals lack medicine, when pupils learn under the trees, when so many social amenities are not available," said 53-year-old Elizabeth Tambala, who hawks doughnuts on the streets of Blantyre. A much-awaited report by British auditors -- commissioned by President Joyce Banda  -- showed this week that $30 million (22 million euros) was stolen in six months from April to September in 2013, her second year in office. That equates to more than one percent of GDP, in one of the world's poorest countries where life expectancy is just 54 years. Protest organisers on Thursday handed a petition to a senior city official for Banda who is away in Nigeria.  Among their demands, they want government to name all suspects involved in the so-called Cashgate scandal, which first broke last year. The marchers walked under police escort in drizzling rain, carrying placards and chanting songs that ridiculed the government. Mhone said another of their demands was that parliament should urgently convene within two weeks to debate the Cashgate scandal.

In the commercial capital Blantyre, thousands of people queued in chilly morning temperatures at a major polling station where voting finally began four hours late. Impatient residents sang and shouted their discontent. Around 50 angry youths staged an impromptu mini-protest carrying branches and chanting anti-government slogans.

Notes: One person was killed Friday when police clashed with protesters demanding a recount of Malawi's disputed presidential elections, as the country nervously awaited a court decision on last week's vote. In the southeastern town of Mangochi, police fired teargas and rubber bullets at more than a hundred demonstrators who claimed that the election was rigged, witnesses said. A teenager was "killed by a teargas cannister, which exploded in his hands as he was trying to throw it back at us," Mangochi police officer Elijah Kachikuwo told AFP. Many of the protesters in Mangochi were members of the People's Party of President Joyce Banda, who was trailing in third place in early results from the election. Others were from the Malawi Congress Party (MCP), whose candidate Lazarus Chakwera was in second place and has asked the court to order a recount. Demonstrators in the Mangochi district, in the southern part of Malawi, smashed shop windows and burned tyres along the road, prompting police to fire tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse them. "In the ensuing fracas one person has been shot dead as police tried to defend themselves after being overpowered by angry protesters," police officer Elijah Kachikuwo told Reuters.

BLANTYRE, Malawi (AP) - About 500 schoolchildren broke classroom windows and damaged cars to protest a strike by their teachers in Malawi's commercial capital, Blantyre, on Wednesday. The students, aged between six and 12, smashed at least 40 cars, according to police. "We're not learning," the pupils chanted in the local Chichewa language as they blocked one of the city's main roads with rocks and tree branches. "We want the president to know we are angry," said Thoko, a 12-year-old student, who would not give her last name for fear of retribution. "He must pay our teachers so that we can go back to class." Dressed in their school uniforms, the students marched toward President Peter Mutharika's official home in the city. Mutharika was away, attending a graduation ceremony at the University of Malawi. Police fired tear gas to disperse the children but none of them were injured according to police.

Malawi leader Peter Mutharika has ordered that public university fees must be reduced by 50,000 Malawi Kwacha ($69) across the board. The students'Â protestsÂ in Malawi come months after their counterparts in South Africa staged nationwideÂ protests.

On Wednesday, pupils mostly from primary schools in Lilongwe took to the streets in hundreds, marching and singing against the delay in addressing their teachers' concerns which they said was affecting the pupils'schooling. TheÂ protestÂ was generally peaceful except for a few incidents where the children blocked the traffic in some roads in the city and threw debris to passing cars, forcing the Malawi Police Service to intervene to disperse the protesters with teargas.

Black students and their parents demanded nullification of high school exams that 58 percent of them failed, and they urged the failing youths to re-enroll in defiance of government rules. The steps were endorsed at a meeting of more than 1,000 people, called to focus on a crisis in black education. Nationally, only 42 percent of more than 190,000 black high school seniors passed standardized exams last year, compared to more than 95 percent of white students.

About 1,200 black rail workers marched through central Cape Town protesting the killing of at least six railwaymen Tuesday, when strikers and non-strikers clashed on a station platform in Germiston, near Johannesburg. Some trade unionists said police did not try to stop Tuesday's clash at Germiston.

Rumours that Mike Gatting's English cricketers had arrived in South Africa secretly overnight led to an immediate demonstration yesterday outside a leading hotel in the city centre here. After an hour the protesters dispersed peacefully when they learned that the Englishmen were not in the country. The incident was a forerunner of what Gatting's players can expect when they arrive here nearer the weekend. It involved about 100 protesters representing the Pan Africanist Movement, a black political group, which is affiliated to the banned Pan Africanist Congress. Most of the demonstrators carried banners which demanded land rights as well as objecting to the cricket tour.

Two hours before Mike Gatting's team of English cricketers had even arrived yesterday, the South African police used Alsatian dogs and tear gas to disperse about 150 anti-apartheid demonstrators outside the main building at Jan Smuts airport outside Johannesburg. This early violence of the sort that the South African cricket authorities had dreaded and the protesters had hoped to avoid must surely have put the future of the tour in immediate jeopardy. Mrs Winnie Mandela, the wife of the jailed African National Congress leader, was among the protesters who arrived in buses at the airport. The protesters were given one minute to disperse, but almost immediately, eye witnesses said, the tear gas sprays were fired at them and they were harassed by the dogs and hit by batons.

Mr. Cohen summarized his impressions in a statement saying he thought both the Government and the anti-apartheid movement were making commitments to negotiations. Hours before he spoke, the police opened fire on a crowd in a black township, killing two people and wounding two others after a crowd of about 5,000 gathered outside the mining town of Carletonville, 50 miles southwest of Johannesburg, to protest the death of a 17-year-old black youth. According to a police report, police fired tear gas and birdshot at demonstrators, who were throwing stones at them and their cars after attending a rally to protest the death in police custody last week of a 16-year-old black. Two men were killed and at least three others wounded, the report said.

Angry clashes broke out today between police and demonstrators in a black township near here, and anti-apartheid violence continued in black residential areas elsewhere, underscoring the uncertainty that has overtaken South Africa in the wake of measures announced on Friday by President F.W. de Klerk. The day's events marked an apparent shift in the national mood. The euphoria that swept the country after Mr. de Klerk told Parliament that the Government had lifted bans on the African National Congress and other leading anti-apartheid groups gave way to concern on the part of many blacks and whites that the Government's program might prove too limited to draw its black opponents into the negotiations over the country's future. As maneuvering continued over terms set by the Congress and its leaders for entering political talks, an anti-apartheid protest erupted into violence in Tembisa, one of the biggest black townships that ring Johannesburg. All day, and into the night, heavily armed police officers fired tear gas canisters into crowds of young blacks protesting, among other things, Mr. de Klerk's failure to include some Tembisa residents in the amnesty he declared for banned and restricted persons in his speech to Parliament. The violence in Tembisa came as gangs of black youths threw stones, set fire to tires and mounted an arson attack on the home of Tembisa's Mayor. Doctors at a local hospital said that at least 18 blacks were injured, including an 8-month-old infant. Given how long the clashes between protesters and police occurred, as well as the policeÈs response, this protest is believed to have at least 100 participants.

Tens of thousands of blacks joined protest marches in South Africa yesterday as police reported the deaths of 13 more people in violence following the release of Mr Nelson Mandela. The state-run South African Broadcasting Corporation estimated that 100 blacks have died since Mr Mandela was released on Sunday. Four of yesterday's deaths occurred in two black townships in Natal province, while nine died in KwaNobuhle, near Uitenhage in the Cape province. This rising violence, in Natal especially, is casting a dark and growing shadow over the land. About 3,000 blacks have already died in the savage fighting, and well over 100,000 have been made homeless. Feelings run high, and the story you get depends on who you listen to.

About 15,000 people, one of the largest crowds to attend any white political gathering in South Africa in years, turned out today for a right-wing rally in protest against the Government's actions in freeing Nelson Mandela and legalizing the African National Congress. The rally was called by the opposition Conservative Party, which has vowed to arouse white anger against President F. W. de Klerk and to unseat him at the next election, or at least to defeat any plan he may bring forward in a referendum to transfer a share of power to blacks. Although the rally was peaceful, with only a few police officers on hand at the edges of the crowd, the mood was one of bitterness and determination, as Mr. Treurnicht expressed it, to see that ''the wagon wheel'' of Afrikaner history rolls forward and crushes any attempt to deprive whites of their right to rule themselves. Thousands of Afrikaners brought traffic in Pretoria to a standstill yesterday with a huge demonstration denouncing President de Klerk, and vowing to begin their own ''freedom struggle''. Official permission had been granted for the demonstration, and police lining the street and observing the proceedings from side-streets did not intervene.

About 340 prisoners at Robben Island Prison off Cape Town began a hunger strike yesterday. Outside Parliament in Cape Town, about 30 relatives of prisoners demonstrated in conjunction with the strike. The prisoners say they should be released because the groups to which they belong are now legal. The South African Government said it will not free prisoners convicted of violent crimes. Several hundred South African political prisoners have begun a hunger strike to force President F. W. de Klerk to release them under a general amnesty that could strengthen the negotiating position of the African National Congress. The hunger strike was started a week ago by 343 prisoners at Robben Island, the country's highest-security prison, and has spread since to include some convicts elsewhere, including several whites jailed in Pretoria. In a rare display of political unity, the strikers include members of the African National Congress, the rival Pan-Africanist Congress and the Black Consciousness Movement. In a statement said to have been smuggled from Robben Island, the hunger strikers defined as political prisoners ''all incarcerated people who have engaged themselves in various ways in the struggle against the system of apartheid, its various structures and forces of reaction whose role is to maintain and sustain the apartheid system.''

Rioting spread yesterday from Ciskei to Bophuthatswana, where seven people were reported killed and hundreds wounded in clashes with territorial security forces firing live ammunition and tear gas from armoured vehicles. President de Klerk said on state television last night that troops would be sent to Bophuthatswana if necessary, in consultation with its government. He was determined to pursue his liberal reforms, but they required stability, and steps would be taken to prevent the country from sliding into anarchy and chaos. As in Ciskei, where an army officer who staged a coup last weekend is calling for reintegration in South Africa, the demonstrators in Bophuthatswana were demanding an end to their illusory independence. The violence flared after an estimated 50,000 people converged on a magistrate's court in Garankuwa township, near Pretoria, to demand the immediate resignation of Mr Mangope. Within minutes of Bophuthatswana security forces arriving on the scene, pitched battles broke out and spread throughout the township.  The latest outburst of violence occurred yesterday here in GaRankuwa, A crowd of as many as 120,000 demonstrators complaining about living conditions tried to deliver their grievances to a magistrate and clashed with homeland police. At least seven people were killed. The GaRankuwa hospital reported today that it had treated 350 injured people, most of them for gunshot wounds. Many protests are against electricity and water rates, house rents and education issues that have sent hundreds of thousands of blacks into the streets to march on local town halls or government offices in scores of townships. But some marches have degenerated into violence as youthful bands heading home begin throwing rocks at the police.

The unrest is spreading to black townships within South Africa, notably Katlehong on the East Rand and Khutsong in the western Transvaal. At least 28 people were injured in Katlehong yesterday when riot police fired shotguns to disperse thousands of residents demanding lower rents and electricity tariffs.

The South African police opened fire today on black anti-apartheid and hospital workers reported that eight people were killed and hundreds wounded. The police said they could not confirm any deaths in the clash in the black township of Sebokeng, south of Johannesburg, where thousands of residents had taken to the streets to protest high rents and racially segregated housing. Witnesses said the police opened fire with rubber bullets and shotguns after the protest march was declared illegal under South Africa's three-year-old state of emergency. Bloodstained protesters were guarding roadblocks, they said, as men in civilian clothes drove through the township in unmarked cars shooting at random. Most of the casualties were in Sebokeng, south of the Johannesburg, which resembled a battlefield after police opened fire with shotguns on tens of thousands of people protesting against high rents and racially segregated town councils. The order to fire was given by senior officers at the scene when the crowd ignored a judicial ban on the demonstration. Witnesses said the crowd fled in panic when the police opened fire, and shortly afterwards the local police station was pelted with stones and the town council offices were set on fire. A hospital employee identified one of the dead as a girl, aged 14, and said hundreds had been wounded by shotgun fire. Many, the employee said, had been shot in the back. On Monday, the police in Sebokeng, a black township 50 miles south of Johannesburg, fired tear gas, shotgun and rubber bullets to disperse a crowd of thousands who had gathered to deliver a petition complaining about living conditions in their township and demanding the resignation of municipal council. A local magistrate had previously denied permission for the march.

Today, thousands of postal, rail and municipal employees, including 200 suspended workers from the Johannesburg prison, marched here and in Pretoria to protest government plans to turn many state-run services over to the private sector. The socialist-oriented black unions oppose the plan on ideological grounds and also fear it will mean loss of jobs. In Pretoria, police broke up the march in the city center using dogs and tear gas and arrested 39 union members. The march here took place without incident.

In the Orange Free State yesterday, police shot dead four boys, said by activists to be aged under 16, and wounded at least one person in a black township near Viljoenskroon. A police spokesman said the police had used shotguns and rubber bullets after a crowd ignored warnings to disperse and threw stones at a police patrol. Black anti-apartheid campaigners in Rammulotsi township in the Orange Free State said the police opened fire on a peaceful demonstrtion, killing four youths and wounding 19. Local black anti-apartheid campaigners, reached by telephone in nearby Kroonstad, said that about 400 youths, mainly of high school age, were marching peacefully, singing and chanting, when police officers in a van pulled across their path, got out and opened fire without warning. Four victims died at the scene after the police opened fire on a crowd that had gathered to demand the resignation of the township's council. A fifth person died at a nearby hospital.

Riots shook the black township of Rammulotsi in the Orange Free State today after five youths were shot to death by the police on Thursday. In response, youths today set fire to at least two houses and a funeral home owned by two of the township councilors. The police guarded the property of five other councilors. The police rode through the shabby township in an armored car, chasing rioters and firing tear gas. The youths emerged from behind rows of small houses to pelt the armored car ineffectually with rocks and stones. Police and hundreds of youth clashed throughout the day today in this Orange Free State township outside of Viljoenskroon, 125 miles southwest of Johannesburg. Youth threw stones at two police armored cars that patroled the streets. Occasionally, white and black policemen emerged from the "Hippos," as they are known, to shoot tear-gas canisters and rubber bullets to disperse the crowds. But today no shotguns were used by police, local residents said.

Three blacks were killed today and scores of others were injured in a confrontation with police in Thabong township near the racially tense mining town of Welkom, according to police, hospital and other sources there. Police fired on a crowd emerging from a public meeting where a decision had been made to end a nearly two-week-old black boycott of white businesses in Welkom, according to the first sketchy reports of the incident. It was not immediately clear why police had fired on the crowd, but the South African Press Association (SAPA) reported that stones had been thrown and property set on fire in the township. Welkom hospital officials said 12 other blacks had been admitted with birdshot or rubber bullet wounds. The Government announcement came a day after an eruption of violence between blacks and police officers in Thabong, a township near the mining town of Welkom in the Orange Free State. The toll in that incident, in which the police fired on a crowd of black protesters, reached 7 dead and 40 wounded today. The violence erupted in Thabong on Sunday, shortly after a community meeting decided to suspend a black boycott of white businesses in the adjacent gold-mining town of Welkom. As the rally dispersed, about 1,000 miners and 500 youths formed a procession, apparently intending to march to the town. Police allowed the workers to catch transport to mine hostels, but ordered the youths back into the township. Angered by the decision to lift the boycott and by police action, the youths began attacking police vehicles with stones and petrol bombs. A police spokesman said tear gas, rubber bullets and birdshot were fired at mobs which set fire to buildings and built roadblocks of burning tyres.

South African proponents of apartheid held the largest gathering of whites in nearly three decades today and heard Conservative Party leader Andries Treurnicht call for the ouster of President Frederik W. de Klerk and the establishment of an all-white state. Treurnicht warned de Klerk that South African conservatives are not about to accept black majority rule "without bitter struggle" and demanded recognition for "our right to our own territory and the right to rule ourselves." The rally, held beneath the imposing Afrikaner Voortrekker Monument on a knoll outside Pretoria, drew an estimated 60,000 right-wing and conservative whites strongly opposed to de Klerk's policies of legalizing the African National Congress and other anti-apartheid groups and opening negotiations with them for an end to the apartheid policies of racial segregation and white domination. Massed below the Voortrekker Monument, which marks the Boer trek northward from the British-ruled Cape Colony in the 1830s, the demonstrators were asked by one speaker whether they wanted de Klerk to negotiate on their behalf. "No, no, no, no," they shouted back. The gathering, attended by many extended white families, from grandparents to small babies in carriages, was a measure of the considerable white resistance de Klerk is certain to face as he presses forward with his announced plans to phase out apartheid legislation and pursue talks with black leaders.

Tonight, the police also reported that tear gas and rubber bullets were used to disperse 1,000 blacks in the township of Mamelodi east of Pretoria. The police said the crowd had been burning vehicles, setting fire to trash and throwing firebombs and stones. A police spokesman said he had no information about any injuries. However, Moses Chikane, an official of the United Democratic Front, said that more than 100 people were injured in the confrontation with police, who he said surrounded a soccer stadium where a public meeting was held to discuss a rent boycott. Mr. Chikane charged that the police had blocked the main entrance to the stadium and then fired tear gas into the crowd. He said the United Democratic Front would formally protest the incident to Mr. Vlok. The South African Press Association quoted a spokeswoman for two local hospitals as confirming that more than 100 people had been admitted for treatment.

Riot police attempting to arrest two protesters yesterday during clashes that took at least 30 lives in Port Elizabeth, in a neighborhood set aside by apartheid legislation for persons of mixed racial descent. AT LEAST 33 people have been killed and more than 100 injured in riots sweeping through Coloured areas of Port Elizabeth in South Africa for the past three days, according to police figures yesterday. One of the dead was a baby shot in its mother's lap. Rampaging mobs, fuelled on looted drink, have set fire to entire blocks of Indian and Chinese-owned shops in the city's northern areas. The disturbances have caused millions of pounds of damage to shops, factories and schools, the government said. The rioters have proclaimed one district, the Chatty area, an ''ANC-liberated zone'', but the ANC strongly denied that it was involved. The violence has been triggered by rent increases and a critical housing shortage in an area of high unemployment. In Port Elizabeth, police said 32 shops, six houses, two factories, a church, three schools and 41 police vehicles had been destroyed by fire as hundreds of protesters and rioters set up blazing barricades, stoned police and drew police and army fire. Witnesses contacted by telephone said many of the properties damaged or destroyed had been linked to Mr. Hendrickse's Labor Party, accused by its critics of collaborating with apartheid by participating in the segregated three-chamber Parliament. Rioting spread from Port Elizabeth to neighboring Uitenhage yesterday, and South African police said 42 people had been killed since Monday. Maj. Bill Dennis said police and soldiers worked through the night to bring rioting under control in mixed-race, or Colored, areas of Port Elizabeth, a coastal city in eastern Cape Province. But he said the violence spread to the neighboring car-making town of Uitenhage, about 20 miles away, where black and Colored crowds burned and looted shops.

Andre Erasmus peered down the broad, straight road outside his tin-roofed home in a whites-only suburb here and gazed with a baleful eye on the advance of 15,000 black protest marchers, chanting through the dust clouds raised by many stamping feet. The unprecedented march by blacks through white suburbs in this conservative town south of Johannesburg, he said, shows that ''the A.N.C. is winning'' in its campaign to end apartheid. It was the first time white officials had permitted blacks to enter Vereeniging to make a legal protest, he said, and that in itself was a victory. Although they did not meet in today's march, called to protest killings in Sebokeng township near here, both men seemed to say that whatever else has happened since the freeing of the congress leader Nelson Mandela from prison in February, old certainties are gone beyond recall.
