And bolder political demonstrations by blacks, like today's march in Vereeniging, seem to strengthen uncertainty and hatred of blacks among relatively low-income whites like Mr. Erasmus who stand to lose most from black advance and who question Mr. de Klerk's avowed commitment to a new political order.

Police used birdshot, batons and tear gas to disperse student marches against violence in black townships. Three blacks died in new fighting, raising the toll to 518 in less than three weeks. Given the police response and the widespread violence these students were marching against, this protest is believed to have at least 100 participants.

Meanwhile, the fragile calm in the townships since the police and army launched its Operation Iron Fist last week is being threatened by the 9pm to 4am curfew that comes into operation tomorrow. About 3,000 people marched in Soweto on Saturday, and handed a protest note to the mayor warning that they would defy the curfew. But if the townships are beginning gradually to return to normality, it means the delicate negotiation process has survived its sternest test so far.

In Pretoria, the Conservative Party, which opposes the dismantling of apartheid, gathered several thousand white supporters for a march to the Union Buildings, where Mr. de Klerk's offices are situated, to deliver a petition contending that he had no mandate to dismantle white minority rule. They demanded that he call a new election for white voters. The Conservative Party contends that Mr. de Klerk has betrayed whites, and particularly Afrikaners, by meeting with the African National Congress, which was banned for 30 years. If apartheid cannot be maintained, the Conservatives want the country partitioned into separate homelands for whites and blacks.

In Soweto, nearly 50 miles to the south, several thousand black supporters of the Pan-Africanist Congress, which regards whites as "settlers" who must return the land to its original inhabitants, gathered in a soccer stadium for the funeral of their leader, Zephania Mothopeng. He died of cancer Oct. 23 at the age of 77. The Pan-Africanist Congress has accused the African National Congress of selling out the country's black majority by agreeing to talk to the Government. It says white minority rule can be toppled only by armed struggle, which the African National Congress suspended three months ago.

South African police clashed with anti-apartheid activists for three hours here today as a campaign to force the collapse of all black township councils accelerated with marches and rallies around the country. Riot police and army reinforcements, seeking to disperse groups of demonstrators, opened fire on them repeatedly with birdshot, tear gas and rubber bullets, and also used dogs. Protesters pelted police with bottles, stones and chunks of cement from buildings in a four-block downtown area. Police said 15 people were injured, six of them seriously from gunshot wounds, in the worst outbreak of violence in the city since Feb. 2, the day President Frederik W. de Klerk announced the legalization of all anti-apartheid groups. One person thought to have been caught up in the confrontation died in the hospital, police said. The street violence here was touched off by a local magistrate's last-minute rejection of a march request after the organizers had reportedly obtained permission from the Johannesburg town council and traffic police. Given policy response and the amount of damage that the protesters were able to cause, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

A JUDGE granted an urgent application by the Pretoria town council yesterday to end an occupation of the South African capital by an estimated 10,000 white farmers. The judge was ferried from his home by motorcycle because the farmers had barricaded the city centre. The farmers, however, vowed to continue their protest. Police said they had arrested 120 farmers but most of them were warned and released. The farmers had invaded Pretoria with their tractors, trailers and pick-up trucks to protest about the government's perceived lack of interest in their plight. Farmers' debt in South Africa totals more than 15 billion rands (Pounds 3 billion). The farmers maintain their distress is made worse by high interest rates, a poor return on production, high input costs and, most important, disquiet over the government's proposed revision of the Land Act, which will enable blacks to buy farms in hitherto white areas. The 10,000 farmers who brought chaos to Pretoria for 24 hours by blocking streets with tractors and lorries in a protest at what they see as government indifference to their economic situation trekked back to their farms yesterday in heavy rain. The end came after the city council was awarded a supreme court injunction declaring their presence in the city illegal, after the judge was taken to court on the back of a motorcycle because of the traffic jams.

The speech by Mr. de Klerk today lent further momentum to a process that the President began at the opening of Parliament last year, when the African National Congress and other anti-apartheid organizations were legalized and Mr. de Klerk announced his Government's intention to release the congress's leader, Nelson Mandela. Mr. Mandela walked out of a prison farm nine days later. "In the short span of a single year," Mr. de Klerk said today, "substantial progress was made. The Government is determined to build on the foundations laid purposefully, efficiently and with due speed. As he spoke, the African National Congress, conducted mass marches in Cape Town, Johannesburg, Pretoria and some other cities to put pressure on the Government in advance of looming but as yet undefined Constitutinal talks. The anti-apartheid group also sought to underscore the reality that blacks remain excluded from Parliament and from institutional political life. In Cape Town, Walter Sisulu, a senior leader of the congress, addressed a crowd of perhaps 15,000 people who had gathered outside City Hall.

RIGHT-WING extremists, angered by the detention of fellow activists, have clashed with police in the biggest confrontation of its kind since the South African government began dismantling apartheid a year ago. Several hundred khaki-clad demonstrators broke through police cordons round Pretoria's central prison on Tuesday night, before being forced back by tear gas. At least one shot was fired, but no serious injuries were reported and there were no arrests. Eugene Terre Blanche, the leader of the Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB), said ''all hell would break loose'' if 40 right-wing activists, detained for acts of political violence, were not released. He made the threat after his supporters had been prevented from delivering a television set to the prisoners. Police said permission had been granted for a protest rally, but they had stopped an illegal march on the prison.

Miss Marcus said in a telephone interview that the congress would probably reserve decision on whether to break off talks until a second deadline of May 9, by when it has called on the Government to stop the current factional violence. The congress has again threatened to stop talking to the Government about the country's future unless Mr. de Klerk meets a number of its demands. These include dismissing two Cabinet ministers who supervise the security forces, which the congress accuses of abetting the violence. The congress has also demanded an end to all politically related trials, but Miss Marcus said more than 200 political trials were still under way, affecting 1,200 or more defendants. "You're not actually emptying the prisons," she asserted. "You're putting more in." The expiration of today's deadline ushered in a new wave of nationwide protests by members of the African National Congress and its allies that is expected to be conspicuous in May Day rallies on Wednesday. More than 150 protesters were reported arrested by this evening; some were protesting the continuing incarceration of political prisoners. This protest is recorded as in the 100s because of how many people nationwide who were arrested.  Not enough information was given to record it as more than that.

Nearly 200 jailed South Africans have gone on a hunger strike to press their case that they are political prisoners who should have been released under an agreement between the African National Congress and the government. Several human rights groups have accused prison authorities of mistreating the hunger strikers. They said the government on Wednesday removed the last 28 political prisoners from Robben Island and took them to Pollsmoor Prison on the mainland. Lawyers say that more than 100 prisoners, convicted of what they regard as politically related offences, are refusing food. The mass hunger strike began on May 1 and the health of some of the strikers is said to be precarious. The detainees are demanding freedom under an agreement between Pretoria and the African National Congress. President de Klerk said he was satisfied that all prisoners who clearly qualified for political status had been released, but officials were still sifting through petitions. Although technically a strike, this was included as a protest due to the coordinated effort and the clear political message to the government.  Seven prisoners were freed yesterday on the orders of Mr de Kl erk as the government moved to neutralise a hunger strike campaign by dozens of inmates claiming their freedom as political prisoners. However, the rapid deterioration in the hunger strikers' health was clearly a factor. Nelson Mandela, the ANC deputy president, and Archbishop Desmond Tutu said that the government had accepted that if a hunger striker died it would seriously jeopardise the chances of political negotiations.

Outdoor gatherings would be prohibited for two weeks, Mr. Vlok's statement said, with exceptions for church and sports events and funerals. Recent political rallies held by the Inkatha Freedom Party have become catalysts for bloodshed. Mr. Vlok's statement said nothing about banning weapons, including traditional spears, clubs and other arms brandished by Inkatha supporters. The issue of eliminating such weapons figured prominently in talks that President de Klerk held yesterday with the Inkatha leader, Chief Mangosuthu Gatsha Buthelezi. The Government mounted a similar crackdown last September after violence became intense, but the effort only temporarily stopped the killing. Today, hundreds of members of the women's and youth leagues of the congress mounted demonstrations and sit-ins to call attention to the issue. At least 155 people were reported arrested. In its April 5 ultimatum, the African National Congress set these conditions: that Mr. Vlok and Defense Minister Magnus Malan be dismissed; that weapons be banned at public rallies and marches; that counterinsurgency units be dismantled; that police officers involved in two fatal confrontations be suspended; that police officers assigned to crowd control not be issued live ammunition; that single-sex migrant workers' hostels, which have been flashpoints for violence, be phased out; and that an independent commission of inquiry be established to investigate complaints of misconduct by the security forces.

Winnie Mandela, the wife of the African National Congress leader Nelson Mandela, was sentenced today to six years in prison in the kidnapping and beating of four young men in Soweto in late 1988. The sentences stunned spectators in the courtroom, some of whom expected Mrs. Mandela to get a suspended sentence. But her lawyer immediately filed an appeal, postponing for months the prospect that Mrs. Mandela will actually go to prison. And there has been speculation that President F. W. de Klerk may yet step in and pardon her in order not to jeopardize proposed negotiations on the nation's future with Mr. Mandela and the African National Congress. Released on a modest bail equivalent to $72, Mrs. Mandela looked defiant as she walked out of the courthouse to cheers from several hundred waiting supporters, some of whom held placards declaring "Stop harassing our mother Winnie Mandela" and "No justice under an unjust government."

Mrs Mandela was arrested for obstruction after an all-night vigil in central Johannesburg over the fate of political prisoners on hunger strike for 22 days. The demonstration was staged by the ANC Women's League. A minibus secured by a heavy chain was used to block off one of the city's main thoroughfares. Fifteen other protesters were also arrested, and taken to police headquarters at John Vorster Square. They were released after appearing before a magistrate, who set a hearing for June 21. Meanwhile, about 200 members of the women's league, led by Albertina Sisulu, the organisation's national vice-president, had been arrested outside police headquarters after staging a protest against Mrs Mandela's arrest. Mr Mandela telephoned President de Klerk, but was told that he was still asleep. Adriaan Vlok, the minister of law and order whom the ANC is demanding should be sacked from the cabinet, said that he would investigate what had happened. When the two groups were released from police headquarters, Mrs Mandela led another march of about 100 supporters back to the scene of her arrest. This time police went into action swiftly and for the first time in a so-called ''unrest'' situation used stun grenades and tear gas to disperse the crowd. Winnie Mandela was arrested twice after scuffles with police during demonstrations demanding the release of hunger-striking political prisoners.  Mandela was released after appearing in court on charges of resisting arrest and obstructing traffic. She was sentenced to six years in prison last week after being convicted in connection with the 1988 abduction and beating of four young men. She is appealing the conviction.

Five people were killed overnight in 30 incidents of black factional fighting and anti-apartheid protests in South African townships, the police said today. Policemen and soldiers patrolling the Johannesburg township of Katlehong shot and killed a man armed with an AK-47 automatic rifle. Three other blacks were killed in the Natal township of Tongaat and in Soweto. Rioting groups shot dead a policeman in the eastern Cape province township of Komga. Three people were arrested. Other incidents of unrest reported across South Africa included police dispersing of anti-Government protesters, stoning of government buildings, and fighting between rival black political groups. Given that this protest is national (with 30 incidents) and involved the deaths of 5 people, this protest is assumed to have at least 100 participants.

MID-TERM exams at East Bank high school in the South African township of Alexandra were disrupted yesterday by political activists, television crews and 200 riot police supported by armoured vehicles and a helicopter. The incident was designed to focus attention on the enduring injustice of the education system, with white schools being closed for lack of pupils while black institutions are overcrowded and ill-equipped. The National Education Co-ordinating Committee, a black community organisation, had intended to transport 300 pupils from the township to occupy a vacant primary school in a white Johannesburg suburb five miles away. The government, while sympathising with black aspirations, ordered the security forces to prevent what it termed illegal seizure of private property. Recently anti-apartheid activists began to force the disparity issue by seeking to occupy an empty white school with 300 black schoolchildren who attend overcrowded and dilapidated schools. The police turned them back.

Hundreds of policemen and white protesters battled with guns and tear gas today when pro-apartheid militants tried to stop President F. W. de Klerk from speaking. At least 2 people were killed and 54 wounded. Pitched battles raged through the main street of this conservative town as members of the Afrikaner Resistance Movement tried to fight their way into the hall where President de Klerk was giving a speech. It was the worst outbreak of violence between white right-wingers and security forces. A minivan carrying blacks along the highway that cuts through the center of town careened out of control into the fighting crowd and flipped on its back. The police said one white militant had been killed by the van. Enraged whites then surrounded it and opened fire, wounding four black passengers. The other person killed was a white protester shot to death by the police, Col. Johan Mostert said, adding that there were unconfirmed reports of at least three other deaths. Six policemen were wounded, three critically, Colonel Mostert said, adding that at least 12 blacks, 9 white protesters and 27 white bystanders were injured. Ventersdorp is the headquarters of an extreme right-wing group known as the Afrikaner Resistance Movement, which opposes Mr. de Klerk's policy of racial liberalization. Hundreds of khaki-clad members waving flags with the group's swastika-like symbol marched toward the hall in theevening as Mr. de Klerk began to speak. Right-wingers then besieged the police station while their leader, Eugene Terre Blanche, negotiated with senior officers. With tension at fever pitch, AWB members spray-painted police vehicles with slogans and deflated their tyres to prevent the police from leaving. The situation was defused when six AWB men who had been arrested were released, pending a court appearance on Monday.

Since the agreement is meant to prevent provocative public displays or actions, and specifically imposes a voluntary ban on the carrying of weapons to meetings, the demonstration today by Inkatha supporters, outside the luxury downtown hotel where the accord was signed, immediately called into question Inkatha's commitment to it. Thousands of supporters of the Zulu-dominated movement and its leader, Chief Mangosuthu Gatsha Buthelezi, chanted, sang and staged mock battles, to the obvious displeasure of heavily armed Government soldiers in armored cars. The Zulus disregarded police requests to surrender their weapons. "The people outside the hotel, while they apparently enjoyed themselves, according to all the reports I received, at no stage posed a threat to anyone," Mr. de Klerk said.

Millions of black South Africans stayed home from work today in protest over a new general tax and the government's attempts to carry out economic and other reforms without the agreement of black labor and political groups. It was the largest nationwide strike in the nation's history. The strike's start was marred by a battle Sunday night between pro- and anti-strike workers at a mine outside Welkom, 160 miles south of here, where 15 miners died and 43 were injured. Elsewhere, the strike proceeded relatively peacefully today, although police said they arrested 108 people during 16 protest marches and demonstrations held without permission.

President F. W. de Klerk promised today to include South Africa's disfranchised black majority in any referendum on political change, but at the same time he reiterated that the white minority would have an opportunity to veto the terms of transition to a new nonracist constitution. Mr. de Klerk's nationally televised speech, which lasted nearly an hour, was criticized by the African National Congress, whose executive committee in Johannesburg accused him of "an insensitivity, uncaring attitude and complacency towards the plight of millions of people whose lives have been ruined by the system of apartheid." As Mr. de Klerk finished speaking, at least 20,000 black demonstrators surged through downtown Cape Town in what the congress, which organized the protest, billed as a "people's parliament." It endorsed the congress's demand that the Government be replaced by an interim government within six months and that a constituent assembly be elected by the end of 1992 to draw up a new constitution.

Police arrested a leader of South Africa's radical Pan Africanist Congress and fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse a crowd of demonstrators who were protesting high rents and electricity fees in the black township of Ennerdale. PAC spokesmen said more than 1,000 people attended the protest rally and that several were wounded by police gunfire. Police estimated the number of protesters at 500 and said they had no reports of casualties. A police spokesman said the officers opened fire after the crowd ignored orders to disperse and began throwing stones. PAC is campaigning against constitutional talks that the larger African National Congress and other black groups are holding with President Frederik W. de Klerk's minority white government.

They marched by the hundreds in black and khaki uniforms with swastika-like armbands, singing: "This land is for the Boers. Shoot the kaffirs. Shoot." They belong to the Afrikaner Resistance Movement, a neo-Nazi movement in style, language and garb, if not objective.  All day Saturday, the group put on a multi-act performance of the skills of its growing private army for local and international media in the streets of this rural village, about 90 miles west of Johannesburg. Saturday's parade, however, numbered no more than 500. They are up in arms over constitutional negotiations that are moving toward the end of white-minority rule here, and so they are preparing a last stand in the name of a separate white nation. The rise of the Afrikaner Resistance, unopposed by the government despite the group's declaration of readiness to do battle against the state, appears to be another sign of such a trend.

The most violent confrontation between police and township residents in more than a year in South Africa took place in Alexandra township Thursday. About 100 residents were treated at the black township's clinic for birdshot and rubber-bullet wounds, but probably because nobody was killed, it went largely unnoticed and unreported abroad. Yet the running street battles between rock-throwing youths and heavily armed special riot police said a lot about the simmering grass-roots tensions and unresolved conflicts that continue to weigh heavily on South Africa's fragile peace process. Alexandra, one of several satellite black townships around Johannesburg, teetered today on the brink of chaos as residents battled each other in politically tinged violence and angry mobs surged into the streets. The violence, which first erupted in Alexandra last month, has involved migrants living in workers' hostels and residents of the surrounding township, which in its organization is similar to but smaller than the better-known Soweto township. It quickly took on political overtones because the migrants are mostly Zulus loyal to the tribally based Inkatha Freedom Party, while the long-term residents of the township largely support the African National Congress. In Alexandra today, young people erected barricades of burning tires, large rocks and the scorched carcass of an overturned car. The stench of tear gas and scorched rubber hung in the air at some intersections, which glittered with shards of glass. Many Alexandra residents want two men's hostels closed down and converted into more stable family housing. The rage in Alexandra's streets was redirected today from the hostel dwellers to the South African Police, whose armored cars attracted volleys of stones as they patrolled the township. Since the shootings and killings appear to not be done by police, but rather by the hostel-dwellers, the response for this protest is only coded as crowd dispersal.  Also, even though this protest involved fighting between two groups of citizens, the Alexandra residents have a political demand in that they want the hostels closed and converted into proper housing.

FRESH from his triumphant visit to Nigeria, President de Klerk returned abruptly to the confused and volatile situation in his backyard at the weekend when he was pelted with gravel and forced to abandon the National party's first rally outside white areas. Although he was cheered by thousands of Coloureds at Mitchell's Plain outside Cape Town, a township created in the 1970s as a result of apartheid's forced removal policies, he was booed and jeered equally as loudly by supporters of the African National Congress and the New Unity Movement. His address in a marquee erected in the centre of the township was almost inaudible. As the protesters hurled handfuls of gravel at the platform, police advised the president to cut short the proceedings in case somebody was hurt. He cancelled a walkabout in a shopping centre and a luncheon and was driven back to his official residence. The ANC, which also opposed Mr de Klerk's visit to Nigeria, said the rally had been an extravagant flop after the National party (NP) had spent 250,000 rand (Pounds 49,700) on its organisation. The number of protesters is assumed to be in the 1000s, because the number of supporters of the president was listed to be this much, and then it was said that the opposition (the protesters) had an equally loud voice, thus implying that it had similar numbers.

The ANC has denounced the call-up, saying it amounts to "declaring war against the people" and that it marks a return to "the old ways of coercion and repression." The ANC asked in a statement Saturday why the government never ordered such a call-up when Inkatha had marched through the streets carrying "traditional weapons" that formally are banned at political rallies. The alleged police bias in favor of Inkatha seemed in evidence in Soweto today. Down the main road in front of the township's Baragwanath Hospital, hundreds of Inkatha youths marched armed with the banned iron spears, sharpened wooden sticks and poles. The marchers took over half of the road, but police in an empty patrol wagon and riot police in an armored personnel carrier made no attempt to disarm the marchers or get them off the road. Later, however, police said they arrested 20 people, apparently Inkatha members, and confiscated "thousands of weapons" at Soweto's New Canada railroad station.

The African National Congress began an open-ended campaign of public protest today with a day of rallies, work stoppages and threats of a crippling general strike by the summer's end if the white minority Government does not move more quickly to give blacks full voting rights. In what black leaders conceded was a high-risk return to the unpredictable theater of the street, Nelson Mandela, the president of the Congress, said the "mass action" campaign would continue until the Government agreed to terms for creation of an interim government and an elected assembly to write a new South African constitution. Addressing 30,000 supporters packed into a soccer stadium in this sprawling metropolis of black slums south of Johannesburg, Mr. Mandela implored his followers to ignore growing calls by impatient blacks to mount a guerrilla war against the white suburbs. ''Do not be provoked into violence,'' Mr Mandela told a 40,000-strong crowd in the Orlando football stadium in Soweto. ''By killing and revenge you do not help the community. Carrying violence to the white areas would be a disaster of the first magnitude.''

President F. W. de Klerk ventured into this bitter black township today in a show of concern for victims of a massacre on Wednesday, but was chased away by angry residents, leaving behind an ugly mood that soon exploded into more violence. About 90 minutes after Mr. de Klerk's motorcade fled before residents blaming him for the Wednesday violence, police officers fired assault rifles into a hostile crowd in a skirmish over the body of a man shot by the police a short time earlier. The number of casualties was not immediately known. "To hell with de Klerk -- go away, go away!" chanted a throng of several hundred people, kept back from Mr. de Klerk's caravan by guards on foot carrying machine guns. Hundreds of furious residents forced President Frederik W. de Klerk out of this tense black township today, chasing his car through the dusty streets and shouting, "Go away" and "Shoot, shoot." Shortly after his hasty departure, police opened fire without warning and at close range on a crowd that had gathered in a field inside the township. At least three people were killed and 20 seriously wounded, according to a journalist who witnessed the incident. Armed residents living in nearby homes then responded with sniper fire, leading to a shootout that lasted more than 15 minutes, the witness said.

Mandela today issued a stern warning to de Klerk not to declare a state of emergency, saying, "Let me warn him that the introduction of anti-democratic measures today will result in a defiance campaign with me leading [it]." Mandela led an earlier "defiance campaign" by blacks against apartheid laws during the early 1950s. The ANC leader, addressing a militant crowd of 20,000 followers in Evaton, said the Boipatong massacre had changed the face of South African politics and that the gulf "between the oppressed and the oppressor has become unbreachable." Many ANC supporters have accused the government of complicity in the Boipatong massacre. Although a rally for the ANC, there is a clear protest message among the crowd, and thus this was coded as a protest rather than excluded as just a political rally.

In the dusty amateur soccer stadium of this previously uncelebrated black township, the leadership of black South Africa and a crowd of 25,000 today eulogized victims of the reform era's worst massacre and roared their bitterness at the white Government. The funeral service for 37 of the people killed on June 17 in a night rampage through Boipatong united black leaders from moderate to militant in calling for the ouster of President F. W. de Klerk. They disagreed over whether he should be driven from office by force or allowed to negotiate his own surrender. "Remember, Mr. de Klerk, we are not your kitchen maids, we are not your garden boys," jeered Jay Naidoo, the president of the Congress of South African Trade Unions, who led a thunderous chant of "de Klerk must go!"

Thousands of angry blacks marched meanwhile today through the black township of Boipatong, south of Johannesburg, to protest the killings last month of more than 40 people and demand action against the attackers. A line of heavily armed police officers watched as 5,000 chanting, singing demonstrators stopped at the township's edge, separated by black protest marshals who formed a human chain. The crowd gestured toward a Zulu hostel that is believed to have been the staging area for the attack June 17. Leaders told the hostel's owners that the building must be demolished and the attackers brought to justice.

Vance arrived on the second day of the latest phase of the ANC's "mass action campaign" designed to pressure the government into making more concessions through strikes, marches and the occupation of government buildings. Hundreds of protesters have been arrested the past two days for occupying police stations, hospitals, courts and government offices. Police said they arrested 273 people for trespassing or participating in illegal demonstrations on Monday. Police estimated that 16,000 people joined in 27 protests that police called "isolated mass actions."

Thousands of African National Congress supporters singing freedom songs marched on government and police buildings across South Africa in a run-up to mass protests planned to topple the government. The demonstrations in four main cities came as President Frederik W. de Klerk said that South Africa urgently needs to elect a transitional government but that the stalled talks on multi-racial rule will have to be resumed first. The protest marches drew less than 10,000 demonstrators -- short of the huge crowds the ANC had predicted it would mobilize to call for majority rule and peace.

A FIVE-HOUR confrontation on the veld with 30,000 cheering demonstrators facing a line of guns and armoured cars ended miraculously without bloodshed at sunset last night. The demonstrators, supporters of the African National Congress, danced and sang their way into the territory of the so-called independent black homeland of Ciskei as darkness fell. The 30,000 marched out of King Williams Town in the Eastern Cape at midday, determined to confront the military ruler of Ciskei, Brigadier Oupa Gqozo, who had vowed that no ANC demonstrator would set foot in his realm. He was accompanied throughout the day by Jose Campino, one of ten United Nations observers invited to monitor this week's intensification of mass action which is aimed at forcing the South African government to yield to the ANC's demands for constitutional reform. The leaders insisted they were going to enter Ciskei to deliver a memo to the Ciskei ministers. The troops insisted, equally vehemently, that they would not. Stalemate. Then the negotiations of Dr Geldenhuys began. The stadium then became the goal of the negotiators. Dr Geldenhuys and Senhor Campino went back to the ministers and suddenly the ministers agreed. All at once it was over. The crowd surged towards the stadium. Their leaders addressed them. The memorandum was delivered. It called for the immediate installation of an intermediate administration in Ciskei to supervise its peaceful reintegration into South Africa. The protesters had marched out of King Williams Town in the Eastern Cape at midday to deliver a demand that an intermediate administration be set up in Bisho immediately to supervise Ciskei's peaceful reintegration into South Africa.

As the March 17 referendum among the white community showed that President de Klerk had their overwhelming support, so this week has shown that Mr Mandela has the support of blacks. While it is true that the success of a general strike can be ensured by intimidation and those wanting to work can be kept at home by the absence of transport, it is more difficult to intimidate people into turning out for mass marches. The vast numbers who poured into city centres on Wednesday were testimony to the strength of feeling, as well as to the organising ability of the ANC cadres, who transported thousands of protesters from rural and small urban districts into the big towns. Estimates varied between 200,000 and 400,000. There were two other impressive things about the mass mobilisation. First, the crowds were well-disciplined by marshals. There were few incidents of violence, or destruction. True, in Pietermaritzburg four cars had their tyres slashed, and after thedemonstrations a couple of petrol bombs were thrown unsuccessfully in Cape townships. But during the Cape Town demonstration, marshals handed over to the police a young man caught breaking shop windows. The same marshals insisted on protesters putting down sticks or anything that might be construed as a weapon. Second, and equally impressive, was the restraint shown by the security forces. Though in many cases police and soldiers were armed with shotguns and rifles, with tear-gas pistols and batons, though they were dressed in bullet-proof vests, steel helmets and gas masks, they stood and watched and joshed the crowd just like policemen in other less socially divided countries. It was possible yesterday to attribute only one death to Wednesday's demonstrations, and that was of a man who fell from a train going home from the Cape Town events.

Nelson Mandela led a huge and orderly throng of black protesters to the capital of apartheid today to raise the flag of the African National Congress on the front porch of the white Government and demand that President F. W. de Klerk make way for majority rule. Mr. Mandela, president of the congress, told supporters who marched to a park beneath the Union Buildings, the seat of the South African executive branch, that he hoped to resume negotiations on the country's future but that South African blacks would make peace "standing on our feet, not kneeling on our knees." There, under the sculptured glare of Gen. J. B. M. Hertzog, one of the spiritual fathers of Afrikaner nationalism, the professorial liberation leader lectured on democracy before 50,000 still disenfranchised blacks. Mr. de Klerk spent the day sequestered in a windowless Cabinet room, an aide said, and saw nothing of the events below. Later he [de Klerk] emerged to tell reporters that "certain discussions have been taking place" between the Government and the congress, and that he expected formal talks to resume shortly. Since the president addressed the crowd saying that discussions are and will take place, the response to this protest is recorded as accommodation. The most noticeable effect was in Pretoria, where a vast crowd estimated at up to 70,000 watched by armed troops and police, marched behind Nelson Mandela, the ANC president, to the Union Buildings on the hill overlooking the town.

Soldiers of the black South African homeland called Ciskei rained machine-gun fire today into a fleeing throng of African National Congress supporters who marched on the enclave vowing to topple its military ruler. The three-minute volley left at least 24 black marchers dead and scores more wounded or trampled in the panic. It also dashed any hope of a rapid reconciliation between blacks and whites on South Africa's political future, because while South Africa insists Ciskei is an independent country beyond its control, almost everyone else here and abroad regards it as a province, if not a puppet, of South Africa. "We are blaming de Klerk for this, and we do it without hesitation," said Cyril Ramaphosa, secretary general of the African National Congress, one of several black leaders who dived to the ground alongside journalists and mediators to avoid the intense gunfire. The march, which set off with more than 50,000 strong from King William's Town, on the South African side of the ostensible border, marked an intensification of the A.N.C.'s battle to end white minority rule. The first fusillade continued for nearly two minutes. After a series of percussions, apparently a belated round of tear-gas grenades, the gunfire again raked the retreating crowd for a minute. AT LEAST 28 people died and nearly 200 were injured when Ciskei armed forces opened fire yesterday on a march of 70,000 ANC-led demonstrators seeking to occupy Bisho, the capital of the nominally independent homeland. A tense standoff continued tonight as thousands of protesters -- out of a demonstration that initially numbered between 50,000 and 80,000 -- camped in an all-night vigil near the scene of the shooting.

On a day of mourning and recrimination, African National Congress leader Nelson Mandela today bitterly accused President Frederik W. de Klerk of deceiving him during an exchange of letters prior to a march here Monday in which 24 demonstrators were killed. "While he was soliciting me to give my cooperation, he was preparing for war against the people," Mandela told a rally of 15,000 ANC supporters who gathered near the site of the massacre. It was some of the harshest language he has ever leveled at the man who has been his on-again, off-again negotiating partner for 2 1/2 years. Although the dead were killed by defense forces of Brig. Oupo Gqozo, military leader of the nominally independent South African homeland of Ciskei, Mandela made it clear he held de Klerk's white-minority government partly responsible. Although technically a rally for ANC supporters, there is a clear protest message against the government at this demonstration.

About 15,000 spear-carrying, stick-wielding Zulus affiliated with the Inkatha Freedom Party marched through downtown Johannesburg today in open defiance of a ban, negotiated by the government and the African National Congress, on the carrying of dangerous weapons. The demonstration was peaceful, and police, who monitored it with videocameras, made no arrests on the scene. A police spokesman said authorities would decide later whether to bring charges against march leaders for flouting the ban. The demonstration reflected a bitter rift that has developed between the government and Inkatha -- onetime allies -- in the wake of the Sept. 26 meeting between de Klerk and Nelson Mandela, president of the ANC, the nation's biggest predominantly black political party and a bitter foe of Inkatha. Political violence, much of it between the ANC and Inkatha, has claimed about 6,000 lives in the past two years.

Riot police officers fired tear gas and rubber bullets yesterday to disperse rock-throwing taxi drivers who blockaded central Johannesburg. The drivers demanded subsidies and complained of discrimination by traffic officers. At least 13 people, including 9 police officers, were injured. Cab drivers, complaining that the traffic police harass them, blocked intersections in Johannesburg for a second day. A civilian pleaded with advancing troops not to use their guns and tear gas to quell the demonstrators. In the clash, one person was left dead and three hurt. Law and Order Minister Hernus Kriel declared Johannesburg an emergency area, giving police special search and arrest powers after the deaths of two men in violent demonstrations by black taxi drivers. Police killed one man and wounded at least three others when they opened fire on a mob attacking a white motorist in central Johannesburg, police said. Witnesses said a second man died when police opened fire to clear a blockade erected by the protesting taxi drivers. Kriel told Parliament that police had been fired on as they towed away minibus taxis parked across major intersections by some of the 800 striking black drivers. The killings climaxed two days of violence around the strike by taxi drivers alleging harassment. They virtually paralyzed traffic in South Africa's commercial capital Monday and said they repeated the protest yesterday to demand the release of seven arrested colleagues. VIOLENCE swept the Soweto township for the third day in succession yesterday, with two buses set on fire, but a heavy police presence kept rioters off the streets in Johannesburg. After a tense and angry meeting at which a list of demands was drawn up, the city council reported that no progress had been made in settling the dispute.

TENS of thousands of black protesters took to South African streets yesterday as black anger at the assassination of Chris Hani boiled over into calls for arms to be taken up against whites. Shots were fired by black radicals, police were stoned and vehicles set ablaze. But younger leaders of the ANC rejected the peace calls at one mass rally, in the Pretoria township of Mamelodi. They demanded to know how they could be expected to act responsibly in the face of the assassination on Saturday of Hani, general secretary of the South African Communist party, which was blamed on the government by several speakers. The rally began in a high state of anger after a police car had been stoned, injuring one of the occupants. Police reacted by firing tear gas at the gathering crowds, and broke them into smaller processions. The rally ended peacefully with the crowd marching back to the township, shouting and singing freedom songs. A thousand blacks, many carrying spears and axes, marched on Hani's home in a suburb of Boksburg, near Johannesburg, where the alleged assassin, Janusz Walus, 40, appears in court today. ANC youth leaders told the crowd: ''We want power. We want it now.'' There was chaos in three East Rand townships, Katlehong, Thokoza and Tsikane, as protesters began to set vehicles alight. Security reinforcements were rushed to the townships as angry youths tried to burn police trucks, vans and cars. In Katlehong a number of black and white reporters and television crews were fired on as they tried to film a blazing truck. Juda Ngwenya, a photographer for Reuters news agency, said he was ''nearly killed'', but that no one was injured. Police fired rubber bullets to disperse a crowd that had burnt down a house belonging to a police sergeant in Katlehong. The crowd of about 200 people was returning from Hani's Boksburg house when it began stoning the police station, breaking the windows of buildings and vehicles. The terrified inhabitants of Boksburg were visited by more than 5,000 marchers anxious to pay their respects to the dead leader. In Cape Province, where the worst of the violence broke out at the weekend, the townships were mainly quiet. After a black man had been killed during an exchange of shots between police and demonstrators in the Chicken Farm squatter camp in Soweto on Sunday, two white men were burned to death at Lwandle township 25 miles from Cape Town. A third white man, who was also set alight and had his tongue cut during the same attack, died yesterday.

A nationwide day of mourning for the slain black leader Chris Hani burst out of control today, as angry young blacks rioted through several cities in defiance of pleas for order. In the worst single incident, panicky police officers here fired without warning into a throng milling outside the main police station, killing three and critically wounding five, and replenishing the rage that black leaders hoped would be spent by this day of protest. Across the country, crowd-control marshals deployed by the African National Congress struggled to hold angry youths in check, and often failed. In Cape Town, Durban, Port Elizabeth, Pietermaritzburg and other cities, rallies turned into rampages of looting, burning and clashes with the police. Organizers of the day's events said the casualty toll -- at least seven people were reported killed and hundreds hurt -- could have been much worse, given the hundreds of thousands who took part and the pitch of emotion after the killing Saturday of Mr. Hani, the Communist Party leader and a popular figure in the African National Congress. Journalists and other witnesses at the police station said the crowd was preparing to disperse when an armored police vehicle roared back and forth through the crowd, followed by a police wagon. When a few young men showered stones on the vehicles, the witnesses said, a line of about 30 police, most of them white, opened fire with tear gas, shotguns and pistols. In Soweto THREE demonstrators were killed yesterday as police opened fire on a huge crowd outside Soweto's Protea Park police station. Two others were shot and killed in Cape Town, and two deaths were reported in townships east of Johannesburg, bringing the total toll for the day to seven.

As stone-throwing youths and riot police faced off in running battles outside a soccer stadium here today, African National Congress President Nelson Mandela urged 80,000 mourners inside to honor Hani's memory by forming peace brigades. Overhead, black smoke wafted past from nearby houses that had been torched by demonstrators. "We, the victims of violence, have been blamed for the very acts that take our lives," he said. "Black lives are cheap and will remain so as long as apartheid continues to exist. And let there be no mistake about it: There have been many changes, and negotiations have started, but for the ordinary black person of this country, apartheid is alive and well." "Who killed Chris Hani?" Slovo asked. "It was not just the brute who pulled the trigger. He was killed by a system that turns people into animals, a system that has made our own people foreigners in our own land. . . . Let us warn the right wing that however many they kill, they represent a dying cause. They are the cave men of South Africa . . . and they must not test the patience of our people."

At Ceres, 60 miles northeast of Cape Town, police fired rubber bullets and tear gas at school children marching to the town hall to protest against a visit by President de Klerk's wife, Marike. In the ensuing violence two youths were arrested, a policeman's home was attacked by stone-throwing youths, police vehicles were attacked and a shop window was smashed, but Mrs de Klerk's address to a local women's church organisation went ahead as planned.  Given the response from police and the destruction caused, this protest is assumed to have at least 50 participants.

About 20 extremist groups met near Pretoria Friday to form an Afrikaner People's Front and called for the immediate suspension of multiparty talks on a transition from white rule to democracy. "The extremist right-wing pressure groups are playing with fire and violations of the law by their side will be dealt with just as strictly as violations by left-wing extremists," Mr. de Klerk said in response to their mobilization. "The Government will not bow to pressure from the right. Those who imagine that negotiations and a new, just dispensation can be stopped are naive." With 20 groups meeting, this protest is assumed to have at least 100 participants.

In Johannesburg, about 6,000 members of the Inkatha Freedom Party, most of whose members are Zulus, marched with spears, axes and shields to the offices of the state-run television and radio service to protest a perceived anti-Inkatha bias. Vitus Mvelase, a member of Inkatha's central committee, called for an urgent meeting between Mr. Mandela and Inkatha President Mangosuthu Buthelezi to halt violence that has killed about 8,000 people in four years.

Hundreds of armed white separatists stormed South Africa's constitutional negotiations this morning, smashing through the plate-glass front of the World Trade Center in an armored truck and holding many of the country's senior politicians under siege to dramatize their bitterness at the approach of black majority rule. After two hours of swaggering through the convention center just outside Johannesburg, spraying graffiti and throwing punches, the khaki-clad mob dispersed without causing any serious casualties. About 1,500 followers of the white separatist front, many armed with shotguns and pistols, massed outside the trade center complex this morning to complain that negotiators had rejected their demand for an independent Afrikaner homeland. The demonstration was timed to coincide with the negotiators' vote confirming the date of the first election for voters of all races next April, which separatists see as the date of their ethnic demise. But the ratification of the election date was put off until next week before the protest occurred. Riot policemen put up no resistance as the crowd poured through the building, occupying the main conference room, waving guns and roughing up black journalists and an Indian negotiator.

If the slaughter a week ago was pure terrorism, in which the very senselessness seemed intended to announce that anyone is vulnerable, the attack Saturday night was old-fashioned vendetta, with deep roots in the local muck of ethnic and political hates. But to Mr. Dwera and his neighbors, and to many other South Africans, both attacks were connected to the prospect of the country's first universal elections, which has given desperate new purpose to those, black and white, who feel endangered by the new order. The two groups have been at odds in Tembisa for more than a decade. The hostility began as inevitable friction between settled township residents, whose political tone is set by young militants loyal to the African National Congress, and the migrants, mainly rural Zulus whose only stake was their jobs in the local factories. As night fell, according to the police and witnesses, a crowd of about 200 Zulus descended from the hostel onto the four-lane highway, shooting and torching taxis and attacking pedestrians, leaving the asphalt littered with bodies. The highway is used by travelers of all political leanings, but the attackers seemed not to care. At the Ngabayena house, the family left supper bubbling on the stove and fled. Mxolisi Ngabayena took his wife, Nokwanda, and their five-month-old son, Bathando, to a bedroom and locked the door. But someone staved in the window above their heads. Mother and son were shot dead where they lay. Mr. Ngabayena was dragged outside and killed. Skirmishes continued through the night.

WITWATERSRAND university, a former bastion of white liberalism which for years defied the architects of apartheid, has for the first time called in the South African police to restrain students. A hundred and thirty four people were arrested after demonstrations by mobs of mainly black undergraduates disrupted lectures, scattered rubbish around the campus, barricaded entrances and flooded lecture halls with fire hoses. Windows were broken and an attempt was made to seize control of the administration offices. Senior staff were manhandled. The protests started three days ago, and yesterday lectures were disrupted while a crowd of demonstrators, which at one point was a few hundred strong, paraded through the corridors of the senate building, singing liberation songs. The South African Students Congress (Sasco), which is leading the student protests, yesterday called for the resignation of the university council and the senate, and for its replacement by a transitional forum. ''It should be representative of students, academics, workers and the community,'' said Makhukhu Mampuru, Sasco's chairman. ''The council is overflowing with representatives of the apartheid regime.''

"If Mandela wants war, he'll get it," said Eugene TerreBlanche, leader of the neo-Nazi Afrikaner Resistance Movement, referring to the African National Congress president, Nelson Mandela. He spoke before about 3,000 cheering supporters, many dressed in khaki uniforms, wearing pistols tucked into their belts or carrying riot sticks. Today, the crowd of Afrikaners swelled to about 10,000 as speaker after speaker deplored the desecration of their homeland by blacks and Jews. Ferdi Hartzenberg, another right-wing leader, told fellow Afrikaners: "All we ask is our own land, our own country, our own government, our own constitution, our own civil service, our own budget. We will not give up this freedom. We will never, never, never surrender."

TENS of thousands of Zulus, many dressed in traditional leopard-skins and almost all carrying weapons, axes, spears, assegais and knobkerries, massed on the lawns below the Union Buildings here yesterday, while their king, Goodwill Zwelethini, met President de Klerk inside. A five-minute volley of shots in the air came from the crowd during the talks. Afterwards two people were reported hurt and another bitten by a dog. The king told President de Klerk: ''Neither I nor the Amakhosi (chiefs) who serve the people under me could possibly advise the Zulu people to participate in the proposed April 27 election while the present constitution remains what it is.'' After three hours of talks, the king seemed mollified, and an agreed statement promised establishment of a joint committee to examine KwaZulu's status in the new South Africa. Members of Chief Buthelezi's party who back participation in the elections were upbeat. ''This has been very good for us,'' said one delegate. ''It gives us a way out.'' A thunderstorm scattered the crowd, estimated by police at 45,000, before the leaders' meeting ended. One man was killed, stabbed with an assegai in Pretoria's city centre. The incident was blamed on over-indulgence in sorghum beer. An off-duty policeman had his jaw broken by a knobkerrie blow, and a bystander suffered an axe wound.

AS MANY as 68 black demonstrators were hurt, and seven taken to hospital, when riot police fired rubber bullets and tear-gas at a crowd of 2,000 trying to march from the Sakhile township to this agricultural town in Transvaal. They were lying in wait for the marchers on the other side of the railway which divides Standerton, 100 miles southeast of Johannesburg, from its Indian and black townships. However, the uniformed and armed AWB storm-troopers avoided the attention of the police by staying under cover at the town's cattle market and claiming to be holding a farmers' bazaar. Tensions have been rising for the past fortnight as the sacking of two supermarket employees for theft led to a strike at the store, and then to a general boycott of the town's shops by the black community. Farmers staged a mass protest, driving their tractors through the streets and claiming that Standerton was part of an Afrikaner volkstaat.

Police in the black homeland of Bophuthatswana used tear gas today to disperse striking civil servants and other demonstrators protesting the refusal of their government to take part in South Africa's first multiracial election. The tensions were expected to come to a head over the next few days, as South African authorities threatened coercive measures -- possibly including cutoff of funds -- to compel the homeland government to allow free political activity for the April 26-28 election. The homeland government has refused to take part in the election, contending that South Africa's new constitution does not allow sufficient power for regions. Here in the streets of Bophuthatswana's showcase capital, protesters confronted skittish police in skirmishes that left more than 30 injured today. They taunted police officers with showers of rocks and built barricades in the streets. Some said they planned raiding parties tonight to set fire to the homes of members of Mr. Mangope's police force -- a tactic employed in many South African townships. ARMED police fired round after round of tear gas, rubber bullets and birdshot in an effort to control crowds of striking workers and students rioting in Mmabatho, the Bophuthatswana capital, which swiftly spread to outlying townships.The rioters replied with stones and petrol bombs, and blockaded streets with burning tyres, stones and traffic signs. Eventually the police resorted to firing live rounds and a number of people were taken to hospital badly hurt.  THOUSANDS of rioters stormed through the capital of the South African homeland of Bophuthatswana yesterday, declaring victory over President Mangope, who was seen leaving the city in a helicopter for an unknown destination. Mr Mangope's refusal on Wednesday to allow his subjects to take part in the South African elections in April sparked widespread rioting in which two people, one a policeman, were killed and at least 60 injured. The government of the tribal "homeland" of Bophuthatswana appeared near collapse at daybreak today as thousands of demonstrators demanding the right to take part in South Africa's first democratic election marched and looted their way through the area's capital, Mmabatho, while police and soldiers made virtually no effort to restrain them. The leader of the apartheid homeland of Bophuthatswana today bowed to a popular uprising and agreed to let his ostensibly independent domain take part in the first nonracial elections in South Africa.

PRISONERS rioting for the right to vote in next month's multi-racial election set fire to a cell in Pretoria last night, starting a blaze that killed 21 people, while 2,400 inmates rampaged through another prison. The deaths came after a weekend of protests in at least 15 prisons by inmates demanding the right to vote. Two prisoners died in a fire in Paarl, near Cape Town, on Saturday. At Pietermaritzburg, in Natal, 2,400 prisoners rampaged through the city's prison, destroying cells. WITH the stench of the burnt-out cells still hanging in the air, heavily armed reinforcements were called in to assist prison officers in Pietermaritzburg last night after jail riots led to a decision by the Transitional Executive Council to give the vote in next month's elections to every inmate in the country.

Gun battles rattled incongruously through the high-rise canyons of downtown Johannesburg today as a protest by Zulu nationalists opposed to elections degenerated into the deadliest melee the city could remember. Armed marchers, police officers and snipers hidden in the surrounding buildings blazed away at each other along several blocks of banks and offices, leaving at least 31 people dead and scores wounded. In the worst single battle of the day, eight Zulus were killed by rifle-wielding African National Congress security guards who fired into a crowd of protesters they said was trying to storm the congress's headquarters. Merchants shuttered their stores and office workers fled for home when Zulus by the thousands converged to demand that KwaZulu, the homeland created under apartheid for the Zulu people, be excluded from the elections, set for April 26 through 28. The Zulu nationalists want their homeland declared a sovereign monarchy. Today's clashes began after about 10,000 heavily armed Zulus marched in protest against the election. The Zulus -- supporters of Inkatha -- fought backers of the ANC, which is expected to gain a landslide victory in the vote.

SOUTH African Defence Force troops and homeland police officers patrolled the streets of Phuthadijhada, the QwaQwa capital, in armoured vehicles yesterday with the city on a knife edge following clashes and looting after an African National Congress march 24 hours earlier. More than 200 people were arrested and troops deployed in the tiny homeland, wedged between the Orange Free State and Natal, when a group of youths broke away from a march by thousands of civil servants to the homeland parliament and ran amok through a shopping centre. Up to 60 people were injured. Members of the ANC-aligned National Education, Health and Allied Workers' Union are refusing to return to work unless the homeland government is dissolved.

More than 20,000 Zulus armed with traditional weapons such as clubs, spears and machetes marched today in support of their King's demand for a sovereign state and in defiance of the emergency decree that prohibits the carrying of weapons. The march was meant as a show of force not only to protest the Government's proclamation of a state of emergency in Natal province but also the shooting deaths last week of Zulu marchers in Johannesburg. Heavily armed police officers and troops initially tried to search the marchers as they arrived in this small town in Natal, 90 miles north of Durban, but they pulled back as thousands of Zulus continued to pour in on overloaded buses, many bare-chested, chanting and doing war dances. Police and the army deployed about 1,000 men to monitor the march. It was the first major political rally held under the new regulations and had been billed in advance as a major test of political will.

Thousands of Zulus gathered at a stadium in Vryheid, northern Natal, yesterday before marching through the town in protest against the election. Many were armed with spears and axes in defiance of emergency regulations, but no attempt was made to disarm them. The Transitional Executive Council (TEC) overseeing the move towards the elections announced yesterday that it was considering extending the voting period in NatalKwaZulu and broadening emergency legislation to allow it to ''commandeer'' KwaZulu government property for use as polling stations. That was greeted with dismay by members of the Independent Electoral Commission.

President Nelson Mandela's Government cut six months off virtually all prison sentences today to halt rioting in several prisons. Two people were killed and scores were hurt in the violence. The concession fell short of demands by a prisoners' rights group for the release of all prisoners who present no threat to the community. But the group called off mass protests it had advocated earlier this week, and unrest in at least six prisons appeared to have ended. Rioting began Thursday at the 4,000-inmate prison at Modderbee. One prisoner was killed on Thursday and another was shot to death by guards today during an attempted escape. About 600 South African prisoners rioted today and held the head of their jail hostage, one day after the Government said it would cut jail terms for common criminals in reaction to earlier riots. A Correctional Services spokesman, Brig. Chris Olckers, said the hostage was the head of the medium-security prison at St. Albans jail, outside the Eastern Cape city of Port Elizabeth. One inmate was killed and 25 were injured today at Victor Verster Prison near Cape Town in the fourth day of disturbances in South Africa's prisons. A spokesman for the Department of Correctional Services said that 270 prison guards regained control of the prison around noon from 665 inmates, some of whom were heavily armed with homemade weapons. The term regaining control implies beatings on part of the guards, and so is included as a response.

LESS than three months after South Africa's first democratic election, cracks are beginning to appear in the African National Congress's alliance with the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu) as a wave of strikes over wage demands and union militancy sweeps the country. The talks followed a week in which hundreds of members of the South African Catering, Commercial and Allied Workers' Union, a Cosatu affiliate, were arrested during violent demonstrations at supermarkets owned by Pick'n Pay, one of the country's biggest retail chains. They were involved in clashes with police little different from those seen under the National Party government. More than 70 strikers were injured by rubber bullets and dog bites. Mr Shilowa said Cosatu expected ANC ministers to remove repressive labour legislation. ''We are being asked by our members if democracy will ever mean anything more than the right to vote every five years.'' Although this protest was against a private company, it was coded due to the demand that the union members have for the government to repeal certain legislation.

SEVERAL thousand trade unionists marched through the centre of Johannesburg yesterday as South Africa's winter of discontent continued to gather momentum. Cosatu repeated a threat to call a national one-day strike on August 8 unless employers met all union demands by the end of this month. Langa Zita, Cosatu's regional secretary, said the march was the ''first campaign of workers in the new society with the object of putting workers' demands at the top of the new agenda''.

A wildcat trucking strike that turned many miles of Africa's most modern highway system into a fuming gridlock ended tonight, but not before creating new fears of anarchy to bedevil President Nelson Mandela in his courtship of foreign investors. The protest began on Monday when hundreds of truckers demanding better pay parked across a tollgate on the country's busiest freight highway, near the Indian Ocean port of Durban. It spread quickly to three other major routes, as the truckers rallied one another to choke points on citizens' band radios. Mr. Mandela's Minister of Labor, Tito Mboweni, mediated a deal in which the truckers agreed to open the roadblocks in exchange for a promise that the employers would meet them in a nationwide bargaining council and that wages would be "changed radically." The drivers said their campaign, which began without warning or union approval, was a spontaneous explosion of frustration sparked by a feeling that they deserved some reward for helping elect Mr. Mandela. Truck drivers are mostly black and less than half belong to unions. Julius Matroose, a spokesman for the union, said many workers were disappointed that the election of Mr. Mandela's African National Congress had not produced quick dividends for workers, and that Mr. Mandela was counseling patience. Mr. Matroose said full-time truckers now get a minimum wage of about $400 a month, plus large amounts of overtime, but they work exhausting hours in trucks that are often badly maintained.

STUDENT unrest has spread like a veld fire in South Africa as black undergraduates fight the mainly white, often liberal, administrations of higher education institutions. Police used teargas and dogs to clear rioting black students from the University of South Africa campus in Pretoria. Six staff members were injured, and the authorities have banned students from the university's premises there and in Johannesburg. At Vanderbijl Park, south of here, majority white students and their black colleagues fought with baseball bats and knobkerries at the Vaal Triangle Technikon, a college of advanced technology. The clash was provoked by rightwingers declaring a hall of residence to be a ''Boerestaat'' (white homeland), and expelling blacks. In Bloemfontein, black students occupied the administration block of the University of the Orange Free State, protesting at the ''unsatisfactory'' results of elections to the student representative council. Perhaps saddest of all, however, is the havoc wrought at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, where rampaging black students threw stones, broke windows, turned on fire hoses and threw rubbish everywhere. Black student demands differ from college to college but they essentially concern the inability of many of the students to pay fees or to meet rigorous ''culturally based'' examination requirements. They are demanding black student control of college administrations and, at Wits, the sacking of Professor Robert Charlton, the Vice-Chancellor. This protest is believed to have at least 1000 people due to how widespread it is and that it is taking place in large universities across the nation.

The riotous scenes were reminiscent of Soweto in the days of anti-apartheid fervor: barricades of burning tires, rocks flying, buildings in flames, white police firing stun grenades and rubber bullets, and a smoldering racial resentment. But the target of the uprising today, in this and several other customarily sleepy townships just west of Johannesburg, was Nelson Mandela's Government, and the protesters were the country's often invisible mixed-race minority, who call themselves "coloreds." Asserting that after decades of short shrift from white rulers they are now victims of favoritism for blacks in housing, services and jobs, the mixed-race townships organized a one-day general strike and began a boycott of rent and utility payments. The day ended without deaths and with few serious injuries -- a young woman shot in the face with a police rubber bullet, and several residents hit by birdshot when police officers fired on a crowd. Although the protest technically took place in townships just outside of Johannesburg, their names were not given, and Johannesburg is very close, so that was the city chosen to represent the location of this protest. Given the violence and the reaction to the protest, as well as how it spanned across multiple townships, it is believed there were at least 100 participants.

Defense Minister Joe Modise said today that more than 2,200 former guerrillas had been dismissed from the army for failing to meet a midnight deadline to report for duty after they left their base during a protest. Mr. Modise said there would be no last-minute reprieve for the men and women who left the Walmansthal base near Pretoria last week to protest conditions, wages and the pace of their integration into the South African National Defense Force. He also warned against any effort by those who left to set up an underground movement. He said that 4,000 of the former guerrillas who had left the base had responded to his warnings and had returned.

More immediately, they must deal with the issue of racism which has been made more pressing after a black policeman was shot dead by white riot police in Soweto on Friday during an attempt to end a strike. The latest racial clash within the force led several polic stations in Soweto to shut down or go slow at the weekend in protest against the killing and to demand the removal of white officers.   After a strike by black policemen in the Orlando area of Soweto, about 400 residents gathered outside the station yesterday to call for the suspension of Brigadier Chris Earle, the district commissioner. The protesters believed that he had given the order for an internal stability unit to open fire on striking policemen at the station on Friday; one striking officer was killed. The demonstrators wanted Sidney Mufamadi, the Safety and Security Minister, to accept their petition personally.

Right-wing whites with sticks and dogs shouted racist insults and attacked black schoolchildren near Cape Town in an attempt to disrupt post-apartheid South Africa's tentative steps toward school integration. A white man was arrested after beating a youth with a whip as blacks and whites faced off across a street in Ruyterwacht, a low-income white suburb. About 100 police protected about 3,000 black children bused into the area from the Khayelitsha township nine miles away in a campaign organized by the National Education Coordination Committee to occupy abandoned white schools. A spokesman for the committee, a nongovernmental lobbying group, said a black youth had been fatally stabbed on the school grounds, probably by a fellow student. About 150 whites, some armed with chains or sticks and several holding snarling dogs, tried to prevent the children from entering the school, but police kept them at bay. Police stood by throughout the day and escorted the children to their buses shortly after noon.

Protester Group Identity: Objectors to new Labour Relations Bill
Notes: MORE than 100,000 people marched through the centre of Johannesburg yesterday in a peaceful demonstration organised by the African National Congress-aligned Confederation of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu). They were marching in support of Cosatu objections to a new Labour Relations Bill. The demands included a ban on management lockouts, the right to strike, and central bargaining. The real motivation was the feeling that not enough has been done to fulfil the aspirations of the black majority after the elections last year. At least one marcher bore a placard reading: ''Let's get South Africa working. Jobs. Jobs. Jobs.'' Recognising the strength of numbers on the streets of the commercial and industrial capital, President Mandela surprised everybody by arriving at the head of the procession to address the crowd from the back of a lorry. He offered the demonstrators his support, and blessed their efforts, and while reminding them that the ANC had always used the right to strike and demonstrate in its freedom struggle, he asked them to be disciplined.

At least three people were killed today when some 2,000 African National Congress supporters marched to protest violence in South Africa's Zulu heartland, the police said. The latest deaths, in Umlazi township outside the port city of Durban, brought to at least 35 the number of people killed in the province since Friday. The A.N.C. supporters marched to the magistrate's courts to protest the violence. The demand for this protest is coded as political process, since the protesters are angry about violence and therefore the governmentÈs inability to curb it.

Nurses' representatives have given the Health Minister ten days to meet a demand for a 33 per cent pay increase, postal workers have downed mailbags in Pretoria, and train drivers have gone on strike on the Cape Town commuter network, stranding 200,000 workers. The municipal workers are seeking a minimum wage of 1,500 rands a month (Pounds 265). The nurses, who brought the giant Baragwanath hospital in Soweto to a standstill two weeks ago, were told flatly that the Government has no money for increases this year. Police fired rubber bullets at demonstrations in the East Rand outside Johannesburg yesterday. The only casualties reported were two police hit by stones thrown by strikers. In Pretoria, 2,000 strikers danced in protest outside the municipal offices, waving clubs and knobkerries, despite a court order forbidding demonstrations within 100 yards of the building.

Thousands of police officers and soldiers patrolled the streets, the railroad stations and migrant workers' hostels. Sections of downtown were cordoned off with razor wire, and many businesses closed, their employees too frightened to be downtown when the Zulus marched. The fear was that the rally, planned to commemorate the 1994 killings of eight Zulus by guards at the African National Congress's headquarters, would turn into the big showdown between the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party and what is now the A.N.C.-led Government. The immediate issue leading up to today's rally was the Zulus' rights to carry spears, clubs and other weapons at political rallies. But that was just the latest fight in the continuing feud between the Congress and its most powerful black rival. But by evening, to nearly everyone's surprise, thousands of Zulus had marched peacefully through downtown and both sides were claiming moral victory. Each side, it seems, had given a little. The marchers were virtually all armed, and the police took away only a handful of weapons. The catch was that the weaponry had been toned down compared with earlier Zulu rallies. Virtually no marchers had rifles, axes or big panga knives. Less than 10 percent had spears -- and many of those had their points wrapped in plastic or corked with corncobs. Most carried knobby-headed clubs, stout or sharpened sticks and small oxhide shields. A few carried only umbrellas or even mock weapons, like cardboard shields and cardboard tubes. Due to the presence of 1000s of police officers, this protest is assumed to also have 1000s of participants.

Protester Group Identity: Confederation of South African Trade Unions
Notes: A general strike, called to fight a constitutional provision, seemed to fizzle today. With a deadline looming for constitutional negotiators to complete their work, the strike had been called to prevent the insertion in the new charter of language giving employers the right to lock out workers. For the Confederation of South African Trade Unions, it was its first nationwide strike under black majority rule. The confederation, a powerful backer of the African National Congress government, may lose some of its credibility as a result of today's lukewarm showing. It said there was 100 percent participation in some areas and 40 to 70 percent in others and said 350,000 workers took to the streets in different cities. But journalists estimated no more than 10,000 in Johannesburg, 8,000 in Cape Town and Pretoria and fewer in smaller cities. Though technically a strike, article pointed to the fact that workers took to the streets; hence, this gathering makes this a codeable protest.

EMERGENCY talks were held at the weekend by President Mandela after a gun battle between policemen and Zulu marchers in Durban threatened to disrupt plans for local government elections in the province of KwaZulu/Natal this month. Three policemen and 20 other people were injured on Saturday when the police fought running gun battles with marchers among 7,000 Zulus who descended on the city to protest against the ban on carrying traditional weapons in public. Soon after a memorandum was handed in at the city hall, gunfire broke out from the crowd, sending people running for cover. Police officers chased demonstrators carrying automatic weapons and searched for a sniper in an arcade. The South African leader summoned senior security officials to talks on Saturday evening, hours after armoured troop carriers rolled into a barricaded Durban city centre. The fact that a gun battleÈ happened shows that one of the responses to this protest was shootings as well as crowd dispersal.

An electric-baton attack by security guards on railway fare dodgers led to a riot and a narrow escape from a violent crowd for Inigo Gilmore.
