YOUTHS fought running battles with police yesterday in Tembisa township, 20 miles northeast of Johannesburg, as they vented their anger after a rush-hour railway station stampede left 15 people dead and more than 50 injured. In rare scenes of township violence since the end of apartheid, hundreds of youths rampaged through the dusty streets around the station vowing to kill the security guards. They also set upon journalists at the scene. Riot police, firing rubber bullets and teargas, chased the mob across waste ground where I was standing. As they took up positions, a white policeman beckoned aggressively to his tormentors as they hurled rocks at him. More than 50 people were reportedly admitted to a hospital in the township with injuries caused by electric shocks.  Residents have pledged to conduct an arson campaign to protest at transport conditions in the township and the heavy-handed use of force by security guards at the main commuter station. The guards have been accused of provoking a stampede by firing shots and using electric batons on commuters. Metro Rail yesterday withdrew its security personnel for fear of aggravating the situation. The bizarre incident occurred during morning rush hour as thousands of workers and students in this black township 15 miles north of Johannesburg tried to board the trains, but were greeted by ticket-checking security guards on a mission to stop fare evasion. Tembisa station, which handles 17,000 commuters a day from this sprawling township of several hundred thousand, draws an especially heavy crowd of non-payers, Mateya said. Metrorail tried to crack down this week by adding 14 extra security guards to the usual contingent of eight. Faced with a rush of commuters Wednesday, the guards used their electric prods to try to stop ticketless passengers from assembling on the station platforms.  Since the rail is a state-owned enterprise and this riot was triggered by a change in policy (number of security guards and checking tickets), this was considered a codeable protest.

Rioting erupted here [Cape Town] today when South African police and troops moved in on a march by armed Muslim protesters who have vowed to eradicate drug dealing by local criminal gangs. The police fired rubber bullets and tear gas at the vanguard of some 5,000 marchers, mostly young men wearing headscarves and chanting "God is Great!" who tried to break through a police roadblock. Soldiers with rifles and gas masks poured in to support the police. A police spokesman said nine people had been wounded in the rioting, most of them by a hand grenade that was thrown at the police but that landed in the crowd instead. The clashes died down when demonstrators later headed to Gatesville, the largest mosque in the area, for evening prayers, some chanting, "One gangster, one bullet!" The marchers vowed to become vigilantes because the local police has been inadequate in doing so.  Thus, the demand for this protest was considered to be political process.  In recent months, masked Muslim vigilantes allegedly have shot up the homes of drug dealers. They besieged the home of the nation's justice minister, also a Muslim, to protest law enforcement inaction. Then last week, with police and cameramen watching, vigilantes shrouded in masks and traditional kaffiyeh scarves shot and burned to death an infamous drug merchant. Although many Muslims supported the anti-apartheid struggle waged by President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, they are growing concerned about the new government's liberalism, including its abolition of the death penalty and its support for abortion rights, a Muslim leader said. Some Muslims, who under apartheid were classified as mixed-race "Coloreds," feel alienated from the black majority, with whom they share neither language nor culture. In a nation whose crime rate is said to be the highest in the world, the neighborhoods of the Flats have been ravaged by gangsters and drug dealers. Scores of gangs have been operating here for two decades, and they have become more entrenched during this transition to full democracy and the influx of the international drug trade. They also have been strengthened by police collusion -- first for political aims under apartheid, when some gangsters were recruited as informants, and now for monetary gain as well as protection from their past malfeasance, according to criminologist Wilfried Scharf of the University of Cape Town.

A protester makes a peace sign after South African police fired teargas and stun grenades yesterday at hundreds of Zulus, some armed with handguns and traditional weapons, demonstrating on the East Rand over eviction from a township. About 800 residents associated with the Inkatha Freedom Party in the township of Thokoza had started marching towards council offices in the nearby town of Alberton after chasing away officials who tried to serve eviction notices (Inigo Gilmore writes). The residents fired shots before police cordoned off roads and fired stun grenades to disperse the crowd. The trouble had its roots in violence during the run-up to the 1994 election, in which Thokoza was a focal point. Supporters of President Mandela's African National Congress fled their homes when Inkatha supporters occupied them. Since then the township has been divided, with ANC supporters living in one half and Inkatha supporters in the other.

MUSLIM vigilantes fought running battles with police for more than an hour at Cape Town's international airport yesterday over their demands that drug-detection equipment be installed at customs posts. The illegal protest by People Against Gangsterism and Drugs (Pagad) and the subsequent riot caused disruption as hundreds of British tourists began arriving in South Africa for a Christmas break. The group's gambit of demonstrating at the airport and other choice tourist venues has brought it into direct conflict with the Government. Five people were injured in the riot, including two journalists, after 200 Pagad members pelted police with stones. Police retaliated with rubber bullets and teargas. The violence erupted near the airport entrance when Pagad refused to disperse. Witnesses said the marchers, chanting "Mandela is a dictator", were given ten minutes to leave. As the march leader tried to turn them back, a woman hurled an object at police, triggering the riot. The Government has banned Pagad from carrying weapons and wearing masks during its protests. Last week President Mandela warned it that the Government would not tolerate protests at airports and other tourist venues.

Residents of mainly mixed-race neighborhoods around Johannesburg took to the streets today, blocking roads with debris and burning tires, throwing rocks and in some cases looting stores to protest what they say is discrimination by South Africa's new Government. Early in the day the police used tear gas and rubber bullets to quell the protests, but later they turned to buckshot and live rounds of ammunition. There were unconfirmed reports that four people, including one young boy, had been killed and hospitals in the area reported treating more than 30 people for various injuries. Under apartheid, mixed-race people had more privileges than blacks and are generally richer and better educated. But the community group that organized the protest is questioning why the mixed-race community is paying fees based on meter readings when vast areas of Soweto are being asked to pay a small fixed fee. But in addition to objecting to the fees, many of the protesters expressed a far broader anger at a sense that they were being left out of the new South Africa. In Westbury, hundreds of people clustered at intersections along the main road building barricades and taunting police officers. Whenever the officers tried to take the barriers away, demonstrators would restore them within minutes. At one point, a taxi driver who tried to get through was hauled from his car and slapped by the demonstrators. The police eventually scattered the crowd with tear gas and rubber bullets. The most dramatic incidents were in the Eldorado Park neighborhood where the protesters and the police clashed repeatedly during the day. At one point, a mob smashed the windows of a service station and convenience store and began making off with cartons of sodas and bags of rolls. A police helicopter began circling and firing from the air and riot police officers arrived with tear gas. But half an hour later, the police had moved off and the crowd continued its work until every shelf was stripped bare. TROOPS moved into Coloured suburbs of Johannesburg last night after a day of running gun battles between police and residents in which at least four people - one a boy, aged seven - were reported killed and 200 injured. Police, who tackled rampaging mobs with buckshot, rubber bullets and teargas, said they had been forced to open fire in the rundown mixed-race Eldorado Park and Westbury districts, where a one-day work stoppage was called to protest against evictions and the cutting of electricity supplies over non-payment of rent.

Thousands of Zulus marched angrily through downtown Johannesburg today in a show of strength that ended in gunfire, reminding South Africa of its simmering political rivalries. The protest marked the unpunished killings of eight people in a similar demonstration in 1994, shortly before the country's first all-race election that ended apartheid. The police reported at least two deaths and nine injuries -- eight from gunshots -- during the day, which began with violence in black townships as Zulu nationalists traveled to Johannesburg for a rally at the central library. Zulu leaders dressed in tribal costumes led regiments of their followers armed with everything from traditional wooden clubs to rusty mop handles. Speakers at the rally called for justice for the killings three years ago, when security guards at African National Congress headquarters opened fire on approaching Zulu marchers. When the rally ended, shooting began in the downtown streets, causing marchers, police and bystanders to dive for cover. The sound of pistols and automatic weapons echoed off the tall buildings for several minutes. The police said eight people were arrested. The angryÈ marching and the fact that the Zulus were armed pointed towards the fact that the protesters were violent. At a rally in the Library Gardens in central Johannesburg a man in the massed ranks of Zulu marchers, allegedly aligned to the Inkatha Freedom Party, began firing into the air. As shots rang out, demonstrators among the estimated 18,000 crowd fled along nearby streets as policemen took up positions behind parked cars.

Hundreds of black demonstrators in South Africa marched in support of black students at a high school beset by racial violence. The marchers demanded that the school, in a white area that has resisted racial integration, be closed and its principal and governing body be removed. The center of it all, the formerly all-white Vryburg High, now is shut down and ringed by a wall of razor wire -- the latest unsettling symbol of just how fragile South Africa's new democracy is in the nation's remote reaches.

Protester Group Identity: The People Against Gangsterism and Drugs
Notes: South African police officers fired tear gas at hundreds of Muslims to break up an illegal march against widespread gangsterism. The People Against Gangsterism and Drugs had permission to march against drug lords in the Cape Flats township, which houses most of Cape Town's poor. But the crowd took an unauthorized route after police said every protester had to submit to a body search.

Johannesburg: Tens of thousands of trade unionists staged a one-day general strike across South Africa in protest against the Government's economic policies and rising unemployment. The stoppage cost the economy millions of pounds. At the same time the currency touched a new low of 10.86 rands to the pound and 7.16 rands to the dollar.

Thousands of people held a protest rally at City Hall before the meeting opened, with Winnie Madikizela-Mandela and others in the crowd berating the government for failing to speak frankly about the link between H.I.V. and AIDS and lagging in its efforts to fight the epidemic. "AIDS exists," said Mrs. Madikizela-Mandela, the ex-wife of former President Nelson Mandela and a political leader in her own right. "H.I.V. causes AIDS. We cannot proclaim this century the African century and then ignore the AIDS pandemic as some political leaders are."

HUNDREDS of white farmers gathered at the Dutch Reformed Church here to protest against the return of the first white-owned property to its original black owners yesterday, and accused the South African Government of Thabo Mbeki of carrying out a "Mugabe-style" land grab. About 300 white farmers and their supporters from the Lydenburg area, once a heartland of the extreme right-wing AWB movement, started a legal campaign against what they called a "monstrous assault" on white property rights. The accusation comes after Pretoria's decision to press ahead with the expropriation of a 3,000-acre property belonging to Willem Pretorius, a white farmer from Lydenburg in Mpumalanga Province, to return the land to its original black owners. Kwape Mmela, of the Commission on the Restitution of Land Rights, dismissed Mr Pretorius's accusations of a Zimbabwe-style land grab. "You cannot use state money to develop a farm and expect the Government to give more state money to buy it back."

HUNDREDS of policemen swooped on a squatter camp outside Johannesburg yesterday after the Pretoria Government announced that it would move swiftly to prevent any Zimbabwe-style land grabs in South Africa. Armoured vehicles were sent at dawn to a field at Bredell, near the city's international airport, where thousands of landless black people had been queuing for days to "buy" a plot of land for 25 rand (Pounds 2). The Pan African Congress (PAC), a small radical party, began "selling" plots of land owned by the local council in protest at the slow pace of the Government's land reform programme. More than 70 people, including two members of the PAC, were arrested for trespassing after police armed with shotguns blocked access to the field and began patrolling the camp to prevent the squatters bringing in building materials to erect makeshift homes. About 20,000 people were estimated to have been at the site.

In riot gear and armored cars, the police arrived at noon, escorting construction workers who tore through the warren of tin shacks with crowbars, leaving one home after another in a heap of scrap metal and ripped tarpaulin. With nowhere to go, hundreds of squatters who settled on the sprawling, dusty patch of land known as Elandsfontein Farm 12 watched as their homes were flattened. Men shook their fists defiantly at the police, while women chanted anti-government slogans and danced in protest, baring their breasts to taunt the demolition crews. Authorities arrested 110 of the squatters last week, and most of the others packed up and left, leaving a few hundred still on the land.

About 200 angry squatters occupied land in Khayelitsha township in Cape Town, emulating a larger land invasion outside Johannesburg earlier this month. The squatters moved onto the private land during the afternoon, the police said, and demanded that the government build them houses. The squatters measured out plots, marked them with wire and started digging trenches around them.

South Africa has lost thousands of jobs even as Mr. Mbeki's government has been praised by the International Monetary Fund for reducing the deficit and inflation and improving tax collection. Ordinary people say they have suffered from economic restructuring. In August, thousands of workers marched to protest plans to privatize state enterprises. Today, the union said it was a planning a similar march for early next year. "This is not what we expected from the government we voted for," said Mbulelo Bara, 30, an assembly worker who attended the meeting. "Huge numbers of jobs are being lost. The dissatisfaction of workers must be dealt with." Since this article discussed a past protest, wires were then searched to see if any specific information could be found: Tens of thousands of trade unionists demonstrated in cities across South Africa on Thursday to demand that the government abandon plans to privatise state-owned enterprises.

Fifty-two protesters were arrested after about 2,000 landless South Africans marched in Johannesburg to demand an end to forced removals from squatter camps. Those arrested refused to move away from a government office they had put under siege, a police spokeswoman said.  Under siege implies protester violence.

The black protesters marched by the thousands today through the gritty heart of this mining city. They shouted angry slogans, waved fiery banners and, for a moment, it felt like the old days when blacks took to the streets to oppose the white apartheid government. The demonstrators accused the government of losing touch with the poor, who are struggling to cope with deep unemployment and surging food prices. They demanded an end to the nation's privatization of state assets, which they say has resulted in job losses. "Create decent jobs!" the marchers cried. "Privatization is born-again apartheid!"

Stepping up a civil disobedience campaign aimed at forcing the government to provide drugs for AIDS patients, about 50 activists shouted down the country's health minister, Manto Tshabalala-Msimang, as she made a speech in Cape Town, and called for her resignation. The government contends that the antiretroviral drugs are too expensive.

Activists jeered South Africa's health minister today at the opening of a national AIDS conference, reflecting mounting anger at the government's tepid response to the disease, which activists say kills 600 South Africans a day. Protesters holding up signs reading "Save Our Youth, Save Our Future, Treat AIDS Now" heckled the health minister, Manto Tshabalala-Msimang, as she opened the conference attended by 2,500 delegates in the port city of Durban. Critics say that South Africa has moved too slowly in addressing HIV-AIDS and that the government's refusal to permit public sector hospitals to use anti-retroviral drugs, the only medicines that have proved effective against AIDS, has stoked anger. President Thabo Mbeki's government has questioned the drugs as expensive, potentially dangerous and difficult to take, arguing that South Africa's priority must be on fighting the widespread black poverty that remains nine years after the end of white rule. The number of protesters is coded as 100+ because although there were 2500 people attending the conference, it is not known whether all 2500 of these attendees were protesters.

Protester Group Identity: Victims of Crimes and their Allies
Notes: THE centre of Johannesburg was brought to a standstill yesterday as thousands of demonstrators took to the streets in an unprecedented protest against murder, hijackings, violent robbery and rape. In scenes reminiscent of the mass marches against apartheid, people of every race and creed walked side by side demanding urgent government action to end the high crime rates that are blighting their lives. Impoverished shack-dwellers from black townships and squatter camps linked arms with the well-heeled residents of the affluent white suburbs, chanting "Enough is enough". Many of the protesters in South Africa's first multiracial march against violent crime had lost relatives in robberies, car hijackings and assaults, or had been the victims of crime during the ten years since black majority rule. Representatives of every political party took part in the march, except the ANC, which reneged on a promise to join the protesters and accept a memorandum from the organisers demanding a nationwide anti-crime campaign. Mrs Vince-Jillings, who founded the Alive Campaign to encourage the Government to take more effective action against crime, has given the ANC three months to respond to Alive's demand to publish the crime statistics, increase police numbers in urban areas and allocate far more resources to prosecute the perpetrators of violent offences.

Thousands of public workers staged some of the biggest protests since the end of apartheid, pressuring the government for wage increases for teachers, nurses and other workers. The police estimated that more than 12,000 people jammed the streets of Johannesburg while another 2,000 protesters gathered in front of Parliament in Cape Town. Union officials reported large turnouts in other cities. The protests follow a string of other demonstrations demanding better housing and more jobs. The sustained public pressure is intended to make the governing African National Congress deliver on promises that helped it win the elections in April.

His visit provoked protests by hundreds of Muslim South Africans who staged marches in three cities over the weekend demanding that their country cut economic ties with Israel. A handful of picketers gathered Wednesday outside the Sandton Convention Center, where the investment agreement was due to be signed, chanting "Free Palestine" and holding placards reading "Boycott apartheid Israel." Police moved the demonstrators across the street, and they dispersed before Olmert arrived. Since this protest included calls for the South African government to cut ties with Israel, this was considered as being against the government.

Police officers used rubber bullets and water cannons against 1,000 students at Tshwane University of Technology protesting tuition increases and housing shortages at their campus in Soshanguve, north of Pretoria. The riot was spawned by the students' contention that the university had doubled tuition instead of raising it by a promised 6 percent. The university says that fees had been sharply raised for some individual courses but that the basic tuition rate was not greatly increased. The students set fire to a police vehicle and stoned motorists and police officers before being dispersed. Michael Wines (NYT)

Sending what some call an ominous signal to this nation's leaders, South Africa's sprawling shantytowns have begun to erupt, sometimes violently, in protest over the government's inability to deliver the better life that the end of apartheid seemed to herald a dozen years ago. At a hillside shantytown in Durban called Foreman Road, riot police officers fired rubber bullets in mid-November to disperse 2,000 residents marching to the municipal mayor's office downtown. Two protesters were injured; 45 were arrested. The rest burned an effigy of the city's mayor, Obed Mlaba. Lacking cars, taxi fare or even bicycles to commute to work, the residents marched in protest on Nov. 14, defying the city's refusal to issue a permit. The demonstration quickly turned violent. This article also refers to other protests but unfortunately there is not enough information available to confidently code them.

Thousands of South Africans marched through Cape Town to Parliament on Saturday to demand sanctions against Israel for its strikes against Lebanon and the Palestinian territories. They urged the South African government to recall its ambassador from Israel and sever diplomatic ties impose trade sanctions and prosecute South Africans who serve in the Israeli Defense Force. Since the protesters are demanding action from their government and are not just protesting the actions of a foreign nation, this demonstration was coded.

Thousands of South African workers marched in sympathy with striking civil servants yesterday in the biggest show of force against the Government since the end of apartheid. Bringing city centres across the country to a halt, demonstrators demanded higher salaries for teachers nurses and policemen, highlighting the divide between the ruling African National Congress (ANC)and its trade union allies. The powerful Confederation of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu), one of the main allies of the ANC-led liberation movement, called the demonstrations to support a 12-day strike by public sector unions, in which about 600 nurses have been sacked amid intimidation of non-strikers. Patrick Craven, a Cosatu spokesman, estimated that the march in Johannesburg's central business district attracted about 15,000 people. "We just hope this show of force will convince the Government to enter serious negotiations," he said.

Police officers fired water cannons and rubber bullets at about 500 protesters in Soweto after crowds gathered in two neighborhoods, Protea and Kliptown, to complain about municipal services. The Kliptown protest was calm, but the Protea crowd blocked a highway and threw stones at the police and journalists, sending one photographer to a hospital. One protester was killed when a bakery van accidentally backed over him; several others were arrested. Protests over poor services have become common in the country's poorest neighborhoods as the government struggles to provide water, power and other basic utilities to shantytowns and low-income areas.

Almost a quarter of a million mineworkers downed tools yesterday in South Africa, the world's top gold and platinum producer, in the country's first strike over safety conditions in some of the world's deepest mines. Many attended rallies, such as the one in central Johannesburg, organised by the NUM -still by far the most powerful member of the Confederation of South African Trade Unions, which is backing Mr Mbeki's rival Jacob Zuma for the leadership of the party and the country. The protesters handed in a petition outlining their grievances to the Chamber of Mines, the organisation that regulates the industry. Although the strike was national, the actual gathering appears to have taken place mainly in Johannesburg, and so, the location of the protest is coded as that. All the miners were rescued, but state officials subsequently ordered a safety inspection of all 2,800 mines. The audit is to begin later this month.

Hundreds of South African women took to the streets yesterday calling for an end to sexual harassment after a young woman was assaulted by taxi drivers for wearing a miniskirt. The demonstrators marched to the Johannesburg taxi rank where the attack took place, demanding action from the Government and for taxi associations to punish those responsible for such acts. Minibus taxis are notorious for packing in as many passengers as possible and for their poor safety record. Women passengers are often exposed to taunts, jeers and drunken sexual advances from drivers and male travellers. Women activists blame senior African National Congress leaders for not helping to change the way women are treated. They point to the rape trial of Jacob Zuma, president of the ANC, who was acquitted in May 2006, but said in court he knew from the way a woman sat if she wanted sex.

Thousands of members of the national labor federation marched through Johannesburg earlier this month to protest higher food and electricity prices. Since there was a lack of specific information, wires were looked into as well.  Hundreds of trade unionists marched in South Africa's largest city on Thursday in a protest over rising food prices and the country's electricity crisis. Around 1,500 demonstrators marched on a branch of retail chain Pick'n'Pay in Johannesburg city centre to demand a hold on food prices and an end to price-fixing.

Thousands of people marched through Johannesburg on Saturday, calling for an end to the violence that has killed at least 50 African migrants and forced tens of thousands to flee their homes. Demonstrators carrying placards saying "Xenophobia hurts like apartheid" and "We stand against xenophobia" brought traffic to a standstill in the city center. Police said that townships around Johannesburg were quiet but that shops were looted and burned outside Cape Town late Friday. The South African government has been criticized for its slow reaction to the violence, the worst since apartheid ended 14 years ago, and for not addressing the poverty that many blame for the bloodshed. South Africa has been disgraced by a wave of violence against foreigners that has left at least 50 dead, President Thabo Mbeki  said. In a nationally televised address, Mbeki said South Africans' heads were "bowed" and called the violence an "absolute disgrace.?ó? "The shameful actions of a few have blemished the name of South Africa," he said. Mbeki said South Africans should remember that their economy was built with the help of migrants and that its neighbors had helped fight apartheid and some had died for their efforts.

Last week there were demonstrations in major cities of South Africa, with calls for the government to impose price controls on foods. Due to a lack of specific information in the original article, wires were searched as well.  A protest march by thousands of trade unionists against rising fuel and food costs closed down businesses and disrupted public transport in South Africa's port city of Durban on Wednesday. COSATU, a junior partner in President Thabo Mbeki's governing coalition, has organised a series of protests in the coming weeks against the rise in costs of household goods as well as a threatened major hike in electricity bills. However a similar march in central Cape Town attracted only around 2,000 people in the pouring rain.

The South African police fired tear gas and rubber bullets at protesters demanding improved services and more jobs on Wednesday in a township near Balfour, in one of the biggest challenges to President Jacob Zuma  since he took office. The marchers, numbering in the thousands, said they would escalate the demonstrations if local officials from the governing African National Congress failed to deliver swiftly on promises to provide jobs, housing and medical care. Some protesters burned tires and hurled stones at police officers in armored vehicles, who responded with tear gas. Wires were looked into as well, since not enough information was available in the original search. Protesters have again brought violence to township streets throughout South Africa over state failure to deliver on longstanding promises of housing and social services for all, but the discontent and frustration run much deeper. By 23 July the media had reported widespread violent protests in the provinces of Mpumalanga, Gauteng, North West and Western Cape over poor access to housing, electricity, water and health care.

Hundreds of council workers rampaged through central Johannesburg yesterday in a "trash" protest marking the first day of a nationwide strike over wages and benefits by 150,000 municipal employees. Singing and chanting liberation songs from the struggle era, protesters emptied rubbish bins and scattered litter across the roads as a long column of T-shirt-clad strikers danced and weaved its way through the nearly deserted heart of South Africa's commercial centre. The current strike is in pursuit of a 15 per cent wage increase. The employers have offered 11.5 per cent. Inflation is put at just over 8 per cent, but the country - heavily dependent on commodities - is in recession for the first time in 17 years.

Cape Town As many as 1,300 soldiers who clashed with police during a violent wage protest last week are to be dismissed. Some military experts fear, however, that the move will create a backlash that could threaten national security in South Africa. "There are between 1,500 and 2,000 people we are looking at. We have sent out letters of dismissal and they will have ten days to come and make representations," ministry spokesman Ndivhuwo Mabaya told AFP. The government has lashed out at the protest on August 26, when soldiers tried to scale the fence at the Union Buildings where President Jacob Zuma has his office. Police used teargas, rubber bullets and water cannons to disperse the soldiers, who marched despite a court order barring their protest. The soldiers were marching to demand higher wages, but the unruly protest has raised questions about the discipline of South Africa's 62,000-strong military.

Thousands of children marched to City Hall this week in sensible black shoes, a stream of boys and girls from township schools across this seaside city that extended for blocks, passing in a blur of pleated skirts, blazers and rep ties. Their polite demand: Give us libraries and librarians. The new protest movement, with its practical goals, youthful organizers and idealistic moniker, Equal Education, is a quintessentially South African answer to a failing education system, one that self-consciously acknowledged its debt to the past in the march to City Hall. The marchers, stretched out Tuesday along Main Road in the shadow of majestic Table Mountain, were themselves a wealth of stories.

The African National Congress party said Thursday that it had fired the mayor and other officials in the Lekwa municipality in Mpumalanga Province to show ''zero tolerance'' for mismanagement and corruption. Sakhile Township there has been racked by protests against what residents see as crooked, incompetent local leaders. In another protest in Sakhile township, also in Mpumalanga, police had to use rubber bullets to disperse a group of protesters who were calling for the resignation of the mayor and councillors. Residents in South Africa's impoverished townships burnt tyres and barricaded streets on Tuesday, in a fresh wave of violent protests over poor service delivery. A further protest, near Johannesburg, saw police arrest three people after a municipal councillor's house was set on fire. Although the articles discuss how these protests began before the 13th and some continued after, no specifics were given and it is unknown if these are continued overnight protests.  Thus, this is coded as just being a one-day protest.

DURBAN, South Africa - A World Cup Sunday that began at the soaring new arch of Durban Stadium ended in smoke and shrieks as police officers fired tear gas and what witnesses said were rubber bullets to break up a large group of protesting security guards. It began in the parking area underneath the stadium, where some administrative offices are located. It soon spilled into the streets outside as several hundred panicked protesters sprinted away as about 40 police officers advanced toward them on foot. Several of the guards said they and their colleagues were upset at being underpaid or, in some cases, not being paid for their work Sunday, the first day of competition in Durban. Controversy over the vuvuzela dominated South Africa news even as the World Cup was hit by its first violence - riot police clashed with 500 security staff in a pay dispute at Durban's Moses Mabhida stadium after Germany's 4-0 win over Australia on Sunday night. Officers fired rubber bullets and stun grenades.

More than a million public sector workers went on strike yesterday across South Africa, threatening chaos as the country faces the bill for hosting the World Cup (writes Jonathan Clayton).Scuffles were reported outside schools and hospitals as the biggest stoppage for almost four years got under way. Workers held placards stating their demands as they danced and sang. Some shouted and spat at non-strikers, including hospital patients and volunteer teachers.The Government has offered a 7 per cent salary increase and a 700 rand (£60) monthly housing allowance. The unions, led by the mighty Confederation of South African Trade Unions are demanding an 8.6 per cent increase. Although technically a strike, there is enough indication that there were actual gatherings to protest for the wage increase.

Thousands of public service workers marched through cities across South Africa on the ninth day of a crippling strike, with unions threatening a total industrial shutdown. The workers sang and waved placards as they marched, vowing that the strike would continue until the Government granted their pay demands. Unions are insisting on an 8.6 per cent salary increase and a 1,000 rand (£88) housing allowance. The Government is offering a 7 per cent rise and a 700 rand allowance.

Hundreds of members of the youth movement of the African National Congress (ANC) brought chaos to the centre of Johannesburg yesterday, throwing bottles and stones and demanding the removal of President Zuma. The violent protest, prompted by moves within the ruling party to bring its firebrand youth leaders before a disciplinary committee, was met by police using stun grenades and water cannon. Helicopters hovered and police reinforcements waited in side streets as angry supporters of Julius Malema, the ANC Youth League (ANCYL) President, hurled insults at local and foreign journalists and set ablaze T-shirts bearing the picture of President Zuma. At least one policeman was taken to hospital and five journalists injured.

South Africa's ruling party pushed a Bill through parliament yesterday to protect state secrets, sparking an outcry over threats to democracy and fears that it would make it easier for officials to conceal corruption. Journalists who dressed in black as a protest, walked out of the chamber after the Bill was approved by 229 votes to 107 with the backing of the African National Congress (ANC). Editors of the country's 17 major newspapers published a joint editorial calling it a "day of reckoning for democracy". Tens of thousands of South Africans marched in the streets of the nation's major cities on Wednesday in a national strike called by Cosatu, the powerful group of trade unions, a crucial ally of the governing African National Congress that is growing increasingly critical of its policies. The stated reason for the strike was to protest new highway tolls and the practice of contracting out jobs through temporary-employment firms, at lower pay and with fewer benefits than permanent workers get, a practice known here as labor broking. But the strike tapped a deep undercurrent of dissatisfaction with the A.N.C., which has governed South Africa since white minority rule ended in 1994. Zwelinzima Vavi, the secretary general of Cosatu, said in a fiery speech that racial apartheid was increasingly being replaced by economic apartheid. He said there would be civil disobedience if the government went ahead with its plans to charge tolls on highways that were built with tax money. South Africa is often roiled by protest. Demonstrations, sometimes violent, happen almost daily in the townships where the poor struggle to live without basic services like electricity, water and toilets. But the outpouring on Wednesday came from working people, not the destitute, and their protests took place not in distant townships but in the heart of South Africa's cities. The toll issue was a flashpoint for their anger.  ''We already paid once, why should we pay again?'' said Busi Harishe, 34, a shop clerk who joined the protest. ''Petrol prices are already high. Working people are suffering too much.''

South African police arrested 59 people and the army was called in overnight to quell post-election protests in a Johannesburg slum, the police and news media said Saturday, as the government clamped down on disorder after the victory of the African National Congress at the polls. Neville Malila, said. Alexandra was ''calm this morning,'' he said, adding that security forces remained in the area. Although the ruling African National Congress remains popular with South Africa's black majority after it dismantled the apartheid system in 1994, there is rising discontent among the millions stuck in grinding poverty and without access to running water or electricity. About 500 people gathered in Johannesburg on Saturday to join the international fight to save dwindling rhino and elephant populations. They marched through South Africa's largest city as part of global gatherings for rhinos and elephants that were planned in 136 cities to mark World Animal Day, according to organizers. The demonstrations aimed to raise awareness of the international ivory trade and to press governments to use stricter legal measures to prevent poaching. "We want the South African government also to make changes in legislation," said Dex Kotze, one of the organizers. South African authorities have made more than 100 arrests related to poaching this year and have introduced longer prison sentences, but that has done little to deter poachers. More than 550 rhinos have been killed in South Africa during that time. Another emphasis of the march was to conserve wildlife populations for future generations, and many marchers brought along children.

"We were called in to come to Oshakati in order to get jobs or to be told where we are going to work, but when we came here, travelled long distances, many of us were not taken in for the jobs as promised, why?" the ex-combatants asked. They vowed that they would not return to their villages until they had received firm offers of jobs. From the Governor's office, the demonstrating fighters marched the three kilometres back to the Swapo headquarters on Friday, where they have been camped out ever since. They are sleeping outside in the open air with their children. In a tense standoff at Oshakati, ex-combatants protesting for jobs held four Regional Councillors hostage for nearly five hours at the Swapo head office yesterday afternoon. Initially it appeared as if the officials would be held overnight, with the large group of ex-Plan fighters warning that they would not release them until their demands for work had been met. Although the situation was resolved peacefully and the officials are free, the situation remained tense last night, with more than 600 fighters still entrenched at the Swapo HQ. Since then the group, including many women with young babies, has set up camp outside the building, sleeping in the open air. Their numbers are growing by the day as disgruntled ex-fighters from the regions join the protest. The majority of protesting ex-combatants at Oshakati yesterday vowed not to budge from the premises of the Swapo headquarters until they had 'jobs in hand', and lashed out at the decision to deploy the Special Field Force and Police against them on Tuesday. The ex-combatants were up in arms over the use of the paramilitary forces. "They came in Casspirs with sjamboks and guns as if they were coming to the enemies," outraged protesters told The Namibian. When Regional Councillor and Swapo Regional Co-ordinator Klemens Kashuupulwa, one of the four Councillors held hostage, and Ashipala arrived, they told the ex-combatants that each and every one of them should go back to their constituency as the registration and allocation of jobs would be done there, according to Cabinet policy.

President Sam Nujoma's controversial announcement last week that public demonstrations or processions required written permission from the Police is unlikely to stop a series of peaceful protests on violence against women and children. Protesters approached for comment at last Thursday's weekly gathering in central Windhoek, the fourth of its kind, were unanimous in saying that they would continue to hold peaceful demonstrations and that the barring of demonstrations was undemocratic. Another demonstrator, Helle Jensen, said that citizens of a democratic country should have the right to call demonstrations on issues of public concern and that the prohibition of peaceful demonstrations only happened in military states. "What has happened to the struggle," she asked, saying that she and many other activists from the pre-independence era regularly used to demonstrate in front of the South African Embassy in London when Swapo members were detained. Last Thursday's anti-violence demonstration was attended by around 60 people, including many school children. The weekly protests against the rape and abuse of women and children were sparked by the brutal rape of a two-year-old toddler which left the young child severely injured. Although articles said that these protests took place every Thursday, the number of protesters was only given for this one, and so was the only one which was coded.

Hospital nurses in Windhoek have given the Ministry of Health until the end of the month to pay outstanding overtime payments of around N$20 million, or face further action. The demand was made by nurses at Windhoek and Katutura hospitals yesterday following a protest march from Katutura Hospital to their Ministry's headquarters, where a petition outlining grievances was presented to officials. In a letter signed by Akwenye, management told the nurses that their complaints were being attended to, but a committee representing the nurses insisted that this be told by Akwenye person to a meeting of approximately 1 200 nurses affected by the overtime payments. The Ministry of Health and Social Services has apparently told aggrieved nurses pushing for long outstanding overtime claims that there is no money in the State coffers to pay the N$20 million. Minister Dr Libertina Amathila was this week quoted as saying, "There is no money whether you strike or not." A well-placed source said the Minister told a meeting last week that nurses at State hospitals would have to wait until the next financial year as there was no money in the budget this year.

There was a mixed reaction to the Council of Churches (CCN) call for countrywide demonstrations against the Abortion and Sterilisation Bill yesterday, which appeared to go largely unheeded. In Windhoek around 200 Christians marched on the Swapo Headquarters in Katutura to voice their opposition to the bill, while members of one congregation at Ongwediwa spent half an hour on their knees praying that the bill might not become law. Close to 200 Christians held prayers and a march outside the Swapo Head Office in Katutura, protesting against the proposed Bill. The group, led by Nakamhela, petitioned Health and Social Services Minister Dr Libertina Amathila not to bring the proposed Bill on Abortion and Sterilisation before Parliament, saying that abortion should not be given "on demand".

A crowd of around 250 jobless ex-fighters and other former exiles have camped out in the Parliament Gardens in Windhoek after failing to meet with both President Sam Nujoma and Prime Minister Hage Geingob yesterday. The group marched from Swapo headquarters in Katutura to State House in Windhoek in a bid to have an audience with President Sam Nujoma. But the Deputy Secretary to the President Kondja Kambala informed the protesters that Nujoma had jetted out of the country to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Scotland. "We ex-combatants we need jobs because we have been here for eight years without having jobs," one of the placards read. In their petition, the protesters demanded that they be given jobs before the end of the year. They also voiced dissatisfaction at that fact that a number of Ministries had not recruited former combatants this year. Several hundred former fighters have been camped out in the gardens for just over two weeks. They are demanding jobs from Government, and have vowed not to leave the gardens until President Sam Nujoma addresses them on their grievances. Josef said they would stick to their decision not to leave the gardens. "We will not leave this place until the President comes. Let hunger kill us. He must come or send someone to talk to us," Josef told The Namibian. President Sam Nujoma is to deliver a statement on national television "in the near future" about the issue of demonstrations by ex- combatants. This was announced by Minister of Information and Broadcasting Ben Amathila during Cabinet's weekly press briefing yesterday. At present around 200 former fighters are camped out in the Parliament Gardens in Windhoek demanding jobs. They marched on State House on October 23 demanding an audience with the President, who had just left the country to attend a series of international engagements. He returned on Friday.

About 200 former fighters have gathered at President Sam Nujoma's home town of Okahao in the northern Omusati region to demand that Government give them jobs. Like other similar protests going on around the country, the demonstrators have vowed not to disperse until Nujoma has addressed them and listened to their grievances. And a group of about 200 ex-fighters are also camping at Okahao, Nujoma's home town. These two groups have also vowed not to abandon their protest until the President has addressed them. Another 400-plus ex-fighters have gathered at the President's home village of Okahao and have vowed not to budge until Nujoma has addressed them and listened to their grievances.

Namibian men who can be respected as role models and family leaders are fast becoming "an endangered species", Minister of Lands, Resettlement and Rehabilitation, Pendukeni Iiluva-Ithana, told a demonstration against rape and sexual abuse staged by Swakopmund parents this weekend. Speaking to an audience of about 100 people who had gathered in town after a peaceful march through Mondesa and Tamariskia, Ithana asked, "Where are the men today? Do they not consider this occasion to be worthy of support or notice?" The demonstrators, including a number of small children, wore placards asking the same questions put by other grieving women in other stricken towns over the past two years as reports of child rape escalate and legal reform lumbers on in low gear. "Where are the new laws?", "Why are sentences so light?", "Why are we not protected?", "What say our menfolk?"

Pensioners from the Katutura and Khomasdal areas of Windhoek participated in an angry demonstration against high-priced municipal services in front of the municipal buildings in the capital's Independence Avenue Tuesday. The demonstration was organised by Ada/Gui, which means "Let's Unite", an organisation representing senior citizens of the city. Johannes Hendricks, an Ada/Gui representative, said pensioners could not afford to pay high electricity and water bills with their meagre state pensions. He added that several pensioners' houses had been repossessed by the municipality following non-payment of accounts. He said it was also unfair to expect pensioners to pay these amounts in full before they could purchase houses under the city's alienation scheme. Hoabeb and Ueitele expressed sympathy with the pensioners, but said they should see municipal officials on a personal basis, rather than en masse as they had done. Speaking in Afrikaans, Hoabeb said he wanted to see people come to the municipality to discuss their financial problems on a "person to person" basis. The officials said they did not want to condemn anyone, but that they had to consider each case on its own merits. The pensioners meeting en masseÈ implies that pensioners met as a large group, so the number of protesters is recorded as 50+.

Loud cheers of approval greeted each demand of the Namibia National Teachers Union (Nantu) petition as it was read out at Swakopmund on Wednesday before being handed to Regional Director for Education, Linus Garoeb. A particularly resounding cheer was reserved for the final point condemning "current tendencies of self-enrichment of political office- bearers at the expense of the Namibian population", as the crowd of about 250 teachers, learners and parents made their feelings known. Speaking just before the start of the march, Jantjies said that while Swakop teachers' grievances were generally in line with the national demonstration, they were particularly concerned about low staffing levels and poor maintenance of buildings. Receiving the petition on behalf of the Regional Education Director, De Castro said he would forward a copy to both Garoeb and the Minister of Basic Education with his own comments attached.

Teachers countrywide yesterday gave Government two weeks to act on their grievances or face action, as thousands of educationalists countrywide took to the streets. The teachers did not spell out what action they planned to take, but presented Government with a comprehensive list of matters they want dealt with. In Windhoek a petition outlining the grievances and demands was handed to Basic Education Minister John Mutorwa by Namibia National Teachers' Union (Nantu) President Elias Manga following a demonstration by an estimated 1 000 teachers through the streets of the capital. Similar demos were held in other regions where the same petition was handed to senior regional Basic Education Ministry officials. The Namibian's Oswald Shivute reported that between 4 000 to 5 000 teachers marched at Ondangwa, with teachers streaming from outlying schools - some up to 200 kilometres away - to join the demonstration. From the coast, The Namibian's Kate Burling reported that there had been a good turn-out at both Swakopmund and Walvis Bay, with around 250 teachers, drawn from a wide spectrum of the teaching profession, staging a spirited protest at both the coastal towns. They demanded: * that the Ministry of Basic Education immediately stop the illegal implementation of the staffing norms * that their pay structure be revised and improved within two weeks and that all civil servants receive salary increments with the exception of the management cadre which consists of deputy directors_etc.

Only one man joined a march by hundreds of women who took time off work and from household chores on Friday to draw the attention of Swakopmund and the entire Namibian nation to the ongoing tragedy of violence against women and children. As expected the peaceful protest, with 'mourners' dressed in black and carrying flickering white candles as they sang age-old anthems of hope, was extremely well attended. By the time it arrived at the Magistrates Court, where Thomas Florin was due to appear charged with the murder of his wife, Monika, more than 800 people had gathered. Beverley Figaji explained to Magistrate Elton Hoff that the petition contained more than 7 000 signatures and asked that bail be denied to anyone accused of a serious crime against women and children. "Courts do not exist in isolation. They live among the community. They are not there to please themselves but to serve us," she said, underlining the 'no bail' demand and calling for stricter sentences for people convicted of serious crimes against women and children.

Women at Rehoboth feel that the town's Magistrate 'must go' and deem him incompetent to deal with matters relating to violence against women and children. The group of approximately 60 women went to hand over a petition to express concern over violence against women and children at Rehoboth. They were reportedly told to "f. . .k off" by Nangula when they congregated in front of his office. The group of women have forwarded a statement to the offices of the Multi Media Campaign on Violence Against Women and Children in Windhoek who have requested the Ministry of Justice to investigate the matter.

The number of protesting former Swapo combatants at Okahao grew to over 200 yesterday with some of the ex-fighters saying they were prepared to maintain their vigil "until death" if they were not given jobs. Demonstrators Ilya Nakambale and Ndategapo Shipulwa said yesterday that no regional leaders from either the Government or Swapo had come to speak to them since they started their protest six days ago. They said they would stay at Okahao until President Sam Nujoma came to address them. "The kids are feeling cold, we do not have proper blankets, we do not have enough food, but we are going to stay here at Okahao until our demands have been met by the Government," Nakambale said. The ex-fighters started their demonstration last Thursday. Around 330 former Plan fighters protesting their plight at Okahao town in the Omusati Region have shifted their battle front to Outapi, and have vowed to march on Oshakati and even Windhoek if their pleas continue to be ignored. The ex-combatants, now in their third week of demonstrations, have directed a desperate plea to the authorities and President Sam Nujoma in particular to help find them employment. So far their call for help has fallen on deaf ears. Former Plan fighters protesting for jobs in northern Namibia say they will stay put at Ondangwa airport until Government helps them find employment despite an appeal by President Sam Nujoma on Friday that they return home. The now more than 480 ex-fighters in the North, including pregnant women and mothers with their small children, marched on foot from Outapi to Oshakati on Thursday and initially planned to take their 'march for jobs' to Windhoek. However, Swapo's chief for the Oshana Region, Klemence Kashuupulwa, stopped them as they marched towards Ondangwa on Friday and told them the President would speak to them. However, when the leaders briefed the group, which had swelled to 650 by Friday evening, they responded by saying that when they had gone home in the past nothing had happened. Three weeks of protests by former Plan fighters in the North has resulted in jobs being lined up for at least 100 of the ex- combatants. The Namibia Protection Service company (NPS) has offered employment to about 100 of the 650 ex-fighters who have now converged on Ondangwa Airport calling on Government to help them find work. A source told The Namibian yesterday that President Sam Nujoma had met with the head of NPS, Alfonso Ngeama at Ondangwa Airport yesterday afternoon and had discussed the employment of 100 ex-fighters in the security company. Hundreds of former fighters have vowed to remain camped at Ondangwa airport despite a call from the Cabinet Technical Committee on Ex- Combatants that they should return to their homes and await news on jobs they have been promised. Some 580 ex-fighters are currently at the airport, where they have lived since August as part of a long-running protest demanding jobs. Yesterday the former combatants said they would remain at the airport until they had received clarification about the process through which they are supposed to obtain jobs in the Government. The next phase of the socio-economic integration programme would not cover Ondangwa airport but regional capitals. The Government last week said it would employ or give pensions to some 9 500 unemployed ex- fighters. In August there were 3000 people there, but the Government said last week that only 1392 of this group qualify for jobs under the new scheme. Only former Plan fighters and those who are currently without means of subsistence who were in exile, but too young to fight in Plan can be registered for jobs.

And in Windhoek a growing number of ex-combatants, now well over 100, have also vowed to stand their ground until they are given solid offers of work. They are camped out in Zoo Park in the heart of the capital and close to State House. On Friday night the Windhoek group slept on one side of Peter Muller Street, opposite Luderitz Street, braving windy and sometimes wet conditions as odd showers fell during the night. The number of mainly ex-fighters and former Namibian exiles currently camping out in the heart of the capital demanding that Government help them find jobs has now increased to 780, one of the leaders of the group told The Namibian yesterday. After marching from Katutura last Thursday, the group, which at that time numbered around 100, has set up home in Zoo Park. More than 1 000 ex-Plan fighters and war orphans currently camped at Zoo Park in downtown Windhoek say they will march on State House today if the President or any other senior Government official does not address them. The ex-fighters and orphans are calling on Government to help them find jobs. By yesterday afternoon the number of protesters in the Zoo Park had increased to 1 026, with more and more streaming in from different parts of the country. A spokesperson for the Windhoek demonstrators said yesterday that she and her colleagues were happy that their recent protests had jolted the Government into seeking a technical rather than a political solution to their plight. The demonstrators had previously complained that no senior Government official had addressed them since they started their protest 11 days ago. More than 1 500 former 'war disadvantaged' have been camped out in Windhoek since early this month, first at Zoo Park in the centre of the capital's central business district and subsequently at the Showgrounds. Since the registration exercise ended on Friday, the group - which earlier last week numbered over 1 500 - has gradually dwindled to about 300 people who have been sleeping outside the Windhoek Showgrounds.

A Decision on proposed massive salary hikes for top Municipal officials were put on ice - for now - at last night's Windhoek City Council meeting, which also attracted a public demonstration. The proposals, which were were originally due to be discussed at last night's meeting, included upping the pay of the Municipality's Chief Executive Officer to N$637 000 a year and increases of between 39 and 44 per cent for other highly-paid officials. Shortly before the meeting around 100 placard-waving Windhoek residents opposed to the 'gravy train' hikes converged on Town Hall to make their views on the huge salaries clear. 'Stop The Blood Suckers', 'Stop The Increases, 'Shame on You Council' and 'Municipality Fat Cats' were some of the messages articulated on the posters. The protesters also attended the meeting. However, the meeting, which was chaired by Matthew Shikongo and attended by all Councillors, decided that the issue should be discussed further at a Management Council meeting to be called soon. The delay is recorded as accommodation in that the protesters were able to temporarily get what they desired.

Residents from a number of villages close to Namibia's border with Angola in the west of Ohangwena Region on Friday staged a march to back earlier appeals to Government to protect them from armed gangs in military uniforms that are terrorising them. They believe that the best solution would be for Government to set up a military base in the area. Gang members are accused by residents of abducting women across the border into Angola where they are raped and then sent back into Namibia. The Namibian spoke to some of the alleged victims at Ohangwena last Friday. Placard-brandishing villagers, most of them women and children, held a peaceful march on Friday, starting from their villages in the west of Ohangwena and Oshikango towns and proceeding to Ohangwena Police Station, where they handed their petition to the Commander of the Ohangwena Police, Inspector I Hainghumbi. Hainghumbi also told them that he had deployed Police and Special Field Force officers in the affected areas to protect the villagers and arrest criminals found there. The villagers said this was inadequate and felt a military base in the area would be the best solution. Although the villagers are protesting against the violence from Angolan citizens, they are also critiquing the lack of adequate protection from their own government; hence this protest was included.  It is coded as 50+ due to the number of villages which took place in the protest.

Students at the Polytechnic of Namibia boycotted classes yesterday to demand the removal of a white lecturer in Nature Conservation whom they allege is racist. Around 150 students demonstrated in front of the main office building at the Polytechnic for about two hours demanding that Willem Adank be sacked. They alleged that Adank gave higher marks to white students and made racist remarks during classes. Dean of Students, Frieda Shimbuli, promised to investigate the allegations. At times the demonstration threatened to get out of hand as the student leaders battled to control the emotional protesters. The students also vowed to approach the Office of the Ombudsman about Adank and his alleged racism.

About 100 NamRail employees at Keetmanshoop took to the streets to protest the moved on Tuesday, demanding that the management of TransNamib be dismissed instead. The group, which marched from the train station in the town to TransNamib's regional office, maintained that the poor performance of the parastatal was not caused by over-staffing but rather by an incompetent management cadre inherited from the colonial era. They also lashed out at TransNamib for failing to implement affirmative action in its top management structure after nine years of independence. The demonstrators accused a senior NamRail manager in the South of abusing his powers by using company property, employees and time for work on his farm. Natau has urged Government to get to the root of the real problems causing the companies falling under the parastatal to incur huge losses. It maintained that the losses being incurred were mainly due to mismanagement and to the management cadre offering itself "abnormal salaries, perks, benefits and expenditures".

Members of the Okahandja community, where the late Regina Kastoor grew up, packed the public gallery in the court room where Judge Mavis Gibson presided over the trial of Kastoor's former boyfriend, 28-year-old Efraim Rachimo Haradoeb. An estimated 200 to 300 people staged a demonstration at Okahandja earlier yesterday, which culminated with the presentation of a petition to the town's Magistrate, Eileen Gous. In the petition the protesters demanded still tougher treatment for men charged with violence directed at women.

100-strong, placard-waving crowd consisting mainly of farmworkers protested on Sunday against an alleged assault on a Swapo politician at a farm in the Omaheke region. During a highly-charged meeting at the remote Okanjetu Farm, Swapo Regional Co-ordinator Kauku Hengari claimed "the beating of blacks on farms by whites has progressively continued and can't be allowed to continue unabated. We are saying enough is enough." Citing alleged threats to use guns by some farmers as an indication that "they are ready for war and they want war, Hengari charged, "therefore we have no other alternative, we have to retaliate against the white farm owners in Steinhausen Constituency in a manner befitting them, with all means at our disposal". In the petition Swapo demanded that Dippenaar apologise publicly for the incident. Other demands were that the Ministry of Labour must ensure that Labour Inspectors have full access to private property in that area, while Government officials must be exempted from making appointments before they can visit farmworkers.

Gobabis residents on Friday protested against the employment of ex-combatants in regions other than where they hail from. About 150 people, organised by DTA leaders in the town, also complained about a lack of medicine at state-run clinics and hospitals in Omaheke Region. After marching from Epako township to the town centre under the watchful eyes of the Police, they handed a petition to Governor of the Region, Paulo Thataone. Residents also demanded improved medical services in their region. disclosed recently that the 65 000 inhabitants of Omaheke face the possibility of being turned away from the Gobabis district hospital or clinics in the region because of a shortage of essential medicines.

More than 700 communal farmers from across the country, who say they are fed up with being ignored by Government, marched on Parliament yesterday. The farmers, some holding traditional weapons such as bows and arrows, handed a petition to the Speaker of Parliament, Dr Mose Tjitendero, wholeft a Cabinet meeting to receive it. Namibia National Farmers' Union President Gabes Shihepo said the placard-waving farmers decided to march after their proposals on resettlement and communal land administration were "ignored" and "sidelined" by the Ministry of Lands, Resettlement and Rehabilitation. "We are one. I receive your petition very humbly on behalf of Parliament. The only reason that you stand here is because you have elected us to be here. We don't have a different agenda," he said. State House and the Office of the Speaker have yet to respond to concerns raised by some 800 communal farmers from across Namibia who last month took to the streets of the capital to press home their dissatisfaction with the slow pace of land reform.

Some 1,000 people staged a march at Aussenkehr near the South African border on Friday, demanding that the Ministry of Mines withdraw its decision to grant prospecting rights to the land on which the community is housed. Davis Mushitu, spokesperson for the community, told The Namibian they were protesting against the Mineral Rights Commission for granting exclusive diamond prospecting rights to Northbank Diamonds to mine the land on which some 1,000 Aussenkehr workers and their 6,500 relatives live. The workers, together with the management of the Aussenkehr grape farm, have already appealed against the decision and a High Court hearing is scheduled for October 25. The Ministry of Mines and Energy, in a statement, claimed that the workers were "mobilised and instigated" by the farm management and said the employers were "greedy, incorrigible and bent on frustrating and chasing away investors from a potentially lucrative venture".

A group of some 300 protesters marched on the Grootfontein Magistrate's Court yesterday to hand over a petition opposing bail for the Caprivi accused. Grootfontein Mayor Engelhardt Gariseb handed over an 11-point petition to Magistrate Christie Liebenberg, who is hearing the bail applications. "We the community of Grootfontein are hereby strongly condemning the bail application for the secessionists," stated the petitioners, who added, "they (secregion as well as the rest of Namibia." The petition threatened that "if bail is granted to the rebels remember that you will bear the consequences. And remember that rebels will go and reorganise themselves for another possible attack".

Caprivi residents, including Government employees and school pupils, yesterday protested at Katima Mulilo against the recent granting of bail to four alleged secessionists. On September 13 Divisional Magistrate Cassie Carstens granted bail of N$1 000 each to Dino Dias, NDF soldier Kashuka Eugene Kamashungu (19), Beaven Kabwana Namitala and Hoster Shimwe Kulisesa (22). Regional Police Commander in the Caprivi, Chief Inspector Hieronymus Goraseb, said the crowd which he estimated at between 1 500 and 2 000 people, handed a petition to the Governor Bernard Sibalatani at around 10h00. Goraseb has been implicated in the torture of suspects in evidence heard at the bail hearings currently proceeding at Grootfontein. The petition read: " The first four rebels released by Magistrate Carstens must go back to jail where they belong. These people are criminals of the highest order who are bent towards causing trouble and insecurity in the region." However, Justice Permanent Secretary, Dr Albert Kawana, confirmed that the Ministry had received petitions from both Grootfontein and Katima Mulilo.

Eleven Caprivi high treason suspects, including former MP Geoffrey Mwilima, on Friday became the fourth group of alleged secessionists to be refused bail by the Grootfontein Magistrate's Court. The refusal of bail by Magistrate Clemens Hausiko came after some 200 people staged a vocal demonstration opposing bail outside the court. In a repeat of open threats made against Magistrate Christie Liebenberg at the previous bail hearings in the northern town in September, the protesters also handed a petition to Magistrate Hausiko warning against the granting of bail. It included a statement that the Magistrate would be held responsible if any of the suspects absconded after being granted bail. In addition, the petition read: "The justice system should protect the citizens country by all means and if fails we will protect ourselves and we are capable of doing so! WE CAN DO IT!"

Loud cheers of approval and acknowledging drum beats reverberated through Zoo Park yesterday in the first celebration of what is intended to become an annual celebration of Girl Child Day. Normal business activities came to a halt at lunch-time when about 400 young women streamed down Independence Avenue to protest violence against women, discrimination against young women and other women's rights issues as part of the Sister Namibia-organised Gender Awareness Month.

More than 100 disgruntled workers from the Ministry of Regional, Local Government and Housing on secondment to the Rehoboth Municipality, yesterday staged a peaceful demonstration listing a litany of grievances. The 120-strong group, mostly staff of the Rehoboth Town Council, are chiefly dissatisfied that their period of secondment has elapsed with nothing transpiring from the interim arrangement. The aggrieved workers handed a petition to Rehoboth's Town Clerk Neville Smith, which stated: "There is a general feeling of unhappiness and dissatisfaction as we don't have any job security, and we don't know who our employer is as the contract stipulating the employment conditions has yet to be implemented. The workers' demands include the reinstatement of the 13th cheque, a salary review, a bonus for every five years of service, access to housing loans and they have called on the Council to stop further recruitments until their status at the authority is clarified.

Over 100 Swapo liberation war veterans, including disabled former combatants, Friday embarked on a long march to see President Sam Nujoma in Windhoek, to remind him to fulfil his promise to pay 75,000 Namibian dollars per person as compensation for their role in bringing about independence. The group's spokesperson, Petrus Julius, told the national news agency Friday that the former bush war fighters were staging a peaceful march to protest against the hunger and poverty they have experienced for the past 10 years after independence. So far, there has been no response to their demand yet, Julius said, adding that they were prepared to even spend their Christmas in front of the State House, if Nujoma does not come up with a satisfactory answer. Around 108 ex-combatants maimed during the liberation struggle are demanding the N$75 000 each they say they were promised by Government, Swapo and President Sam Nujoma in 1997, a promise they say has 'vanished'. Quietly determined, they left Oshakati for Windhoek on Friday morning - on foot, on crutches and in wheelchairs. Since this protest marched for several days through several cities, this protest is considered national. President Sam Nujoma is reported to have told Ministers that he will not meet with demonstrating ex-fighters camped outside the Osona army base. Government yesterday denied that either it or the ruling Swapo party had ever promised to compensate people for their part in the struggle for the country's independence. Over 100 war victims and veterans are currently camped at Osona demanding payments of N$75 000. Kalomoh said that when people joined the struggle for liberation they were never promised that they would later receive a reward. The Namibian Police Thursday used police dogs to block over 100 former SWAPO liberation fighters and war victims from marching to State House to see President Sam Nujoma.

About 400 students hailing from Namibia's Kavango region staged a peaceful demonstration in Windhoek Sunday morning against what they called ongoing banditry activities alleged committed in that region by suspected UNITA rebels. Although the demonstration was under police escort and supervision there was no official from State House available to receive a petition the protesters wanted to deliver to President Sam Nujoma. Some of the placards the students carried read: "We are tired of sleeping in the bush. Kavango is not a war zone. We need peace and tranquility in the Kavango region now." Others read: "Unita is not AIDS, why don't you (President Nujoma) stop them killing our family and relatives", and "What did we do wrong in Kavango?". In a scene reminiscent of the colonial era, more than 30 armed law enforcement agents, from the Police riot unit and the Special Field Force, prevented the group from marching to State House by erecting a barricade at the junction of Robert Mugabe Avenue and Daniel Munamava Street. Some members of the Police were armed with batons and tear gas canisters, while there were gas masks in one of the vehicles that rushed officers to the demonstration.

Some 1,000 Namibian civil servants took to the streets of the capital Saturday in protest against what they called "meagre wage" increases for civil servants in the country. [P]olice barred the marchers from proceeding to the State House where they had intended to hand over a petition to President Sam Nujoma, who is currently in northern Namibia. In the petition read by TUN president Gert Jansen, the unions expressed dismay at the disgusting 83.5-dollar-per month salary paid a civil servant from the last increment in April.

Some 200 Namibians Monday took to the streets to express their dissatisfaction with the imbalance in the representation between women and men in elected positions at all levels of government in the country. With shouts of "we want 50-50 in government now and we want more women as Ministers now", the demonstrators marched from Kudu Park through Independence Avenue to the Parliament to hand a petition to the Speaker of the National Assembly, Mose Tjitendero.

The Khomas regional branch of the Swapo Party staged an outspoken demonstration at the High Court yesterday, calling for Home Affairs Minister Jerry Ekandjo to be acquitted of contempt of court in a judgement set to be delivered today. Their ruling will be announced in the shadow of a demonstration that made it clear that the Khomas regional branch of the ruling party wanted to see Ekandjo let off the hook, while they further called for Sikunda's release not to be ordered and for him to be deported from Namibia instead. Some 400 demonstrators refused to heed Police instructions not to proceed to the steps of the High Court with their demonstration around lunch hour yesterday. The flag- and placard-waving crowd surged past Police officers trying to stop them three times on their way to the court. The petition further says that the Khomas Swapo branch encourages "all patriotic Judges in our country to continue to serve the interests of the Namibian people first and foremost", and that they "should not give in to the intimidation by the unpatriotic and unprincipled hostile print media operators who have chosen to fight in the interests of the imperialists, the bandits and disgruntled elements in our society".

Residents of Karibib yesterday took up President Sam Nujoma's call for a clampdown on official waste. About 300 people demonstrated at the Municipal offices and handed over a petition to the Mayor listing their grievances, including allegations that Municipal vehicles are being abused by Councillors and Municipal employees. They also requested that auditors look at the Council's books. "We are very unhappy with the way in which the town is managed," said Sara Brunzel, a member of the Community Development Committee which organised the demonstration. Hoeseb said they had tried to explain this to residents many times. He said he suspected that the demonstration was politically motivated, charging that "some individuals want to be seen and heard". He said the petition would be discussed today and the Council would then decide on how to respond.
