Last Saturday, more than 200 Tjeye residents, 20km east of Rundu, held a peaceful demonstration and accused the FAA and Unita of being responsible for several attacks at the village.

Chanting 'Whose bank is it?' and 'We feed the nation, take us seriously', members of the Namibia National Farmers Union (NNFU) yesterday demonstrated at all six Agricultural Bank of Namibia branches countrywide. Demonstrations took place simultaneously at the bank's branches at Mariental, Windhoek, Otjiwarongo, Oshakati, Rundu and Katima Mulilo. The union, which describes itself as "the sole and authentic voice of communal farmers", organised the protest action after accusing Agribank of brushing aside their arguments.

Demonstrators from Kuisebmond yesterday demanded the resignation of the Mayor of Walvis Bay and the suspension of the Municipality's chief executive officer and other councillors. It requests Swapo headquarters and the Ministry of Local Government and Housing to investigate alleged corruption in the Municipality. "We therefore request the suspension of all our local councillors who are involved in this issue including Liboly Haufiku, the CEO of Walvis Bay Municipality, Augustinus Katiti, and King Mandume Muatunga. The Mayor of Walvis Bay, Theresia Samaria must resign or alternatively she must not stand for the coming election." Further demands by the protesters, which have been mentioned in two previous petitions over the past month by the same group, are their rejection of the Tutaleni low-cost housing project, a request for an electricity card system and that serviced land be made available to residents at a reasonable price. "We want to make it categorically clear that we the community of Walvis Bay will never support or defend any people who are making corruption in Namibia," the petition, signed by unionist Benhard Petrus on behalf of the roughly 700 protesters, says.

More than 100 ex-combatants, who say they were in the People's Liberation Army of Namibia in exile, have started gathering at Swapo headquarters in Windhoek in the latest of a series of protests that have taken place since the mid-1990s. Over 120 people were gathered at the Swapo HQ yesterday morning. "At the moment we have no proper homes to live with our children. We live in a shanty house on the outskirts of Okahandja," she said. " Speaking on behalf of the ex-Plan fighters, Fiina Tuyeni, a youth who was born in exile, said the younger ones in the demonstrating group had been told by the Swapo leadership that they were too young to be considered in the same category as ex-combatants." Niilo Taapopi, head of the Technical Committee dealing with the plight of ex-combatants and Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs, told The Namibian the committee's mandate has been extended by Cabinet to deal with the demonstrating ex-combatants. "We are working very hard to find a solution to this problem," he said.

CLOSE to 4 000 pupils from Walvis Bay took to the streets yesterday to express shock and outrage at the gang rape of a 14-year-old girl at the town last week. Claire Campbell, the Junior Mayor, read out the petition to Magistrate Pietie Husselmann. It reads: "If the very persons we entrust to ensure that our children and women travel to and from home perpetrate barbaric crimes, it is time to step in and say 'Enough'. What is happening to our society when the fabric of decency is torn apart senselessly? Families are suffering. The town is suffering. The country is suffering." In the petition they ask that the perpetrators' drivers' licences be revoked, that harsher sentences be imposed on rapists and that no parole be granted to convicted perpetrators of crimes of this nature.

OVER 100 workers at the University of Namibia (Unam) yesterday protested over management's alleged failure to act on wage and other problems. The demonstrators were members of the Namibia National Teachers Union (Nantu) and the Namibia Public Workers' Union (Napwu). The demonstrators were members of the Namibia National Teachers Union (Nantu) and the Namibia Public Workers' Union (Napwu). The workers accuse their employer of reneging on an earlier commitment that it would implement an across-the-board wage increase of 8,5 per cent for the next three years, and a separate 16,5 per cent increase. Unam spokesman, Edwin Tjiramba said the negotiations were ongoing on the issues raised by the workers and had already been presented to management.

About 300 Namibians demonstrated peacefully this week in protest against the recent killing of a German tourist at Ameib, about 25km from Usakos. Renate Engeborg Gruber (48) died a week ago after the vehicle she was travelling in with her husband came under fire. Hermut Gruber (58) was wounded in the legs. The mainly youthful demonstrators carried placards and marched to Usakos police station where they handed a petition to the station commander. Some of the placards read: "We the community of Usakos will make sure that the criminals are brought to justice", "Viva Tourists" and "Usako's Youth against Crime know how to deal with these kind of criminals". Aksel Muafangeyo, chairperson of Usakos Youth against Crime, said the people of Usakos wanted to show the world that attacks on innocent people could not be tolerated any longer as there were many tourist attractions in the Erongo region.

THE Rehoboth Town Council is to hold an emergency meeting on Monday to decide whether to sign a contract for the installation of pre-paid water meters at the town. The meeting follows a demonstration last Friday by residents who demanded that the Council sign a contract with the company, Nossob River System, for the installation of 1 315 pre-paid water meters. The pre-paid water meters were donated by the Ministry of Regional, Local Government and Housing to help alleviate the water problems at the town. Around 300 demonstrators marched on the Council offices last Friday and ended up emptying the 'slop buckets' in the offices in the presence of the Police.

POLICE on Friday prevented a second attempt by Swapo Party Youth League-led demonstrators to occupy a farm near Gobabis, following the eviction of 30 people who had lived on the land for decades. Over 100 angry demonstrators, organised by the SPYL, entered the farm on Thursday for several hours in response to the eviction. They slashed the tyres of vehicles on the farm and broke at least one window in the farmhouse. Special Field Force members, armed with teargas and automatic weapons, were on guard at Kalkpan from Thursday until Friday.

OMARURU residents yesterday expressed outrage over the continuous murderous attacks on women and children in Namibia. About 50 people marched to the town's Magistrate's Court to hand over a petition before the appearance of a 45-year-old man charged with murdering his girlfriend. The residents carried posters protesting violence against women and children and calling for the speedy implementation of the Domestic Violence Bill.

POLICEMEN yesterday cocked their guns to prevent angry women and children from lobbying legislators to pass the Domestic Violence Bill. The Police officers threatened to fire at the demonstrators, who were determined to seek President Sam Nujoma's support for the enactment the Domestic Violence Bill. The women chanted "stop violence against women and children" as Police officers cocked and pointed their AK-47 rifles at the demonstrators. "There is no threat coming from women and children for the Police to threaten us with guns. Given the protest the day before in another city over the same issue, as well as the response received, this protest is believed to have had at least 50 people.

GOVERNMENT must make the world a place to live in and not a place to die in, pleaded Anthony Plaatjies, who is HIV positive, at a candlelight vigil at Walvis Bay on Tuesday night. Three vigils, organised by the Treatment Action Forum, were held - in Windhoek and at Walvis Bay and Opuwo. The aim was to remember all those who have died from HIV-AIDS and to protest the continuing lack of affordable medication for those still living with the disease. A tearful Herlyn Uiras (18) told the more than 100 people at the vigil that their group had lost six people over the past couple of months. Hafeni Ndemula, a National Councillor, accepted petitions from three speakers saying "Government has heard your message".

Residents of the Rundu Rural Constituency yesterday staged a demonstration demanding the immediate resumption of drought food relief distribution which was stopped at the beginning of the year. Moses Nyundu handed over a petition to the Governor of the region on behalf of the demonstrators, the majority of whom were women. Nyundu said they were protesting the move to stop drought food relief as no clear explanation was provided by the Regional Emergency Management Unit (Remu). Karupu assured the demonstrators that Remu would discuss their petition with the Emergency Management Unit (EMU) in the Office of the Prime Minister to seek an amicable solution to the problem.

IMMIGRATION officers whose main functions are to be handed over to the Police have petitioned Home Affairs Minister Jerry Ekandjo demanding that he stop dismantling their division. The petition was to be handed over to Ekandjo yesterday, but he refused to receive it and told Police to block a demonstration by the immigration officials.  Police threatened to use teargas to disperse the marchers whom they pushed and shoved. They were armed with rifles, handguns, teargas and batons. In July there was an outcry among the country's estimated 400 immigration officials who protested against the Ministry's move, accusing Minister Jerry Ekandjo of unilaterally changing their conditions of service.

KARASBURG residents, angered over a controversial contract their Municipality has signed with the South African-owned Southern Electricity Service Company (SELCo), are threatening to stage more street protests this week. A week ago hundreds of Karasburg residents demonstrated outside the Municipal offices, accusing their councillors of "gross negligence" for entering into the agreement. They say that since the contract for the operation and management of their town's electricity network was given to SELCo, electricity charges have spiralled by between 100 to 250 per cent. They had given the Council until Thursday to come up with an explanation on why the contract was signed - but the Council failed to meet the deadline. They had given the Council until Thursday to come up with an explanation on why the contract was signed - but the Council failed to meet the deadline. This protest took place a week ago, and so it has been coded as taking place on the 15th only.

The bail application attracted a crowd of around 60 Gobabis residents who staged a peaceful demonstration outside the court building to oppose the granting of bail to the two.  In a petition handed over to Magistrate Wouter Maske, the demonstrators called for an independent and unbiased hearing and a life sentence for those found guilty. Maske postponed the bail application hearing until today.

HUNDREDS of placard-carrying demonstrators yesterday marched on government offices at Katima Mulilo, where they protested against 13 secessionist suspects. We the people of Caprivi Region condemn the idea of seceding the region from the rest of Namibia. We therefore call upon the masses in the region to remain united, as divided we fall," read the 16-point petition. "We demand the government to follow up all the secessionist sympathisers and their supporters as they are the people engineering political instability in the Caprivi Region," the petition stated. The petitioners further demanded that the 13 suspects "should remain in custody for the rest of their lives" as they are apparently a threat to peace and development. And more radically the demonstrators called upon the government "to revise the judicial system as it is seen as a threat to the national security of the country". The petitioners further appealed to the government to introduce a "screening system of judges as they are seen and viewed as representing their legal interests and not the people's interests."

Last weekend, women from all walks of life in the capital took to the streets to mobilise men and women to protest against killing, rape and abuse of women and children. Dressed in traditional attire ranging from Nama-Damara, Oshivambo, Otjiherero, Tsetswana, Caprivian and Rukavango and German, the women paraded the streets of Windhoek. At around 9h25 last Saturday, the mother of the nation, First Lady Kovambo Nujoma arrived at the Katutura UN Plaza to address the nation on the eve of the International Women's Day which is celebrated all over the world on March 8.

RESIDENTS of the former mining town of Uis on Monday protested against alleged irregularities and mismanagement in the Village Council. Residents said Monday's march was organised after the Council refused to agree to a demand for a community meeting on March 24. The town's newly elected Mayor, Annelise Tauros, sent one of her Councillors to accept the petition on Monday, with a message that Council was working on a response to issues raised in the petition. Apart from concerns on water problems, poor communication between Council and the community, maintenance of houses and new developments, residents want to know about the Council's financial situation and the distribution of drought relief food. More than 100 residents signed a petition that was handed to Council for the second time 10 days ago.

HUNDREDS of supporters of President Sam Nujoma took to the streets of Oshakati on Wednesday to hand over a petition demanding that he be allowed to serve a fourth term in office by way of a referendum. The petition that was handed over to the Governor of the Oshana Region, Clemens Kashuupulwa, appealed to the SWAPO Party's Central Committee to look into the "urgent" request of the majority of the people during the party's Extraordinary Congress to be held in May, and nominate President Nujoma for a fourth term. Despite eleventh-hour mass demonstrations calling for a referendum on a fourth term, Nujoma announced on Saturday that he would not be available.

MEMBERS of the Hardap Women's Voice staged a demonstration in Rehoboth yesterday condemning the continued occurrence of rape and other social evils at the southern town. Led by the group's chairperson in the region Rachel Cloete, a large number of women accompanied by youths marched to the town's magistrate's court, where they delivered a petition to Rehoboth Magistrate, Gaynor Poulton. In the petition, the women detailed their grievances, which include rape, alcohol and drug abuse, mushrooming of shebeens and non-payment of child maintenance by especially run-away fathers. Handing over the petition, Cloete said women in the town of Rehoboth were not living a safe life anymore, because they have become victims of their husbands, brothers and relatives as a result of rampant alcohol and drug abuse. Cloete, who was disappointed by the low turnout for the march, said the march was to highlight the mistreatment of women in society.  The petition was signed by 1 057 people. Although there was a low turnout, the article mentions a large crowd of protesters, and the high number of signatories to the petition implies a protest of at least 50 people.   Magistrate Poulton promised to forward the petition to the line ministry who should ensure that police would do their part, adding that all problems raised were more relevant to the police.

INFORMAL traders consisting of members of the Oshakati open market informal traders and street hawkers staged a peaceful demonstration yesterday against informal trading regulations in the Oshakati Town Council suburb. The group handed a petition to Oshana Regional Governor Clemens Kashuupulwa who called an emergency meeting with the group and the management members of Oshakati and Ongwediva town councils to harness the differences between the traders and the town council. The traders told New Era over the weekend that they were unhappy with the new regulations saying that it was not proper and that these restrictions interfere with their business activities and operations. New Era learnt that since Monday, more than 200 informal traders were instructed and moved to new sites, while more than 200 rejected the council's order to move to newly allocated areas. More than 500 informal traders are expected to hand the petition to the office of the mayor tomorrow morning. Given how many people ignored the order as well as how many traders are expected in the next day?ó»s march, this demonstration is believed to have at least 50 people.

THE murder of a Swakopmund resident on the beach on Friday morning united the coastal community yesterday morning, when about 500 people took part in a silent march to the Magistrate's Court. Residents marched side by side in memory of Alexandra Mooren (44) and other victims of crime at the coast. Quietly singing hymns and carrying candles, flowers and placards the procession down Sam Nujoma Avenue brought the early morning traffic to a standstill, with many onlookers observing a moment of silence in respect. Making a statement A section of the crowd of about 500 people who took part in a march at Swakopmund yesterday to protest against violent crime.

RESIDENTS of Swakopmund who took part in an anti-crime demonstration yesterday stormed a Police van carrying three suspects in the Mooren beach murder case. More than 300 people took part in the protest in front of the Magistrate's Court to speak out against crime and demand more Police officers for the town. She said the crowd shouted: "They are in there, they are in there" and ran after the van. "They shook the van and shouted angrily at the suspects."

THE Police at Karibib had to calm a group of about 80 residents who took part in a peaceful demonstration to hand over a petition to the Mayor yesterday. The group, known as the Karibib Community Delegation, which is chaired by Sara Brunzel, demanded answers from the Town Council on a host of issues. The main concerns raised by residents are access to and service at the new health centre, pre-payment electricity meters, refuse removal and outstanding money to NamWater and NamPower. They have also raised a number of issues to be investigated by auditors concerning the alleged abuse of Council vehicles by Municipal staff, allocation of projects on tender to Municipal employees, insurance of vehicles and homes of former Councillors, housing allowances to employees in Municipal houses, loans to staff members and Councillors and overtime. The Mayor said he would not be able to give much feedback to the community tonight, as the auditors had not yet completed their task.

WORKERS at Coimbra OK Foods, saddened by police inaction to arrest two Portuguese bosses who allegedly assaulted a black worker, now want the Ministry of Home Affairs to probe the incident that smacks of racism. The workers at Coimbra OK Foods want the Ministry of Home Affairs to investigate their complaints jointly with the Ministry of Labour. They argue that had the Portuguese been on the receiving end, the black perpetrator would have been arrested in record time. The ugly incident that left Crispin Lucas bloodied was allegedly committed by one male supervisor and his daughter and it triggered a noisy demonstration involving over 100 workers. The workers, who have since resumed duty at Coim-bra OK Foods after the incident, are further unhappy that their representatives at Nafau have dismally failed to address a list of their grievances. Following the incident, three workers were fired on the spot while others were apparently forced to sign final warning letters from their seemingly unsympathetic bosses. Workers and other residents at Katima Mulilo are unhappy that the police seem to be dragging their feet as they have not yet arrested the alleged perpetrators of the incident.

WOMEN from the DRC informal settlement at Swakopmund yesterday carried burning candles in a peaceful protest march to the Municipality in memory of the mother and two toddlers who died on Saturday when their shack burnt down. "We are forced to use candles and paraffin lamps because there is no electricity," the spokesperson for the group of 50 residents, Louis Barnard Haslund, read from a petition. The provision of electricity has been an ongoing issue raised in several protest marches to the Council. "How long do we still have to suffer without electricity?" and "Have we been forgotten?" were some of the statements, while one woman carried a piece of cardboard above her head simply stating "POWER". Mayor Rosina //Hoabes said she could not give them an answer immediately. She said the procedure was that the petition had to be tabled at the next Council meeting, after which the Management Committee would discuss it and make recommendations.

MORE than 1 000 children and adults on Friday marched to the Swakopmund Magistrate's Court in silent protest at the brutal rape and murder of a six-year-old girl four days earlier. Along the way mothers and fathers expressed feelings of anger and frustration with the crime situation in the country and sentences meted out to those found guilty. "Has the life of a cow more value than that of a child's," asked Sophia Motinga, UDF Town Councillor and member of the Atlantic School Board, referring to the severe mandatory sentences for stock thieves approved in Parliament last year. The Deputy Mayor and Magistrate Gibson Imbili both condemned the crime. "The community of Swakopmund appeals to the President to implement a special law for those raping and killing innocent children, who are the leaders of tomorrow," said Uahimisa Kaapehi, a father and Nudo politician.

HUNDREDS of Windhoek residents, young and old, mainly wearing black and singing solidarity songs, marched from Katutura to the city centre yesterday as Namibians mourned the deaths of two young rape and murder victims. The march, led by spiritual leaders of churches affiliated to the Council of Churches in Namibia, demonstrated people's anger at recent attacks in which two minors, aged three and six, were raped and killed in Windhoek and at Swakopmund. About 500 people, mainly women and children, walked close to 10 kilometres to the Parliamentary Gardens from the scene of the latest crime - the rape and murder of three-year-old Manuela Sofia Hoesemas in the Katutura Old Cinema Hall. "We can't tolerate it any longer. They must just hang them," said one woman in her late 50s as people marched down Independence Avenue.

THE Mayor of Tsumeb, Veueza Kasiringua, over the weekend led a two-thousand strong crowd of aggrieved community members through the town in a demonstration against the abuse and rape of innocent young women and children in the country. Hundreds of men and women, clad in black attire and others weeping, marched through the streets of Nomtsoub carrying posters calling for stiffer sentences for rapists. "It is time for us to stand up against the criminals, no matter whether they are our children, fathers, mothers, family or friends, they do not deserve to be treated with kindness." Given that the mayor herself participated in this demonstration, the response has been recorded as accommodation.

RESIDENTS of Arandis have given the police at the town until Friday this week to remove the suspect in the rape and killing of six-year-old Rachel Hamutundu recently, from the town's holding cells. This ultimatum was given last week at the end of a peaceful demonstration that attracted more or less 1 000 people. Since no specific date is given, the start and end date for this protest is recorded as happening one week earlier than this article.  The march was against the recent rapes and killings of children Hamutundu in Swakopmund and Manuela Sofia Heosemas in Windhoek. The community said in a petition they were shocked by recent brutal and horrific incidences of rape and murder of innocent young children. "We demand that this murderer be taken back to the place where he committed these satanic deeds with immediate effect. If not, we may take the law into own hands," said the petition.

AT least 1 500 women and men staged a peaceful demonstration against violence against women and children in Opuwo yesterday. In submitting the petition, Ujaha said the residents of the Kunene Region were calling on the lawmakers to support the Minister of Women Affairs and Child Welfare by amending the constitution to allow for capital punishment for those who make themselves guilty of these inhuman acts. The petition also had three recommendations on what should be done. The protes-tors recommended counselling for the criminals and that workshops be conducted to inform the public about love, relationships and mutual acceptance. They recommended stringent punitive measures to be put in place to isolate if not eliminate such criminals. The third recommendation called for more holistic, realistic and stringent regulations against alcohol outlets.

HUNDREDS of Outapi town residents held a demonstration against women and child abuse to commemorate International Women's Day. The demonstration was in response to the recent rape and murder of two minor girls in Windhoek and Swakop-mund. The residents are demanding that lawmakers call on witchdoctors to explain how minor children can cure the HIV/AIDS pandemic when they are raped. They are also demanding that rapists and murderers be given capital punishment. They also demand that rape and murder suspects be refused bail. The residents also called on the Ministry of Home Affairs to strengthen measures to control drug trafficking and alcohol and drug abuse by teenagers.

Residents of Mariental yesterday turned out in droves to protest against the ruthless killing of eight people on a farm near Kalkrand in the Mariental District at the weekend. More than a thousand people, most of them wearing black, took part. She said the community was opposed to the two suspects being granted bail and demanded lifelong imprisonment, coupled with hard labour, for all those convicted of rape and murder.

TRAFFIC was brought to a halt as hundreds of students from the University of Namibia (Unam) in Windhoek took to the streets to protest against a recent string of murderous acts that have shocked the nation. Over three hundred students from Unam vigorously marched from Unam under the escort of the traffic police to the National Assembly where they handed over a strongly worded petition to Speaker Dr Mose Tjitendero. Reading the petition, Wise said Unam students are not calling for the re-introduction of capital punishment, but that they find the sentences being meted out to perpetrators too lenient and not enough of a deterrent. The student community further appealed to the National Assembly and to Cabinet to urgently devise strategies aimed at identifying the root causes of this aberrant phenomena and speedily find and prescribe solutions.

ABOUT 200 teachers affiliated to the Teachers' Union of Namibia (TUN) yesterday took to the streets of Windhoek to demonstrate against what they called the "unsatisfactory way" in which their conditions of service are being managed by the Ministry of Basis Education, Sport and Culture, and their "worsening" financial position since 1995. But the TUN march proceeded to the offices of the Ministry of Basic Education, Sport and Culture, where marchers handed a petition to Minister John Mutorwa, demanding clear written indications from the two ministries of education that salaries of all teachers and school secretaries would be translated according to the circular that came into effect in January last year. The union thus, among others, demanded that all teachers be treated equally, and that the difference in salaries between ordinary teachers and school management be addressed. The teachers further demanded that the date of implementation should be no later than the end of April this year. The teachers asked that a fair procedure, as applicable in all ministries, be applied when "over-deductions" are made. "We are encountering serious difficulties when we just observe on our salary advances that deductions are made in such amounts that we cannot afford and which causes us serious financial problems," they explained.

The wave of discontent of ratepayers with their Councils that has been spreading across the country in recent weeks, reached Henties Bay last week when more than 200 residents demonstrated on Thursday and Friday with posters at the Council offices. As the demonstration heated up, residents started demanding that the Town Council should be dissolved. THE Henties Bay Town Council needed a marathon meeting on Monday to answer the accusations made by a concerned community group during a two-day demonstration last week. Kapere, who promised to check some decisions with the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Regional and Local Government and Housing, decided to call another meeting on June 11.

CLOSE to 200 teachers in the Karas Region took to the streets of Keetmanshoop on Tuesday, under the banner of the Teachers Union of Namibia (TUN), to protest against their conditions of employment. Led by local school principals, the teachers from various communities marched to the Karas Regional Education Office to hand over a petition demanding a more equitable salary structure. The teachers demanded equitable salaries for primary and secondary school teachers, claiming that secondary school teachers and newly appointed teachers were earning more than their counterparts in primary schools. The petition called for the timely payment of leave and pension gratuities and other termination benefits as provided for by the Treasury Instructions, State Finance Act and the Labour Act.

ABOUT 250 angry Okahandja residents marched to their Town Council offices yesterday to hand over a petition calling for the immediate removal of the Mayor, Christophine 'Citto' Paulus, and her co-councillors. They are also demanding that all allegations of corruption be immediately investigated. Paulus and her Swapo Party colleagues, namely her deputy Constantia Kahengombo, Hilaria Shilimetindi and Johannes Nande, were nowhere to be seen, as was the case with Sofia Noabes of the UDF, AJ Strauss of the CoD and Agatha Handura of Nudo. Individuals approached The Namibian to complain of collapsing services, payments for pre-paid electricity meters allegedly not being paid into their accounts, abuse of municipal vehicles by councillors and a general disregard for anyone's interests except their own.

CLAIMS of greed and graft rang through the streets of Otjiwarongo yesterday as disgruntled residents demonstrated to demand the immediate removal of the Town Council and the suspension of two senior employees. Toy-toying members of the community levelled a barrage of accusations against officials they allege are enriching themselves at the expense of the town. By 18h00, it was estimated that more than 500 people had tried to cram into the Swanevelder hall. Given how many people wanted to get into this community meeting, this protest is believed to have had at least 100 participants.

THE Namibian Police's Special Field Force and Task Force used teargas and rubber bullets to disperse taxi drivers who blockaded Hosea Kutako Drive near Rhino Park in Windhoek yesterday morning. Taxi drivers want their industry to be more regulated, and the protest was aimed at putting pressure on the relevant authorities to improve the situation. Others parked their taxis in Independence Avenue in the city centre, locked their vehicles and walked away. In the petition, the taxi drivers demanded that the municipality provide them with suitable taxi ranks. Given how disruptive the protest was, this demonstration is believed to have at least 50 people.  But what was initially planned as a peaceful demonstration degenerated into a riotous event that resulted in members of the municipal and the regular police force being called to restore order.

AN attempt to get answers from the Okahandja Town Council on various allegations of mismanagement and corruption fell flat yesterday as Mayor Citto Paulus and her councillors refused to meet with a group of demonstrators. The march consisted of about 50 demonstrators who danced and chanted in front of the municipal offices yesterday just after lunch. Their demands to speak to the Mayor and her councillors however failed to elicit anything more than curious stares from municipal employees.

THE famous kudu statue situated at the corner of John Meinert Street and Independence Avenue in the city centre yesterday played host to dozens of people who protested against a recent string of corruption cases. Carrying placards bearing messages such as "Viva Uncle Pohamba", "Stop Corruption" and "Where Is The N$100m" in reference to the case in which the Offshore Development Company (ODC) invested a fortune in a briefcase company, the protestors made their way to the Office of the Prime Minister. "We the undersigned Namibians demand that Government initiates immediate and effective action against corruption by among other things investigating all allegations of corruption, making the findings public, prosecuting all suspected of corruption and publishing the guilty," read the statement. ?óÖDozens?ó» of people implies that there was at least 50 protesters.

THOUSANDS of angry teachers marched countrywide yesterday to demonstrate against a Cabinet decision to nullify an earlier undertaking to increase salaries and benefits for long-serving teachers. The teachers defied a Government order to refrain from demonstrating, as they are hoping to push the State into bowing to pressure and promised that the next action would be a potentially crippling national strike. Organised by the Namibia National Teachers' Union (Nantu) and supported by the rival Teachers' Union of Namibia (TUN), the teachers demanded that the State get money from the Government Institutions' Pension Fund (GIPF), Social Security Commission (SSC) and the Overseas Development Company (ODC) to increase their salaries and benefits.

ANGRY Keetmanshoop municipal workers and residents staged two separate protests over huge rent increases of more than 1 000 per cent yesterday. About 200 municipal workers downed tools and marched from the Namibia Public Workers Union (Napwu) offices to the local authority building. The petition protested the delay in payment of salaries, the suspension of long-service bonuses and free services, and the exorbitant increases in rent. The Governor instructed the group not to pay any municipal bills (rent, water and basic charges) until next week. He said he would negotiate with the local council and give the group feedback next Tuesday. Mayor Tiboth, when interviewed by The Namibian, said he agreed the rent increases were too high.

WAVING placards and chanting slogans protesting violence against women, Polytechnic students and school children from five Windhoek high schools drew maximum attention to their campaign by taking it to the launch of this year's State of the World Population Report. Accompanied by family members of Juanita Mabula, the 21-year-old woman whose body was found naked and decapitated in Windhoek almost three weeks ago, the students, wearing giant cardboard cut-outs of white ribbons, waited for Prime Minister Nahas Angula to hand over a petition calling for more stringent action against perpetrators of violence. The Polytechnic students called on Government to strengthen policing for the protection of communities and a more efficient judicial system to deal with criminals. Part of the crowd that protested on Wednesday included Mabula's minor daughter and some relatives who were symbolically dressed in black. Leading the pack of close to 250 demonstrators, Rector of the Polytechnic of Namibia Dr Tjama Tjivikua assisted by the Dean of Students Frieda Shimbuli, marched to the NamPower Convention Centre, where Angula was officiating the launch of the 2005 State of the World Population Report. The students demanded swift action and for the protection of women and children from violent men. One of the placards brandished appealed to the police to swiftly find the killer/s, saying the masses were tired of crying.

THE anger and frustrations of hundreds of distressed pensioners, sparked by an apparent misleading parliamentary statement on their plight, yesterday culminated in a protest march and demands for an increase in pensions in Khomasdal. Busloads of pensioners from the marginalised communities yesterday morning gathered from 09h00 near the Khomasdal soccer stadium in preparation for a spontaneous protest march on the offices of the Ministry of Labour and Social Welfare. She went on to say that the present monthly pension of N $300 is totally inadequate for her to maintain a decent, dignified and secure standard of living.

OSHIWAMBO-SPEAKING farmers who have been ordered to remove their cattle from west Kavango say they will not budge unless Government and the Ondonga and Oukwanyama Traditional Authorities give them a place in former Owambo to settle with their animals. "If there is no other way to find a place for us to settle, then we are not moving out of Kavango, whatever the cost, or else we are going to add to the skeletons of our brothers at the Eenhana military base," the farmers said in a petition yesterday. Following a demonstration at Omuthiyagwiipundi yesterday, the farmers handed their petition to the Chief Executive Officer of Omuthiya Constituency, Samuel Mbango, who received it on behalf of the Omuthiya Constituency Councillor Penda Ndakolo, who is also the Governor of Oshikoto Region. An estimated 400 farmers took part in the protest, giving vent to their frustrations by dancing, brandishing placards and chanting.

Over 500 disgruntled members of the Hoachanas community held a peaceful demonstration at the town last week expressing their discontent over the 17-year "corrupt administration" of Chief Petrus Simon Moses Kooper. In a petition handed over to Kooper last Friday, the demonstrators called for the immediate removal of the traditional chief, while at the same time calling for government's intervention into the matter. On Friday, the leader of the demonstration David Topnaar handed over the petition to Kooper at the town's community hall. Speaking to New Era, Topnaar said that many incidents have shown that a lot has gone wrong in the way his chieftainship has administered Hoachanas.

THE Deputy Minister of Lands and Resettlement, Isack Katali says his ministry has no legal powers to evict hundreds of illegal herders occupying communal areas under the Ukwangali Traditional Authority. Hundreds of unhappy residents of the Ukwangali Traditional Authority last Thursday staged a peaceful demonstration expressing their dissatisfaction with Government's inaction on the highly sensitive issue. In a petition handed over to the representative of the Ministry of Lands and Resettlement Vilho Shikumwa, the demonstrators maintained their action had been prompted by government's failure to resolve the matter once and for all since the problem started back in 1992.

Over 25 civil society organisations (CSOs) on Tuesday made a last hour attempt to make lawmakers accommodate their amendments to the Child Status Bill. They said parts of the content of the Bill are not in the best interests of the child, as per the Convention of the Rights of the Child. Scores of school children from different schools and representatives of the CSOs holding placards and shouting slogans made their presence felt at the steps of the National Assembly yesterday to ask Parliament not to pass the Bill in its current form. Given how many organizations were involved, this protest is believed to have at least 1000 people.

Hundreds of Hardap Region's inhabitants took to the streets at Mariental yesterday to demand the immediate removal of the Chief Regional Officer James Sankwasa, as the accounting officer of the region. The demonstrators also complained that people from outside the Hardap Region get jobs, while the local residents are suffering. The Hardap Regional Council suspended its Chief Executive Officer James Sankwasa without remuneration on Friday. He stands accused of unilaterally removing expensive government property from the council premises and taking it to a private farm.

SHEBEEN owners in Walvis Bay on Wednesday demanded that the backyard bars closed by the Police last weekend be reopened and that confiscated alcohol be returned to the proprietors. Some 50 shebeen owners and their clients, mostly young women, rocked up at the Kuisebmond Stadium in Walvis Bay yesterday to protest the closure of illegal shebeens in the town. Many of them said they had applied for liquor licenses unsuccessfully, and did not know why their applications were rejected.

Meanwhile, some 200 protesters dug in their heels at the Walvis Bay Municipality on Wednesday - some even standing firm through a bitterly cold Tuesday night - to convey their dissatisfaction with the closure of their businesses. "We've had meetings with the Mayor, Police Commander, Municipal CEO, Town Council and the Regional Governor. It amounted to nothing. Police officers were sent to the scene to disperse the crowd and, according to Petrus, they were ordered by Regional Commander Andrew Iyambo to use force if necessary. The communications officer of the Municipality of Walvis Bay, Nolita Marques said more than 200 people gathered outside the municipality on Wednesday and Thursday and about 50 spent two nights there. Though this was regarded as a sign of protest, the communications officer indicated that the municipality at the town maintained its stand, adding that this was an action by the police and the municipality had nothing to do with it. Protestors were adamant that they wanted sheebens to be re-opened and all the confiscated liquor be returned to the rightful owners.

Hundreds of shebeen owners angered by the recent decision to close down all unlicensed informal pubs last Saturday braved the cold weather and marched to State House to express their grievances. The protesters footed from Katutura to State House, where they handed over a petition listing their grievances to a senior minister who received it on behalf of President Hifikepunye Pohamba. The march that started from the Namibia Shebeen Association (NASA) offices in Katutura saw hundreds of irate men and women brandishing placards with messages demanding the re-opening of their sheebens. As Kandenge delivered the news that the President still needed time to study the petition before he could attend to their grievances, emotions ran high and the demonstrators threatened they would not leave until they were given an immediate answer to their concerns. Kandenge told New Era that circumstances forced people to operate illegally given the delays in approving licences. It takes two to three years for a licence to be approved, he said.

Scores of villagers at Onyaanya in the Oshikoto region yesterday staged a peaceful demonstration to condemn the disempowerment of traditional authorities from granting trading licenses as was the practice before and after independence. They handed a petition to Onyaanya Constituency Councillor Henock Kankoshi after police at Okatope reportedly threatened to dispose of all liquor and other alcoholic substances should the Liquor Act continue to be violated by the deadline of Wednesday (today). Scores of villagers implies at least a crowd of 100 at the protest.

SAFETY and Security Minister Peter Tsheehama yesterday vowed that the Police would close down all unlicensed liquor outlets in Namibia despite opposition from cuca shop owners. At the weekend, the Police fired rubber bullets and teargas when they clashed with angry shebeen owners at Omuthiya in the North. Tsheehama said two members of the public and three Police officers were slightly injured by stones during the fracas. "The Police further found a large group of people shouting slogans, defying that they will not close their bars and that blood will be shed," he said. Given the police response and the large crowd and the past protests, this demonstration is believed to have at least 100 people.

Hundreds of shebeen owners under the leadership of the Namibia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (NCCI) demonstrated at Ondangwa yesterday demanding the review of the Liquor Act No. 6 of 1998. They also condemned alleged police brutality against shebeen owners. They also called for differential application fees instead of a blanket $400N for all applicants regardless of the size of the enterprise. The group again called for a 12-month extension to give them time to re-apply and also meet the stringent conditions such as brick toilets although they operate their businesses from shanties.

Embittered shebeen owners marched on parliament in the grip of a pervasive mood of anger demanding a moratorium on the Liquor Act. Yesterday thousands of disgruntled shebeen owners marched to the National Assembly where they handed over a petition to Speaker of the National Assembly Theo-Ben Gurirab and Chairman of the National Council Asser Kapere. In the petition, demonstrators adamantly voiced a need for the government to place a moratorium on the implementation of the Liquor Act and the liquor regulations until factors that impede effective and efficient compliance are sorted out. Escorted to the National Assembly under heavy police guard, about 3000 demonstrators from all corners of the country expressed their anger towards the government adding that the current 'No Shebeens Operation' campaigns that have seen the closure of more than 2000 unlicensed shebeens countrywide is subjecting them to hunger. "We are hungry, this is the second petition to the government and no response is forthcoming. Yesterday a group of about 60 protesters remained on the parliamentary premises, promising that more people were on the way to swell their ranks.  DESPITE sober assurances by Government that it is hard at work to ensure the smooth implementation of the Liquor Act, a core group of shebeen protesters yesterday remained camped outside Parliament in Windhoek. Although the numbers dwindled greatly, there were still 50 people in the area for multiple days. Demonstrators, who want Government to give them the go-ahead to re-open their unlicensed shebeens, started the trek home to their respective regions on Saturday.

About 400 Tsumeb residents yesterday took to the streets to voice their dissatisfaction over a range of issues they want resolved by the Tsumeb Town Council. The angry crowd, who were shouting and singing slogans, demanded that their water be turned on and that written proof be submitted to that effect as they claim to be "tired of empty promises". Receiving the petition, Mayor of Tsumeb, Engel Nawatiseb, said the community has the responsibility to contribute to the town's development through the payment of rates, taxes and other consumer service fees as much as the council is expected to render such services to the community. He further said that the town council is not being indifferent to the needs of the people as there can be no greater needs than those of the people. He promised the residents that the town council would have to find some kind of solution to satisfy residents.

After a committee representing the group threatened to march "in thousands", only a small number of former former veterans turned up for the event. About 80 people singing freedom songs gathered outside the Greenwell Matongo Community Hall in Katutura from 08h00 before later dispersing. Despite the low turnout, the demonstrators were ready to march across the city to hand over a petition to Government, but they were stopped in their tracks by their organisers.

RESIDENTS from Oshikango, Omafo, Engela, Ohangwena and Onuno - villages that fall within the boundaries of the new town of Helao Nafidi in the Ohangwena Region - on Friday took to the streets to protest the actions of the Helao Nafidi Town Council. They want the Minister of Regional and Local Government, John Pandeni, to intervene, saying that the council was taking land for new developments without properly compensating villagers. Residents also say they are being charged municipal tariffs although they live in traditional homesteads and not in a town with modern services. Given that residents from five villages participated in this protest, it is assumed to have had at least 50 people.

Close to 300 nurses who held a peaceful demonstration in Windhoek yesterday have given the Ministry of Health and Social Service an ultimatum of 30 working days to address their demands or face a national nurses' strike. In Oshakati, also about 300 nurses, porters and cleaners from Oshakati State Hospital handed a petition to the Director of Health, Dr Naftali Hamata. Issues raised in the petitions included the overtime rate for work done on Sundays and public holidays, the proposed salary structure and an election to be held between Nanu and Napwu to determine who should be the sole bargaining agent for nurses and security orderlies.  " I heard of a nasty experience where one of the clerks was not receiving his salary for four months, and some nurses have not received their claims from as far back as April/May this year," he said, adding that his meeting would help in nurturing transparency amongst all stakeholders in the health sector. The envisaged meeting is expected to be attended by regional health managers, district coordinating committees, directors, general personnel, regional directors and nursing managers.

They gathered near the Okandjengedi Combined School early yesterday morning, from where they marched under Police escort to the Ongwediva Town Council to hand over a petition asking for taxi ranks. They then marched back to the Oshakati Town Council's offices, where they also handed over a petition asking for the taxi ranks in Oshakati.  From there they marched to the Oshakati Police station where the regional Nabta chairman, Pendapala Nakathingo, read a petition addressed to the Police Chief, Lieutenant General Sebastian Ndeitunga...Police Deputy Commissioner Sydney Philander said he would forward the petition to Lieutenant General Sebastian Ndeitunga. Both the CEO of Ongwediva, Damian Egumbo, and the acting CEO of Oshakati, Ores Shilunga, promised to address the lack of taxi ranks in their towns..."

1) "A SURPRISE protest in Windhoek yesterday by hundreds of taxi drivers is threatening to bring the city of Windhoek to a partial standstill in days to come...The strike, which took place at two sites in Katutura, was monitored by the City Police and NamPol officers. Strikers were adamant that a strike could help them solve the issue of high fines, and Nangombe was criticised for his perceived lack of action.  The Nabta boss was described as "useless" and his plea that the strike be called off was ignored...part of the group meeting at Donkerhoek in Katutura yesterday. Taxi drivers say the high fines are "unreasonable" and will ruin their business...City Police Chief Abraham Kanime personally visited both sites of the protest, and attempted to discuss the issues. Kanime stressed that the fines are "not a fee. You have an option. If you don't contravene the law, everything will be good." Kanime warned that the traffic fines are based on law, which cannot be changed on short notice..."; 2) "Two taxi drivers were injured after the Police clashed with a group of striking Windhoek taxi drivers in Katutura yesterday morning. The confrontation between the taxi drivers and a contingent of law-enforcement agents consisting of uniformed and plainclothes Police officers as well as the Police Special Reserve Force started when the drivers decided to march to the city centre in defiance of Police orders. The Police had to fire warning shots in the air to stop the approaching mass of taxi drivers. The unruly taxi drivers retaliated by throwing stones at the Police. The Police were forced to fire rubber bullets at the group. The two taxi drivers who were injured are Mateus Leonard (45), who was hit by rubber bullets in the head and arm, and Simon Shangula (29), who was beaten on the head with the butt of a gun.; 3) "Government yesterday condemned the violent behaviour of protesting taxi drivers, which led to the arrest of 90 taxi drivers and injuries to at least six Police officers and two taxi drivers...Violent scenes played out in Katutura yesterday, as hundreds of taxi drivers scattered in all directions in the Lafrenz area after the Police fired tear gas into the crowd. The Police said several rocks had been thrown at Police officers and their vehicles and several taxi drivers were shooting with live ammunition while the rocks were being thrown. The Police later arrested several men and confiscate their firearms. A number of taxi drivers, who refused to take part in the strike, were beaten up by striking colleagues. The situation was still tense last night, as Police and taxi drivers were again in a standoff as the drivers tried to reach their parked cars in Katutura's Donkerhoek neighbourhood..."

"President Hifikepunye Pohamba yesterday snubbed hundreds of disgruntled civil servants wanting to voice their dismay about the lost millions of the Government Institutions' Pension Fund (GIPF) when he refused to receive their petition at the opening of Parliament. The Police turned back at least 700 peaceful protesters, blocking them at the Zoo Park in Independence Avenue and marching them to GIPF House where a press officer from State House was sent to pick up the petition..."
"On April 6, the nurses submitted proposed salary structures and re-grading to the Ministry of Health and requested a meeting with Kahuure on May 17, but have not had any response?ó_"

turned violent on the third day; 1) "A youth organisation march to the Ministry of Youth yesterday was stopped in its tracks by police in Wanaheda after the group threatened to camp on the ministry's premises until their demands are met. Deputy Commissioner Andreas Nelumbo confirmed that the Wisdom Youth Organisation (WIYO) protesters were ordered to stop the march because of their intention to camp on the Ministry grounds...several members of WIYO decided to camp at the corner of the Wanaheda police station, surrounded by a number of police officers ordered to keep the group calm...WIYO members and organisers agreed that their main goal is to find employment and stop the rising levels of youth unemployment in the country..."; 2) "THE Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Youth and Sport, Dr Peingeondjabi Shipoh, has dismissed demands by a group of young people camping outside the Wanaheda Police Station in Katutura...Shipoh said he met the group two to three weeks ago already..."; 3) "The police stopped a march by a youth group to the Ministry of Youth, National Youth Service, Sport and Culture and arrested three of the protesters. After spending two days camped outside the Wanaheda Police Station in Katutura, the group calling themselves Wisdom Youth Organisation (Wiyo) claimed that they were told by the station commander, Chief Inspector Joshua Shikongo, that they could march to the ministry...The youth organiser said that Deputy Commissioner Andreas Nelumbu had set up a blockade to prevent them from marching further...The Police prevented the protesters from marching further and kept them there for most of the day, until late in the afternoon...At around 15h45, the Police had left the scene where they had set up the blockade and the protesters continued their march...However, 300 metres down the road they were stopped and prevented from moving further...The incident turned violent when the Police began pushing the crowd of largely women and children protesters back in the direction from which they had come. Three of the protestors, all of them male, were arrested by the Police in the scuffle." The Police continued to herd the protesters in the direction of the Wanaheda Police station, constantly pushing the women and children without encountering any real resistance."

Protester Group Identity: Plastic Packaging employees, Metal and Allied Namibian Workers' Union (Manwu)
Notes: "Plastic Packaging employees took to the streets in protest yesterday morning following a breakdown in wage negotiations...207 workers took part in the strike at all three plants and would not return to work until the issue had been resolved...Plastic Packaging management held a meeting with Manwu representatives yesterday afternoon, but the dispute remained unresolved."

"On June 13, nurses in the Khomas region staged another peaceful demonstration to hand over their petition and express their dissatisfaction at the manner in which they were being treated by Government?ó_"

"In early July, approximately 200 employees staged a lunch-time demonstration at the country's main airport over demands for a housing allowance from their employer. Napwu shop-steward and NAC employee Faye Kandjoo said in July that management had called the Airport's Company's employees to the negotiating table approximately one week after the first peaceful protest. Roughly a month after the negotiations began, a senior official inside Napwu yesterday said that the two parties were still in the negotiating process and that progress was being made."

"Between 500 and 700 nurses gathered outside the High Court in Windhoek yesterday, from where they marched down Independence Avenue, and up Fidel Castro Street to deliver a petition to Prime Minister Nahas Angula. yesterday's peaceful demonstration and handing over of the petition was the third public demonstration by nurses in Windhoek this year. Nurses at the Oshakati State Hospital also demonstrated yesterday..."

1) "CHAOS erupted at Herero Mall in Katutura, Windhoek on Friday evening when the Police clashed with an unruly crowd who refused to let the Police close down shebeens which were operating without licences. Herero Mall has recently been at the centre of attention following a bust-up between Khomas Regional Councillor Ambrosius Kandjii and a shebeen owner, and a Police clampdown on illegal alcohol sales...when about three or four Police officers arrived at Herero Mall on Friday evening to close down operations for the evening, they were met by disgruntled and unruly shebeen owners and patrons who demanded that the Police show them the documents authorising the closure of the shebeens. The Police Officers then left the scene only to return about 20 minutes later with about 30 Police and Special Reserve members. The situation quickly spiralled out of control as patrons and shebeen owners refused to allow the Police to close the shops. While the Police fired teargas and bullets into the air to disperse the agitated crowd, the Police themselves faced a barrage of rocks and empty bottles from the crowd...One man at Herero Mall asked why only that place was being targeted by the Police and why shebeens in Eveline Street were allowed to operate until late into the night."; 2) "two men arrested on Friday evening at Herero Mall appeared in the Windhoek Magistrate's court in Katutura on a number of charges. Samson Ngombe, a shebeen owner at Herero Mall, and Ngumenitize Katjimune were arrested on Friday evening when a riot broke out as Police attempted to enforce new operating hours for shebeens and close them down for the evening..."

1) "DISGRUNTLED residents of Bethanie village in the South yesterday padlocked the council's gates in protest against the recent work contract renewal of the council's chief executive officer, Willy Humphries. The residents let in council workers only after Police intervention...";  2) "the council yesterday reconnected water and electricity supply to residents' houses after they protested. Claiming the council had failed to inform them in advance about the cancellation, the protesting residents demanded that the council restore the services and negotiate with affected residents on how to repay their debts. The council suspended water and electricity supply because of residents' outstanding debts. The disgruntled residents claimed the council's administration was in 'shambles' because Humphries allegedly "runs the office from his cellphone"."; 3) "ANGRY residents of Bethanie village in the South are still protesting in front of the Village Council, objecting to the renewal of the work contract of the council's CEO, Willly Humphries. The protest is now a week old?ó_"; 4) "THE Bethanie Town Council is turning to the courts to remove angry residents protesting in front of the council offices. Council's decision to renew an employment contract of its CEO, Willy Humphries, for another five-year term led to the protest now edging towards its second week. The residents want the council to terminate Humphries' contract with immediate effect, claiming that it was renewed ""in a dubious manner"" at the beginning of September...picketing protestors, who have illegally set up tents at a council plot, about 30 meters from the council office..."; 5) "Meanwhile, a group of residents have vowed to continue their two-month-old protest in front of the council office to object to the renewal of Humphries's contract. The group now also demands that Knouwds be removed as a council member."; 6) "A GROUP of Bethanie residents camping in front of the local council offices on Monday voluntarily dismantled their protest camp. Protester Group Identity: NamPower employees, Mineworkers Union of Namibia (MUN)
Notes: "APPROXIMATELY 260 NamPower employees staged a protest outside the power utility's main offices in Windhoek yesterday. They handed over a petition to NamPower managing director (MD) Paulinus Shilamba. The workers are not happy with the deadlock in wage negotiations between NamPower and the Mineworkers Union of Namibia (MUN) and overspending by the company...Accepting the petition, Shilamba said the fact that he personally received the petition was a sign that NamPower was committed to the wellbeing of its employees, whom it regards as the organisation's most important assets. Shilamba told the workers that NamPower had always been a good employer and ensured them that their concerns would receive thorough consideration."

"On Monday local Police used teargas to disperse a mob of local RDP members after they had allegedly stormed the council office and insisted on handing over the recall letter personally to Knouwds. Protestors calling for the termination of Humphries's contract have voiced their disapproval of the "harsh treatment" the RDP members had received at the hands of the Police..."

Protester Group Identity: Polytechnic employees, Namibia Public Workers Union (Napwu)
Notes: "A group of between 60 and 70 Polytechnic employees held a demonstration outside the main gate of the Polytechnic's Windhoek campus yesterday to voice their concern over what they claim to be a general disregard of their concerns by the institution's management. Namibia Public Workers Union (Napwu) senior organiser Cleophas Katuuo read out a petition setting out the Polytechnic employees' grievances, saying that "the unfair labour treatment of Polytechnic of Namibia employees by Dr Tjama Tjivikua cannot be tolerated in an independent Namibia anymore"..."

Location of Protest: Iipandayamiti, Oshoogolo, Ombalala, Omafo and Oheke villages
Protester Group Identity: residents of Iipandayamiti, Oshoogolo, Ombalala, Omafo and Oheke villages
Notes: "RESIDENTS of Iipandayamiti, Oshoogolo, Ombalala, Omafo and Oheke villages in the Omusati Region held a demonstration last week, demanding that pre-paid electricity metres be installed at their churches, settlements and businesses...The villagers also said that they do not have roads in the constituency and it seems that earlier promises of roads have died a natural death. The residents than called upon their councillor and Omusati governor Sophia Shaningwa to consider their petition as an urgent matter."

"RESIDENTS of Tsumeb on Friday demonstrated, demanding the immediate halt of copper concentrate imports for refining at the Namibia Custom Smelters (NCS). They also called on the Government to ban the import of copper, especially from Bulgaria. The demonstration was led by Swapo regional coordinator for the Oshikoto Region Armas Amukwiyu and joined by some Oshikoto regional councillors and the senior headman of Oshivelo Traditional District, Nation Nashikaku...Accepting the petition, Councillor Tobias said he is also concerned about this issue, and promised that he will forward the petition to the Office of the Oshikoto governor Penda yaNdakolo for his immediate attention."

"ABOUT 500 Khorixas residents yesterday demonstrated against corruption at the local council, calling for the removal of the chief executive officer. The demonstrators in no uncertain terms called for the current CEO Nicodemus Gaeseb to be replaced with a new chief executive...closely monitored by armed Police. Some protesters threw stones at the council offices before the Police intervened. After much argument between the CEO and the demonstrators and with the intervention of the Police the petition was later handed to the CEO, who promised to forward it to the Minister of Regional, Local Government and Housing, Jerry Ekandjo, to whom it is addressed..."

Protester Group Identity: Municipal bus drivers, Namibia Public Workers Union (Napwu)
Notes: Daily protests began on February 23rd, but after approximately two weeks of no response, the bus drivers marches on the mayor's office on March 15th; 1) "MUNICIPAL bus drivers took to the streets of Windhoek yesterday to voice their dissatisfaction with their employer's refusal to pay them overtime backdated to 2007. The group of about 60 drivers also expressed unhappiness over the manner in which the municipality's Public Transport Division is being run...alleged that nepotism and favouritism are rife in the division, adding that Rupingena does not follow any of the municipality's policies and procedures..."; 2) "MUNICIPAL bus drivers in Windhoek have still not received any response from the Windhoek Municipality following daily demonstrations which started last Thursday over a dispute relating to overtime payments..."; 3) "MUNICIPAL bus drivers in Windhoek yesterday marched to the mayor's office to hand over a petition demanding overdue overtime payments as well as the axing of their department head. Roughly two weeks ago municipal bus divers in Windhoek engaged in a daily peaceful protests outside the City's public transport division to voice their disappointment over a number of issues...The group also expressed their unhappiness over the manner in which the municipality's public transport division is run by its manager, Clarence Rupingena. However, over the last two weeks the drivers' protest action has fallen on deaf ears, prompting the drivers to engage in a march and hand over the petition...Deputy mayor Gerson Kamatuka received the petition on behalf of mayor Elaine Trepper, who is out of town. Kamatuka said he would discuss the issues contained in the petition with Trepper and raise them at the City Council's management committee meeting on Monday."

"Close to 70 residents led by community activist Ernst Jash on Friday staged a protest march and presented a petition containing the so-called 'no-confidence vote' against the council and its CEO to Karas governor Bernadus Swartbooi's special advisor, Lucia Basson..."

"Street vendors, who were evicted by the Rundu Town Council and ordered not to sell their goods in the central business district (CBD), indicated after the meeting that they will go back on the streets to conduct their businesses in the usual manner. The town council last week abandoned an eviction order, after they apparently received instructions from Kavango Regional Governor Maurus Nekaro that the Namibian Police should allow the vendors to continue selling on the streets.  Last week's eviction was the second time in two years that street vendors were ordered away from the CBD. The latest eviction was met with fierce resistance from more than 600 street vendors who flocked to the municipal offices, demanding to see Rundu mayor Hilka Levi...After failing to see the mayor, the street vendors then resorted to an unsanctioned demonstration through the town's main street, despite several reminders from police officers that what they were doing was illegal. The street vendors claimed that the Open Markets are too small and cannot accommodate all of them, and that is why they opted to sell in the streets. They also indicated that they cannot afford to pay rental fees at the Open Market, as they do not generate significant profits from their businesses."

"ANGRY residents of Maltahí?he yesterday staged a protest march against the village council. The protest march, spearheaded by a pressure group calling itself the Maltahí?he Community Advocacy committee, called for the removal of the entire council...The residents also took issue with alleged interference by the Local Government Ministry in appointing senior council staff..."

although the source says this is the third demonstration in recent months, only two are reported in our sources; "Maltahí?he residents yesterday staged a third peaceful demonstration in less than two months against alleged corruption, poor service delivery and incompetence in their village council. Because of their alleged ignorance, the councillors are being manipulated by council's top administrative staff, the residents claimed. Handing over a petition to the council following a protest march spearheaded by the Community Advocacy Committee (CAC)...The council's chief executive officer, Eliphas Shipanga, received the petition and promised to forward it to the council..."

"WORKERS from almost every department of the Walvis Bay Municipality stopped working yesterday to stage a protest march and hand over a petition containing labour grievances. They wanted to give it to either the mayor, Derek Klazen, or chief executive officer Muronga Haingura but it was received by the general manager of communications, Kevin Adams, in the presence of councillor Romeo Goseb...Brand said the workers want the municipality to honour the recognition agreement signed in 1999. According to the workers, the council has been ignoring the agreement by issuing directives that allegedly have had an adverse effect on employees' working environment, benefits and work relationships..."

"SIX football clubs in the Omusati Region staged a demonstration against the Outapi Town Council on Wednesday after their grounds were taken away from them. The protesters accuse the council of having demolished their four sport fields at Onakayale village without their consent. They claim to have been allocated the piece of land by the late village headman Blasius Nangolo, who died earlier this year...Led by a police escort, the demonstrators marched to the office of Governor Sophia Shaningwa who told their leader, Jona 'Dlamini' Ndinoshiho, that she cannot receive their petition as the right person to receive it is the mayor of Outapi. The town council is said to have earmarked the area - situated less than 50 metres from the Nangolo homestead - for unspecified development..."

Protester Group Identity: Rally for Democracy and Progress (RDP) supporters, other opposition party supporters
Notes: 1) "THE Rally for Democracy and Progress yesterday accused the police of using a "colonial" law which prohibits a demonstration in or near a court building to remove their supporters from the Supreme Court. The party had staged a sit-in since Sunday to demand the verdict of the 2009 National Assembly election court challenge, but the police gave them until 16h00 yesterday to pack up and go or face the law...Since Sunday noon, more than 200 demonstrators have arrived at the Supreme Court from most regions of the country..."The election verdict is three years outstanding; we want this matter to be finally dealt with so that we know which way we are going."..."; 2) "RALLY for Democracy and Progress (RDP) demonstrators who moved their tents from the Supreme Court to the Parliament Gardens on Monday have been ordered to move again. The party's secretary for information and publicity, Jeremiah Nambinga, yesterday said the police were not against the demonstration and sit-in at the start, blaming political interference for the police's decision to have them removed from the area in front of the Supreme Court...the party has decided to withdraw from the Parliament Gardens in order to avoid a confrontation with the police...The demonstrators will be moved to the Shalom Centre in the Goreangab Dam area where they will sleep, and return to the Supreme Court during the day where they will continue with their demonstration..."

1) "THE 195 'struggle kids' still camping out at Brakwater may soon get entry-level jobs in the public service....the Brakwater area outside Windhoek yesterday, where 195 'struggle kids' have been staying since July 17, they were in high spirits, performing dances and songs for a filming crew of Namrights that is doing a documentary on the struggle kids who have staged protests at various locations since September 2008...The news of possible jobs for the youths came as a very welcome reprief and proof that when pressured, Government can come up with the goods, commented the executive director of Namrights, Phil ya Nangoloh."; 2) "...A group of about 200 'struggle kids' have camped at a Swapo plot at Brakwater north of Windhoek since July 17 after their protests in the city were stopped by the authorities."

"close to 300 teachers who staged a demonstration at the office of the Namibian National Teachers Union (Nantu) yesterday afternoon to hand over a petition calling on general secretary Basilius Haingura to report on the status of salary negotiations..."

Protester Group Identity: residents of Swakopmund DRC informal settlement
Notes: "POLICE at Swakopmund used pepper spray yesterday to disperse hundreds of people who demonstrated outside the town's municipal building for better service in the DRC informal settlement. The demonstration turned violent when the protesters became frustrated with police officers who were summoned to disperse the crowds after they refused to leave the premises and opted to stay on until last night s ordinary council meeting at 19h00. The protest was in response to the town council s alleged procrastination when it came to the formalisation of the shantytown on the north-eastern fringe of Swakopmund. Residents of all ages marched about five kilometres from the DRC to the municipality to air their frustration and to hand over another petition to Swakopmund CEO Eckart Demasius. Demasius assured them that the matter would be addressed at last night s council meeting, but the protestors refused to accept this as an official acknowledgment of their petition. Instead they opted to occupy the municipal grounds until the meeting where they expected an official response. The police were called in while the town s managers applied for a court order to stop the protest. The protestors however stood their ground...At lunchtime, residents started arguing with officers who were ordering them to leave the premises and scuffles broke out. One man involved in a tussle with an officer was handcuffed and dragged to a police van. Protestors then stormed the police, demanding that they let the man go. Some ran toward the van, shouting their dissatisfaction and making threats, and the police used pepper spray to disperse the crowd..."

Location of Protest: Khomas region and Otjiwarongo, Oshana Region, Oshakati, Ompundja and Onamutai, Omaheke, Karas, Erongo, Ohangwena and Otjozondjupa regions and Windhoek
Notes: related to October 17th event.  When Khomas & Otjozondjupa protest on Oct. 29th there is no response (source 1).  When teachers in additional locations protest on Nov. 1 police try to disperse the crowd and arrest some teachers (source 2).  1) "More than 400 teachers from the Khomas Region who took part in a strike yesterday stated that until their demands for a salary increase are met, they will not return to school and will continue to demonstrate at the Ministry of Education office premises.
