The strike has been declared illegal by the Ministry of Education and the Office of the Prime Minister. The Oshana teachers first met at the Oshakati Independence Stadium but the police chased them away. They then set up camp in Othingo village on the Oshakati-Okahao main road, where some were arrested and the rest were ordered to leave...Meanwhile, in Windhoek, more than 500 teachers picketing at the offices of the Ministry of Education were informed by the police of the correct procedures to follow before picketing..."; 3) "The more than 500 Khomas Region teachers who have been striking in front of the head office of the Ministry of Education since Monday said they would be marching to the High Court today as from 12h00. Attempts by the teachers to march to the offices of the Prime Minister on Tuesday were blocked by the police because of the illegality of the strike..."; 6) "THE Namibian teachers' nation-wide strike, that lasted almost two weeks from the 29th of October until the 8th of November 2012..."

"The Namibia National Students Organisation (Nanso) yesterday led a march by close to 1 000 pupils from schools in Khomasdal and Katutura, which started at the Dawid Bezuidenhout Secondary School and ended at the Immanuel Shifidi Secondary School. Nanso and the pupils are asking the government to meet the demands of their teachers so that the teachers could return to school for the examinations that started this week..."
"Hundreds of nurses and other health workers, including hospital cleaning staff, gathered at the Katutura State Hospital s nurses home yesterday where they decided to go on strike on Tuesday...

"HIMBA and Zemba people from the Omuhonga and Epupa areas on Saturday marched from their villages to Okanguati, 120 kilometres from Opuwo, to protest against human rights violations against them?ó_In these declarations, they denounced the planned hydro-electric dam in the Baynes Mountains, which they said would threaten their way of life and the natural environment that sustains it, and lead to a potential loss of land..."

"HIMBA and Zemba communities have again taken to the streets to amplify their demand for more control over their traditional lands. The groups first demonstrated at Okanguati, 120 kilometres from Opuwo, in late November, and on December 5 took a petition straight to the government offices at Opuwo, capital of the Kunene Region, to repeat their dismay at a planned hydro-electric dam in the Baynes Mountains..."

"ABOUT 100 placard-waving Khorixas residents on Monday demanded the suspension of town council officials who have been charged with corruption...The demonstration gathered at Eddie Bowe Soccer Field in front of the Khorixas Town Council offices and chanted slogans calling for the removal of the three officials. They also demanded the reconnection of water supply that was disconnected over unpaid bills and that a new debtors' system be implemented within 60 days..."

"SWAPO Party secretary general Nangolo Mbumba says he has neither the power nor the capacity to provide the 'children of the liberation struggle' with jobs. Mbumba told Nampa yesterday that as part of his duties as SG he can meet them, and nothing else. He was responding to demands by a group of about 80 'struggle kids' - as they are often referred to - on January 11 to meet him specifically..."

"A GROUP of 'children of the liberation struggle' have been camping outside the Swapo regional office at Outapi in the Omusati Region since late last week, demanding employment by the government...They accuse the Ministry of Youth, National Service, Sport and Culture of failing to deliver on its promises of public service jobs made when it registered them in 2008 and 2009..."We will camp here until our demands for employment are met," said Amutenya. They want to meet with Prime Minister Hage Geingob, Defence Minister Nahas Angula and Youth Minister Jerry Ekandjo to discuss their situation. The protesters are from 12 constituencies of Omusati, namely Outapi, Anamulenge, Ruacana, Onesi, Tsandi, Okahao, Otamanzi, Elim, Oshikuku, Etayi, Ogongo and Okalongo..."

"ABOUT 800 'children of the liberation struggle' from the Ohangwena Region are camping at the regional Swapo office at Eenhana, demanding government jobs. One of the spokespersons of the group, Asteria Patrick, confirmed to The Namibian over the weekend that more than 800 of them from all over the Ohangwena Region have been camping at the Swapo office since January 28 and will remain there until their demand is met.  She said they have handed a petition to the Ohangwena governor, Usko Nghaamwa, who promised to forward it to the relevant authorities. They said they were registered by the Ministry of Youth in 2009 and were promised jobs in the public service, but this never materialised..."

"THE police stopped a group of demonstrators under the Home Owners Association (HOA) from continuing with their march on Friday. The march was intended to petition the High Court against alienating houses from poor households?ó_"

"WHAT started with a controversial statement by the Inspector General of the Namibian Police ended with a protest by a large crowd of women, and even some men, dressed in miniskirts. In last week Tuesday's edition of The Namibian, Lieutenant General Sebastian Ndeitunga was quoted as saying that women must stop wearing skimpy miniskirts and hot-pants or face arrest. Ndeitunga was said although the police do not want to interfere in citizens' constitutional freedom, skirts that are too short and revealing "are not acceptable in African culture" and amount to public indecency. "Those who are behaving outside the normal tradition of an African will be dealt with," he said...others called it an abuse of women's rights and called for peaceful protests which led to hundreds of protesters coming together at the Zoo Park in Windhoek on Friday. At around lunchtime, a crowd of female protesters, and even some men, showed up in miniskirts and skimpy shorts in defiance of the police's view that wearing short skirts and shorts amounts to public indecency...There are already a number of cases of women being threatened with arrest because of wearing miniskirts. The miniskirt came under the spotlight over the festive season when more than 40 girls wearing hot-pants were arrested at Rundu. Kavango Deputy Commissioner Willie Bampton told Nampa earlier this year that the police would continue arresting those who are not "properly" dressed..."

Protester Group Identity: struggle children, Namibian Exile Kids Association (Neka)
Notes: started as a 700km march from the north to Windhoek & setting up of a tent camp (source 2) then turned into a march & police confrontation (source 1).  Source 3 indicates the camp lasted from March 1-April 22.  1) "THE police yesterday blocked an illegal march in Windhoek's Robert Mugabe Avenue by a group of 'children of the liberation struggle' who wanted to petition the Office of the Prime Minister. A scuffle erupted between the police and the marchers after one male member of the group hit a police officer. Some members of the group were lying in the street to block it and were removed to the pavement. "We wanted to go to the Office of the Prime Minister but the police blocked the road and shot [at] us with rubber bullets," Conrad claimed later. One police officer was hit in the face with a stone while another was hit on the leg. "Stones were raining, these people are a nuisance," one police officer said when The Namibian arrived at the scene. The police used teargas to disperse the protesters and about 40 of them were arrested. Inspector Ismael Basson said the march was illegal and was therefore stopped by the police. "Two of the officers were injured seriously and we rounded up 40 of them [protesters]," Basson said. Officers and some injured 'struggle kids' were taken to hospital for treatment. Later in the day, some of the 'struggle kids' again had a scuffle with the police at the gates of the Swapo headquarters where they sang liberation songs and chanted "give us work". "'Our mothers and fathers died, we are alone," some shouted. Later about 50 police officers arrived in riot gear and an estimated 100 tents were removed from opposite the Swapo headquarters."; 2) "Talk of a national protest by Neka comes after a group of more than 50 so-called 'struggle kids' arrived in Windhoek last month after allegedly covering more than 700 kilometres on foot from Outapi in northern Namibia. Affiliated to no specific political party, the youth decided to break their silence on topical issues, taking to the streets and marching to Parliament to hand over their petition, signed by about 900 people. In order to demonstrate their support against gender-based violence (GBV) hundreds of men, the majority of whom wore high heels while a few featured in feminine attire such as mini-skirts and long dresses, on Saturday protested against the violence that has skyrocketed in recent months. The 'Walk a Mile in Her Shoes' campaign that coincided with International Women's Day saw men bravely sporting heels and skirts to demonstrate in Independence Avenue, with the protest march starting from the offices of the Ministry of Gender Equality and Child Welfare and ending at Zoo Park in the city centre. Only on Thursday, with help from 200 Botswanan troops, was some order restored in Maseru. By then little was left standing.

?óìIt came as a shock to all and sundry on August 23 to see thousands of protestors buzzing around the streets of Maseru demanding an audience with Prime Minister Pakalitha Mosisili in order to air their grievances.?ó?  Thousands of protestors in Maseru.  ?óìHe was followed by people from all walks of life - from ordinary people to trade union leaders, from youth activists to officials from non-governmental organisations, with a few opposition party leaders following the masses.?ó? A diverse group of protestors.   ?óìPrime Minister Mosisili declined to meet the demonstrators, who had demanded that he receive their petition in person. Protester Group Identity: IndustriALL Global Union; IDUL; the Lesotho Council of NGOs; Lentsoe La Sechaba
Notes: IndustriALL Global Union affiliate the Independent Democratic Union of Lesotho (IDUL) joined civil society organizations in aÂ demonstrationÂ in the capital, Maseru, on Sunday 27 November 2016 to demand a return to the rule of law. about 55,000 industrial workers across botswana embarked on peaceful demonstrations this week for higher wages. according to the "guardian" newspaper of botswana today, the national manual workers union, which organized the protest, said it resorted todemonstrations after its hopes of negotiated salary increment faded away when its talks with the minister for presidential affairs and public administration mompati merafhe came to a stalmate on march 12 this year.

Botswana university students stopped cars here Friday to protest against the mass firing of at least 18,000 striking manual workers by the government. Students boycotted classes Friday and decided on the lunchtime action to press demands that the workers be reinstated in government departments and parastatals. The government has not budged on the demands and reports indicated certain workers would be re-hired if they accepted the low wage. Given how massive the firing was and how the students were able to stop traffic in the capital, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

At least three people were injured after Botswana deployed paramilitary police in a village near here Wednesday to quell riots sparked by the ritual killing of a teenage girl, South Africa's SAPA news agency said. The police Special Support Group (SSG) was sent to Mochudi village, 40 kilometres (24 miles) from the capital Gaborone, after schoolchildren attacked a restaurant belonging to a man they believe mutilated and killed their classmate, Segametsi Mogomotsi, on November 6 last year. Last month Mogomotsi's friends went on the rampage to avenge her death and to protest perceived police inefficiency in apprehending the killer. It was unclear if any demonstrators in Gaborone were hurt, but at least one student was hospitalized in a similar protest in nearby Mochudi after reportedly being struck by 14 rubber bullets. Given the destruction that the students caused, as well as the presence of the paramilitary police, this protest is believed to have at least 50 participants.

Rampaging students outraged over the suspected ritual murder of a teen-age girl clashed with riot police Thursday in Gabarone. At least two people were injured. Police fired rubber bullets and tear-gas to disperse the students as they tried to enter the National Assembly to protest what they see as inefficiency in investigating the girl's murder. The students, estimated by journalists to number about 1,000 from the capital's university and high schools, retaliated by stoning government vehicles parked on the assembly grounds. Club-wielding riot police chased them through the downtown, beating students and bystanders. The students smashed bank and shop windows. Most merchants closed to prevent looting. The rioting continued in the capital Friday when stone-throwing crowds blocked motorists from Gaborone's central business district. Police fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse protesters. Police spokesman Edwin Batshu said 300 people were arrested overnight Thursday in an attempt to prevent further violence in the capital, the South African Press Association reported. botswanan president ketumile masire today called for calm in the capital gaborone after three days of riots left at least one youth dead and two policemen seriously wounded. according to the south african press association tonight, a 24-year-old teacher was also in a critical condition in hospital after she was stabbed during the riots. more than 60 people have been arrested and the university of botswana has been closed indefinitely following student demonstrations.

Press freedom is under attack in Botswana and a bill scheduled to be introduced in the current session of Parliament has unleashed a wave of protest by journalists. So strong have been the protests that the Minister of Presidential Affairs and Public Administration, Ponatshego Kedikilwe, has agreed to delay the controversial Mass Media Communications Bill and hold more discussions. The bill comes at a time when private radio and television stations are waiting for licenses to operate. Observers say that the bill will stifle the operations of the private stations. The country's only radio station and only daily newspaper are both owned by the government. There is no television channel. Given the strength of the protest (being enough to force accommodation), this protest is assumed to have at least 100 participants.

Demonstrating University of Botswana students Friday gave president Festus Mogae 14 days to reject a controversial parliamentary motion urging the government to increase salaries of lawmakers, cabinet ministers, councillors and traditional leaders. The students, who marched from the university through the capital Gaborone, said they would mobilise the nation to mass action if Mogae did not heed their demands.  Given that the students believed they could mobilize mass national action, this protest is believed to have at least 50 participants.   The students braved a chilly morning to stage a peaceful protest to present their petition to parliament and the president's office. They demanded, among other things, that Mogae should not endorse the motion and should recall parliament as a matter of national urgency to reverse the issue. Chanting slogans and waving green twigs and posters, the students condemned the MPs and called them names, with Ngwaketse West legislator Michael Tshipinare, who moved the motion, bitterly villified. The students further called on a cabinet minister, Margaret Nasha, whose constituency covers the university, to dissociate herself from the motion.

Police threw a security cordon around the University of Botswana Friday as students rioted to protest against the management style of its Vice Chancellor, Prof. Sharon Siverts. The students also called for better learning conditions and demanded an increase in their study allowances and the improvement of their diet. The students have made an impassioned plea to University Council Chairman Justice Elijah Legwaila to intervene and bring what they call Siverts' uncontrolled spending to a stop. The University of Botswana's Student Representative Council (SRC) has decided to sue the police for refusing to issue it with a permit to hold a demonstration and subsequently, for injuring 17 of its members. According to the SRC president, James Mathokgwane, the students feel that the police, who fired teargas and rubber bullets last Friday to disperse them, have violated their rights. The student leader said that what the police did on Friday is unconstitutional because it limits the people's rights. When asked why there were a lot of police officers to quell the demonstration, Mbulawa said they had to leave their duties and control the students who were behaving violently. Given how the police responded and the amount of people who were injured, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

In one of the largest demonstrations ever seen in the capital, thousands of workers poured onto the streets of Gaborone on November 21 to back Bulgsa. The march also served as a vehicle for trade unionists to vent pent-up frustrations over labour laws. While the strike had been suspended, signs were that trade unions were not content to put up with the status quo. "It is time that trade unions in this country should take a stand and be fully involved in the salary negotiations," said Manual Workers Union organising secretary Johnson Motshwarakgole .

Parents, teachers and students took to the streets on Monday to protest the stalled construction and refurbishment of Francistown Senior Secondary School (FSSS) buildings. The placard wielding demonstrators petitioned Vice President, Ian Khama, to look into the matter. The petition was received by Francistown District Commissioner Sylvia Muzila on behalf of the V-P. The petitioners are worried that three years following the abandonment of the FSSS project, there is still no sign that construction and refurbishment will resume. The demonstrators felt that Khama's intervention is required since the officials have failed to make sure the project is re-started. The shortage of facilities at FSSS is said to have severely affected learning at the institution. Some classes are reportedly being held at the library and the dining hall because of the shortage, which was meant to be solved by the stalled construction and refurbishment. The dining hall was built 25 years ago to cater for only 400 students. The current student population at FSS is well over 1000. After receiving the petition, Muzila said she will forward it to the Office of the VP.  Given the population of the school and the fact that teachers, parents and students all came together to protest, this demonstration is believed to have at least 100 participants.

Second year students at Tonota College of Education (TCE) caused a disturbance at the institution yesterday over delayed allowances. Deputy principal, Gabasotlwe Gobotswang told Mmegi that the students wanted to be paid immediately with third years who were going for practicals in the field. According to Gobotswang, the students started assembling at the main hall and demanded to meet the college principal. The principal promised to meet them but was held up with other matters. On Tuesday matters came to a head as students marched to the college library where the principal was locked in a meeting. They demanded to meet with the principal whom they embarrassed in front of her juniors. Gobotswang indicated that by yesterday afternoon they were yet to assess damage caused to the college property. "Well, as we speak now, we are not yet certain if any property has been damaged or not," he said. The president of the Student Representative Council (SRC), Bofitlhile Lewanika, told Mmegi yesterday that the college authorities have themselves to blame for not taking heed of the students' demands. "The current crop of second year students were promised last year that some of their unpaid allowances will be paid accordingly this year. But the college was seemingly ignoring this factor, hence the demonstrations," he asserted. Because the administration kept saying it would meet the students, the response is believed to be accommodation, despite being unable to meet them due to other circumstances.  Also, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

THOUSANDS of street hawkers and vendors poured into the streets of Gaborone yesterday jamming traffic for close to an hour as they demonstrated against what they called "a tide of terrorism at the hands of the council". They also dismissed the Monday national budget as a rich man's budget. About 2000 demonstrators shutdown their operation in Gaborone yesterday morning to participate in the first ever March in the history of the country by the informal sector. In a petition, which was read out to the Local Government Minister, Michael Tshipinare, the angry demonstrators accused the Gaborone City Council and the police of harassment and confiscation of their goods, hence denying them a source of living. The association furiously attacked the government policies of neglecting their sector and urged for formulation of policies that will bring equality to the nation.

Stop corruption. Stop stealing land. Crooks should be fired. State media should belong to the people. These were some of the messages on placards carried by the Botswana National Front (BNF) supporters, marching to protest the way the ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) runs the affairs of the country. The protest march started at Old Naledi on Saturday morning and ended in front of the Botswana National Library Services (BNLS). The party leaders and supporters marched to the Office of the President to deliver the petition before assembling in front of BNLS where the petition was read out to the public. The party relayed their messages through placards and party songs, alleging acts of corruption and misuse of state media by the ruling BDP. Some placards carried messages, which implied that the Minister of Communication, Science and Technology, Boyce Sebetela should be removed from office, together with other ministers implicated in corruption. "Sebetela should resign," read a placard carried by one of the BNF supporters. The hyped supporters, while awaiting the formal delivery of the petition message, talked about their displeasures with the ruling party. Some of them alleged that the ruling party refused to accept their petition because it is a party of cowards. Given that this party is the main opposition to the ruling party, this protest is assumed to have had at least 100 people.

University of Botswana (UB) students boycotted classes and held a demonstration yesterday to protest the delay in paying allowances for first-year students. The students were annoyed that the UB administration failed to keep its promise to remit the allowances by Monday this week. By 10 o'clock in the morning, crowds of angry students started banging doors, chanting and generally creating havoc at the campus.  The ability of the students to create havoc and that there are multiple crowds banging on doors, etc., gives the impression of this protest having at least 100 people.  UB's public affairs director, Samuel Moribame, released a statement expressing regret that students had chosen demonstrations over other avenues of conflict resolution. "We take all concerns of the students seriously and will continue to do so. We, however, believe that most, if not all the concerns can be better tackled by engaging management in fruitful discussions in a spirit of give and take rather than boycotting classes...or forcing students out of classes, or damaging property such as happened (today)," the statement said. There was no explicit statement of trying to resolve this issue, and therefore this is coded as an ?óÖignore?ó» response.  Also, ?óÖdamaging property?ó» implies a certain level of violence on the side of the protesters.

University of Botswana (UB) students took to the streets yesterday to protest against what they term meagre off campus allowances. The students waved placards, some of which read: "Kgoroba mosola wa gago ke eng? [Kgoroba (George - Education Minister) what is your usefulness?)] "Taxi drivers or students, Kgoroba who is important?". They submitted a petition to the Ministry of Education and the UB administration. In their petition to the ministry, they want an undertaking that an adjustment of students' allowances would be made by September 20. The ministry has been given seven days to make this undertaking. The students demanded that the adjustment should be done in accordance with the Students' Representative Council's (SRC) proposal which was submitted to the Department of Student Placement and Welfare last month. The Director of Student Placement and Welfare, Florence Stoneham who received the petition, said they would respond in due course. UB Vice Chancellor, Bojosi Otlhogile assured the students that the management would respond to their concerns accordingly. Given the demonstrations two days prior and the population of the total student body, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

Four teacher organisations commemorated the World Teachers' Day on Tuesday by registering their displeasure with the way the Ministry of Education is handling complains about conditions of service and professional matters. The Botswana Teachers Union (BTU), Botswana Federation of Secondary School Teachers (BOFESETE), Association of Botswana Tertiary Lecturers (ABOTEL) and Botswana Primary Teachers Association (BOPRITA) staged a motorcade from BTU offices before assembling at the Gaborone Secondary School grounds to deliver the protest message. Given the participation of four different organizations, this protest is believed to have at least 50 participants.

More than 20 people have been arrested in Botswana's Central Kalahari Game Reserve after violence over the government's policy of relocating San Bushmen. President Festus Mogae's office said people had tried to enter the reserve, which government officials closed, citing a disease outbreak. Given that 20 people were arrested, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.  The Government says the reserve is closed because of animal disease, but the bushmen believe it is a ploy to destroy their nomadic way of life. "The demonstrators broke into a riot and attacked the police with an assortment of weapons," a statement from the president's office said yesterday.

Top opposition officials converged in Bobonong on Sunday to lead a demonstration against plans to introduce school fees next term. The demonstrators urged the government not to introduce school fees and condemned the ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) for not having the welfare of people at heart. They said the introduction of school fees will weigh heavily on the already impoverished Batswana. Among the people who participated in the demonstration are the Botswana Congress Party (BCP) president Gilson Saleshando, his deputy Kesitegile Gobotswang, secretary general Taolo Lucas, publicity secretary Dumelang Saleshando and Botswana National Front (BNF) vice president Kathleen Letshabo. Other opposition leaders in the demonstration were Billy Makuku, Vain Mamela and Phillip Bulawa. The demonstrators have tasked the only opposition councillor in Bobirwa constituency, Abel Madome to hand the petition to the acting District Officer, Innocent Maotwe. Bulawa assured Batswana that the opposition will continue to mobilise people to protest against the injustices perpetuated by the BDP government. He called on the government to take heed of their demands in the interest of the nation. Given the collusion of the various opposition parties, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

After eight days of class boycotts and demonstrations by students following a hike in food prices, the University of Botswana (UB) was closed yesterday. The UB Council indefinitely closed the institution at 3pm and gave the students one hour to leave. By 4.30pm, there were no students inside the main campus as UB security guards and police patrolled around. The closure came as a surprise to some students who thought peace would prevail. Two lecturers at the University of Botswana (UB) were beaten up by a mob of rioting students hours before the institution was shut down on Wednesday. UB's chief security officer, Robert Kalasi told Mmegi yesterday that the students also injured two foreigners using the university library. One student was caught with a scanner and has been taken to court. Kalasi said there were violent incidents the night before UB was closed as students turned against one another. This protest, given how destructive it was and the fact that it closed the school down, is believed to have at least 100 participants.

The president of the Botswana National Front Youth League (BNFYL) and Gaborone mayor, Nelson Ramaotwana did not mince words on Saturday when the planned handing of their petition to Mochudi District Commissioner (DC) failed. BNFYL marched from Phaphane complex to Segale Primary School in commemoration of June 16 Day of the African Child. Ramaotwana said that not only did they have to wait until Friday to receive the permit for their demonstration but the DC, who is paid by taxpayers, refused to take the petition and stated that they hand it in during the week. Ramaotwana said that the DC could have delegated someone else to take the petition. The petition read by Ramaotwana, called on the Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) government to release the Segametsi Mogomotsi death report to the public because millions of taxpayers' money was used to hire Scotland Yard investigators and that Batswana deserved to know the truth. He said the youth of Botswana have a task to advocate for the elimination of socials ill such as ritual murders, passion killings, child labour, child sexual abuse, child trafficking, poverty, disease and cultural unity in diversity.

Trade unions have told the Chief Justice Julian Nganunu to quit for delivering judgements that are not favourable to workers. Through BULGASA official Pelotshweu Baeng, the trade unionists said at a massive demonstration in Selebi-Phikwe that Nganunu has delayed the hearing of workers' cases brought before the him for too long. He called on the government to take all the ownership of the mines in Botswana because the current situation is what causes general managers to be insensitive to workers and behave the way they want. "Batswana must have a hand in the running of the mines so that management of the mines can improve," he stressed. "We accordingly demand that government should act swiftly to amend labour laws and give maximum protection to workers from indiscriminate expulsion from work by some employers," the petition said. Members of BULGASA, BOSETU, BHTTWU attended the handing over of the petition to show solidarity with BMWU. ?óìMassive?ó? demonstration has been taken to imply a presence of at least 1000 people.  The District Officer promised to hand over the petition to the relevant ministry.

Police on Wednesday released 45 Kumakwane residents who were arrested in connection with the damage of motor vehicles on Sunday evening. The residents went on rampage when a man died on the spot after he was hit by a motor vehicle. The residents blocked the Kanye-Gaborone 'Highway of Death' in protest against Government's refusal to erect speed humps along the road. At least six vehicles were damaged and police had to fire shots in the air to disperse the stone-throwing mob. Superintendent Andrew Bosilong told Mmegi yesterday that 18 youths, aged between 13 and 18, received two strokes and were freed while 21 others, aged between 20 and 25, refused to be punished and demanded to be charged and tried as required by the law. They will be tried on December 6 when six of them will face six counts of malicious damage to property. Bosilong said police were waiting for quotations from car owners. Given how many people were arrested, this protest is believed to have had at least 50 participants.

Speaking at the beginning of the demonstration at the Urban Freedom Square in White City, Motswakgakala Gaoberekwe, a Mosarwa rights activist, castigated the government for its violent treatment of the relocation victims. He pointed a finger at analysts and political pundits who, he says, are always quick to blame foreign influences whenever Basarwa call for their rights, stating that, Basarwa are human beings who are intelligent enough to wage their own struggle. "People should stop blaming foreigners for our protests. It is very patronising for people to assume that we are incapable of waging our own struggle without the input of so-called foreign elements," stated Gaoberekwe. The demonstration involving hundreds of people and a motorcade started at White City and travelled through the city streets to the Office of President.  After allegations that the Botswana National Front (BNF) is courting the notorious Survival International (SI) for funds, the party staged a demonstration on Saturday that could be likened to those usually organised by the British NGO to taint the image of Botswana. The BNF organised the demonstration to show support for Basarwa in their fight against relocation from the Central Kalahari Game Reserve (CKGR) by the government.

Students waited for the Ministry of Education to credit their allowances at 12pm but when they failed, about 300 of them quickly assembled for a peaceful demonstration. They went to the administration block and protested even though they were supposed to go to the MoE's head offices with their grievances. After toyi-toying around the campus, the students were told by the Student Representative Council (SRC) president that the ministry had promised to credit the money before 4pm.

Just a day before Botswana celebrated her 41st anniversary, members of the opposition Botswana National Front (BNF) in Kanye mounted a demonstration to protest the introduction of school fees. A long motorcade carrying young activists started at the BG Mall and proceeded to the Rural Administration Centre where a petition was read out before being handed to the District Commissioner's office. In the petition headed "No to Commercialisation of Education", the BNF demanded re-instatement of the right to free education with immediate effect. This protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

The students, who decided to march to the MoE head offices without a police permit, were stopped in their tracks by the police at the Gaborone Secondary School (GSS) grounds and driven back to the university campus.  In their excitement all the students approached the amateur photographer with sticks demanding that he delete the pictures forthwith. In those few seconds the man was shoved and pushed while others tried to beat him as he sprinted into the administration block as the SRC president tried to intervene to no avail. When reached for comment, SRC president Thutlwe explained that they were angered by the ministry's decision to ignore changes that the students made this year. He said since semensterisation was introduced in 2004 they have had the option of changing their meal plans and to choose whether they move off campus with each new semester.

The University of Botswana (UB) student demonstration turned violent when police intercepted the illegal march, apparently en route to Parliament to coincide with Finance Minister, Baledzi Gaolathe's presentation of his 2009 budget proposal. The male students got their fair share of the baton as the females retreated under a barrage of the stick. Some students stoned cars as they beat a retreat, redirecting some away from their path back home. The students have been boycotting classes since the beginning of the month in protest against the Ministry of Education action to stop paying allowances for those who had failed, and wanted to repeat their courses.

Speaking at a BNF demonstration held last week, the party's youthful parliamentary candidate for Gaborone Central said that reducing students' allowances was not the solution to the sponsorship crisis gripping the Ministry of Education and Skills Development. The BNF held a mass demonstration calling for the resignation of Education Minister Jacob Nkate. The match, which started at the national stadium, ended with a rally at Old Naledi in Gaborone South.  Mass demonstration implies a crowd of at least 1000.

Employees of Kgalagadi Breweries Limited (KBL) and Botswana Breweries Limited (BBL) yesterday marched in protest against the 30 percent alcohol levy because the surcharge had resulted in serious problems occasioned by massive job losses and posed a threat to the whole industry. They called on the government to rescind the levy or reduce it to save further job losses.  Given the involvement of two different companies, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

After being subjected to red tape for some time, the Botswana National Front (BNF) staged peaceful demonstrations to protest against extra judicial killings on Saturday. The demonstrations commenced at Gaborone West and culminated in a rally at Ledumang. However, both the march and rally were poorly attended. Party officials attributed the poor attendance to the Desert Race, which was taking place at the same time as well as the initiation ceremony in Mochudi. Despite poor attendance, this protest is still believed to have at least 50 people, given the involvement of the BNF.

An assembly of six junior secondary schools from around Molepolole turned into a battlefield after police allegedly fired rubber bullets and teargas at protesting students on Friday. The students had gathered at the entrance to Kgari Sechele Senior Secondary School where the previous day they had threatened violence over the fact that they had not been taught because their teachers have joined other public service employees in the ongoing strike that is now in its third week. Then all hell broke loose. Gathered in a place awash with stones, the irate students picked up the only weapons available to them and retaliated. The police found the missiles too much to bear. Their perspex shields offered little protection from the thousands of pellets from over 3,000 children.  It sounds as though the students are angered over the government?ó»s lack of action over the public workers?ó» strike, and thus, it is counted.

Opposition parties have told President Ian Khama to resign because he has failed to lead the country. Speaking at a rally organized by opposition parties in Gaborone over the weekend to support the on-going strike by government employees, Botswana National Front (BNF) president Duma Boko said Khama has been overburdened with the mantle of power and is failing to rule the country. He said Khama must resign and try his hand at being a special constable or something else because Botswana needs a good leader not a Father Christmas, "who goes around donating blankets when there is a national crisis". Given the fact that the workers?ó» strike includes over 50,000 people, and that all opposition parties were present at this rally, this protest is believed to have at least 1000 people.

After violent protests, frustrated Botswana unions call off their strike to plan a way forward. Shattered glass, large stones and bricks littered the ground at Gaborone's Main Mall after violent protests by Botswana's public service workers, who are embroiled in a wage dispute with President Ian Khama's government. In the run-up to the violent outbreaks angry workers marched and sang and denounced Khama's rule as "autocratic". Some of the workers, taking a cue from the North African protests, demanded that Khama be removed. A cool Khama recently told a community meeting that "the workers can strike for another five years but they will not get any money". Given the amount of participants in the strike, this protest is assumed to have at least 1000 people.

Police clashed with students at Swaziland University, injuring 80 of them in a melee that caused $$40,000 in damage, authorities said Friday. Four of the students were reported in critical condition, university officials told the independent South African Press Association. The riot Wednesday night involved student grievances over campus life, including the quality of food. Fighting erupted when a group of about 400 refused to leave the Kwaluseni campus peacefully, erected barricades and smashed furniture and windows, the government-run South African Broadcasting Corp. reported.

The Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions called the strike to press for workers' rights legislation, adding its plea for reform to demands for more political openness in this usually quiet monarchy. Police fired tear gas at a crowd of protesters in Mbabane, the South African Press Association reported. The news agency said it was the biggest stay-away since nationwide strikes in 1977. hundreds of striking workers and students today went to the main street of swaziland's capital mbabane to go on the kingdom's largest-ever national strike. striking workers and students in swaziland's capital of mbabane continued their protest last night and at least three workers were shot and serious wounded, a local newspaper "the citizen" reported today.

Scores of people were injured during a clash between more than 500 street vendors and police during a protest in the town centre here Wednesday, witnesses said. It quoted witnesses as saying baton-wielding police fired teargas and rubber bullets to disperse the Manzini vendors, who were protesting against enforcement of a clampdown on unlicensed street trading. The crowd retaliated by throwing stones before police waded in with batons, beating several protestors to the ground before arresting them, SAPA said.

Vendors also staged protests in the capital Mbabane but no injuries were immediately reported, the South African news agency SAPA said. In the Mbabane protest, several hundred people, mainly women who sell fruit and vegetables, marched on the council-controlled market where they overturned and looted stalls of licensed vendors, SAPA said. Protestors complained of corruption and favouritism in the granting of vending licences by the council.

Labor unions and student organizations launched peaceful demonstrations Monday in Swaziland, demanding the restoration of multi-party democracy in the small southern African kingdom. The South African Press Association reported the protests appeared to enjoy widespread support, with most factories and shops in the capital Mbabane closed. Police and troops maintained a heavy presence in public areas and sealed roads leading into Mbabane and the city of Manzini to minimize disruptions. No incidents of violence were reported by early evening. The demonstrators called for indefinite action to press for an end to the absolute monarchy established in that country of 800,000 people in 1972, when all political parties were banned.  Protestors gathered in several parts of the capital Mbabane and shopkeepers kept their blinds down for fear of trouble, Swaziland police said, according to the South African news agency SAPA. The violence erupted after three leaders of the Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions were arrested here Monday night, the South African Press Association (SAPA) reported. Given the presence of the police and the fact that both the labour unions and student organizations were involved, this protest is believed to have at least 100 participants.

Striking students and workers Tuesday clashed with police and troops who retaliated with rubber bullets and tear gas in Manzini, 42 kilometers (26 miles) east of here, opposition spokesmen said. The violence erupted after three leaders of the Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions were arrested here Monday night, the South African Press Association (SAPA) reported. Benedict Tsabedze, president of the Swaziland Youth Congress, told SAPA that six people were hospitalized, while People's United Democratic Movement leader Kislon Shongwe said the exact number of wounded could not be determined because many protesters had gone into hiding. They are seeking an end to the non-party political system established with the 1972 banning of political parties in the landlocked kingdom wedged between South Africa and Mozambique. State-run television later reported that a 16-year-old girl was killed by police gunfire in unclear circumstances in Manzini, the country's industrial center, when the strike began Monday. Soldiers and police patrolled throughout Mbabane, the capital, and the industrial center of Manzini, 30 miles (50 kilometers) to the south, on Tuesday in a show of force, according to residents reached by telephone from Johannesburg. On Tuesday, police used tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse marching strikers in Mbabane and Manzini, according to residents and labor leaders.

The leaders of a pro-democracy strike, freed from prison and embraced by cheering supporters Thursday, vowed to continue their campaign against Swaziland's monarchy. The men were carried on the shoulders of the chanting, singing crowd such displays normally draw a brutal police response. They were then driven to Mbabane, where several hundred more supporters danced in the streets. Riot police in helmets and armed with rifles stood in the streets and fired two rounds of tear gas as a crowd of demonstrators ran toward a central Mbabane square, sending people fleeing with shirts pulled over their faces. There were no injuries. Later Thursday, police later fired two rounds of tear gas to break up crowds that ran to a central square in Mbabane after the freed labor leaders rode into town with car horns blaring.

About 100 pro-democracy demonstrators defied a government ban Friday to march on government offices as they protested against a 23-year old ban on political activity in this tiny mountain kingdom. Prime Minister Mbilini Dlamini on Thursday banned what was heralded as two mass rallies organized by the umbrella opposition Swaziland Democratic Alliance to mark the 23rd anniversary Friday of an April 12, 1973, state of emergency restricting personal freedoms and banning political parties.

Swaziland's civil servants resolved Thursday to embark on an indefinite strike from Friday in support of their demand for an 18 percent wage increase, a senior official said. The decision was taken at a meeting attended by some 7,000 civil servants in the central town of Manzini, according to the acting president of the Swaziland National Association of Civil Servants, Paul Dlamini. Schools and colleges have been closed since Thursday last week and students have begun street protests in support of the striking teachers.

Teachers resolved at a mass meeting in this central Swaziland town on Wednesday to continue a strike they began 12 days ago pending a second hearing on Friday by the Industrial Court. Some 6,000 teachers, members of the Swaziland National Association of Teachers, gathered at the trade fair grounds here where they unanimously resolved to continue striking until their demand for an 18 percent wage hike is met.

In another protest meeting here Saturday, about 4,000 teachers resolved to continue a three-week-long strike, which has crippled the country's education system and prompted 25 student leaders to go on hunger strike in sympathy. The teachers, who have called for 18 percent wage increases, rejected the government's latest offer of 10.9 percent and agreed to continue their battle in Swaziland's industrial court on Monday.

Police on Saturday dispersed a demonstration here of about 4,000 opposition party supporters calling on Swaziland's government to institute democratic reforms. The gathering, which had been called at Manzini's Freedom Square by leaders of the opposition People's United Democratic Movement to announce a new "defiance campaign" against the government, was peacefully ended by several thousand police officers.

Six people were injured when police opened fire on striking sugar workers at Big Bend, in Swaziland's central Lubombo region, the SAPA news agency said Tuesday. The incident, which occurred on Monday, is the first reported violent confrontation between strikers and the security forces of the tiny southern African kingdom since a national strike was launched by the Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU) on February 3. The report said the shootings occurred when striking workers wanted to enter the premises of Ubombo Ranches Sugar Company and force out workers who were maintaining essential services and machinery under an agreement between the union and the company. About 50 policemen, some in riot gear, fired teargas and warning shots in the air, prompting the workers to begin stoning them. Police then opened fire on the workers, wounding six of them. The SFTU, backed by outlawed political groups, is demanding that King Mswati III lift a 1973 decree that bans all political parties, and reinstate constitutional rule. Even though the immediate desire of the demonstrators was to take people away from working so they could strike, this is a direct consequence of the strikeÈs demand for democracy.  Given the presence of 50 police and the popularity of the strike, this demonstration is believed to have at least 100 people.

Riot squads clashed with several hundred protestors outside a venue here Wednesday where four leaders of a mass 10-day strike appeared in court. Police beat protestors with batons, although it was unclear if anyone was hurt, the SAPA news agency said.

Police in Swaziland police on Saturday arrested 15 youths protesting against the country's 24-year-old royal decree banning opposition political activity. The protestors were seized by baton-wielding police during a pro-democracy demonstration organised by the Swaziland Youth Congress (SWAYOCO), a youth wing of the country's largest banned opposition party, the People's Democratic Movement (PUDEMO). At least two of the 200-odd protestors -- who were dispersed just as the demonstration was beginning at the Manzini bus rank -- were assaulted with police batons, the AFP correspondent said. The demonstrators were calling on Swaziland's youthful King Mswati III, who rules by decree, to lift a 1973 law banning all political parties in the tiny mountain kingdom, which is sandwiched between South Africa and Mozambique.

Media workers in Swaziland today held a public protest against a decision of government to approve a media bill which will introduce licenses and a government imposed ethics code. The journalists marched to the office of the country's Prime Minister Sibusiso Dlamini to present a written petition to government. Dlamini was reportedly out of the office but the petition was handed over to the Director of the Public Policy Co-ordinating Unit, Mishek Shongwe. In the petition presented to government, journalists have demanded an immediate withdrawal of the bill in the light of its drafting without any consultation with media workers as stake holders. They also claim the bill will affect the operations of the media and ultimately media freedom. There has been no government response to the petition. Last week, the Swaziland National Association of Journalists led a march of close to 100 media workers to Cabinet offices to deliver a petition to the Prime Minister, Sibusiso Dlamini, calling for the unconditional withdrawal of the draft Bill.

Police hurled tear gas at striking educators in Swaziland Thursday, trying unsuccessfully to break up a demonstration by 7,000 teachers and headmasters. Teachers have been striking for nearly two weeks for an 18 percent pay raise dating back to 1996. The government offered an 8 percent raise after a similar monthlong action earlier this year, but teachers turned it down.

Armed paramilitary police fired tear gas at about 2,000 demonstrators awaiting Swaziland's King Mswati III on his return from the Commonwealth Heads of State Conference in Scotland, South African radio said. Swaziland has been plagued by actions from trade unions demanding constitutional changes to institute democracy. The protest campaign accelerated Tuesday when police fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse a crowd of about 500 demonstrators who tried to block King Mswati's exit from the airport on his return from the Commonwealth summit in Scotland. The protesters, who want democratic reforms and higher pay for teachers, threatened to demonstrate again when Charles arrived, but police banned the gathering.

Swaziland's media faces new challenges following the cabinet's approval of the proposed Media Council Bill 1997 which restricts press freedom. Incensed, hundreds of angry journalists from the country's five media houses, The Times of Swaziland, Swazi Observer, Nation Magazine, Broadcasting and Information Services and Television Broadcasting Corporation, marched to the Prime Minister's office to protest. National Association of Journalists president Mbuso Mtsenjwa handed over a petition demanding an immediate withdrawal of the media bill by Prime Minister Dr. Sibusiso Dlamini. The association has said it is prepared to fight the matter in the court. But Minister of Information, Muntu Mswane, argues that the journalists' fears are groundless because the core objective of the bill is to promote professionalism.

Swazi students are taking their yearly exams under police and army watch this year as a teachers' strike rocks the kingdom. Over 6,000 people marched to the cabinet offices in Mbabane recently to deliver a petition to Prime Minister Dr. Sibusiso Dlamini asking him to grant an 18 percent salary increase to teachers. Parents, teachers, students, unionists, and political activists joined in the protest with petitions from the National Association of Teachers, the National Parent/Teacher Association, and a women's rights group, Women and the Law in Southern Africa.
Police used tear gas to break up a demonstration by about 100 protesters calling for greater democracy, but no arrests were reported.

Teachers in Swaziland on Thursday staged a march in the capital in protest against the eviction of two chiefs by police in an action that has disrupted schooling in eastern Swaziland. About 2,000 people marched from the University of Swaziland to the palace yesterday to demand a meeting with the King.

Protester Group Identity: Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions and Swaziland National Teachers Association
Notes: Several people were injured on Monday when Swaziland's armed forces broke up anti-government protests in the capital, Mbabane, and in the industrial city of Manzini. Eyewitness said police and army officers disrupted a march on the king's palace outside the capital led by the Swaziland National Association of Teachers (SNAT) with teargas and batons. The teacher's association called the action to protest against the eviction of subjects of two chiefs deposed by a member of the royal family two weeks ago. "We were beaten up severely by police who dispersed us with teargas," Swaziland National Teachers Association (SNAT) president Musa Dlamini, who led some 300 teachers in the action, told IRIN.

The first state witness, Senior Superintendent Jomo Mavuso, testified that on November 7, 2000, about 250 members of the Swaziland Democratic Alliance gathered at the old Mbabane bus station, heading for the prime minister's office. The police officer said he ordered them to disperse, but they started to march and chant songs with lyrics including "Even if we die!" After a three-hour standoff with police, Masuku addressed the crowd, when he allegedly said: "Away with the king and the system!", "Away with Mswati's reign" and "Away with the dictator's government." Since the arrest of Masuku did not take place during the same day as the protest, arrests is not considered a response.

Thousands of pro-democracy protestors in Swaziland dispersed peacefully on Monday after crippling the business centres in the kingdom's two major cities of Mbabane and Manzini for over three-hours at the start of a two-day anti-government strike. Large police and army squads surrounded the chanting protestors, but no damage or injuries were reported and demonstrators dispersed voluntarily after midday Police also used a dreaded 60-day detention-without-trial law on Monday to arrest Swaziland National Association of Civil Servants (SNACS) executive member Quentin Dlamini, Swaziland Youth Congress (Swayoco) secretary general Sandile Bhembe and Swayoco executive member Sibusiso Dlamini during demonstrations in Manzini and Swaziland's southern district of Nhlengano. The strike continued on Tuesday, without public demonstrations, and without any significant disruption of public or commercial services. Therefore, this is coded as a 1-day protest only. Mass action is taking place today in Swaziland, and will continue tomorrow, calling for an end to the gross violation of human and trade union rights and the oppression of the people.

FIFTY women bared their buttocks in protest at the seizure of land in Swaziland, Africa's last absolute monarchy, by the brother of King Mswati III. The sight of a woman's buttocks is a strong insult in Swazi culture, and was intended to show their anger over the loss of land in Macetjeni and kaMkhweli. Manzini (Swaziland) - Swazi women are flashing more than their backsides in their campaign against oppression in the tiny kingdom. While Swazi police were busy questioning some of the elderly rural women who made headlines last week when they staged a pantyless protest outside a chief's homestead, their urban counterparts gathered in Mbabane to discuss how to find justice.

About 300 young women marched to a royal residence outside of the capital of Mbabane and laid down their symbolic chastity belts - a multicolored tasseled scarf - in protest of King Mswati III's choosing a 17-year-old as his ninth wife. There -- ululating and chanting -- they demanded redress, and the king capitulated. Swaziland's young absolute monarch bowed to pressure from the maidens of his kingdom Sunday and delivered up an ox as a fine for taking a second fiancee after demanding that all young women take a vow of chastity.

Almost 200 Christians gathered Saturday at the Silesian High School in Manzini in central Swaziland to pray for jailed opposition leader Mario Masuku and protest royal rule. "We want to make it part of our agenda that the church in Swaziland plays a leading role in cases of human rights abuse," he added. Worshippers in the largely Christian country also prayed for more than 200 families who were evicted from their homes in eastern Swaziland about two years ago. They had refused to recognise King Mswati's older brother Prince Maguga as chief.

Protester Group Identity: Swaziland branch of Women in Law in Southern Africa and the Swaziland Action Group against Abuse
Notes: An ad hoc gender rights consortium, consisting of the Swaziland branch of Women in Law in Southern Africa and the Swaziland Action Group against Abuse, showed up at the high court wearing black mourning outfits, not in anticipation of the outcome, which seemed preordained, but in protest against women's minority status in the country. Given the two groups?ó» involvement, this protest is coded with the belief that there were at least 50 people present.

Several hundred took to the streets of Manzini both Thursday and Friday, chanting anti-government slogans and listening to speeches from labor and political leaders. Several thousand workers and opposition activists took to the streets of Swaziland's two main cities Thursday to protest against profligacy by Africa's last absolute monarch in the face of crushing poverty. They also called for democracy and a return to the rule of law. A petrol bomb was thrown at a house occupied by police some hours before the marches started, but police were not immediately able to establish a link between the attack and the demonstrations, which were set to continue Friday. A small bomb exploded at a police compound in Swaziland overnight that authorities said may have been linked to a nationwide anti-government strike that began Thursday. No one was injured in the gasoline bomb blast on the outskirts of the capital, Mbabane, police officials said, but the building where it blew up. Police said they suspected an underground opposition organization, the People's United Democratic Movement was involved in the attack. Monarch tried to stop protests with the court, but the court was on strike, so the response is coded as ignore. Also, since the bomb attack could not be explicitly linked to the protest, it is not considered violence.

Thousands of marchers took to the streets in Swaziland's two main cities Tuesday on the first of a two-day mass action to protest escalating poverty and a lack of rule of law in Africa's last absolute monarchy. The protest is the second in a series called by Swaziland's largest Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU) and other pro-democracy groups, lobbying for the return of democracy in the small kingdom landlocked by South African and Mozambique. In Manzini, Swaziland's second largest city, an estimated 7,000 marchers, many of them wearing red SFTU T-shirts, walked through the streets, while about 1,200 people gathered in the capital Mbabane. A total of 6,000 Swazi workers launched a protest on Tuesday, demanding democratic reforms and limit the endless emperor power in this small southern African country. The workers protested peacefully in the industrial city of Manzini and the capital Mbabane in the national anti-government strike. They chanted slogans calling for the country's king to take a back seat to government and for the institution of democratic reforms, the South African Press Association reported. Thousands of Swaziland's workers took to the streets Wednesday on the second of two days of protest against escalating poverty and a lack of the rule of law in Africa's last monarchy.

Police fired teargas at demonstrators who gathered at the sourthern Swaziland town of Lavumisa on Saturday to protest the 30th anniversary of the ban of party politics, an opposition official said. A leader of Swaziland's banned main opposition, the People's United Democratic Movement (PUDEMO), Bong'nkosi Dlamini, said the 300 demonstrators ignored a warning from the police's riot squad to disperse.

Thousands of public sector workers demonstrated in Swaziland on Tuesday to protest after the government awarded politicians a pay rise but withdrew a planned increase for civil servants. Around 5,000 teachers, nurses, civil servants and pro-democracy activists took to the streets of Mbabane early on Tuesday, carrying placards demanding that the government raise their pay immediately to match the 30-percent increase it awarded politicians.

Some 2,000 people poured into the streets of Manzini while the secretary general of the Swaziland Federation of Labour (SFL), Vincent Ncongwane, led an estimated 3,500 protesters to Prime Minister Sibusiso Dlamini's office in Mbabane. However, Dlamini was not in his office to receive a memorandum from the crowd on their salary increases, which have been frozen by the government. Angry protestors in Mbabane mobbed the motorcade of Deputy Prime Minister Arthur Khoza when he left his office, but police officers were on hand to defuse a potentially explosive situation. Some 5,000 protestors gathered in the capital, Mbabane, and 1,000 in the central commercial city of Manzini. Demonstrators broke windows and caused minor vandalism in Mbabane and riot police responded with teargas. When the protestors attempted to reassemble, they were beaten by baton-wielding security forces. Agence France-Presse reported a trade union official as saying that one man was beaten to death by the police. The police cracked down on protests in this African kingdom today as a Commonwealth summit meeting began and as demonstrators angrily criticized what they described as the king's increasingly autocratic rule. Swazi police, however, insisted that the protesters move their picket to a location outside the city. When the protesters refused, police opened fire on them, hitting at least two protesters and injuring many, Ncongwane said. Cosatu spokesman Norman Mokoena told Sapa: "The Swazi police beat up and terrorised the protesters. They started shooting live ammunition at them. As I speak there are a lot of people in hospital in Manzini and Mbabane. The march has been disrupted by police and the security forces." Swazi trade unionists vowed to fight government and police oppression at a pro-democracy protest Friday, describing an international conference under way outside Mbabane as a "picnic" that excluded ordinary Swazis.

Swazi police clashed at the weekend with protesters demanding political reform in Swaziland, where King Mswati III wields absolute power, witnesses, anti-monarchist activists and reports said Sunday. A gunbattle broke out after police fired tear gas during a protest held Saturday in a township in Matsapha in central Swaziland, eyewitnesses said. But a youth activist insisted that the protesters had not opened fire on the police in the southern African kingdom, wedged between South Africa and Mozambique. The protesters than started throwing stones at the police, the report said. Given the response and the desire to block this group from the capital, this protest is taken as having at least 50 members.

Swazi women took to the streets in an unprecedented protest march on Thursday following the public gang rape of a teenage girl at a bus rank in the commercial city Manzini. About 1,000 marchers, including school children, joined the protest action at the bus rank on Thursday, with speakers demanding the abolishment of outmoded customs that keep Swazi women in minority status. "Abuse of women is getting worse, and we must stop it because the next time there might be a public murder," said one of the march organisers, Brenda Nhlabatsi, of the Swaziland chapter of the International Community of Women Living with HIV/AIDS. "We are talking to the bus owners. We want them to make a code of conduct. We are urging the Road Transportation Board to revoke the operating licences of the involved buses," she said.

Over the next few weeks, Pungwayo answered that question by helping to organize the first-ever women's march in Swaziland, a mountain kingdom of 1.2 million people. She also successfully lobbied for police and other authorities to take action. Three men have been arrested, but the activists are pressing for dozens more to be charged. Fueling the outrage of activists such as Pungwayo is their conviction that the traditional subjugation of women is one reason that Swaziland has an HIV infection rate of nearly 40 percent, the highest in the world. Their protests of the assault have initiated uncommonly passionate public debate over what it means to be Swazi in the age of AIDS. When about 1,000 women demonstrated Sunday against the attack, drivers and conductors threatened to do the same again. Although some members of the government commented on the attack, nothing substantial was done, and therefore, the response is coded as ignore.

Protester Group Identity: Union Workers and the Swaziland Federation of Labor
Notes: About a thousand workers marched through the capital in a peaceful demonstration on Wednesday to protest against taxation on their retirement benefits and poor constitutional reform. Sithole's union and the Swaziland Federation of Labor (SFL) organized the one-day protest. The workers delivered a memorandum to the finance ministry before dispersing peacefully.

The 80,000-strong Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU), and the smaller Swaziland Federation of Labour, were only able to muster a few hundred demonstrators for a march along the main commercial street of the capital, Mbabane.  He said 1,000 unionists and members of Swaziland's banned political parties took part in the protest march, but police spokesman Superintendent Vusie Masuku and eyewitnesses interviewed by IRIN placed the number at 400 to 500. A poor response to a general strike called by Swazi labour to demand political reforms on Tuesday has exposed the limitations of the pro-democracy movement. Police had deployed two water cannons near the gathering point of the protesters who in the end, numbered only a few hundred, wearing red t-shirts that read "Enough is enough !".

Only some 300 people took part Wednesday in the protest called by trade unions in the economic capital of Manzini, about the same turnout as the previous day in the political capital Mbabane, where thousands of police outnumbered protesters. The unions were calling for democratic reform in Swaziland, Africa's last absolute monarchy where Mswati has been accused of living high on the hog while his subjects struggle with grinding poverty and the world's highest AIDS infection rate.

A near riot at a Swazi primary school this week, when parents tried to register their children as orphans to qualify for government support, has underlined the resentment created by efforts to help the growing numbers of vulnerable children. Coded as tax policy/price increases because the protest was about non-orphaned children?ó»s parents having to pay while orphaned children received free schooling.  "Children whose parents can afford to pay school fees felt it was unfair that they had to pay, when government was paying for orphans. They said, 'Why should these children be rewarded because their parents got AIDS and died?'" a teacher at Khuphuka Primary School near the capital, Mbabane, told IRIN. The teacher said that out of 761 registered pupils, only 86 paid their school fees on the opening day of school - the rest were sent home. Police had to disperse an unruly crowd of parents who protested that they were being discriminated against because their children were not orphans. Based on how many students were sent home, this protest is coded as having 100 people at least.

About 500 people representing church groups in Swaziland, Africa's last absolute monarchy, staged a protest Thursday against a new draft constitution that they said gave King Mswati III too much power. The protesters led by Catholic and Anglican bishops marched to the offices of the prime minister in the capital Mbabane to deliver a petition opposing the proposed new basic law currently before parliament. The protesters, who had received police permission for the march, sang hymns and many wore religious dress. Since they received police permission, this is coded as accommodation.

Swaziland's public schools were either closed or being run by a skeleton staff on Thursday as teachers took to the streets to demand higher salaries. A major complaint has been the discrepancy between salary increments awarded to members of the armed forces earlier this year, compared to those of teachers. Based on the fact that most schools were closed, this protest is coding as having at least 100 people.

Diminishing economic resources led to the suspension of scholarships at the University of Swaziland and a rise in student activism at start of the academic year this week. Late on Thursday afternoon, 10 students were injured when police broke up a march by 1,000 undergraduates seeking an audience with Prime Minister Themba Dlamini to demand the restoration of government scholarships that had always been available to tertiary students. The prime minister's office, overlooking downtown Mbabane, the capital, is close to the city hospital, where students injured by water cannon and in a resulting stampede were admitted, treated and released. According to The Swazi Observer newspaper on Friday, before firing teargas at the students assembled at the gate to the prime minister's office, one police officer said, "They are spoiled brats. They deserve a thorough beating." Angry senators questioned Minister of Finance Majozi Sithole, saying this was the first time in the University of Swaziland's 30-year history that government had suspended the scholarships, claiming poverty. This is coded as price increases/tax policy, since without the scholarships, the price of university schooling drastically increased.

In one of the biggest demonstrations seen in Swaziland in years, HIV-positive people marched on the offices of the prime minister and the national AIDS council this week to protest an "insulting" new media campaign. The project by the National Emergency Response Council on HIV/AIDS (NERCHA) seems to suggest that HIV is caused by sexual infidelity. It was launched last month without consulting people living with the virus. "The campaign further stigmatises the HIV infected. It is an insult, we are angry. It is time we are involved in matters pertaining to us," said protest leader Vusi Matsebula, chairperson of the Swaziland National Network of People Living with HIV/AIDS (SWANNEPHA). Around 1,000 people participated in the demonstration. NERCHA did not return IRIN's phone calls on Friday, but in previous press statements the organisation, which falls under the authority of the Prime Minister's office, has argued that Makhwapheni was a dramatic attempt to change people's behaviour. However, SWANNEPHA has accused NERCHA of arrogance, and its staff of making a living off the AIDS crisis, which NERCHA has denied. The protestors also claimed NERCHA was concentrating its media efforts on uninfected Swazis while ignoring people in the advanced stages of opportunistic diseases brought on by AIDS. Von Wissell refused to meet the throng, but a few days later, he gave in to the complaints and suspended the campaign.

Recent clashes between Swazi university students and riot police have brought a burgeoning education crisis into sharp relief, but went unreported by the state radio and television networks. Street battles erupted after students marched on Prime Minister Themba Dlamini's offices demanding that the government honour its university scholarship commitments. Musa Hlope, a member of government's semi-autonomous National Curriculum Centre, said "reasonable people should have seen this crisis in education coming." In a report released last week, the centre said a lack of government policy on school fees, curriculum development, assessment and evaluation, and availability of schoolbooks was responsible. "An analysis of various policy documents shows fragmentation and inconsistency within the Ministry of Education," the study commented. Of immediate concern to the university students was the imminent expulsion of students who had expected government scholarships. The education ministry at first said 182 students had been affected by scholarship reduction, but the announcement that 521 students were to be deprived of scholarships provoked the protests and subsequent student unrest. Based on how many students would be deprived of scholarships, this protest is coded as having at least 100 people. Demand is coded as both price increases (due to lack of scholarships causing an increase in fees for most students) and political behaviour/process due to the expulsions and policies.

At least one person was injured when police clashed with protesters yesterday at the hub as tempers flared during the first lap of the national mass action. The about 3,000 marchers could only watch helplessly as one of their members was beaten with batons by police officers after a verbal confrontation. He was later loaded into a police vehicle. At least two shops were looted and one person detained for violent acts when marchers brought the city to a standstill. There were, however, contained elements of violence as certain individuals in the crowd occasionally threw stones at some of the stores and other businesses in the city. These people, who trailed in the rear of the protesting group, also looted clothing that was on display outside some of the shops as they passed by. As a result some shop owners would shut down when the protesters approached.

Swaziland ground to a halt Thursday as thousands of workers staged the country's biggest demonstration for over a decade in a push for multi-party democracy in Africa's last absolute monarchy. As riot police and plain-clothed officers kept a close eye on a mass march in the capital Mbabane, union leaders warned such shows of strength would be repeated if King Mswati III and his government did not meet their demands. Tens of thousands of striking public sector workers gathered Thursday in Swaziland's capital for a second day of mass protests to demand the introduction of multi-party democracy. Authorities gave Thursday's demonstration the go-ahead and there were only minor skirmishes. Some 5,000 demonstrators gathered amid tight security in the capital Mbabane to press their grievances against King Mswati III's sweeping powers as well as economic issues like plans to tax pensions. There are differing numbers, so the range is recorded as 5000+ The marchers stoned a furniture shop but there were no other reports of violence. Riot police and water cannons were deployed for the demonstration after isolated acts of violence and looting by demonstrating workers in the second city of Manzini?ó_

In the strike action, which began on 3 March, workers participating in peaceful marches to demand better salaries have been teargassed and beaten by police, and at least a dozen have reportedly been injured. More than 16,000 workers, most of them women, have been affected by the strike action. Local media reported that the Swaziland police carried out unprovoked attacks on peaceful marchers on the first day of the strike. Several injuries were reported after riot police shot teargas into a line of marchers in the Matsapha Industrial Estate outside the central commercial town of Manzini. On 5 March, several marchers were beaten and teargassed after vandals sealed the lock on the gate of a textile factory with glue. Uncertain of the culprits' identities, the police randomly struck at marchers, some of whom had to be hospitalised. One policewoman was injured by a thrown stone. The Ministry of Enterprise and Employment, which brought the textile industry to Swaziland, called workers and management to a resolution conference in Manzini for the evening of 6 March. On the table will be the wage dispute, but another less tangible issue will likely remain unresolved when workers return to their jobs: the workers' complaint about lack of respect.

Tired of being taken for granted, Swaziland's nurses have opted for industrial action after the government ignored a deadline to improve conditions of service. After marching to the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare in the capital, Mbabane, on Friday to deliver their ultimatum, Swaziland's nurses registered their anger with an overtime ban beginning on Monday to protest delayed pay, unsafe working conditions, and crumbling facilities. The 2,016 nurses registered by the SNA, who have stayed in Swaziland rather than going abroad to work, have watched the deterioration of hospitals and clinics with dismay.
