Earlier this year, the Health Inspector of Mbabane declared the city's hospital, the largest in the country, unfit for human habitation. Given the amount of nurses registered with the SNA and the widespread nationwide problems this particular group of workers has faced, this protest is coded as having at least 100 people.

Public transport workers were teargassed at the downtown bus station in the central commercial town of Manzini on 17 March. Manzini, the country's transport hub, was shut down by mini-bus operators to show solidarity with textile workers, who have been on strike since 3 March. Police officers have been heard telling the women to 'get back to work.' What is their role here - protection of law and order or politically motivated strikebreaking? Dozens of shops were vandalised and the bus station's entrance was barricaded in this week's protest. Members of banned political parties had also urged onlookers to participate in the strike action. The police responded with rubber bullets and six people were hospitalised with gunshot wounds. More than 16,000 workers, most of them women, have been affected by the strike action.

More than 1000 demonstrators, mainly HIV-positive women, took to the streets last week to express outrage at the expensive 40-40 celebrations. WOMEN'S rights activists in Swaziland have mounted a rare protest march against the extravagance of the royal family, triggered by a shopping trip for eight of its queens. The demonstration in the capital Mbabane was organised by the Women's Coalition of Swaziland. The protocol also calls for gender-specific approaches to treatment and prevention of HIV/AIDS which the more than 1,000 demonstrators, mainly women and people living with HIV/AIDS, demanded in petitions to the Minister of Finance, Majozi Sithole, and Prime Minister Themba Dlamini.

At least 10,000 pro-democracy activists crowded the usually quiet streets of Manzini, the country's central commercial hub, on 3 September, before reassembling in the capital, Mbabane, the following day. The march in Mbabane was marred by the detonation of two small explosive devices: the first, planted in a trash bin in a shopping mall, did no damage, and the second, inside an empty bus, blew a hole in the vehicle. No one claimed responsibility, and march organisers were furious that the blasts might distract from their humanitarian message.

Demonstrators stoned shops, looted a market and bombed a bus as a second day of protests for democratic reform in Swaziland turned violent yesterday. About 5,000 people marched in Mbabane, the capital of the southern African monarchy, calling for multi-party democracy and criticising the lavish lifestyle of King Mswati III. Police used water cannon and teargas to disperse protesters, and a bomb squad was sent in after a small blast damaged a bus.

Organised by civil society organisations, churches, non-governmental organisations, labour formations, student groups, teachers, parents, women movements and the business community, thousands took to the streets on Apr. 16 to protestgovernment's refusal to adhere to the constitution. In January, a week before the start of the first school term of the year, the Swazi were outraged when the education department announced it would not implement FPE this year and remained noncommittal when asked what year the programme will start. The widowed mother of six was among parents who took to the streets of Manzini this month to hold government to its promise of free primary school education. To prevent parents' anger from escalating, government issued a statement on the eve of the protest march, promising that FPE will start next year - but only for some - not for all - primary school pupils. According to government press secretary Macanjana Motsa, contrary to the court verdict, only pupils attending Grades One and Two will be exempt from school fees next year. "The implementation of FPE will be carried out in an incremental manner, covering one grade each year until all the grades are included by 2015," said Motsa. Even though this sounds as though the government is accommodating the protesters, it is coded as ignore because it is not addressing the current issue of this year?ó»s fees.

Global rights group Amnesty International has denounced the use of excessive force by Swaziland's correctional services officers against journalists and political activists after a demonstration at one of the main country's prisons turned violent. The attack on 21 September by prison security guards at Matsapha Central Prison, a maximum security facility 25km east of the capital, Mbabane, occurred shortly after Mario Masuku, head of the banned opposition People's United Democratic Movement, was acquitted of terrorism charges. "The security officers reacted aggressively to the presence at the prison gate of some 50 noisy but peaceful, unarmed supporters awaiting Mario Masuku's release from the prison ... Without any official warning to disperse, security officers charged into the group at the gate," said a statement by Amnesty.

On the eve of the Global Day of Action for Swaziland, police in Swaziland this afternoon broke up a peaceful meeting of pro-democracy activists at the Tum s George Hotel in Manzini before loading scores of them into police vans and taking them away to the Manzini Regional Police headquarters. While exact details are still unclear, it seems as if up to 50 people have been detained, including Swazi activists and representatives from the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), who were in the country to lend their voices to the call for democracy and the protection of human rights.

Police removed at least three people from the march, including Pudemo president Mario Masuku, who was driven to his home 40 kilometres (25 miles) away in the capital Mbabane after being taken to the regional police headquarters, he said. Mabuza estimated that nearly 1,000 people took part in the march in Swaziland's biggest city Manzini ahead of a second demonstration planned for the capital on Wednesday where demands will be handed to the government. The march took place under a heavy police presence after nearly 50 people were arrested on the eve of the planned protests in Manzini. At the core is the demand for multi-party democracy because all the problems that workers and the general public are facing comes from the lack of democracy in the country. A leading Zimbabwe democracy activist has been banned from entering Swaziland for the next five years, after he was arrested on Tuesday taking part in a protest to mark the Global Day of Action in Manzini. On Tuesday, about 250 democracy activists marched through the nearby commercial capital of Manzini amid a heavy police presence.

Two leading activists in Swaziland were briefly detained Wednesday during a pro-democracy march in the capital of sub-Saharan Africa's last absolute monarchy, while supporters said a third leader also has been released. Police plucked the president of the Swaziland Youth Congress, Wandile Dludlu, and unionist Wonder Mkhonza, from among 350 marchers. Both were released after several hours in police custody.

ZIMBABWE football players plying their trade in the mountainous Kingdom of Swaziland stayed indoors yesterday following civil servants salary protests that broke out on Friday. Hundreds of police officers and special armed units were deployed on the streets of Mbabane and roads leading to a park where hundreds of protesters gathered were blocked off.  Salaries of civil servants have been frozen after the country suffered a 60% drop in income from the Southern African Customs Union, which accounts for two-thirds of state revenues.

Thousands have marched on the prime minister s office in a rare protest to demand the resignation of the tiny southern African kingdom s government. Thousands of Swazis marched on the prime minister s office yesterday in a rare protest to demand the resignation of the tiny southern African kingdom s government. Swaziland, which has an absolute monarchy, is in the grip of a serious financial crisis and civil servants fear they will not be paid this month. The king was reacting to a mass protest by close to 3000 people on Friday against the country's government as well as the growing economic crisis. Scores of workers and students took to the streets demanding a regime change and calling for the arrest of senior government officials for corruption. The protestors brought the city to a grinding halt as they demonstrated and sang struggle songs, demanding pay hikes for civil servants and the reinstatement of pension and disability funds that were withdrawn by Mswati's administration two months ago.

Swazi police use tear gas to disperse protesters in Manzini. SCORES of baton-wielding police prevented thousands of protesters from entering Swaziland's commercial centre yesterday on the first day of a pro-democracy stayaway due to end tomorrow, writes Loyiso Langeni. Police used tear gas and water cannons on a crowd of protesters marching to the city centre, including more than 1 000 people from a teachers' training centre who were singing and chanting peacefully. Protesters and passers-by fled from the tear gas, leaving the usually bustling streets of Manzini deserted. Shops were closed and the main taxi rank was cordoned off amid a heavy police presence. Riot police have fired teargas and water cannons, beaten demonstrators and arrested union leaders, activists and journalists in an attempt to stop pro-democracy protests in Swaziland, Africa's last absolute monarchy. The Manzini demonstration was called in protest at the lack of freedoms and the dire economic crisis in the tiny mountain kingdom. Nearly broke, the government recently announced it would have to cut civil servants' salaries, which were raised last year following an outcry over plans to raise politicians' allowances.

Mbabane Hundreds of teachers marched through the capital of Swaziland calling on the US and South Africa to push for democratic and economic reform in the country. The move followed an austerity budget that would freeze state salaries for three years.

The revelations come as uncertainty over the availability of ARVs prompted Khoza and hundreds of other HIV-positive people to mount an unprecedented protest in Mbabane on 27 July. Police refused members of SWANNEPHA permission to march in the streets, so 500 members took buses to the Health Ministry to deliver a petition. The umbrella organization also petitioned the National Emergency Response Council on (NERCHA), the government unit that finances SWANNEPHA and other AIDS organizations, which is itself facing a funding crisis.

Swazi police in bullet-proof vests and armed with shotguns and tear gas canisters invaded a meeting of lawyers in the Swaziland High Court. The lawyers were meeting to discuss their on-going campaign to get Michael Ramodibedi, the Swaziland Chief Justice removed from office. The lawyers were angered by the growing signs of authoritarian rule in Swaziland, including the suspension (and eventual sacking) of a Supreme Court judge who had allegedly shown disloyalty to the King. The judge was accused of supporting "regime change" in Swaziland, but analysts say he was suspended because he insisted on judicial independence. When the lawyers held a meeting to discuss the issue, it was stormed by police armed with shotguns and tear gas. But they continued their boycott for months, holding frequent protests in the streets to demand the rule of law. Of the 180 members of Swaziland's law society, nearly all joined the boycott - even though it meant the loss of more than half their income. They faced harassment and surveillance by the police, threats to their families, and monitoring of their phone calls and e-mails, yet they refused to bow to the pressure.

PUDEMO says the marches will spread to other towns tomorrow and throughout the whole week. The people are demanding the unbanning of political parties, return of exiles, a democratic constitution, release of political prisoners, end to corruption, the freezing of a government process to retrench over 7000 public workers, availability of medication in public hospitals and suspension of the proposed scholarship policy which effectively makes education the preserve of the rich elite. 5,000 protestors converged on Gwamile Street in the centre of the Swazi capital Mbabane today on the first day of the Global Week of Action for Swaziland. Generally, protests in Swaziland are largely peaceful and habitually involve picketing and then submitting petitions with a list of demands and grievances to relevant authorities. Picketers are mainly members of trade unions and labour associations, the only organisations legally allowed to exist, organise and demonstrate in Swaziland. Reports coming out of Swaziland are that protestors and by-standers have been injured by police teargas as the Global Week of Action entered day three today.

In the regional Town of Siteki, a large assembly of youth, students, workers and the unemployed in Swaziland was violently disrupted by the armed forced when they sought to prevent COSATU 2nd Deputy President Zingiswa Losi from addressing the crowds.  In its desperate attempt to stave off mass resistance, the Swazi regime resorted to ruthlessly attacking activists, including those from international solidarity groups. PUDEMO, a banned political party in Swaziland, says 2,000 people marched in Siteki another 1,000 protested in Nhlangano, in the south of Swaziland. In Manzini, the kingdom's main business city, there was also a reported stand-off with the police refusing to allow a march to continue. Police are said to have fired teargas at demonstrators. In September, Swazi citizens groups and South African labor union organizers conducted a week-long campaign of protests against the Swazi regime and against South Africa's 2.4 million rand loan to Swaziland's King Mswati III, whose government has run out of money. In the provincial town of Siteki, nearly 3,000 protesters were reported on the streets on Sept. 8, a remarkable feat in a country with just under 2 million people. And in the nation's commercial capital, another 5,000 marchers brought the city to a halt.

The Southern Africa Development Community Lawyers Association (SADC LA) and the Southern Africa Litigation Centre (SALC) note the unprecedented action on the part of Swaziland lawyers who, on Wednesday 21 September, marched in large numbers through the streets of the capital, Mbabane, to protest Swaziland's ongoing judicial crisis and the role of the Chief Justice in instigating this crisis. ?óìLarge numbers?ó? means this protest is assumed to have at least 100 people.

With the health sector hard hit by the absence of drugs for chronic and acute diseases, schools unable to open due to lack of government funding, and bus and taxi workers vying hard for custom, hair-trigger protests are increasing. This was seen in the violent clashes between over 1 500 transport workers and the police in and around Manzini last week, which was sparked by the arrest of taxi operators for operating outside their designated limits. Violent clashes implies violence on both sides, and also assumes beatings and/or crowd dispersal as the police response.

Yesterday, over 2, 000 University of Swaziland students marched to deliver a petition to the Minister of Labour and Social Security over unpaid allowances. As is to be expected these days, the march was characterized by clashes between the students and the police over routes and other issues. Fortunately, no one was seriously hurt or arrested. This protest is also not an isolated student demonstration since the William Pitcher Teachers' College was this indefinitely closed this week after students undertook a sit-in strike over allowances and a host of other issues.

Meanwhile, lawyers and civil society activists led by the Law Society of Swaziland staged another protest march today to deliver a petition to the Prime Minister voicing their dismay at the deployment of police at the High Court. The petition was received by the government spokesperson, Percy Simelane, who promised, as usual, to pass it on to the premier. Of the 180 members of Swaziland's law society, nearly all joined the boycott - even though it meant the loss of more than half their income. They faced harassment and surveillance by the police, threats to their families, and monitoring of their phone calls and e-mails, yet they refused to bow to the pressure. Given that this is another meeting of a popular boycott among lawyers, this protest is coded as 100+, following the other previous meetings of this particular group.

A woman protester was shot at close range by Swazi police as she was walking from them. Local media report that it is not known if she was hit by live ammunition or a rubber bullet. Rose Fakudze was part of a protest march in Siteki, Swaziland, called by vendors and transport operators over plans by the town hall to move the local bus rank. A court order had been obtained from the magistrate court to stop the march but this angered the vendors as the town board has agreed that it would go ahead. The vendors and transport operators demanded to continue with the march, but riot police were called and they moved in. The incident proved outrage among local residents who marched on the regional police headquarters demanding to know why police had shot a defenceless woman who was walking away from them. Given the response of police and the inclusion of local residents, this protest is coded as having at least 50 people.

Yesterday (14 February 2012), the Swaziland College of Technology (SCOT) was closed indefinitely, following class boycotts by students. Both sets of students are angry with the Swazi Government for not paying them their due allowances. Swaziland is on the brink of financial meltdown and the government is finding it increasingly difficult to pay its bills. Armed police fired teargas on students at SCOT where about 120 third-year students are demanding about E7 000 each which they said was supposed to have been part of their allowances while they were on attachment with different companies during the last academic year.

Classes across Swaziland were abandoned and some colleges and universities closed altogether yesterday (26 March 2012) as students took to the streets to peacefully protest against government scholarship cuts. Swazi media reported that between 600 and 1,000 students were on the march and the SNUS said 3,000 took part. Riot police sealed off roads to stop the students reaching the city centre. Since an arrest was attempted (though not successful), arrests is still included in the response category.

Public sector unions in Swaziland have started a series of demonstrations ahead of a national strike next week over pay. Since Tuesday (3 April 2012) they have been picketing during their lunch hour at more than 20 places across the kingdom. They want cost-of-living increases of 4.5 percent, but the Swazi Government has refused because the kingdom is broke. It has had difficulty in recent months in paying public sector salaries and wants to cut salaries by 10 percent. Given its nationwide appeal and the history of protests by this particular group, this protest is coded as having at least 100 people.

Police in Swaziland beat up demonstrators with batons and used teargas against them as protests spread across the kingdom. Yesterday (11 April 2012), on the first day of what some activists are calling an 'indefinite protest action', large numbers of police and soldiers were present in all major towns and cities. Although the 11th is considered the ?óÖstart?ó» of the protest, marching did not occur until the next day ?óñ April 12th.  Activists are protesting against the undemocratic regime of King Mswati III, sub-Saharan Africa's last absolute monarch. All political parties and opposition groups are banned in the kingdom. More arrests of protest leaders are reported from Swaziland this morning (12 April 2012). Trade union leaders were detained by police and roads blocked to stop protesters gathering. Barnabas Dlamini, the Swaziland Prime Minister, had ordered a ban on all protests. Police said the protests were against national security. The crackdown was so effective that by midday yesterday (12 April 2012) workers' leaders called off the protest, which had been planned to last up to four days. This protest is coded as only 100+ because it was largely stopped before it could gain the momentum that leaders had promised and desired.

Hospitals are not protecting their workers from tuberculosis (TB) infection, say nurses in Swaziland, who recently staged a rare public demonstration to draw attention to how vulnerable they are to this highly infectious disease. Nurses attached to the National TB Hospital in Swaziland's commercial hub, Manzini, are blaming inadequate infection measures at the hospital for the risk they face. TB is one of the primary killers and the main opportunistic disease in people living with HIV and AIDS.  Given the involvement of nurses, who have gone on strike before in large numbers, this protest is coded as having at least 50 people.

Teachers in Swaziland managed to deliver their petition to the government this afternoon (13 June 2102), despite being blocked by riot police. Police stopped about 3,000 members of the Swaziland National Association of Teachers (SNAT) marching across Mbabane city centre this morning. They had wanted to deliver a petition for a 4.5 percent salary increase, but were stopped from doing so. The Centre for Human Rights, Swaziland, reports, 'The march was characterised by threats of violence from security agents. Two workers were unlawfully detained by riot police, and this seemed to anger workers who retaliated by throwing stones at the police vehicles into which the two were taken. They were promptly released and the march continued.'

Scores of people were injured, some seriously, by police in Swaziland who fired rubber bullets and tear gas and used batons to attack striking public servants. More than 200 police officers attacked strikers in Coronation Park, Mbabane, the Swazi capital, as they prepared to march in support of a 4.5 percent wage increase. Police imprisoned the strikers in the park for most of the morning yesterday (11 July 2012) and refused to allow them to leave for a march through the city. At about 2pm some strikers tried to leave the park to get lunch. It was then that police commanders ordered officers to fire rubber bullets and teargas at the strikers. POLICE have fired rubber bullets and tear gas to stop a protest by thousands of government workers demanding higher wages.

In a two-day protest action that ended yesterday by public transport operators in the city of Manzini, police shot an innocent bystander, Bonginkosi Mkhonto, in the stomach for watching protesting transport operators. Other incidents of police brutality were reported during this protest action. 'The public operators' protest action came after a public bus driver was fined R4800 by a court, when police refused to let him pay a R60 on-the-spot fine. Swaziland police shot an innocent bystander in the stomach with a rubber bullet as they attacked a protest of transport workers. The Centre for Human Rights, Swaziland, reported that several other people were injured by police who were seen 'ransacking' the Manzini bus rank in an attempt to arrest protesting transport operators. The Centre said, 'Several protesters and pedestrians have been arrested by the police who are going for any person they suspect to be taking part in the on-going protest action. 'The police fired teargas all over the town as a result harming vendors and other people in the town. Scenes of violent police have been observed all over the town as police beat up protesters using batons and fists.' Given the response by police and the fact that this protest is taking place alongside a much larger strike, this is coded as having at least 100 people.

About 1,000 parents and teachers were stopped 500m from parliament yesterday (18 July 2012) and told they could go no further. They were calling on the Swazi Government to find a solution to the indefinite teachers' strike over pay that has been going on for a month. They also want parliament to pass a vote of no confidence in the government; scrap the recently introduced 14 percent Value Added Tax; and scrap 'circular No. 1', an order that allows government ministers and parliamentarians inflated financial benefits.

Teachers in Swaziland are marching in the streets of the capital Mbabane today (3 August 2012) following their successful court action to stop the government sacking striking teachers. The Centre for Human Rights, Swaziland, reports that close to 200 teachers are singing and chanting struggle songs as they march from the Industrial Court to the Ministry of Education. They want to deliver a petition calling on the Swazi Government to stop further sackings and to hold talks with the teachers.

Heavily-armed state forces stopped students in Swaziland from marching on government to protest about the non-payment of tuition fees and scholarships. More than 100 students today (16 August 2012) gathered at the University of Swaziland campus in the kingdom's capital Mbabane, but they were blocked from leaving for about four hours by police and prison wardens. The students hoped to march on the Labour and Social Security to deliver a petition concerning a continuing scholarship crisis. Three university students in Swaziland were shot by police - two in the head - while security forces stopped a protest march against scholarship cuts. Reports from the Centre for Human Rights and Development, Swaziland, say several other students were injured by police batons and kicks. He said police assaulted Dlamini with batons and kicks. The students retaliated by pelting stones at the police officers in an attempt to save their colleague.

Students led by the Swaziland Union of Students (SNUS) will be marching to the Ministry of Education in Mbabane this morning (4 September 2012).The march is part of a global week of action for Swaziland. The students are marching to demand education for all in Swaziland. The Centre for Human Rights and Development, Swaziland, reports more than 100 students are now gathered in Manzini in preparation to proceed to Mbabane where they will be meeting other students to proceed to the Ministry. Students fought with police in Mbabane, the Swazi capital, this lunchtime (4 September 2012) as they tried to arrest Swaziland National Union of Students leader, Maxwell Dlamini. Reports from the scene at the Mbabane bus rank say that police and security forces vastly outnumber the students. State security forces fired teargas, beat up students and activists and drove them away from the bus rank towards the University of Swaziland, Mbabane Campus, the People's United Democratic Movement (PUDEMO) reported.  Police have fired teargas and made indiscriminate arrests as they blocked a prodemocracy protest led by students in Swaziland today (4 September 2012). The SDC reports that a student from William Pitcher College who fled with the SNUS banner during the police attack has been arrested.

Last month saw the establishment of a new group - the Swaziland Young Women's Network - which announced its launch with a march through the streets of the capital, Mbabane, to protest the prevalence of sexual harassment. The police blocked the march on the grounds that some of the women were wearing miniskirts. "The government's first response to women seeking our rights was to block us and threaten us with arrest, and to control us by telling us what to wear. That is their instinct, and it is going to be hard to overcome, but we are determined not only for our own sake but for the sake of the country," said Simelane. Police recently halted a protest march by women who wore mini-skirts to draw attention to the harassment they face. This protest is coded as having at least 50 people given the history of women?ó»s marches and the rampant prevalence of rape in the nation.

This follows police action that yesterday (12 April 2013) broke up a public meeting to discuss the lack of democracy in the kingdom. About 80 armed police stopped the meeting taking place at a restaurant in Manzini, the main business city in Swaziland. Police, who did not have a court order for the action, said the meeting 'presented a threat to national security'. Given how many police showed up to break up the gathering, this protest is coded as having at least 50 people.

The Swaziland Youth Congress (SWAYOCO) tried to hold a rally in Msunduza Township, Mbabane, on Friday (19 April 2013) at the same time that King Mswati III was holding an E10 million (US$1.1 million) party in another part of the kingdom to celebrate his 45th birthday. The Swazi Police Commissioner Isaac Magagula had warned SWAYOCO in advance that his officers would stop any attempt at meeting. SWAYOCO supporters went ahead with their attempt to meet with residents to discuss with them why they should boycott the national election due later this year. Political parties are not allowed to contest the so-called Tinkhundla election and the parliament that is selected is not independent, but serves the wishes of King Mswati, who is sub-Saharan Africa's last absolute monarch. Police said two people were arrested at the rally. Given the importance of the group involved in this particular rally and the police desperation to stymie it, this protest is coded as having at least 50 people.

Members of the Royal Swaziland Police Service yesterday quashed a march intended by over 100 women against the recent spate of attacks against women. The event was organized by the Swaziland Rural Women's Association (SRWA). About 100 women ended up loitering around Siphofaneni under the watchful eye of the police. The police staged roadblocks between Siphofaneni and Phuzumoya, where they monitored passengers aboard public transport vehicles. They also searched cars they suspected to have been transporting people who intended to join the march.  SRWA decided to defy the ban and continue with the march.

Swaziland police are out in force in Manzini, the country's second largest city and centre of recent protests against the absolute monarchy. The police have set up a blockade on the west side of the town and almost every street corner has some form of police presence, uniformed and plain clothes. Throughout yesterday, activists and advocates were followed and recorded by plain clothes police. Then, Vincent Ncongwane, General Secretary of the Trade Union Congress of Swaziland (TUCOSWA), was arrested in his office by ten police as he prepared to lead his members in protest. No warrant was produced. Given the swift and harsh put down of this protest, and given the history of protests during this particular week, this demonstration is assumed to have at least 100 people.

Walter Dlamini, of the Times Sunday, had taken photos at Gege where police had broken up a peaceful protest march by youth in the area. They were protesting against alleged irregularities at the recent election. 'The casual work-a-day savagery of these police officers and their sense of entitlement to brutalising Swazi citizens with impunity goes a long way to explaining why they would attack with teargas and batons what was a peaceful protest march before their intervention; once again proving the police are responsible for much of the violence that erupts during protests.' The bashing of protestors -- who are unhappy with what they believe to be unfair and unfree elections -- and intimidation of journalists last Saturday, adds to the growing reality of police repression and muzzling of civil and media freedoms in the southern African kingdom. Given the harsh and brutal suppression of the protest and the history of youth protests in the nation, this is coded as having at least 50 demonstrators.

Three people were killed and 20 injured in a failed coup attempt in Madagascar early yesterday, hospital sources said, after armed rebels seized the national radio station to announce the overthrow of the President, Admiral Didier Ratsiraka. Residents said that 4,000 to 5,000 policemen loyal to Mr Ratsiraka ringed the radio station after the coup announcement, while about 300 protesters responded to the rebel appeal, chanting anti- government slogans and stoning police who responded with tear gas. Although a coup was going on, the protest is coded as only the 300 people protesting against the government and not the actual coup itself.  Therefore, the killings that took part against the coup members are not counted as a response to the protest.

More than 100,000 protesters took to the streets of Madagascar's capital yesterday on the eighth day of demonstrations for democratic reforms. Diplomats say the protests pose the greatest challenge yet to President Didier Ratsiraka's 16-year-old rule. The protests have been orchestrated by the Opposition Platform that includes Marxists and right wingers which wants a new transitional government to supervise the introduction of a new constitution. Protests that brought out 100,000 people in Madagascar on June 11 were the beginning of a series of demonstrations against the regime of President Didier Ratsiraka that have continued to mount. The protesters in Antananarivo, capital of the Indian Ocean island nation, have been calling for an end to Ratsiraka's 16-year rule and for a national conference to draft a new constitution.

On Monday, the Prime Minister, Victor Ramahatra, threatened the opposition with legal action if it persisted in claiming that it had appointed a new government. Thousands took to the streets in response.

Opposition parties in Madagascar led up to 100,000 protestors through the streets of the apital to mark yesterday's independene anniversary by demanding democratic reforms. Some estimates put the size of the demonstration at 200,000, or one-third of Antananarivo's population. The 16-party opposition coalition had agreed with the city authorities to keep the march peaceful and no violence was reported. An official military parade to mark the country's 31 years of independence attracted around 10,000 people. The opposition has accused President Didier Ratsiraka of rigging a 1989 election which gave him a third term in office. President Ratsiraka, a former naval officer who seized power in 1975, has attempted to introduce a degree of democracy and economic liberalisation.

Up to 300,000 people poured into the streets of the Madagascan capital yesterday, demonstrating in support of opposition calls for a new constitution and a national conference. A general strike to try to force President Didier Ratsiraka to step down has been called for tomorrow.

The opposition paralysed the capital of Madagascar with a strike, and an estimated 400,000 people took to the streets demanding the resignation of President Didier Ratsiraka. Protest organisers have also demanded democratic elections and the replacement of the socialist constitution. Tens of thousands of people took to the streets, partially paralysing Madagascar's capital for the second day in response to an opposition general strike call to bring down the government. Madagascar's government alliance has agreed to talks with the island's coalition of opposition parties on a new constitution, following a month of huge demonstrations calling on President Ratsiraka to step down. A large part of the capital was still strikebound yesterday and thousands of demonstrators thronged the city centre as the opposition maintained its call for an open- ended general strike. Almost half a million people took to the streets on Monday and Tuesday.

MADAGASCAR'S opposition yesterday partially called off an effective week-old general strike held to precipitate the resignation of President Didier Ratsiraka. Party leaders insisted it was a small concession that would achieve their aim. But opposition supporters were angered at their leaders' climbdown and thousands filled the streets of the capital, Antananarivo, in the mood to take a more confrontational tack than the peaceful protests of recent weeks. Riot police were in evidence for the first time. However, opposition supporters, who have blocked the heart of the capital with almost daily demonstrations, were not content. About 60,000 largely middle- class protesters filed with remarkable order into Independence Avenue yesterday morning. President Ratsiraka abandoned his Marxist experiment 11 years ago after dragging Madagascar from relative prosperity to its present position as the world's 12th poorest nation. But the opposition is not convinced by his conversion to privatisation, with the considerable incentive of World Bank loans. Today the President is seen as more opportunist than Marxist. The opposition resents his claims of credit for a substantial increase in foreign aid, mainly from the French, especially when much of it is diverted from the causes for which it was intended.

Demonstrators breached security cordons around two Madagascar government ministries to try to install opposition ''ministers'' of finance and post and telecommunications in office. Their action followed a rally of several hundred thousand people seeking to end President Didier Ratsiraka's rule. Anti-government protesters and soldiers clashed outside Madagascar's state radio station as President Didier Ratsiraka ordered a security crackdown after weeks of peaceful demonstrations.  Witnesses said one soldier and several demonstrators were injured before opposition leaders told their supporters to withdraw. Police commandos seized another minister in the opposition's self-declared government today, while protests continued against President Didier Ratsiraka. The seizure of Rahantavololona Andrianmanjato at the Public Works Ministry was the government's boldest move since Ratsiraka declared a state of emergency Tuesday to stop the takeover. Prime Minister Victor Ramahatra announced his resignation and the dissolution of his Cabinet today. He acted hours after President Didier Ratsiraka made his first concession to seven weeks of huge pro-democracy demonstrations and offered to open talks with opponents seeking his ouster.

MADAGASCAR'S opposition has rejected political concessions made by President Didier Ratsiraka and in a meeting of tens of thousands of demonstrators yesterday vowed to continue its seven-week campaign of strikes and protests until he steps down. 'What we demand is your (Ratsiraka's) resignation,' opposition leader Jean Rakotoharison told protesters in the capital, Antananarivo. THE President of Madagascar, Mr Didier Ratsiraka, bowing to a seven-week campaign of strikes and protests, says he will sack his government and bring in a new constitution by the end of the year. But his concessions may not satisfy tens of thousands of anti-government protesters in the capital Antananarivo who have thrown the Indian Ocean island into turmoil and insist that he must resign.

Opposition leaders rejected President Didier Ratsiraka's offer to form a coalition government, and anti-government protesters occupied two more ministries. Ratsiraka, the target of almost daily mass protests since June 10, said he would not bow to demands to resign. He invited the opposition to work with him in forming a "government of reconciliation" to rule this island nation off the southeast coast of Africa. But retired Gen. Jean Rakotoharison, president of the opposition's self-declared alternative government, told more than than 100,000 demonstrators that protests and a general strike would continue until Ratsiraka ends his 16-year rule.

Madagascar's opposition said two anti-government protesters were killed in clashes with security forces in the port of Toamasina. The Active Forces opposition coalition said 37 opposition supporters were arrested at the port. The word clashes implies mutual violence.  Also, since these are related to the protests in the capital, and due to the number of people injured, this protest is assumed to have at least 100 participants.

An opposition official said at least 20 people were killed Saturday in the northeastern port town of Mahajanga. Four people were killed and at least 20 wounded in Anjouan on Saturday in fighting between Government troops and secessionists on the island, which holds few employment opportunities for its 190,000 population. The government on Monday lifted a 4-day-old curfew imposed to quell unrest in this Indian Ocean nation that left as many as three people dead and 19 injured. It also announced the opening of negotiations with teachers, whose three-month strike triggered the conflict.

Gendarmes shot dead two demonstrators on the Comoran island of Anjouan Monday as a crowd in Matsamudu, its principal town, called for secession, a Radio Comores official told AFP in Nairobi by telephone. Some gendarmes were injured, he said, and reinforcements were being sent there from Grande Comore, the main island in the Indian Ocean archipelago between Madagascar and mainland Africa. He said the demonstrations on Monday -- France's national day -- had lasted all day, with Anjouanians raising French flags and the flag of Sultan Mawana, who ruled last century. This protest is believed to have at least 100 people due to the killing of two individuals and the need for reinforcements to deal with the protesters.

Two police officers were seriously hurt Tuesday in clashes with protestors on the Comorian island of Anjouan over Monday's arrest of a separatist leader, sources said here. The worst clashes came in the town of Domoni where the residence of new governor Sheikh Allaoui was set alight by protestors. There was also unrest in Mutsamudu, Anjouan's main town. Backers of the Organization for the Independence of Anjouan, who want the island reattached to the former colonial power France, renounced the authority of Moroni at the weekend and called for their own leaders to be installed in Anjouan. The soldiers moved in after violent clashes between security forces and separatist militants on the island, one of three in the Comoros archipelago between Madagascar and the east coast of Africa. Soldiers have closed off some of the main roads leading into Anjouan's main town Mutsamudu and mounted patrols throughout the town, said residents reached by telephone from the Comorian capital Moroni. Reinforcements were also sent to Domoni among some 120 police and soldiers who have been sent recently to Anjouan to bolster an existing force of between 200 and 250 troops. Given how many police and soldiers were needed to quell the rioting, this demonstration is assumed to have at least 100 people.

Secessionists on the Comoros Island of Anjouan who want France to take them back into the colonial fold have intensified their protests, French media reported Sunday. Protests have been staging protests on Anjouan and Moheli over the past several weeks. Islanders claim the current government of President Abdallah Taki Abdoulkarim is corrupt and they would be better off under French rule. The crowd of some 7,000 who rallied in the central square of Mutsamudu, Anjouan's main town, marched to the governor's palace - abandoned on Saturday - and hoisted the flags of France and the sultans who ruled Anjouan in pre-colonial days, tearing up the Comoran flag that had been flying there.  Meanwhile Comoran troops went on "red alert" Monday, prepared at a moment's notice to deploy in Mutsamudu, Anjouan's main town. The total armed forces of the Comoro Islands amounts to some 1,200 men -- about 600 soldiers and 500 to 600 gendarmes. The 200 to 250 gendarmes and soldiers normally stationed on Anjouan have been reinforced by 100 to 125 men since the clashes began. Reliable sources in Mutsamudu say they are almost out of tear gas, but still have stocks of live ammunition.

With the secessionist revolt spreading from Anjouan to Moheli, two of the four islands that make up the Comoran archipelago, what began as an odd, even flattering anachronism is fast turning into an embarrassing crisis for France.  Riot police yesterday clashed with demonstrators on the smaller island of Moheli, after they raised the French tricolour over government buildings. The separatists in Fomboni, the main town on Moheli, were reported to have hoisted the yellow-and-black flag of Queen Fatima Djoumbe, the last ruler of Moheli before colonisation. Given the popularity of the separatist movement, and that major clashes occurred between protesters and police, this demonstration is assumed to have at least 50 people.

But on Thursday, separatists captured a police station and arrested an emissary of President Mohamed Taki Abdoulkarim, French newspapers reported. A government delegation, sent to Anjouan from Grand Comoros where the government is based, has sparked unease among the secessionists. On Anjouan, rebels have erected barricades across the island, preventing traffic from circulating. New barricades appeared this week in the town of Mutsamudu, which has not fully supported the move for reunification with France. The demonstrations, described in news reports as reflecting the desires of a vast majority of Anjouan's 200,000 largely impoverished people, culminated in a declaration of independence by rebel leaders on the island and the establishment of a new provisional government headed by a 71-year-old Koranic scholar, Abdallah Ibrahim. Given the popularity of secession among the islanders, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

In the Comoran capital Moroni, meanwhile, most residents, who were initially sympathetic to the separatists, have grown resentful over being made to shoulder the blame for their economic deprivation. But Moroni residents do share a desire for President Mohamed Taki Abdoulkarim's ouster. At a rally late Tuesday, while backing Comoran unity, some 300 residents called for his resignation.

Three hundred people on the separatist Comoros island of Moheli went on a rampage Thursday, storming the main town's administrative offices and setting fire to one of the governor's houses. The crowd became infuriated after a demonstration demanding the resignation of the governor was set upon by tear-gas-firing police, a reliable witness at the scene in Fomboni town said. Two of the protesters were slightly hurt. The demonstrators, some of whom carried grenades, wrecked the prefecture building, setting fire to documents and furniture which they had heaped up in the street and set up road blocks. Moheli, like the neighbouring island of Anjouan, has declared independence from the Comoros archipelago government in the capital Moroni. Anjouan has demanded to be reattached to the former colonial power France.

Meanwhile some 500 Comoran oppositionists rallied in Moroni on Tuesday, demanding to be included in the OAU-sponsored talks. The OAU-sponsored negotiations are to bring together government officials and separatists from Anjouan and Moheli.

Troops opened fire Thursday on a group of separatist activists on the island of Moheli in the Comoros, where at least two people were wounded, local sources told AFP. The army used automatic weapons and tear-gas grenades against the protesters in Fomboni, capital of the smallest island in the Indian Ocean republic, several sources said. Separatist movements have emerged recently on Moheli and the island of Anjouan in protest at perceived domination by Grand Comore, the main island in the archipelago. One resident reached by telephone said that two or three people were injured. However, separate sources gave different reasons for the clashes, which lasted several hours. However, another source said trouble broke out after separatists persuaded the governor to resign and then went to the gendarmerie (paramilitary police post) to demand the keys to official buildings. "The gendarmes turned them down and incidents broke out," the source said, adding that several homes were razed and the gates of the governor's residence were smashed. Given the popularity of the separatist movement and the clashes between the protesters and police, this demonstration is assumed to have at least 50 participants.

Police clashed with opposition demonstrators Saturday who were protesting the government's military intervention on the separatist island of Anjouan. At least one person was injured as police used tear gas and batons to break up the march of some 500 people representing a coalition of parties opposed to President Mohamed Taki's attempt to put down the secession on Anjouan by force. Clashes broke out Saturday in the Comoros capital Moroni between security forces and opposition demonstrators protesting against government intervention to quell a separatist uprising, witnesses said here.

Several hundred youths protested Tuesday in the centre of the Comoran capital Moroni in protest at the police seizure of an independent radio station. The protesters erected barriers in the south of the city but there were no reported incidents involving the security forces who maintained a discreet presence.

The Comoro islands capital Moroni ground to a halt Monday when government workers went on strike and held street protests to press demands for payment of 15 months of salary arrears. Strikers blocked about 20 city streets with tree trunks, cars and rocks, with each roadblock guarded by dozens of young people. Many set fire to tyres to dramatize the strike, which forced offices, markets and schools to close across the capital. State employees have not been paid since January. Previously, the government owed them 12 months' worth of pay arrears, and workers have said back payments must be settled before they would return to work. A few minor incidents occurred early Monday, pitting security forces against stone-throwing youths who broke windows at the police headquarters and the foreign and education ministries. A strike by Comoros civil servants developed on Tuesday into a strong protest against the government as witnesses reported arrests and increasing numbers of troops deployed in the capital Moroni. Sources said that about a score of youths were arrested in the old part of the main town in the Indian Ocean republic, while soldiers fired shots into the air and turned out with heavy machinery to shift street barricades. Meanwhile the Comoros authorities charged that the barricades were set up by "groups of young people to protest the closing of the private radio station Tropic FM" last week. Striking civil servants brought the Comoros capital Moroni to a standstill on Tuesday after a tense night under curfew, when troops patrolled central streets and fired live rounds into the air. Protests started on Monday when thousands of civil servants went on strike and protested against not being paid for up to 15 months. They were joined by hundreds of young unemployed and students voicing their displeasure at last week's closure of a local radio station by the authorities. However, during the protests, several demonstrators clearly said they wanted to get rid of Taki. The Organisation of African Unity (OAU), which has already sought in vain to mediate an end to the secession crisis, proposed to help in the trouble on Grande Comore itself.

Gendarmes in the Comoros used tear-gas Thursday to disperse demonstrating school pupils, a Radio Comores journalist told AFP by telephone from Moroni. The pupils, aged between 10 and 15, were protesting against a government refusal to delay examinations despite a scholastic year marked by strikes and perturbations. The gendarmes broke up demonstrations in Moroni, on the main island of Grande Comore, and in the nearby village of Vuvuni, the radio reporter said, adding that a number of people, including a cameraman, suffered minor injuries. The examinations were held Thursday as planned in other towns on Grande Comore, but were cancelled in the capital. Given the protests taking place between two cities and the apparent need for teargas to disperse the protesters, this demonstration is assumed to have at least 50 participants.

Some 150 protesters in the Comoran capital reacted angrily Tuesday after representatives from the separatist island of Anjouan declined to sign a deal to end the archipelago's political crisis. Staging a second day of demonstrations, mostly young protestors called on Anjouanese families to leave their civil servants' accommodation. They also called for the resignation of Comoran interim President Tadjidine Ben Said Massounde, himself from Anjouan, whose plans for a government of national unity have been rebuffed by Anjouanese leaders. That led to violent protests earlier this week in Moroni, on the main island of Grande Comore, and hundreds of Anjouanese fled the capital to return to Anjouan. Soldiers stood-by without acting as hordes of youths, mostly the unemployed, attacked people from Anjoua islands, after delegates from the separatist island refused to sign the meeting's final document. Col. Azaly Assoumani said he ousted the government of president Tadjiddine Ben Said Massonde to restore order after three days of violent protests against the autonomy deal reached last weekend.

Security forces used teargas Saturday to break up a small demonstration in Moroni called to protest a sovereignty deal struck by the Comoran junta chief and the separatist leader on the island of Anjouan. Some 200 people took part in the demonstration, which was broken up less than a minute after it began.

Several demonstrators took to the streets of Moroni Friday to protest against the rise of the price of fuel and other basic goods. Traffic was totally blocked by barricades that were erected very early in the morning - from 3 AM - by rather dissatisfied youths. Riot police threw tear gas to disperse the protesters. There was hardly any traffic in Moroni by late morning, and most business concerns and schools remained closed during the day. About 30 people were arrested and some of them were later released, according to witnesses. The worst violence took place in Irougoudjani, a working class district near the port. Police here were repeatedly forced to beat a retreat under a hail of stones. The protests were sparked by the government's decision to raise the price of fuel from 390 francs to 450 francs and that of kerosene from 100 francs to 150 francs per litre. Given the response and the traffic problems which occurred due to the protesters, this protest is assumed to have at least 100 people.

Police in the Comoran capital on Saturday used tear gas to break up an anti-junta demonstration, raided houses and made arrests inside a mosque during prayers. Events appeared to have been sparked by a protest staged by women in the Mtsangani district against the repression of the military regime, which came to power in April 1999. About 20 people were arrested. Given how many people were arrested and the lengths the police went to stop the demonstrations, this protest is taken to have at least 50 people.

Some 150 demonstrators staged a peaceful protest Thursday in Moroni, the Comorian capital, to oppose the implementtion of the Fomboni accord. The protest march organised by a Reunion-based Comorian lawyer, Larifou Sai, who heads the "National Public Salvation Committee" opposed to the authorities in Moroni as well the separatists in Mutsamudu (Anjouan), went off without any violence. The protestors waved banners with words hostile to the military government and the Fomboni accord.

Police clashed with protesters overnight on the road leading to the main airport on the Comoran separatist island of Anjouan, residents told AFP by telephone Tuesday.  Security forces heavy-handedly dealt with the protests, according to the same sources. [A]rrests were made after protesters clashed with security forces on Monday night and blocked the airport road. Security forces intervened overnight Monday after protesters said to oppose reconciliation with the Comoro Islands' central government on Moroni blocked the airport road and poured sand on the runway. Those taken into custody were Andili Massoundi and Ridjali Abdou, who had been members of a parliament dissolved by Anjouan leader Lieutenant-Colonel Said Abeid Abderemane in October, and Halifa Said and Takidine Salim, according to an OPIA spokesman reached by telephone. Given the ability of the protesters to block the airport road and pour sand on the runway, as well as the involvement of two prominent former PMs, this protest is assumed to have had at least 50 people involved.

Sporadic gunfire rang out Wednesday in the breakaway Comoran island of Anjouan, where a protest by soldiers led to the closure of the airport and port, residents contacted by phone told AFP. The soldiers, from the island's main town, Mutsamudu, occupied the port to protest perceived discrimination and to demand promotions.  The soldiers, from the island's main town, Mutsamudu, occupied the two facilities to protest perceived discrimination and to demand promotions. The residents, who had reported sporadic gunfire Wednesday morning, said the soldiers in the afternoon left the port and airport, which had since reopened. They said, however, that at one stage the situation had become "critical", with confrontation between loyal troops and mutineers who had occupied the port narrowly being averted. They gave no further details. Given how the mutineers occupied two facilities, created a critical situation, and were able to prevent two aircrafts from landing, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

Residents of the capital of the Comoro islands woke to gunfire Monday, when several streets were barricaded in the wake of protests against police corruption and unpaid salaries, witnesses said. The gunfire echoed for about an hour in the north of Moroni, where a series of strikes and demonstrations have been held in recent days, an AFP journalist reported. There were no reports of casualties resulting from the gunfire, which residents put down to police attempts to disperse protestors trying to erect new barricades. Armed police in the capital of the Indian Ocean island nation patrolled several streets Monday morning, looking for "rioters". About 10 taxi drivers were arrested over the weekend and were still being held Monday morning. Since October 5, drivers' protests have resulted in the frequent closure of many roads leading out of the capital, virtually cutting off the south of the island of Grande Comore. Given the response and the need for barricades, this protest is assumed to have at least 100 people.

About 400 people in 26 towns and villages in the north protested earlier in the day at the headquarters in Moroni of the Comoran company for Electricity and Water (CEE) about electricity cuts that have been going on for months. Clashes between the police and protesters left several injured, one seriously, said the hospital in Moroni. This prompted the protesters to attack a police station before returning to their villages to block the roads. The police retaliated by erecting a roadblock about 30 kilometres (20 miles) outside Moroni. The roadblock was still in place on Wednesday evening. Some 100 people have been arrested in the north of the Comoran island of Grande Comore after a police station was attacked by people protesting about utility services, local inhabitants said. Although this protest started out against a private company (and therefore would not have been counted), the protesters turned on police after witnessing the harsh treatment they were receiving.  Thus, this protest has been coded as against police brutality; the demands of the protesters for the company are left out.

Angry youths set up barricades in the capital of the Indian Ocean archipelago of Comoros on Monday to protest at former military leader Colonel Azali Assoumani's declaration that he had won presidential elections. Roadblocks were put up in the centre of the capital, Moroni, shops remained closed the old market was practically deserted in protest of Azali's announcement of victory. A number of the demonstrators were seen marching towards the Volo-Volo district in the north of Moroni, where the capital's largest market is located. Given that roadblocks were set up and the old market was deserted, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

A 12-year-old boy was shot in the chest Wednesday as troops armed with rifles and tear gas clashed with anti-government protesters in Moroni, capital of the Comoro islands, a witness told AFP. An AFP journalist saw sporadic skirmishes in Moroni, where youths had set up barricades overnight as a protest against Colonel Azali Assoumani, president of the Union of the Comoros, in the Indian Ocean between Madagascar and the African mainland. On Wednesday, about 50 soldiers were patrolling the streets, taking down the roadblocks made of stones, burning tyres and wrecked cars. In some areas, as soon as the troops moved on, the protesters, many with their faces covered in scarves as protection against the tear gas, reappeared to rebuild the barricades, occasionally throwing stones at their adversaries.

Comoro army troops firing tear gas clashed with masked anti-government protestors on Friday in a second day of unrest in the capital of the Indian Ocean archipelago, witnesses said. The rioting followed similar clashes on Wednesday when three people were wounded. They said soldiers used tear gas as gangs of youths, most of them wearing scarves around their faces, used trees, rocks and vehicles to throw up barricades in Moroni and blocked two major routes into the city. They included a boy of 12 who was wounded after allegedly being shot in the chest. The barricades were set up in protest at a perceived imbalance in power-sharing between Colonel Azali Assoumani, president of the Union of the Comoros, and President Abdou Soule Elbak of the main island of Grande Comore where the capital is situated.

Six people -- five civilians and a police officer -- were wounded here Monday when police clashed with students protesting to demand better conditions for pursuing studies in the Comores, the Comoran Red Crescent said. A peaceful march by hundreds of Moroni high school students took place Monday morning, and in the afternoon several dozen students built barricades in several parts of the capital. Police, backed by army soldiers, responded to the student protestors with tear gas and fired automatic weapons into the air, AFP witnessed. For their part, middle and high school students fearing the idea of an invalid year took to the streets of Moroni on March 24 to shout their anger. For 48 hours, the capital's activities were disturbed by the youth protests, which were marked by walls of tires on fire on the city's main arteries. Confrontations with the army didn't end until the early evening on March 25, after many people were wounded, including five seriously by shots who had to be hospitalized and undergo operations. The gendarmerie made more than fifty arrests among the students.

The ongoing row over political power in the Comoros now threatens to weaken the country's already fragile economy, analysts said on Thursday, as traders on Grande Comore took to the streets in protest against double taxation. "The strike was a way of showing authorities that businesses on the island are tired of this confusion. Commercial traders are unsure who they should obey, because on the one hand the island authorities are demanding that they pay their taxes, while the Union administration is also asking to be paid," former politician Abdorahim Said Bacar told IRIN. Given the amount of commercial traders who participated in the strike on the previous Tuesday, and the fact that this protest took place across the entire island of Grand Comore, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

On September 15, 1,500 people attended a peaceful RIDJA rally against Azali.  Larifou heads the opposition Ridja party, which earlier this month held demonstrations against Union President Colonel Azali Assoumani. The peaceful protests against the rise in prices, organized throughout Grande Comoros from September 15 to 22 by Franco-Comorian lawyer Said Larifou's Ridja party (ION 1055), was a real success, especially among youth, making Union of Comoros authorities lose their cool. Prior to Larifou's arrest, his Ridja party had on September 15 organised a peaceful protest in Fomboni against Assoumani. Some 1,500 backers of the opposition party attended the demonstration.

At the September 22 protest in Moroni, there were confrontations with the gendarmarie, deployed in the morning to attempt to defeat the protest, which was intended to be peaceful. Busses transporting protesters to Moroni were stopped in the middle of nowhere, and the passengers were stranded for hours. Despite all this, more than 6,000 people, most of them young, participated in the protest against President Assoumani Azali. Then, on September 22, it was Larifou's turn to be arrested when he went to the gendarmerie to check up on his two friends. The Ridja protest then clashed with the police when protester wanted to free the party's leader. ?óìIntent to be peaceful?ó? implies that it turned out to not be a peaceful protest, further implying violence on the end of the protesters.

Political tension simmering between leaders in Comoros came to a head on Wednesday when government troops reportedly opened fire on a group of demonstrators protesting the policies of the country's president, Azali Assoumani. President of Grande-Comore island, Abdou Soule Elbak, who led the march through the main street of the capital, Moroni told said at least 15 people were injured during scuffles with soldiers. He told IRIN: "There was absolutely no provocation from the marchers. We were only exercising our democratic right to protest against policies which we feel are detrimental to our country. The reaction of the army is unjustifiable. Four of those injured are now in critical condition in hospital." "I was walking in the first row, my hands crossed behind my head. The soldiers fired on innocent people," said Elbak, whose entourage said between 3,000 and 6,000 people took part in the march. The government "regretted that the situation should have taken such a bad turn", and called the shooting "an unfortunate event which left some 15 people injured," Inoussa said, quoting the statement. "But we avoided the worst," he said, before quoting the statement again as saying that federal government troops had opened fire "only after giving the usual warnings." The arrests followed unrest in the capital Moroni Wednesday in which troops shot and wounded at least 15 people after officials said a crowd led by Elbak was on its way to the office of the federal president to seize power.

About 150 people demonstrated in the capital of the Comoros islands on Wednesday to call for the release of opposition leader and human rights activist Said Larifou, a French-Comoran who was detained in September. As well as chanting "Free Larifou", the protesters called for the resignation of Colonel Azali Assoumani, the president of the archipelago's federal government. Security forces adopted a low profile during Wednesday's demonstration, which took place without serious incident.

Police arrested an election candidate Sunday after violence in the Comoros as people went to the polls to elect members to new parliaments on each of the three Indian Ocean islands. The candidate, Issa Gauda, was taken in for questioning in the capital Moroni after a gang he had been seen with smashed up four polling stations, but officials otherwise reported that the poll was going smoothly. Gauda was detained after about 50 men burst into polling stations, broke the plastic ballot boxes, tore up electoral lists and threw voting slips on to the floor. He had already upset the calm prevailing in Moroni streets when he pulled his representatives out of one polling station soon after 11:30 am (0830 GMT), to protest at the voters' register, an AFP correspondent saw.

Hundreds of angry students threw up roadblocks of burning tires and large rocks in the capital of the Comoros islands on Tuesday, demanding government action to end a teachers' strike that has closed schools. Several streets in the capital were made impassable by the barricades and several shots were heard as police moved to clear the obstructions, according to an AFP correspondent on the scene. On Monday, police arrested several student protestors following a march through the capital during which incidents of vandalism were reported.

Gunshots were heard on the streets of the Comoros island of Anjouan on Monday as police moved to disperse a crowd of student demonstrators protesting a teachers' strike, witnesses said. At least one person was injured when police broke up the protest and took down barricades of large rocks and burning tires the students had erected in the streets of the Anjouan capital of Mutsamudu, the witnesses said. Comoros Defense Minister Houmedi Msaidie confirmed that there had been "social disturbances" on Anjouan over unpaid wages that led teachers on the island to go on strike. According to Abdul Kamareddine, a teacher, the students were shot and killed on Monday, allegedly by the police, after joining their teachers in a demonstration over months of unpaid salaries, which turned into violent confrontation. Anjouan police commander Ahmed Salim said a teenager hit by an errant bullet had died when police fired into the air on Monday to disperse the students who had erected barricades of burning tires and rocks to protest a teachers strike. "The victim was not directly hit by the bullet, but was hit by a stray bullet," he said, adding that police had been forced to fire warning shots due to the presence of looters in the crowd. Given the joint presence of both teachers and students, as well as the turnout from the previous month?ó»s demonstration, this protest is believed to have at least 100 people.

Hundreds of Comoros government employees took to the streets of the capital Moroni on Thursday to demand payment of salary arrears and protest plans by the government to streamline the public sector. No violence was reported at the second street protest in a month, which came as the IMF team held talks with officials on the status of a monitoring program signed earlier this year with the impoverished Indian Ocean archipelago.

Burning tires and barricades blocked streets in Moroni on Friday as the Comoran capital came to a standstill amid a strike by taxi drivers over plans to boost the price of gasoline on the Indian Ocean archipelago, witnesses said. By late morning most streets were impassable and many businesses, including those at the city's two main markets, had closed fearing possible violence while United Nations employees were ordered not to take UN vehicles outside local offices for security reasons, they said. The taxi strike was called earlier this week to protest government plans to raise the price of gasoline to offset higher world oil prices.  One person was killed and at least 15 others injured in the Comoros islands on Saturday as protests against plans to increase fuel prices in the Indian Ocean archipelago turned violent, hospital officials said. Doctors at Moroni's El-Maarouf hospital said many patients sustained bullet wounds after police opened live fire. The protestors, who first took to the streets on Friday, have paralysed operations in the capital after barricading streets with rocks and burning tyres, bringing the town to a standstill, an AFP correspondent reported. Angry protesters burnt at least five vehicles belonging to senior government officials and looted their houses, including the home of the Vice President Ben Massound Rachid. Comoran President Azali Assoumani has announced a 40% cut in most import tariffs in order to cushion the effect of sharp increases in fuel prices that led to violent protests in the past week.  Given the reaction of the police and the government, as well as the blockage of the streets, this protest is believed to have over 100 people.

Supporters of the third-place finisher in the weekend presidential primary on the coup-plagued Comoros islands staged a protest here Thursday, fearing the country's highest court might disqualify their candidate from May elections. About 100 backers of Ibrahim Halidi gathered outside the Indian Ocean archipelago's Constitutional Court. The protestors chanted slogans to call for the speedy certification of provisional returns from Sunday's primary on the island of Anjouan as soldiers watched, but dispersed peacefully in the late afternoon.

Senior Sunni clerics in the Comoros staged a demonstration here on Thursday, calling for Shia Islam to be banned in the Indian Ocean archipelago. About 60 religious leaders gathering in Moroni also called for the expulsion of foreigners accused of spreading the Shia version of Islam. The clerics also called for the closure of establishments where Shiite practices are taught and urged President Ahmed Abdallah Sambi, who many say is Shia but insists he is Sunni, to intervene.

A government minister in the Indian Ocean archipelago of Comoros was in a serious condition in hospital Wednesday after being beaten by demonstrators near the capital Moroni, hospital officials said. The incident happened in Vanamboini, around 10 kilometres (six miles) from the capital, after security forces fired shots during a demonstration by locals against the siting of a rubbish dump in their area, wounding a youth.  Given the fact that the police felt it necessary to fire shots into the demonstration, as well as the fact that a man was then beaten, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

Some 100 protesters in Wanyi [phonetic], a small town near the Anjouan airport, carried placards calling for peace and unity among Comorans and particularly the resignation of Anjouan President Col Bacar. Many of the slogans were translated into English so as to be better understood by the many diplomats shuttling between Anjouan and Grande Comores. We have had enough of Bacar and we are asking him to step down from power because his mandate has expired. The majority of Anjouan residents do not want to hear about Bacar because he acts like a despot. We do not want the balkanization of our beautiful Comoros. In his palace, in the middle of a forest on the edge of Anjouan, President Bacar said he was not worried about the demonstrations saying that they had been orchestrated by the central government of President [Ahmed Abdallah] Sambi.

A peaceful demonstration took place on Thursday morning, starting from the Karthala Hotel and ending at the Independence Square. The demonstrators expressed their anger over the high cost of life, the six-month salary arrears and the perpetual fuel shortage. "It is time to make sacrifices. Let's have the courage to sacrifice small things so that there can be big changes in this country", Deputy Said Mounir, one of the parliamentary representatives who marched with the trade unions suggested to the present crowd. According to Said Mounir, it is time to face this worsening inflation...[ellipsis as published] Staying with arms crossed while the country is falling deeper into poverty should nolonger be part of the virtues of a peaceful Comoran.  In the face of the distress call made by the trade union group and the association of consumers yesterday Thursday 19 June through their demonstration against the high cost of living, and questioning the union's and autonomous islands' political authorities, the economic advisor and spokesman of the president of Ngazidja has expressed "concern over the situation" and shares the demonstrators' cause. The island's president, Mohamed Abdouloihabi, took note by ordering the cabinet to think about their respective sectors and to without delay start dialogue with social partners. Given the involvement of major political figures as well as turnouts of previous protests with respect to these issues, this protest is believed to have at least 50 people.

Relatives of victims of the Yemenia air crash marched in the Comoros capital Moroni on Thursday to protest against the lack of information from authorities, more than two weeks after the accident. Around 300 demonstrators marched on the headquarters of the search operation to vent their frustration at a lack of information about the circumstances of the crash, which killed all but one of the 153 passengers and crew aboard. The marchers heard calls for the transport minister and the head of the island's civil aviation authority to resign.

Tensions have been mounting over a five-week-old pay conditions strike by public sector teachers which has paralysed the school system. On Friday, 1,500 school students demonstrated in Moroni over the strike.

It is not the first time that arguments over something as seemingly trivial as a photograph have threatened Afghanistan's coalition government, which was brokered by the United States after fraud-strewn elections in 2014. Hard feelings left over from those elections -- between the supporters of Mr. Ghani, who became president, and Abdullah Abdullah, for whom the position of the government's chief executive was created -- have kept the two sides tense over the smallest protocol issues. The strained relations have burdened a government faced with the mounting challenges of an emboldened insurgency and an economic crisis.  The tensions in Balkh are the continuation of the political troubles stirred by the election. Mr. Noor, who was one of Mr. Abdullah's main supporters, has said that his candidate was cheated out of winning and that the president's team is now trying to marginalize Mr. Abdullah as well as replace Mr. Noor as governor of Balkh, a post he has held for 12 years. Mr. Noor denied accusations that he was behind the removal of Mr. Dostum's photos. In a long and at times harsh statement, he placed blame for the episode on ''agitators'' who he promised would be pursued. ''We will not allow the security of our city to be ruined, or us and our people be cursed at, on pretext of the tearing of a photo,'' he wrote."

The crowd of around 5,000 gathered in the main square of the capital near the presidential offices carrying banners with slogans like ''Constitutional Reforms Through Parliament'' and ''Yes to Democracy, Yes to Reforms!''
